BG_C01_INTRO1::block-0: Nārāyaṇa is beyond the Unmanifest; from the Unmanifest the Cosmic Egg is born; within the Egg are these worlds and the earth with its seven continents.
BG_C01_INTRO1::block-1: That Blessed One, having created this universe and wishing to maintain its order, first brought forth Marīci and the other progenitors and made them adopt the path of duty marked by engagement in action (pravṛtti), as set forth in the Veda. Thereafter, having generated others — Sanaka, Sanandana and the rest — He made them adopt the path of duty marked by withdrawal (nivṛtti), characterised by knowledge and dispassion. For the dharma declared by the Veda is twofold — that of engagement and that of withdrawal — and is the cause of the world's stability. That dharma which is directly the cause, for living beings, of prosperity and of the highest good was being practised, over a long course of time, by Brāhmaṇas and the rest among those of the four orders and stages, who sought the supreme welfare. But when, through the rise of desires in the practitioners, dharma came to be overpowered by adharma — adharma whose cause lies in the dwindling of discriminative knowledge — and adharma went on increasing, then that primeval Maker, Viṣṇu known as Nārāyaṇa, wishing to preserve the stability of the world, took birth, as it is said, in the form of Kṛṣṇa, with a portion of Himself, from Vasudeva in the womb of Devakī, for the sake of guarding earthly Brahman, that is, Brāhmaṇa-hood. For when Brāhmaṇa-hood is guarded, the Vedic dharma is guarded, since the distinctions of the orders and stages depend upon it.
BG_C01_INTRO1::block-2: And that Blessed One, ever endowed with knowledge, lordship, power, strength, valour and splendour, having brought under His sway His own māyā — the root Nature constituted of the three guṇas — although He is unborn, undecaying, the Lord of beings, and although His very nature is eternally pure, awakened and free, yet, as it were, by His own māyā, appears as if possessed of a body and as if born, doing favour to the worlds. Although He has no purpose of His own, out of the wish to grace beings, He taught the twofold Vedic dharma to Arjuna, who was sunk in the great ocean of grief and delusion, thinking, "When dharma is grasped and practised by men of pre-eminent qualities, it will spread." That dharma, in the very form in which it was taught by the Blessed One, the all-knowing Bhagavān Veda-vyāsa set forth in the seven hundred verses called the Gītā.
BG_C01_INTRO1::block-3: This Gītā-śāstra is the gathered essence of the meaning of the entire Veda; its meaning is hard to grasp. Although many commentators have expounded the words, the meanings of words and the meanings of sentences with reasoning, observing that ordinary people take it as a thing of mutually contradictory and manifold imports, I shall, with discrimination and concisely, undertake an exposition for the sake of determining its true meaning.
BG_C01_INTRO1::block-4: The purpose of this Gītā-śāstra, in brief, is the supreme good, which consists in the absolute cessation of saṃsāra together with its cause. And that arises from the dharma whose form is steadfastness in knowledge of the Self, preceded by the renunciation of all action. Thus, with reference to this very subject-matter of the Gītā as the dharma, the Blessed One Himself has declared in the Anugītā, "That dharma is amply sufficient for the realisation of the state of Brahman" (Aśv. 16.12). And there itself it is said, "He is neither one of dharma nor of adharma, nor indeed of good or evil; he who, fixed in one seat, sits silent, thinking of nothing" (Aśv. 19.1, 7), and "Knowledge has the mark of renunciation" (Aśv. 43.26). And here too, at the end, it is said to Arjuna, "Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone" (BhG 18.66). Even that dharma of engagement which, aiming at prosperity, is enjoined with reference to the four orders and stages — although it is the cause of attaining the realms of the gods and the like — when practised in the spirit of dedication to the Lord and free from longing for fruits, conduces to purification of the inner being. And in the case of one of purified being, by way of fitness for steadfastness in knowledge and by being the cause of the rise of knowledge, it also turns out to be a means to the supreme good. Having this very meaning in view He will say, "Placing actions in Brahman" (BhG 5.10), and "Yogins perform action, having abandoned attachment, for purifying the self" (BhG 5.11).
BG_C01_INTRO1::block-5: This twofold dharma whose aim is the supreme good, and the supreme reality which is named Vāsudeva — the highest Brahman that is the very subject of discourse — being specially set forth, the Gītā-śāstra is endowed with a distinctive purpose, connection and subject-matter. Since by the cognition of its meaning the accomplishment of all human ends is achieved, therefore the effort at its exposition is being made by me.
BG_C01_V03: Behold, O teacher, this mighty army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up in battle-array by the son of Drupada, your own wise pupil. Duryodhana, addressing Droṇa, points out the formidable Pāṇḍava force, marshalled by Dhṛṣṭadyumna who, though Drupada's son, had been Droṇa's own student.
BG_C01_V04: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna — Yuyudhāna and Virāṭa, and the great chariot-warrior Drupada. Duryodhana enumerates the Pāṇḍava champions whose prowess matches that of Bhīma and Arjuna themselves.
BG_C01_V05: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valorous king of Kāśī; Purujit and Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, foremost of men. The roll of Pāṇḍava warriors continues, naming kings of distinguished valour.
BG_C01_V06: Yudhāmanyu the heroic, and the valorous Uttamaujā, the son of Subhadrā, and the sons of Draupadī — all great chariot-warriors. The recital concludes with further Pāṇḍava heroes, including Abhimanyu and the five sons of Draupadī, all of whom are accomplished mahārathas.
BG_C01_V07: Know, O best of the twice-born, those who are most distinguished among us, the leaders of my army; for your information I name them to you. Turning to Droṇa, Duryodhana now proposes to enumerate the foremost commanders on his own side.
BG_C01_V08: Yourself, and Bhīṣma, and Karṇa, and Kṛpa who is ever victorious in battle; Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, and the son of Somadatta (Bhūriśravas), and Jayadratha. Duryodhana here enumerates the foremost warriors on his own side, naming the venerable Droṇa first by addressing him directly, then the chief heroes upon whom his hopes for victory rest.
BG_C01_V09: And many other heroes too, who have given up their lives for my sake, equipped with various weapons and missiles, and all of them well-skilled in warfare. Duryodhana points out that besides the named champions, there are countless other valiant warriors fully prepared to lay down their lives in his cause, each expert in the use of diverse arms.
BG_C01_V10: That force of ours, guarded by Bhīṣma, is unlimited (or insufficient); whereas this force of theirs, guarded by Bhīma, is limited (or sufficient). Duryodhana, betraying his inner anxiety, contrasts the two armies — though his own appears vast under Bhīṣma's protection, he fears it may yet prove inadequate against the Pāṇḍava host so well guarded by Bhīma.
BG_C01_V11: Therefore, all of you, stationed in your respective divisions at every point of entry, must protect Bhīṣma alone above all. Duryodhana entreats every commander, posted at his allotted station in the army's formations, to make the safeguarding of the grandsire Bhīṣma their paramount duty, recognizing that on him hinges the strength of the entire host.
BG_C01_V12: Bringing joy to him (Duryodhana), the valiant grandsire, the eldest of the Kurus, roared aloud like a lion and blew his conch with great might. Bhīṣma, perceiving Duryodhana's apprehension, gladdened him by his bold demeanor — uttering a lion-like battle cry and sounding his conch, thus signaling his readiness for the fight.
BG_C01_V13: Then conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and cow-horn trumpets were sounded all at once, and that noise became tumultuous. Following Bhīṣma's lead, the entire Kaurava host let loose a deafening din from every kind of war-instrument, the combined uproar filling the sky and shaking the earth.
BG_C01_V14: Then, seated in their grand chariot yoked to white horses, Mādhava (Lord Kṛṣṇa) and the son of Pāṇḍu (Arjuna) blew their divine conches. Now in answer to the Kaurava blasts, Lord Kṛṣṇa together with Arjuna, mounted on a magnificent chariot drawn by white steeds, sounded their celestial conches, signaling the Pāṇḍava response.
BG_C01_V15: Hṛṣīkeśa (Lord Kṛṣṇa, master of the senses) blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya (Arjuna) the Devadatta, and Bhīma of dreadful deeds, the wolf-bellied one, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. Each of the foremost Pāṇḍava warriors then sounded his own celebrated conch — Lord Kṛṣṇa his Pāñcajanya, Arjuna his Devadatta, and the mighty Bhīma his Pauṇḍra — proclaiming their resolve in battle.
BG_C01_V16: King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the conch named Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew the conches Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka respectively. (16)
BG_C01_V17: The king of Kāśī, the supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍī the great warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki — (all blew their conches). (17)
BG_C01_V18: O lord of the earth, Drupada and the sons of Draupadī on every side, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā — all of them blew their respective conches. (18)
BG_C01_V19: That tumultuous sound, reverberating through both sky and earth, rent the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. (19)
BG_C01_V20: Then, O lord of the earth, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bore the emblem of Hanumān, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra arrayed in battle order, raised his bow as the clash of weapons was about to commence. (20)
BG_C01_V21: O lord of the earth, at that moment he addressed these words to Hṛṣīkeśa (Lord Kṛṣṇa). Arjuna said: O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies. (21)
BG_C01_V22: So that I may behold these who stand here eager for battle, and discern with whom I must contend in this undertaking of war. (22)
BG_C01_V23: I wish to behold those who have assembled here ready to fight, eager to do the bidding of the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle. (23)
BG_C01_V25: In front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth, He said: "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled together." Thus, having drawn up the chariot at the appropriate place between the two armies, Lord Kṛṣṇa, the universal Teacher, addressed Arjuna so that he might directly perceive the kinsmen arrayed for battle. The very sight thus shown was meant to evoke in Arjuna that delusion of attachment which would become the occasion for the teaching of the supreme knowledge.
BG_C01_V26: There Pārtha saw, stationed in their positions, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends as well. Beholding kinsmen of every relation present on both sides, his heart became overwhelmed with the sentiment of affection rooted in the notion of "mine," which is the seed of saṃsāra, born of avidyā.
BG_C01_V27: Fathers-in-law and well-wishers also, in both armies — beholding all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed for battle, that son of Kuntī was overcome. Seeing them about to perish in mutual slaughter, the conviction of "these are my own" arose in him with great force, drawing forth the despondency that the Lord would soon dispel through the teaching of the Self.
BG_C01_V28: Filled with profound compassion and despairing, he spoke this. Arjuna said — "O Kṛṣṇa, having seen these my own people, eager to fight, drawn up here." The compassion mentioned is no spiritual virtue but a delusion born of attachment to body and kin; it is what avidyā produces when one mistakes the perishable body-complex for the Self, and which the Lord will remove through the knowledge of Brahman.
BG_C01_V29: "My limbs sink, and my mouth is parched; my body trembles, and the hair stands on end." Arjuna here describes the bodily marks of overpowering grief and fear, which arise when one identifies the Self with the body and clings to relations as one's own. Such symptoms are the natural fruit of avidyā, indicating that the warrior, otherwise valiant, is now subject to delusion.
BG_C01_V30: "The Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, my skin too burns all over; I am unable to stand firm, and my mind seems to whirl about." The famed bow falling from the warrior's grasp signals the collapse of his courage; the burning of the skin betrays inner anguish; the inability to stand and the reeling mind disclose the loss of discrimination — all wrought by the delusion that takes the body-aggregate for the Self.
BG_C01_V31: "And I see contrary omens, O Keśava; nor do I foresee any good from slaying my own kinsmen in battle." Arjuna here cites adverse portents and the absence of any apparent welfare arising from victory through such slaughter, treating the killing of kin as itself contrary to dharma. This is the voice of avidyā mistaking apparent dharma for true dharma; the Lord will reveal that the dharma of the kṣatriya, undertaken without attachment, is in fact the path to liberation.
BG_C01_V32: I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what use to us is a kingdom, O Govinda, of what use are enjoyments or even life itself?
BG_C01_V33: Those very persons for whose sake kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures are desired by us — these stand here arrayed in battle, having renounced their lives and wealth.
BG_C01_V34: Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers; maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen as well.
BG_C01_V35: These I do not wish to slay, O Madhusūdana, even though they slay me — not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, how much less for the earth!
BG_C01_V36: Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, what satisfaction can be ours, O Janārdana? Sin alone would take hold of us by killing these aggressors.
BG_C01_V37: Therefore we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their kin. For how, having killed our own people, could we be happy, O Mādhava?
BG_C01_V38: Even though these, with minds overcome by greed, do not see the evil born of the destruction of family and the sin in betraying friends —
BG_C01_V39: Why should it not be known by us, O Janārdana, who clearly perceive the evil born of the destruction of family, that we must turn away from this sin?
BG_C01_V40: When a family is destroyed, the eternal dharmas of the family perish. When dharma is destroyed, adharma indeed overwhelms the entire family.
BG_C01_V41: O Kṛṣṇa, by the prevalence of adharma the women of the family become corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, an admixture of castes (varṇa-saṅkara) arises.
BG_C01_V42: This admixture leads to hell both for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself. Their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of piṇḍa and water.
BG_C01_V43: By these misdeeds of the destroyers of the family, which generate the admixture of castes, the eternal caste-dharmas and family-dharmas are uprooted.
BG_C01_V44: O Janārdana, for men whose family-dharmas have been destroyed, dwelling in hell is inevitable — thus we have heard repeatedly.
BG_C01_V45: Alas, what a great sin we have resolved to commit, that out of greed for the pleasures of kingship we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen!
BG_C01_V46: If, while I remain unresisting and unarmed, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with weapons in hand were to slay me in battle, that would be far more beneficial for me.
BG_C02_V03:
O Pārtha, do not yield to unmanliness; this does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of foes!

Such cowardice is unworthy of one of your stature; shake off this trivial faintheartedness, which is unbecoming, and stand up, ready for battle.
BG_C02_V05:
Better indeed it would be to live on alms even in this world than to slay these greatly venerable elders; for, having slain my elders — though they seek wealth — I would here itself have to enjoy pleasures stained with their blood.

Arjuna means that begging, though deemed lowly, is preferable to the killing of revered teachers, since the enjoyments won by such slaughter would be drenched in the blood of one's own gurus and would therefore be utterly tainted.
BG_C02_V06:
Nor do we know which of the two is better for us — that we should conquer them, or that they should conquer us. Those very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, slaying whom we should not wish to live, stand arrayed before us.

Arjuna confesses utter perplexity: victory and defeat seem alike calamitous, since the very kinsmen whose death would render life worthless are those now standing as the foe.
BG_C02_V07:
My nature smitten by the taint of pity, my mind bewildered as to dharma, I ask You: tell me decisively that which is for my highest good. I am Your disciple; instruct me who have taken refuge in You.

Overwhelmed by faintheartedness and confused regarding what is dharma and what is not, Arjuna formally surrenders to Lord Kṛṣṇa as his teacher and prays for definitive guidance toward the supreme good.
BG_C02_V08:
For I do not see what could dispel this grief of mine which dries up the senses, even were I to gain on earth an unrivalled and prosperous kingdom, and even lordship over the gods.

No earthly sovereignty, however vast, nor even rulership over the celestials, appears to Arjuna capable of removing the sorrow that is parching his very faculties; this confession of helplessness sets the stage for the Lord's teaching of self-knowledge.
BG_C02_V10: O Bharata (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), to him, Arjuna, sunk in despondency between the two armies, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words. ||10||
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-0: Here, the portion of the text beginning with "Beholding the army of the Pāṇḍavas" (Bh. Gī. 1.2) and ending with "Having said to Govinda, 'I will not fight,' he became silent" (Bh. Gī. 2.9) is to be expounded as serving the purpose of exhibiting the cause of the arising of those defects — sorrow, delusion and the rest — which are the seed of saṁsāra (transmigratory existence) for living beings. Thus: in Arjuna there were displayed his own sorrow and delusion (śoka and moha), occasioned by the severance of the affection arising from such notions as "I belong to these" and "these are mine" with regard to kingdom, elders, sons, friends, well-wishers, kinsmen and relations — as in the verses beginning, "How shall I in battle (encounter) Bhīṣma…" (Bh. Gī. 2.4). For one whose discriminative knowledge is overpowered by sorrow and delusion, even though he had of his own accord engaged in the kṣatra-dharma of war, desisted from that war, and set out to perform another's dharma — the livelihood of begging and so on. In just the same way, for all beings whose minds are possessed by the defects of sorrow, delusion and the rest, there will, by their very nature, follow the abandonment of one's own dharma and the practice of what is forbidden. And even when such persons do engage in their own dharma, the activity of their speech, mind and body is preceded by the expectation of fruit and is accompanied by the sense of "I" (egoism, ahaṅkāra). When this is so, by the accumulation of dharma and adharma, saṁsāra — characterised by the obtaining of desirable and undesirable births, pleasures and pains — never ceases. Therefore, sorrow and delusion, being the seed of saṁsāra, can be removed by nothing other than knowledge of the Self preceded by renunciation of all action (sarva-karma-saṁnyāsa). Wishing, then, to teach this, and for the favour of the whole world, the Lord Vāsudeva — taking Arjuna as the occasion — speaks: "Those who are not to be grieved for…" (Bh. Gī. 2.11), and so on.
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-1: An objector here says: From mere steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self preceded by renunciation of all action — taken alone — kaivalya (final isolation, liberation) is in fact not attained. Then how? It is the settled doctrine of the whole Gītā that liberation is gained from knowledge combined (samuccita) with the śrauta and smārta works such as the agnihotra. And as proof of this they cite — "Now if thou wilt not engage in this righteous battle" (Bh. Gī. 2.33), "Thy right is to action alone" (Bh. Gī. 2.47), "Therefore do thou indeed perform action" (Bh. Gī. 4.15), and the like. Nor, they say, should the apprehension be entertained that, since Vedic action involves injury (hiṁsā) and so on, it would lead to adharma. How? Because the kṣatriya's action — characterised by war, involving the slaying of teachers, brothers, sons and the like, although extremely cruel — being his own dharma, does not lead to adharma; and when the Lord says, in the case of its non-performance, "Then, having forsaken thine own dharma and renown, thou shalt incur sin" (Bh. Gī. 2.33), it follows by clear implication that the actions enjoined by the śruti such as the "life-long" (yāvajjīva) sacrifices, characterised by the slaying of animals and the like, were never adharmic to begin with — so they hold.
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-2: This is not so. For the Lord declares the division of the two niṣṭhās — steadfastness in knowledge and steadfastness in action — as resting upon two distinct intellects (buddhi). What the Lord teaches in the portion beginning with "Those who are not to be grieved for" (Bh. Gī. 2.11) and ending with "And considering also thine own dharma" (Bh. Gī. 2.31) — namely the determination of the highest reality of the Self — is the Sāṅkhya (the discrimination of the real). The intellect concerned with this — the intellect that arises from the establishment of the topic that the Self is non-agent, since the six modifications such as birth do not belong to the Self — is the sāṅkhya buddhi. Those jñānins for whom this intellect is fitting are the Sāṅkhyas (here meaning followers of the Self-knowledge path, not the Kāpila school). Prior to the arising of this intellect, however, with regard to the Self there obtains the yoga — the practice of the means to mokṣa, founded on the discrimination of dharma and adharma, which presupposes the Self's distinctness from the body and so on, and its agency and enjoyership. The intellect concerned with this is the yoga-buddhi. Those karmins for whom this intellect is fitting are the yogins. Thus the Lord has indicated two distinct intellects: "This intellect has been declared to thee in (the path of) Sāṅkhya; now hear (this) in (the path of) Yoga" (Bh. Gī. 2.39). Of these two, the steadfastness based on the sāṅkhya intellect — by way of jñāna-yoga — pertaining to the Sāṅkhyas, He will set forth as distinct: "Of yore I declared (it) in the form of the Veda" (Bh. Gī. 3.3). And the steadfastness based on the yoga intellect — by way of karma-yoga — He will likewise set forth as distinct: "by karma-yoga, for the yogins." Thus, by relying upon the sāṅkhya intellect and the yoga intellect, two niṣṭhās have been declared distinctly by the Lord himself, since He sees the impossibility of jointly resorting in one and the same person at one time to (the paths of) knowledge and action — these resting respectively upon the intellects of non-agency and agency, oneness and manyness. Just as this declaration of division is made here, so the same is shown in the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa: having enjoined renunciation of all action by, "Wishing for this very world (the Self) the brāhmaṇas go forth as wandering monks," it then continues, "What shall we do with progeny, we whose this Self is this (very) world?" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22). And there, prior to taking a wife, the puruṣa is in his natural state; afterwards, when the desire to know dharma arises, three means of attaining the three worlds are shown — a son, and a twofold wealth, the human and the divine. Of these, the human, in the form of action (karma), is the means of attaining the pitṛ-loka; and vidyā, the divine wealth, is the means of attaining the deva-loka. With "He desired" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.17), all those śrauta and other works are shown as belonging only to one who has avidyā and desire. From these — "having risen up (vyutthāya), they go forth" — the going-forth (vyutthāna) is enjoined upon the desireless one who longs for the Self alone as his world. This declaration of division would itself be unintelligible if a combination (samuccaya) of śrauta action and knowledge were the Lord's intent.
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-3: Nor would Arjuna's question, "If knowledge be deemed by Thee superior to action…" (Bh. Gī. 3.1), and so on, be intelligible. If the impossibility of one person performing both intellect (knowledge) and action together had not previously been stated by the Lord, how could Arjuna, never having heard that intellect was superior to action, falsely impute such superiority to the Lord by asking, "If intellect be considered by Thee superior to action…" (Bh. Gī. 3.1)?
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-4: Further: if a combination of intellect and action had been taught for all, it would have been taught for Arjuna also; how then, when both have been instructed, could the question, "Tell me decisively that one of these two which is the better" (Bh. Gī. 5.1), be one referring to only one of them? It is not possible that, when a physician has prescribed to one wishing to allay pitta both sweet and cool things to be eaten, the patient should ask, "Of these two, tell me which is the cause of allaying pitta."
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-5: Even if it be supposed that Arjuna's question arose from a failure to grasp the distinct meanings of the Lord's two utterances, even then the answer given by the Lord ought to have been suited to the question — namely, "By me a combination of intellect and action has been taught; why are you thus deluded?" It is not fitting to give an answer unrelated to what was asked, viz. "Two niṣṭhās were of yore declared by Me" (Bh. Gī. 3.3), which is something altogether other than what was asked.
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-6: Nor, were the combination of intellect with smārta action alone intended, would the declaration of division and all the rest be intelligible. Further — for a kṣatriya who knows war to be a smārta action and his own dharma, the reproach "Then why dost Thou enjoin upon me this terrible action?" (Bh. Gī. 3.1) would be inapplicable.
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-7: Therefore in the Gītā-śāstra a combination of even the slightest śrauta or smārta action with knowledge of the Self cannot be shown by anyone. But for him who, having engaged in action through ignorance or through faults such as attachment, has by sacrifice, gift, and austerity attained purification of the inner being (sattva-śuddhi), and in whom there has arisen knowledge concerning the highest reality, namely "All this is one Brahman alone, and is non-agent" — for him, even after action and the motive of action have ceased, what is seen as activity is what is engaged in, with effort, for the welfare of the world (loka-saṅgraha), in the very same way as before; that activity in form is not karma such that it could be combined (samuccaya) with intellect. Just as the Lord Vāsudeva's discharge of kṣatra-dharma is not combined with knowledge for the attainment of any human goal, so it is with the knower, owing to the equal absence of expectation of its fruit and of egoism. The knower of reality thinks, "I do not act," and does not look forward to its fruit. As, again, in the case of one who has set up the sacred fires for the sake of attaining heaven and so on and has engaged in the kāmya agnihotra and the like — even if his desire be destroyed when the rite is half-performed, the agnihotra and the rest he continues to perform; and yet that agnihotra and so on are no longer kāmya. Thus the Lord shows, here and there, "Even acting, he is not tainted" (Bh. Gī. 5.7), "He neither acts nor is tainted" (Bh. Gī. 13.31).
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-8: And as for the texts, "Done by ancient men of yore" (Bh. Gī. 4.15), "By action alone Janaka and others attained perfection" (Bh. Gī. 3.20) — these must be understood by making a distinction. How? If, on the one hand, those ancients such as Janaka were also knowers of reality and yet remained engaged in action, then they, for the sake of the welfare of the world, with the knowledge that "the guṇas operate among the guṇas" (Bh. Gī. 3.28), attained perfection by knowledge alone — in the sense that, although renunciation of action was open to them, they remained, along with action, in the path of perfection: they did not, that is, take to renunciation of action. If, on the other hand, they were not knowers of reality, then it must be expounded thus: Janaka and others, by action offered up to the Lord and serving as means, attained perfection — that is, purity of inner being (sattva-śuddhi), or the perfection consisting in the arising of knowledge. The Lord himself will state this very meaning: "They perform action for the purification of the inner being" (Bh. Gī. 5.11). Having said, "Worshipping Him by his own action a man attains perfection" (Bh. Gī. 18.46), He will further declare the steadfastness in knowledge that belongs to one who has attained perfection, in the verses beginning, "How, having attained perfection, (he attains) Brahman…" (Bh. Gī. 18.50).
BG_C02_INTRO1::block-9: Therefore in the Gītā-śāstra it is the settled meaning that liberation is attained from knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) alone, and not from such knowledge combined with action. As to how this is so, we shall, dividing it section by section, show in each place.
BG_C02_V11::block-0: There, seeing no other deliverance for Arjuna — whose mind was utterly bewildered with regard to dharma, who was possessed of false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna), and who was sunk in the great ocean of sorrow — except by knowledge of the Self, the Lord Vāsudeva, out of compassion, wishing to lift Arjuna up, undertook to bring him to knowledge of the Self, and said —
BG_C02_V11::block-1: "Those who are not to be grieved for…" — They are not to be grieved for (a-śocyāḥ), namely Bhīṣma, Droṇa and the rest, both because they are of righteous conduct, and because, in their highest reality, they are eternal. These who are not-to-be-grieved-for, thou hast nevertheless grieved over (anvaśocaḥ): "They are dying because of me; bereft of them, what shall I do with kingdom, pleasures and the like?" Yet thou speakest the words of the wise (prajñā-vādān) — the speeches of those endowed with discriminative intellect. The intent is: thou displayest in thyself folly and learnedness commingled in mutually contradictory fashion, like one mad. For the wise — the knowers of the Self (paṇḍitāḥ) — do not grieve for those whose breath has departed (gata-asūn), namely the dead, nor for those whose breath has not departed (a-gata-asūn), namely the living. By etymology (nirvacana), paṇḍā is the intellect concerning the Self; those who possess it are paṇḍitāḥ, as the śruti says, "Having attained learnedness (pāṇḍityaṁ nirvidya)" (Bṛ. Up. 3.5.1). But thou grievest, in truth, for those who are eternal and not to be grieved for; therefore thou art deluded — such is the purport. ||11||
BG_C02_V12: Never indeed was I non-existent, nor thou, nor these rulers of men; nor again shall any of us cease to exist hereafter. ||12||
BG_C02_V12::block-0: Why are they not to be grieved for? Because they are eternal. How so? —
BG_C02_V12::block-1: "Never indeed (na tu eva jātu) at any time was I non-existent (nāsam) — I was, indeed." The intent is: through the past arisings and destructions of bodies — like jars, ghaṭa and the rest — I was, like the sky (vyat), eternally existent. Likewise, "thou wast not non-existent" — rather, thou wast. Likewise, "these rulers of men were not non-existent" — rather, they were. Likewise, "nor shall we cease to be" — rather, we shall exist; "all of us, after this" (ataḥ param) — that is, even after the destruction of the body, in the time to come. The meaning is: in all three times (past, present, future) we are eternal in our true nature as the Self. The plural number is used in conformity with the diversity of bodies, not in the intent of any plurality of Selves. ||12||
BG_C02_V13: Just as for the embodied one (the Self) within this body there is childhood, youth, and old age, so also is the obtaining of another body. The wise man is not deluded therein. ||13||
BG_C02_V13::block-0: How then is the Self eternal? To this He gives an illustration —
BG_C02_V13::block-1: He whose this is, namely "of his is the body" — he is the dehin (the embodied one); for that dehin, the Self possessed of a body, in this present body, in the manner in which kaumāra (the state of being a kumāra, the condition of childhood, bālya), yauvana (the state of being a young man, the condition of middle age, madhyama), and jarā (the decline of age, the worn-out condition, jīrṇa), are these three states, mutually distinct from one another. In the destruction of the first state there is no destruction of the Self; in the arising of the second there is no arising of the Self. What then? The attaining of the second and third states is seen for the Self, which is itself unchanging (avikriya). In the same way, just so — there is another body distinct from this body, called "another body" (deha-antara); the obtaining of it (deha-antara-prāpti) is for the Self which is itself unchanging — such is the meaning. The wise man (dhīraḥ, the discerning one), this being so, is not deluded — he does not fall into delusion. ||13||
BG_C02_V14: But, O son of Kuntī, the contacts of the senses with their objects — productive of cold and heat, pleasure and pain — come and go and are impermanent. Bear with them, O Bhārata. ||14||
BG_C02_V14::block-0: Although for one who knows the Self to be eternal there cannot arise the delusion occasioned by the destruction of the Self, nevertheless there is to be seen, in worldly experience, the delusion occasioned by the obtaining of cold, heat, pleasure and pain — the delusion arising from separation from pleasure, and the sorrow arising from union with pain. Anticipating such a remark on the part of Arjuna, the Lord says —
BG_C02_V14::block-1: Mātrāḥ — those by which sound and the rest are measured (mīyante), namely the senses (indriyāṇi) such as the ear and so on. The contacts (sparśāḥ) of the mātrās are their conjunctions with sound and the like. They are productive of cold and heat, pleasure and pain — that is, they yield (prayacchanti) cold, heat, pleasure and pain. Or alternatively, sparśāḥ means "that which is touched" (spṛśyante iti), namely the objects (viṣayāḥ), sound and the rest. Both the mātrās (the senses) and the sparśāḥ (their objects) are productive of cold, heat, pleasure and pain. Cold is at one time pleasant, at another painful; heat too is of indeterminate nature. Pleasure and pain, on the other hand, are of fixed character, since they do not deviate (from being respectively pleasant and painful). For that reason cold and heat are mentioned separately from them. Inasmuch as those mātrā-contacts and the rest are āgama-apāyinaḥ — having the nature of coming and going (āgama-apāya-śīlāḥ) — for that reason they are impermanent (anityāḥ). Therefore them — those cold, heat and the rest — bear (titikṣasva), endure (prasahasva). The intent is: do not entertain joy or dejection regarding them. ||14||
BG_C02_V15: That wise man, O bull among men, whom these (cold, heat, pleasure and pain) do not afflict, who is the same in pain and pleasure — he becomes fit for immortality. ||15||
BG_C02_V15::block-0: Hear what comes about for him who endures cold, heat and the rest —
BG_C02_V15::block-1: That puruṣa to whom pleasure and pain are equal (sama-duḥkha-sukham) — that is, who is free from joy and dejection at the obtaining of pleasure and pain — that wise one (dhīram), the man of intellect (dhīmantam), whom these aforesaid cold, heat and the rest do not afflict (na vyathayanti), do not shake (na cālayanti), because of his vision of the eternal Self — he, established in the vision of the very nature of the eternal Self, the endurer of the pairs of opposites (dvandva-sahiṣṇuḥ), is fit for amṛtatva — for the state of immortality, that is, for mokṣa (liberation); he becomes capable (samartho bhavati) of it. ||15||
BG_C02_V16: Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no non-being. The conclusion regarding both these has indeed been seen by the seers of truth. (16)
BG_C02_V16::block-0: And for this further reason it is fitting to endure cold, heat and the rest without giving way to grief and delusion — because:
BG_C02_V16::block-1: Of the unreal (asat) — that is, of the non-existent cold, heat and so on, together with their causes — there is no being (bhāva), no actual existing-ness, no real subsistence.
BG_C02_V16::block-2: For cold, heat and the like, together with their causes, when investigated by the means of valid knowledge, do not turn out to be real entities. They are mere modifications (vikāra), and a modification is something that strays from itself (vyabhicarati). Just as the shape of a pot and similar things, when scrutinized by the eye, are unreal because they are not apprehended apart from the clay, so every modification is unreal because it is not apprehended apart from its cause. And because the effect — pot and the like — is not apprehended before its origination or after its destruction, and because its material cause — clay and so on — is itself not apprehended apart from its own cause, both effect and cause are likewise unreal.
BG_C02_V16::block-3: Objection: If they are unreal, then the absence of everything would follow. Reply: No; for everywhere two cognitions are met with — the cognition "it is" (sat-buddhi) and the cognition of the particular object (asat-buddhi). That whose object the cognition does not stray from is real; that whose object it does stray from is unreal. The division into real and unreal thus rests on cognition. Everywhere two cognitions are perceived by all, sharing the same locus — not like "blue lotus" where two qualifying cognitions modify one substance, but like "the pot exists," "the cloth exists," "the elephant exists." Of these two cognitions, the cognition "pot" and the like strays — as has been shown — but the cognition "is" does not. Therefore the object of the cognition "pot" and the like is unreal, because it strays; but the object of the cognition "is" is not unreal, because it does not stray.
BG_C02_V16::block-4: Objection: When the pot is destroyed, the cognition "pot" strays, and along with it the cognition "is" also strays. Reply: No; because the cognition "is" is met with in cloth and other things as well. That cognition pertains only to the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).
BG_C02_V16::block-5: Objection: Just like the cognition "is," the cognition "pot" too is seen in another pot. Reply: No; because it is not seen in cloth and the like.
BG_C02_V16::block-6: Objection: Even the cognition "is" is not seen in the destroyed pot. Reply: No; because in the absence of the qualified (viśeṣya), the cognition "is" — which has the qualifier alone for its object — when, owing to the absence of the qualified, the qualifier-status itself fails, what could it have for its object? Yet this does not amount to the absence of an object for the cognition "is" in itself.
BG_C02_V16::block-7: Objection: Co-locatedness in one substratum is not appropriate when the qualified — pot etc. — is absent. Reply: No; for in expressions like "this is water" with respect to a mirage and the like, co-locatedness is observed even when one of the two terms is absent.
BG_C02_V16::block-8: Therefore, of the unreal — namely the body and so on, and the pairs of opposites with their causes — there is no being. Likewise of the real — namely the Self (Ātman) — there is no non-being, no non-existing-ness, because of non-straying everywhere; this we have already said.
BG_C02_V16::block-9: Thus, of both these — the Self and the not-Self, the real and the unreal — the conclusion (anta), the settled determination, has been seen, that is, apprehended, by the seers of truth (tattva-darśin), namely: the real is precisely real, the unreal is precisely unreal. "Tat" is a pronoun; and all this is Brahman, whose name is "that"; the being-That is tattva, the very what-it-isness of Brahman. Those who have the natural disposition to see That are the tattva-darśins, and "by the seers of truth" means by them. You too, taking your stand on the vision of the seers of truth, abandoning grief and delusion, having ascertained in your mind that "these pairs of opposites — cold, heat and the rest, both the regular and the irregular — are mere modifications, unreal, falsely appearing like the water of a mirage," should endure them. This is the import. (16)
BG_C02_V17: But know That to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. None can bring about the destruction of this Imperishable. (17)
BG_C02_V17::block-0: But what is that which is real always and forever? It is now stated:
BG_C02_V17::block-1: Indestructible — that of which the very nature is not to perish. The word "tu" (but) serves to mark it off from the unreal. "Know That" — recognize That. What? That by which all this — this entire universe, including ākāśa — is pervaded, suffused, namely Brahman known as the Real, just as pots and the like are pervaded by ākāśa. "Vināśa" means non-perception, non-being. "Avyaya" — that which does not waste away, which neither increases nor decreases. Of that which does not waste away. This Brahman, called the Real, does not waste away in its own form, does not stray, because it is partless, unlike the body. Nor does it waste away through what belongs to it, because nothing belongs to it. Just as Devadatta wastes away through the loss of his wealth — Brahman does not waste away in such a manner. Therefore, of this imperishable Brahman, none can bring about destruction; none can destroy the Self — not even Īśvara. For the Self is Brahman, and action toward one's own Self is contradictory. (17)
BG_C02_V18: These bodies of the eternal, indestructible, immeasurable embodied Self are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O descendant of Bharata. (18)
BG_C02_V18::block-0: But what is that unreal which strays from its own being? It is now stated:
BG_C02_V18::block-1: Anta — destruction; "having anta" — those that have an end. Just as in a mirage and the like, the cognition "is" runs on for a while and then, when scrutinized by the means of valid knowledge, snaps off — that snapping is its end; in the same way these bodies, like dream-bodies and bodies conjured by māyā, have an end, while the embodied Self — the eternal possessor of bodies, the indestructible, the immeasurable Ātman — does not. They have been declared to have an end by the discriminating, this is the meaning. "Eternal" and "indestructible" are not redundant, since both eternality and destruction are of two kinds in worldly usage. A body that has been reduced to ashes and gone out of sight is said to be destroyed. So too, even while existing, when it is otherwise transformed and afflicted with disease and the like, it is said to be destroyed. Therefore, by the words "eternal" and "indestructible," what is meant is that the Self has no connection with destruction of either kind. Otherwise the Self would be eternal in the way that earth and the rest are eternal — and so that this should not be supposed, the Lord says "eternal," "indestructible." "Immeasurable" means: not an object of measurement, not capable of being delimited by perception and the other means of valid knowledge.
BG_C02_V18::block-2: Objection: But the Self is delimited by scripture (āgama), and previously by perception and the rest. Reply: No; because the Self is self-established (svataḥ-siddha). Only when the Self, the cognizer, is already established does the desire to cognize and the search for the means of valid knowledge arise. For one does not first set out to delimit other knowables without first having cognized oneself as "I am thus." The Self is never something unknown to anyone. Scripture is the final means of valid knowledge: it attains its status as a means of knowledge for the Self only by being the remover of the superimposition (adhyāropa) upon the Self of properties not its own — not by being a revealer of an unknown thing. Thus the śruti: "That which is direct and immediate, the Brahman that is the Self within all" (Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka 3.5.1).
BG_C02_V18::block-3: Since the Self is thus eternal and changeless, therefore fight; the meaning is — do not desist from battle.
BG_C02_V18::block-4: Here the duty of fighting is not being enjoined. He had already engaged in battle, and only now, hindered by grief and delusion, sits silent. Therefore the Lord is doing nothing more than removing his impediment. Hence "fight" is a mere reiteration (anuvāda) of what is already in progress, not a new injunction (vidhi). (18)
BG_C02_V19: He who knows this Self as the slayer, and he who thinks of it as the slain — both these do not understand. This neither slays nor is slain. (19)
BG_C02_V19::block-0: The Gītā-śāstra is meant for the cessation of grief, delusion, and the rest — the causes of saṃsāra — and not for instigating action; in support of this very meaning the Lord brings forward two ṛk-mantras as witnesses. As for what you think — "In battle Bhīṣma and the others are slain by me; I alone am their slayer" — that notion of yours is utterly false. How? —
BG_C02_V19::block-1: He who knows this — the embodied one under discussion — as a slayer (hantṛ), as the agent of the act of slaying; and another who thinks of this as slain (hata), as the object of the act of slaying through the killing of the body, in the form "I am slain" — both these have not understood, have not known the Self due to non-discrimination. "I am the slayer," "I am slain" — those who, through the killing of the body, know the Self as the object of the I-cognition (aham-pratyaya) are ignorant of the very nature of the Self; this is the meaning. For this Self does not slay — does not become the agent of the act of slaying; nor is it slain — does not become the object of the action; the meaning is, because of its changelessness (avikriyatva). (19)
BG_C02_V20: It is not born, nor does it ever die; nor, having come to be, will it cease to be again. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not slain when the body is slain. (20)
BG_C02_V20::block-0: How is the Self changeless? The second mantra says:
BG_C02_V20::block-1: "Na jāyate" — does not come into being; the modification of substance characterized by birth (jani) does not belong to the Self, this is the meaning. So too "na mriyate vā." The word "vā" stands for "ca" (and). "And does not die" — thus the final modification, characterized by destruction, is denied. The word "kadācit" (ever) is to be construed with all the denials of modification — never is it born, never does it die — and so on. Since this Self does not, having come into being and undergone the act of becoming, afterwards become non-existent again, therefore it does not die. For in the world, that which, having come to be, ceases to be, is said to die. By force of the word "vā" and the word "na," this Self does not, like the body, having not been, come to be again. Therefore it is not born. For that which, having not been, comes to be, is said to be born. Not so the Self. Hence it is not born. Since this is so, therefore it is unborn (aja); since it does not die, therefore it is also eternal (nitya). Although by negating the modifications of beginning and end, all modifications stand denied, still, in order that the modifications occurring in the middle — youth and the rest, all of them, even the unmentioned ones — may be denied, the Lord denies them by their own words, saying "śāśvata," and so on. By "śāśvata," the modification characterized by waning (apakṣaya) is denied. "Śāśvata" means "that which is at all times"; it does not wane in its own form, because it is partless; nor does it wane through the loss of qualities, because it is without qualities (nirguṇa). The modification opposite to waning, namely growth (vṛddhi), is denied by the word "purāṇa." That which is built up by the addition of parts is said to grow and to be new; but this Self, being partless, is ever new even in old times — hence "purāṇa"; the meaning is, it does not grow. So too "na hanyate" — "is not slain." "Hanti" — here it must be taken in the sense of transformation (vipariṇāma), to avoid redundancy. The meaning is: it does not undergo transformation, even when the body is being transformed (slain). In this mantra, the six modifications of being (ṣaḍ-bhāva-vikāra) — worldly modifications of substance — are denied of the Self. The purport of the sentence is: the Self is devoid of every kind of modification. Since this is so, the connection with the previous mantra "both these do not understand" is established. (20)
BG_C02_V21: He who knows this as indestructible, eternal, unborn, undecaying — how, O Pārtha, can such a person slay anyone, or cause anyone to be slain? (21)
BG_C02_V21::block-0: Having declared by the mantra "He who knows this as the slayer" (BG 2.19) that the Self is neither agent nor object of the act of slaying, and having stated changelessness as the reason in "It is not born," the Lord now concludes the proposition just affirmed:
BG_C02_V21::block-1: "Veda" — knows; "avināśin" — devoid of the final modification of being, namely destruction; "nityam" — devoid of transformation. "He who knows" — this is the construction. "This" — the one whose characteristics have been stated in the previous mantra; "aja" — birthless; "avyaya" — devoid of waning. How — by what means — does that wise person, the qualified one (adhikṛta), perform the act of slaying — "hanti" — and how does he cause another to slay ("ghātayati"), employing a slayer? In no way does he slay anyone; in no way does he cause anyone to be slain. The sense in both places is one of denial (ākṣepa), since a question would not fit the context. And since the cause assigned — namely, changelessness — is the same in either case, what the Lord has in view as the topic of the section is the negation of all action for the knower (vidvat). The act of slaying is mentioned only by way of an illustration.
BG_C02_V21::block-2: What special reason for the impossibility of action in the knower does the Lord see, in view of which He sets aside actions in the words "How can such a person…"? Objection: But the changelessness of the Self has already been mentioned, and that itself is the special cause for the impossibility of all action. Reply: True, it has been mentioned. But that is not the special cause as such, since the knower (vidvat) is different from the changeless Self. For surely it is not so that one who has known a stationary post (sthāṇu) to be motionless thereby finds action impossible. Objection: Then no, this argument fails. Reply: Not so; for the knower is verily the Self. Knowership does not belong to the aggregate of body and the rest. Hence by the residual method (pāriśeṣya), the unaggregated Self is the knower and is changeless; so for this knower the impossibility of action is established, and the denial "How can such a person…" is well placed. Just as the Self, though indeed changeless, is, through the non-discrimination of the modifications of the intellect, supposed by avidyā to be the cognizer of sound and the other objects presented by the intellect — so too, by the cognition of the discrimination of Self and not-Self, by the modification of the intellect taking the form of vidyā which is itself ultimately unreal (asatya-rūpa), the Self, though essentially changeless, is called "the knower." Since the impossibility of action for the knower is declared, the Lord's settled view is to be understood thus: the actions enjoined by śāstra are enjoined for the non-knower (avidvat), not for the knower.
BG_C02_V21::block-3: Objection: But knowledge (vidyā) too is enjoined only for the non-knower, since for one who has already grasped the knowledge, enjoining knowledge would be like grinding what is already ground. So the distinction — that actions are enjoined for the non-knower and not for the knower — does not stand. Reply: No; for the difference between what is to be performed (anuṣṭheya) is well established by presence and absence respectively. After the cognition of the meaning of the injunction "agnihotra" and the rest, the agnihotra and other works are to be performed by gathering together their many factors; for the non-knower, who has the cognition "I am the agent, this is my duty," they become things to be performed. But it is not so that, after the cognition of the meaning of the injunction concerning the nature of the Self in "It is not born" and the rest, anything further remains to be performed. On the contrary, from the knowledge whose object is the oneness, agentlessness and so on of the Self — "I am not the agent, I am not the enjoyer" — nothing else arises. This is the special difference that holds. He, on the other hand, who knows the Self as "I am the agent" — for him the cognition "this is to be done by me" is unavoidable; and on its basis he is qualified, and toward him actions are possible. Such a one is the non-knower, by virtue of the saying "both these do not understand" (BG 2.19), and by the negation of action specifically with regard to the qualified knower in "How can such a person…". Therefore, only the qualified knower of the changeless Self, the desirous of liberation (mumukṣu), is qualified for the renunciation of all actions (sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa). Precisely for this reason the Lord Nārāyaṇa, having distinguished the Sāṅkhyas — the knowers — from the karmins — the non-knowers — has them adopt two distinct standpoints (niṣṭhā): "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas, by the yoga of action for the yogins" (BG 3.3). Likewise the Lord Vyāsa addressed his son: "These two are the paths…" (Mahābhārata, Śānti-parva 241.6) and so on. Likewise, "the path of action is first, and renunciation afterwards." The Lord will indicate this very division again and again: the non-knower of truth — "with self deluded by ego, he thinks 'I am the agent'" (BG 3.27); but the knower of truth — "I do nothing." Likewise, "having renounced all actions by the mind, he sits…" (BG 5.13) and so on.
BG_C02_V21::block-4: There certain self-styled scholars (paṇḍitam-manya) say: knowledge of the form "I am the Self, the one, the agentless, devoid of the six modifications of being beginning with birth, the changeless" never arises in anyone — the knowledge upon whose arising the renunciation of all actions is enjoined. Reply: not so; for that would render the scriptural teaching "It is not born" (BG 2.20) and the like meaningless. They are to be questioned: just as, by the power of scriptural teaching, the cognition of the existence of dharma and adharma and the cognition of the agent's connection with another body arise, why should the cognition of the changelessness, agentlessness, oneness and so on of the very same Self not arise from scripture? Objection: because it is not within the range of the instruments of cognition (karaṇa). Reply: not so; by virtue of the śruti "it is to be seen by the mind alone" (Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka 4.4.19). The mind, refined by the teaching of scripture and teacher and by śama, dama, and the rest, is itself the instrument for seeing the Self. And since both inference and scripture are present for attaining that, to say that knowledge does not arise is mere recklessness. And the knowledge that arises must be admitted necessarily to dispel the contrary ignorance. That ignorance has been pointed out — "I am the slayer," "I am slain," "both these do not understand." Here the Self's agency, objecthood, and causal-agency in the act of slaying have been shown to be products of ignorance. And, owing to the changelessness of the Self, this — namely, that agency and the rest are products of avidyā — is uniformly the case in all actions. For one who possesses modification, the agent, employs another, the object, with the command "do." This very same agency and causal-agency in all actions, the Lord Vāsudeva, without distinction, denies of the knower in order to indicate that the knower has no entitlement to action, by the words "He who knows the indestructible … how can such a person …" Where then is the knower's entitlement? That has been stated already — "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas" (BG 3.3). And so He will state the renunciation of all actions: "having renounced all actions by the mind" (BG 5.13) and the rest.
BG_C02_V21::block-5: Objection: Because of the word "by the mind," verbal and bodily renunciation is not meant. Reply: No; for it is qualified by "all actions." Objection: "All actions" means only mental actions. Reply: No; for verbal and bodily activities are preceded by mental activity — in the absence of mental activity they would not occur. Objection: Then what is meant is to renounce by the mind all actions other than the mental actions which are the causes of scriptural verbal and bodily acts. Reply: No; for the qualification "neither acting nor causing to act" (BG 5.13) bars this. Objection: This renunciation of all actions is spoken by the Lord with reference to a dying man, not to a living one. Reply: No; for the qualification "the embodied one dwells in the city of nine gates" (BG 5.13) does not fit then. For after one has renounced all actions in the dying state, his sitting in that body is not possible. Objection: "Having renounced in the body itself, dwelling without acting and without causing to act" — the construction should be: "he does not dwell in the body." Reply: No; because everywhere the changelessness of the Self has been ascertained, and because the act of sitting requires a substratum, while renunciation is independent of any such substratum. The word "nyāsa" preceded by "sam" here means "giving up" (tyāga), not "depositing." Therefore in the Gītā-śāstra, only the knower of the Self is entitled to renunciation, not to action. This we shall show in this place and that, in the relevant sections on Self-knowledge later. (21)
BG_C02_V22: Just as a man, casting off worn-out clothes, takes new ones, so the embodied Self, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new. (22)
BG_C02_V22::block-0: Now we shall take up the topic at hand. There the indestructibility of the Self has been declared. To what is it like? It is now stated:
BG_C02_V22::block-1: "Vāsāṃsi" — clothes; "jīrṇāni" — that have become weak; just as in the world a man, casting them off, abandoning them, takes — assumes — "navāni," "aparāṇi" — new ones, others; so too in the same way, casting off worn-out bodies, the embodied one — the Self — enters, goes to, other new ones. The Self is just like the man — entirely changeless. This is the meaning. (22)
BG_C02_V23: Weapons do not cleave this; fire does not burn it; waters do not wet it; nor does the wind dry it up. (23)
BG_C02_V23::block-0: Why is it changeless? He says:
BG_C02_V23::block-1: Weapons do not cleave this — the embodied one under discussion; because of being partless (niravayava) they do not bring about the division of its parts. "Weapons" — sword and the like. So too "fire does not burn it" — fire too does not reduce it to ashes. Likewise "the waters do not wet it." Water has the capacity to bring about the separation of the parts of an object that has parts by making it moist; this is not possible in the partless Self. Likewise wind destroys oily substances by drying up their oil. But this Self — even the wind does not dry up. (23)
BG_C02_V24: This Self cannot be cleft, cannot be burnt, cannot be wetted, and indeed cannot be dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and primordial.
BG_C02_V24::block-1: Because the weapons and the rest — namely fire, water, and wind — which are the very causes of one another's destruction, are unable to destroy this Self, therefore it is eternal. Because it is eternal, it is all-pervading. Because it is all-pervading, it is like a stake (sthāṇu) — that is to say, firm and motionless. Because it is firm, this Self is immovable (acala). Hence it is sanātana, that is, ancient, never produced from any cause whatsoever; in other words, it is not something newly originated.
BG_C02_V24::block-2:
It should not be objected that there is mere repetition (paunaruktya) in these verses; for already by the single verse beginning "It is not born, nor does it die" (Bh. Gī. 2.20), the Self's eternality and changelessness have been declared. Whatever is said here regarding the Self does not exceed the import of that single verse; some portion is repeated only in word, some in meaning as well.

The Self being a thing exceedingly difficult to grasp, the Lord Vāsudeva, returning to the topic again and again, expounds the very same reality through different words — wishing thus: "How indeed may this unmanifest Reality, which has come within range of the cognition of the transmigrators as something subject to transmigration, become a means for the cessation of transmigration?"
BG_C02_V25: This Self is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unalterable. Therefore, having known it thus, you ought not to grieve.
BG_C02_V25::block-1: Because it is not the object of any of the sense-organs, this Self is not made manifest, hence it is unmanifest (avyakta). For this very reason it is unthinkable (acintya). For whatever falls within the range of the senses becomes an object of thought; but this Self, not being within range of the senses, is unthinkable. For the very same reason it is unalterable (avikārya): just as milk is altered by curd-ferment and the like, this Self is not so altered. And being without parts, it is changeless; for nothing partless has ever been observed to undergo change. Being changeless, this Self is declared to be avikārya. Therefore, having known the Self in the manner just stated,
BG_C02_V25::block-2: you ought not to grieve, thinking, "Alas, I am the slayer of these," or "these are slain by me."
BG_C02_V26: But even if you consider this Self to be perpetually born and perpetually dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve in this way.
BG_C02_V26::block-0: Granting, for the sake of argument, that the Self is non-eternal, this is now spoken —
BG_C02_V26::block-1: The phrase "atha ca" carries the sense of mere concession (abhyupagama). Should you consider this Self under discussion to be perpetually born — that is, taking it according to the popular conception that with the production of each successive body, it is "born and again born" — and likewise should you consider it to be perpetually dead, dying with each one's destruction, "dead and again dead"; even then, that is, even on such a supposition regarding the Self, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve in this way. For of that which has birth, death is inevitable, and of that which has died, birth is inevitable — these two are bound to occur.
BG_C02_V27: For of one who is born, death is certain; and of one who has died, birth is certain. Therefore, with respect to a matter that cannot be averted, you ought not to grieve.
BG_C02_V27::block-1: For one who has come to birth, death is certain — that is, unfailing; and for one who has died, birth is equally certain. Therefore this matter, characterized by birth and death, cannot be averted. With respect to such an unavoidable matter, you ought not to grieve.
BG_C02_V28: Beings have unmanifest beginnings, manifest middles, and unmanifest ends, O Bhārata. What lament can there be over them?
BG_C02_V28::block-0: Even with respect to beings that are simply aggregates of body and instruments (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta), grief is not fit to be indulged in, for the following reason —
BG_C02_V28::block-1: Those beings — namely sons, friends, and the like, who are nothing but aggregates of body and sense-instruments — have the unmanifest as their beginning: "avyakta" means non-perception, non-apprehension; that is the "ādi" or initial state of these beings. Such beings are "avyaktādīni" before their origination; and once originated, they are "vyakta-madhyāni" — manifest only in the middle, prior to death. They are also "avyakta-nidhanāni" — that is, those whose nidhana, namely death, is again the unmanifest, the not-being-perceived. After death too they revert to the very state of unmanifestness — this is the meaning. Thus has it been said: "From non-appearance he has come, and again to non-appearance he has gone. He is not yours, nor are you his — what useless lament is this?" (Mokṣa-dharma 174.17). In such a case, what lament, what wail, can there be over beings that are themselves nothing but the delusion of "unseen, seen, vanished"? — that is the meaning.
BG_C02_V29: Some perceive this Self as a marvel; another likewise speaks of it as a marvel; another hears of it as a marvel; and even having heard, none whatsoever truly knows it.
BG_C02_V29::block-0: This Self under discussion is hard to know; why then do I blame you alone, when the cause of delusion is common to all? How is this Self so hard to know? — to that he replies —
BG_C02_V29::block-1: "Āścaryavat" — āścarya means something never seen before, something wondrous, suddenly revealed; comparable to that, that is, like a marvel — someone perceives this Self. Another likewise speaks of it as a marvel. Another, again, hears of it as a marvel. And having heard, having seen, having spoken, even then no one whatsoever knows this Self. Or alternatively: he who perceives the Self is himself like a marvel; he who speaks of it and he who hears of it — only some rare one among many thousands becomes such. Hence the Self is exceedingly difficult to grasp — this is the import.
BG_C02_V30: This embodied one in the body of every being is forever inviolable, O Bhārata. Therefore you ought not to grieve over any beings whatsoever.
BG_C02_V30::block-0: Now then, summing up the topic of this section, he says —
BG_C02_V30::block-1: The embodied one — that is, the indweller of the body — being partless and eternal, is forever, in every condition, inviolable; in any body whatsoever it is unslayable. In the body of every one — for, being all-pervading, although it abides even in immobile things and the rest, yet in the body of every living creature, even when that body is being slain, this embodied one is not slain. Since this is so, with regard to all those beings beginning with Bhīṣma, you ought not to grieve.
BG_C02_V31: Considering, moreover, your own dharma, you ought not to waver. For there exists nothing more excellent for a kṣatriya than a righteous war.
BG_C02_V31::block-0: It has been stated that, when the highest reality is held in view, neither grief nor delusion is possible. Not only when the highest reality is held in view; but also —
BG_C02_V31::block-1: Considering, moreover, your own dharma — for a kṣatriya, war is his own dharma — you ought not to waver, that is, to swerve from the natural dharma of a kṣatriya, which is to say, from your own innate disposition (ātma-svābhāvya); this is the import. And that war, undertaken by way of the conquest of the earth for the sake of dharma and for the protection of the people, does not deviate from dharma — it is supremely righteous (dharmya). Therefore than such a righteous war there exists nothing else more excellent for a kṣatriya.
BG_C02_V32: And, O Pārtha, happy are the kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle as this — come of itself unsought, an open door to heaven thrown wide.
BG_C02_V32::block-0: And on what further ground is that battle to be fought? It is said:
BG_C02_V32::block-1: By chance — that is, unprayed-for and unsought — there has come to you a battle which is itself an open door to heaven, thrown wide and uncovered. Those kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who light upon such a battle as this — how are they not happy? Surely they are most fortunate.
BG_C02_V33: But if you will not engage in this righteous war, then, having abandoned your own dharma and your fame, you shall incur sin.
BG_C02_V33::block-0: Even though it has thus come into your hands as your bounden duty —
BG_C02_V33::block-1: If, on the other hand, you will not engage in this saṅgrāma — this battle which is dharmya, that is, in no way departing from dharma but ordained by scripture — then, by that very non-performance, having cast aside your own dharma (svadharma) and the fame (kīrti) that would have arisen from your encounter with Mahādeva and the like, you shall reap nothing but sin.
BG_C02_V34: And the world will recount your unending dishonour; and for one held in esteem, dishonour is worse than death.
BG_C02_V34::block-0: It is not only the loss of one's dharma and one's fame —
BG_C02_V34::block-1: And further, in the matter of the battle, beings will recount your akīrti — your dishonour — and that too as avyayā, lasting through long ages. And for one who has been held in high esteem by virtue of qualities such as 'he is righteous, he is a hero,' and so on, dishonour overshoots even death; for one so esteemed,
BG_C02_V34::block-2: the meaning is: death is preferable to such dishonour.
BG_C02_V35: The great chariot-warriors will think that you withdrew from the fight out of fear; and those by whom you were held in high regard will come to make light of you.
BG_C02_V35::block-1: The great chariot-warriors — Duryodhana and the rest — will reckon and think that you turned back from the battle out of fear of Karṇa and the others, not out of compassion. And those very Duryodhana and his fellows, in whose eyes you had till now been bahumata — held in high regard, judged to be 'endowed with many excellences' — to those same persons you shall now go to laghutva, to lightness of esteem, that is, to contempt.
BG_C02_V36: Your enemies will utter many unutterable words, decrying your prowess. What greater pain than that?
BG_C02_V36::block-1: Your enemies — those ill-disposed towards you — will utter many avācya-vādas, words that ought never to be spoken, of various kinds, decrying and reviling your sāmarthya — that prowess of yours which was demonstrated in the battle with the Nivātakavacas and the like. Than that pain — the pain that springs from incurring such censure — what pain is more painful? The meaning is: there is no anguish more grievous than that.
BG_C02_V37: Slain, you shall attain heaven; victorious, you shall enjoy the earth. Therefore rise up, O son of Kuntī, with mind made firm for battle.
BG_C02_V37::block-0: When the battle is, after all, undertaken, by Karṇa and the others —
BG_C02_V37::block-1: 'Slain, you shall attain heaven': being slain, you shall reach the heavenly world. 'Or victorious, you shall enjoy the earth': having conquered Karṇa and the other heroes, you shall enjoy sovereignty over the earth. Either way, the gain is yours alone — that is the import. Since this is so, therefore rise up, O son of Kuntī, for the fight, with firm resolve — that is, having made the resolution, 'I shall conquer the foes, or else I shall die.'
BG_C02_V38: Holding pleasure and pain alike, gain and loss, victory and defeat, then gird yourself for the fight; thus you shall not incur sin.
BG_C02_V38::block-0: There, since the battle is your own dharma, hear this further teaching meant for one who is engaged in fighting —
BG_C02_V38::block-1: Having made pleasure and pain equal, alike — that is, having entertained neither attachment (rāga) nor aversion (dveṣa) towards them. Likewise having made gain and loss, victory and defeat, equal, then gird yourself, exert yourself, for the battle. So fighting, you shall not incur sin. This teaching is, however, prāsaṅgika — incidental, brought in by way of context — and not the principal theme.
BG_C02_V39: This understanding, declared to you in the way of Sāṅkhya — hear now the same understanding as it stands in Yoga; equipped with which understanding, O Pārtha, you shall cast off the bondage of karma.
BG_C02_V39::block-0:
For the removal of grief and delusion, a mundane line of reasoning was advanced through the verses beginning 'Even regarding your own dharma' (BG 2.31), but not by way of the principal purport. The vision of the supreme reality (paramārtha-darśana) is what is properly under treatment here. That very vision, having been set forth, is now summed up by 'This has been declared to you' (BG 2.39), in order to display the division of the scripture's twofold subject-matter. For once this division of the scripture's subject is shown here, the scripture will hereafter unfold easily under the rubric 'by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas, by the yoga of action for the yogins' (BG 3.3) — which sets out the twofold steadfastness (niṣṭhā-dvaya) — and listeners too, with the subject-matter clearly demarcated, will grasp it with ease. Hence he says:

Objection might arise as to whether the foregoing prudential reasoning is itself the Lord's siddhānta. Reply: it is not; that was provisional. The siddhānta — the steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self — is what has been set forth, and to mark this clearly Śaṅkara now distinguishes the two domains of the śāstra.
BG_C02_V39::block-1: 'This' — the buddhi, the knowledge that has been spoken to you, in respect of Sāṅkhya, that is, in respect of the discrimination of the supreme real entity (paramārtha-vastu-viveka) — is the direct cause of the cessation of those defects, grief and delusion and the rest, which are themselves the cause of saṃsāra. 'But in Yoga' — that is, in the means of attaining that very Sāṅkhya knowledge, namely karma-yoga, the performance of action with non-attachment and after relinquishing the pairs of opposites, undertaken for the worship of the Lord (īśvarārādhana), and likewise in the yoga of samādhi — hear now this very understanding which is about to be declared. And he extols that understanding by way of inducement: 'Equipped with that understanding,' that is, with the understanding pertaining to Yoga, O Pārtha, 'you shall cast off the bondage of karma' — for karma itself, going by the names of dharma and adharma, is the bondage; that bondage you shall cast off, the import being: through the attainment of true knowledge brought about by the grace of the Lord (īśvara-prasāda).
BG_C02_V40: Here there is no loss of effort once begun, nor does any contrary result arise. Even a little of this dharma rescues one from the great fear.
BG_C02_V40::block-0: Furthermore, there is yet another point —
BG_C02_V40::block-1: In this — that is, in the path of liberation, the karma-yoga here being taught — there is no abhikrama-nāśa, no destruction of what has been undertaken (abhikramaṇa = abhikrama = the beginning, the inauguration), as there is in agriculture and the like, where, if the proper sequence is broken, the whole effort comes to nothing. The meaning is: in the field of yoga the very commencement does not have an uncertain or non-uniform result; it never proves fruitless. And further — unlike the case of medical treatment, where a wrong dose or omission produces a contrary effect — here no pratyavāya, no adverse consequence, comes to be. On the contrary, even a very little of this dharma — that is, of this yoga-dharma — when actually performed, rescues and protects one from the great fear, namely the fear of saṃsāra characterized by birth, death, and the rest.
BG_C02_V41: The resolute intellect, O joy of the Kurus, is single here; but the intellects of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
BG_C02_V41::block-0: That very buddhi which has been spoken of with reference to Sāṃkhya and to Yoga — the buddhi whose mark is now to be stated — is this:
BG_C02_V41::block-1: Vyavasāyātmikā — having determination as its very nature, decisive — such a buddhi is one alone (eka eva); it is the destroyer of all the variant branches of contrary cognition, because it is born of valid means of knowledge (samyak-pramāṇa-janitatvāt). ‘Iha’ — here, in this path of the supreme good (śreyo-mārga). O joy of the Kurus (Kurunandana). Now those other contrary buddhis, by whose proliferation along divergent branches saṃsāra becomes endless, shoreless, unceasing, ever-spread out and far-extended; and again, when, by the agency of that discriminating buddhi born of valid pramāṇa, those endlessly differentiated buddhis come to rest, saṃsāra too comes to rest — those buddhis are bahu-śākhāḥ: they are the ones whose branches (śākhā) are many; that is to say, whose differentiations are many. For along each separate branch the buddhis are endless. Of whom? Of the avyavasāyins — those devoid of the discriminating buddhi born of pramāṇa: this is the meaning.
BG_C02_V42: This flowery speech, O Pārtha, the unwise utter, delighting in the letter of the Veda and saying ‘there is nothing else’.
BG_C02_V42::block-0: Those in whom there is no resolute determinative buddhi — they are now described:
BG_C02_V42::block-1: ‘This flowery speech which is about to be set forth’ — puṣpitām, like a tree in flower, looking attractive, sweet to the ear when heard — this very vāc, characterized as a sentence (vākya-lakṣaṇām), they utter. Who? The avipaścitaḥ — the witless, those wanting in discrimination (avivekinaḥ): that is the meaning. Veda-vāda-ratāḥ — those engrossed in the Vedic statements that proclaim the abundant artha-vāda passages and the means to various rewards. O Pārtha. ‘There is nothing else than the works which produce results such as heaven, cattle, sons, and the like’ — thus they are vādinaḥ, given to such talk.
BG_C02_V43: Full of desires, holding heaven the highest, they utter that speech which yields rebirth as the fruit of works — abounding in special rites, all aimed at the attainment of enjoyment and lordship.
BG_C02_V43::block-1: ‘Kāmātmānaḥ’ — having desire as their very nature, given over to desire: this is the meaning. ‘Svarga-parāḥ’ — those whose paramount human end (puruṣārtha) is heaven, who therefore make heaven their chief object. ‘Janma-karma-phala-pradām’ — the fruit of action is karma-phala; rebirth itself is the karma-phala here, hence janma-karma-phala; that speech which bestows it (pradadāti) is janma-karma-phala-pradā — that speech they utter (the verb is to be supplied from the previous verse). ‘Kriyā-viśeṣa-bahulām’ — special rites are kriyā-viśeṣāḥ; the speech in which these are many is kriyā-viśeṣa-bahulā, that speech by which the means to heaven, cattle, sons, and the rest are abundantly displayed. ‘Bhogaiśvarya-gatim prati’ — bhoga (enjoyment) and aiśvarya (lordship) are bhoga-aiśvarye; the attainment (gatiḥ = prāptiḥ) of these two is bhoga-aiśvarya-gatiḥ; the special rites that are the means towards that — the speech rich in those rites is the speech they utter. The purport is: deluded, they go round and round in saṃsāra.
BG_C02_V44: For those attached to enjoyment and lordship, whose mind is carried away by such speech, the resolute intellect is not established in samādhi.
BG_C02_V44::block-1: ‘Bhogaiśvarya-prasaktānām’ — of those who, holding ‘enjoyment is to be done; lordship too is to be had,’ are utterly enamoured of bhoga and aiśvarya alone, who have made the two their very self. ‘Tayā’ — by that speech, abounding in special rites, ‘apahṛta-cetasām’ — those whose discriminating wisdom (viveka-prajñā) has been smothered, covered over. The vyavasāyātmikā buddhi — that buddhi which belongs to Sāṃkhya or to Yoga — is not laid down (na vidhīyate), does not arise (na bhavati), in their samādhi.
