Here ‘samādhi’ is to be unpacked: ‘in this antaḥkaraṇa, the buddhi, all is laid up (samādhīyate) for the puruṣa’s enjoyment’ — hence samādhi means antaḥkaraṇa, buddhi; in that samādhi the resolute determinative buddhi does not come forth: this is the sense.
BG_C02_V45: The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, O Arjuna; be free from the three guṇas, free from the pairs of opposites, ever poised in pure sattva, indifferent to acquisition and preservation, in possession of the Self.
BG_C02_V45::block-0: Of those who are thus devoid of discriminating buddhi — those kāmātmans — what is their fruit? That He now states:
BG_C02_V45::block-1: ‘Traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ’ — for whom the traiguṇya, that is, saṃsāra, is the viṣaya, the matter to be illumined: such are the Vedas — they have the three guṇas as their object. (This is precisely how Śaṅkara takes the line: the karma-kāṇḍa of the Veda speaks within the field of the three guṇas; the goal here taught lies beyond it.) But you — be nis-traiguṇyaḥ, beyond the three guṇas, O Arjuna; that is, be desireless (niṣkāma): this is the meaning. ‘Nirdvandvaḥ’ — pleasure and pain, being the two causal opposites, are mutually counter-paired pairs (sa-pratipakṣau padārthau) and are denoted by the word dvandva; departed from those, be nirdvandva. ‘Nitya-sattvasthaḥ’ — be ever resorting to the sattva-guṇa. Likewise ‘niryoga-kṣemaḥ’ — yoga is the acquiring of the unacquired, kṣema is the preserving of what has been acquired; for one whose chief preoccupation is yoga-kṣema, application to the supreme good is hard; therefore be niryoga-kṣemaḥ. ‘Ātmavān’ — and be vigilant, never heedless. This is My teaching to you who follow your own dharma.
BG_C02_V46: As is the use of a small reservoir of water when there is a flood of water on every side, just so is the use of all the Vedas for a brāhmaṇa who has come to know.
BG_C02_V46::block-0: Objection: If, then, in all the works enjoined in the Vedas the endless fruits that are spoken of are not to be looked to, for what purpose are those works to be performed for the sake of the Lord (īśvarāya)? — Reply: hear —
BG_C02_V46::block-1: Just as in the world, in any one limited reservoir — a well, a tank, and the like — whatever artha, that is, fruit, that is, purpose (prayojana), is to be had — bathing, drinking, and the rest — that whole purpose, of whatever measure, is also accomplished, in just that measure, in a flood of water that is overflowing on every side; it is included within it: that is the sense. Just so, in the very same measure is whatever artha — whatever karma-phala — is to be had in all the Vedas, that is, in the works prescribed by the Vedas, also accomplished for the brāhmaṇa, the saṃnyāsin, who is a knower of the supreme reality (paramārtha-tattvaṃ vijānataḥ); whatever artha, whatever fruit of jñāna, is comparable to the all-flooding water — in that the smaller is included: that is the sense. As the śruti says: ‘As, in the case of one who has won at dice with the kṛta-throw, the lower throws devolve upon him, so to him devolves whatever good any creature does — to him who knows what he knows’ (Chānd. Up. 4.1.4). And He will Himself say further on, ‘the whole of action in its entirety…’ (Bh. Gītā 4.33). Therefore, prior to the attainment of the qualification for steadfastness in knowledge (jñāna-niṣṭhā-adhikāra-prāpti), one who is qualified for action must perform action, even though it stands in the position of the well, the tank, and so on.
BG_C02_V47: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Be not the cause of the fruit of action; nor let attachment be yours to inaction.
BG_C02_V47::block-1: Your adhikāra (right, qualification) is in karma alone, not in jñāna-niṣṭhā — for you. (The Bhāṣyakāra makes plain the pravṛtti / nivṛtti distinction: action belongs to the path of pravṛtti for one not yet qualified for steadfastness in knowledge.) And while doing that very action, let there be no adhikāra of yours over fruits — let there be no thirst (tṛṣṇā) for the fruit of action ‘ever’ (kadācana), in any state whatsoever: that is the meaning. For when there were thirst in you for the fruit of action, you would become the cause (hetu) of obtaining the fruit of action; therefore, in this manner, do not become the cause of the fruit of action. For when one is impelled by thirst for the fruit and engages in action, one would be the cause of birth itself, which is the very fruit of action. Now, [Objection:] if the fruit of action is not desired, what is the use of action, which is of the nature of suffering? [Reply:] therefore let there be no saṅga of yours — that is, let there be no fondness for inaction either, for non-doing. (Thus Śaṅkara fences off two false conclusions: neither pravṛtti for the sake of fruit, nor a self-styled nivṛtti that is mere idleness.)
BG_C02_V48: Established in yoga, perform actions, abandoning attachment, O Dhanañjaya, becoming even-minded in success and failure alike — this evenness is called yoga.
BG_C02_V48::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: If action ought not to be undertaken when one is impelled by the fruit of action, then how, indeed, is it to be undertaken? In reply, it is said —
BG_C02_V48::block-1:
Bhāṣya: Being established in yoga, perform actions solely for the sake of the Lord; and even there, abandoning attachment of the form "may the Lord be pleased with me," O Dhanañjaya. When action is performed by one who is empty of craving for the fruit, success (siddhi) is the attainment of knowledge that arises from purity of the inner being (sattva-śuddhi); failure (asiddhi) is what arises from the opposite of that. Becoming even (sama), that is, equal (tulya), with respect to both — success and failure alike — perform actions. 

Objection: What, then, is this yoga, established in which He says "perform"? Reply: This itself is that — the evenness with regard to success and failure is called yoga.
BG_C02_V49: Far inferior, indeed, is mere action to the yoga of buddhi, O Dhanañjaya. Take refuge in buddhi; pitiable are those who are impelled by the fruit.
BG_C02_V49::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: But that action which has been spoken of as conjoined with the cognition of evenness, performed for the worship of the Lord — than this kind of action —
BG_C02_V49::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Far" — by an extreme remove, that is, utterly — "inferior," lowly, despicable, is the action performed by one who craves the fruit, in comparison with the action conjoined with the cognition of evenness, since it (the fruit-driven action) is the cause of birth, death, and the rest. O Dhanañjaya, since this is so, therefore in the buddhi pertaining to yoga, or in the Sāṃkhya-buddhi which is matured from it, seek refuge — that is, the resort which is the cause of attaining fearlessness; pray for it. The meaning is: become one who has taken refuge in the knowledge of the supreme Reality. For those who, performing the inferior (fruit-aimed) action, are kṛpaṇas — wretched ones — being impelled by the craving for fruit, are "causes of fruit" (i.e., act for the sake of fruit), as the Śruti says: "He, O Gārgī, who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable, is a kṛpaṇa" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10).
BG_C02_V50: One conjoined with buddhi casts off here both good deeds and evil deeds; therefore yoke yourself to yoga — yoga is skill in actions.
BG_C02_V50::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: Hear what fruit is attained by him who, being conjoined with the cognition of evenness, performs his own duty —
BG_C02_V50::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Buddhi-yukta" — conjoined with the buddhi pertaining to evenness in regard to action — that one casts off, abandons, here in this world, both — sukṛta-duṣkṛta, that is, merit and demerit — by way of purity of the inner being and the consequent attainment of knowledge. Since this is so, therefore yoke yourself, exert yourself, for the sake of the yoga of evenness-cognition. For yoga is skill (kauśala) in actions: in one who is engaged in actions called one's own duty, that cognition of evenness regarding success and failure, with the mind offered to the Lord — that is the kauśala, the state of being skillful. For this is indeed the kauśala — that even those actions which are by nature binding, by virtue of the cognition of evenness, cease of themselves from their (binding) nature. Therefore become one conjoined with the cognition of evenness.
BG_C02_V51: For the wise, conjoined with buddhi, having abandoned the fruit born of action, become released from the bondage of birth, and attain the abode that is free of all malady.
BG_C02_V51::block-1:
Bhāṣya: "Having abandoned the fruit born of action" — the construction is to be made by joining these distantly placed words. The acquisition of bodies, desired and undesired, is the fruit born of action, that is, born from actions. The buddhi-yuktāḥ — those conjoined with the cognition of evenness — for that very reason, having abandoned the fruit, become manīṣiṇaḥ — wise, men of knowledge — and being janma-bandha-vinirmuktāḥ — birth itself is bondage, the bondage that is birth, freed from that, that is, freed even while alive from the bondage of (further) birth — they attain the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is called liberation, anāmaya — that is, devoid of all afflictions. 

Or else, beginning with "buddhi-yogād Dhanañjaya" (Bhagavad-Gītā 2.49), the buddhi which is the very direct seeing of the supreme Reality — comparable to a flood of waters everywhere — generated from the purity of being that arises through karma-yoga, is what is shown; for it is heard (in the text) to be the direct cause of the dropping off of merit and demerit, and so on.
BG_C02_V52: When your buddhi shall cross beyond the thicket of delusion, then you shall come to feel disgust toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
BG_C02_V52::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: When is the buddhi born of the purity of being arising from the practice of yoga attained? In reply, it is said —
BG_C02_V52::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Yadā" — at whatever time — "te" — your — "moha-kalilam" — turbidity in the form of delusion, the form of non-discrimination, by which the inner organ, having muddied the discriminative cognition between Self and not-Self, proceeds toward the sense-objects — that turbidity, your buddhi shall "vyatitariṣyati," that is, shall transcend, shall attain the state of utter purity — this is the meaning. Then, at that time, you shall "come to," attain, "nirveda" — dispassion (vairāgya) — toward what is to be heard (śrotavya) and what has been heard (śruta); the purport is that, then, the to-be-heard and the heard appear to you as fruitless.
BG_C02_V53: When your buddhi, distracted by Śruti, shall stand unwavering, motionless in samādhi, then you shall attain yoga.
BG_C02_V53::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: "Suppose, having attained the wisdom born of Self-discrimination by way of crossing beyond the thicket of delusion, when shall I attain the supreme yoga that is the fruit of karma-yoga?" If this be asked, hear that —
BG_C02_V53::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Śruti-vipratipannā" — distracted, scattered in many directions, by the Śrutis — that is, by the hearings — which reveal the relations of various ends and means and which are characterized by the [twin] paths of pravṛtti (engagement) and nivṛtti (cessation) — your buddhi being thus scattered, when, at whatever time, it shall stand — shall become firm — "niścalā" — devoid of the wavering of distraction — "in samādhi": that in which the mind is collected together (samādhīyate) is samādhi — namely, the Self (Ātman); "in that Self" is the meaning. "Acalā" — and in that very [samādhi], devoid of mental constructions (vikalpa) as well — this is what is meant. "Buddhi" means the inner organ. Then, at that time, you shall attain yoga — that is, you shall attain the discriminative wisdom which is samādhi.
BG_C02_V54::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: Having received the seed of a question, Arjuna, desirous to know the marks of one whose wisdom in samādhi has become established, said —
BG_C02_V54::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Sthitā" — well established — is the cognition "I am the supreme Brahman" — the one of whom that cognition is so established is sthita-prajña (one of steady wisdom). What is the bhāṣā — the manner of speech, the utterance — of such a sthita-prajña? In what manner is he spoken of by others — he, sthita in samādhi, abiding in samādhi, O Keśava? Or, what does the sthita-dhī, the sthita-prajña, speak of his own accord? "How does he sit, how does he move?" That is, what is his sitting, what is his moving, how is it — this is the meaning. By this verse, the marks of the sthita-prajña are inquired into.
BG_C02_V55::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: For the one who, from the very beginning, having renounced actions, is engaged in the steadfastness of the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga-niṣṭhā), and the one who [is engaged] through karma-yoga — the marks of the sthita-prajña, and the means thereto, for both these, are taught beginning with "prajahāti" up to the conclusion of the chapter. Indeed, everywhere in the spiritual scripture (adhyātma-śāstra), those very marks of one whose purpose has been accomplished are themselves taught as the means [to be cultivated], because they are accomplishable by effort. Those marks which are also accomplishable by effort and serve as means — these the Blessed Lord said —
BG_C02_V55::block-1:
Bhāṣya: "Prajahāti" — utterly casts off, abandons — "yadā" — at whatever time — "sarvān" — all, complete — "kāmān" — the various forms of desire, O Pārtha — "manogatān" — those that have entered the mind, that have entered the heart. 

Objection: When all desires are abandoned, since the cause of contentment is absent, and so long as there remains the residue serving as the occasion for sustaining the body, only behavior like that of one mad or intoxicated would result. Reply: To this it is said — "ātmany eva" — in the very Self, in the form of the inward Ātman — "ātmanā" — by oneself alone, independent of any external acquisition — "tuṣṭaḥ" — content, by reason of the gain of the nectar-essence of the seeing of the supreme Reality, possessed of the conviction "there is enough" with respect to anything else — such a one, sthita-prajña — he in whom the prajñā born of discrimination between Self and not-Self has become sthitā, prati-ṣṭhitā, well established — that knowing one is then said [to be a sthita-prajña]. The meaning is: one who has renounced the threefold longing for sons, wealth, and worlds, the saṃnyāsin, who delights in the Self (ātmārāma), whose play is in the Self (ātma-krīḍa) — he is the sthita-prajña.
BG_C02_V56: He whose mind is unshaken in sorrows, who is free from longing in pleasures, from whom attachment, fear, and anger have departed — such a sage of steady wisdom (sthitadhī) is called a muni. (56)
BG_C02_V56::block-1: "In sorrows" — when miseries of the three kinds, beginning with the bodily (ādhyātmika), present themselves — he whose mind is anudvigna, not agitated, not perturbed at the onset of sorrow, is anudvigna-manāḥ. Likewise, when pleasures arrive, he from whom spṛhā — thirst, craving — has departed, who, unlike fire which only grows the more fuel is heaped on it, does not swell up after pleasures, is vigata-spṛhaḥ. Vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ — he is so called from whom rāga (passion), bhaya (fear), and krodha (anger) have utterly departed (vītāḥ vigatāḥ). Such a one — sthitadhīḥ, of steady wisdom, sthitaprajña — the muni, the saṃnyāsin — is at that time called [a sage of established wisdom].
BG_C02_V57: He who is everywhere without affection, and on encountering this or that good or evil neither rejoices nor hates — his wisdom (prajñā) stands firm. (57)
BG_C02_V57::block-1: That muni who is sarvatra — everywhere, even with respect to the body, life, and the like — anabhisneha, devoid of clinging affection (abhisneha-varjita), and on encountering tat-tat — this or that — śubha or aśubha, that is, gaining now this auspicious thing and now that inauspicious thing, neither nābhinandati nor dveṣṭi: on obtaining the auspicious he is not delighted, does not exult; on obtaining the inauspicious he does not hate. Of such a one, free thus from elation and dejection, the prajñā born of viveka (discrimination) stands established.
BG_C02_V58: And when, like the tortoise its limbs, this one wholly withdraws the senses from the sense-objects — his wisdom stands firm. (58)
BG_C02_V58::block-1: When this yati, engaged in jñāna-niṣṭhā (steadfastness in knowledge), saṃharate — fully withdraws — like the tortoise its limbs: just as a tortoise out of fear withdraws its own limbs sarvaśaḥ, on every side, so this one fixed in jñāna-niṣṭhā withdraws indriyāṇi — the senses — from indriyārthas, all sense-objects. Of him, prajñā pratiṣṭhitā — the meaning of the sentence is as already explained.
BG_C02_V59: Sense-objects turn away from the embodied one who abstains from feeding on them — but the relish (rasa) does not. Even that relish of his ceases, having seen the Supreme. (59)
BG_C02_V59::block-0: Objection: There, in the case even of a sick man who does not partake of sense-objects, the senses do withdraw like the tortoise's limbs, but not the rāga (attachment) directed toward those objects — how then is that withdrawn? Reply —
BG_C02_V59::block-1: Although viṣayāḥ — that is, the senses, denoted by the word "objects" by metonymy of object-and-organ — turn away (vinivartante) even from the dehin, the embodied, who is nirāhāra, who does not feed on the objects — even from a fool engaged in painful tapas — yet they turn away rasavarjam: leaving aside the rasa, the rāga toward objects. The word rasa is well known in the sense of attachment — as in "engaged of his own rasa," "rasika," "rasajña" and the like. That rasa too, subtle in nature, in the form of mere coloring (rañjanā), of this yati who, having seen — that is, directly known — the Supreme (paraṃ paramārtha-tattvaṃ), Brahman, and abides in the cognition "I myself am That," turns back (nivartate); the meaning is that the cognition of objects becomes seedless (nirbīja). Without right vision (samyag-darśana), there is no extirpation of rasa. Hence the intent is that one must establish the steadiness of the prajñā that is the very form of right vision.
BG_C02_V60: For, O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind even of a wise man who strives. (60)
BG_C02_V60::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: For one wishing to bring about the steadiness of the prajñā characterized by right vision, the senses must first be brought under one's own control. The defect in not so establishing them is now stated —
BG_C02_V60::block-1: Yatataḥ — of one making effort; hi — because; Kaunteya — O son of Kuntī; puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ api — of even a discerning, wise man — the connection being made through an intervening word. The senses, pramāthīni — by their very nature given to churning, agitating — turn the man, when he faces the objects, into a state of agitation, throw him into turmoil, and having so thrown him into turmoil, haranti prasabham — they forcibly, by sheer overpowering, carry off the manas — the mind — even though it is endowed with viveka and vijñāna and is gazing only on the Light.
BG_C02_V61: Restraining all those, let him sit yoked, holding Me as the Supreme. He whose senses are under control — his wisdom stands firm. (61)
BG_C02_V61::block-1: Saṃyamya — having effected the saṃyamana, the bringing under control, of all those senses; yuktaḥ — well-collected, samāhita; āsīta — let him sit; matparaḥ — "I, Vāsudeva, the inmost Self of all (sarva-pratyag-ātman), am the Supreme (para) for him" — such a one is matparaḥ; the meaning is, "let him sit thinking, 'I am no other than That.'" Of the yati who sits thus — for him whose senses, by force of practice (abhyāsa-balāt), have come under control — his prajñā stands firmly established.
BG_C02_V62: In the man who broods on sense-objects, attachment to them is born; from attachment is born desire; from desire arises anger. (62)
BG_C02_V62::block-0: Now is told this — the root of every evil — for the one [yet] to be overpowered —
BG_C02_V62::block-1: Of the man dhyāyataḥ — pondering, dwelling on — viṣayān, the particular sense-objects such as sound and the rest, brooding upon them — there arises in those objects saṅga — āsakti, prīti — clinging, fondness. From saṅga, that is, prīti, is born — sañjāyate, comes forth — kāma, thirst (tṛṣṇā). From kāma, when it is thwarted somewhere, krodha — anger — arises (abhijāyate).
BG_C02_V63: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, loss of memory; from loss of memory, destruction of the intellect; from destruction of the intellect, he perishes. (63)
BG_C02_V63::block-0: From krodha there comes saṃmoha — non-discrimination (aviveka) regarding what is to be done and what is not (kārya-akārya). For one who is enraged, becoming bewildered, abuses even his guru. From saṃmoha there is smṛti-vibhrama: the smṛti — the recollection generated by the impressions deposited by the teaching of śāstra and the ācārya — suffers vibhrama, breakdown — namely, the failure of recollection to arise even when the occasions for its arising are present. Then, from smṛti-bhraṃśa comes buddhi-nāśa — destruction of the buddhi. The unfitness of the antaḥkaraṇa, the inner organ, to discriminate between the to-be-done and the not-to-be-done is what is called the destruction of the buddhi. From buddhi-nāśa, he perishes (praṇaśyati). For a person is a person only so long as his antaḥkaraṇa is fit for discriminating between the to-be-done and the not-to-be-done; when it becomes unfit for that, the person is verily lost. Hence, by the destruction of that antaḥkaraṇa, that buddhi, he perishes — that is, becomes unfit for the human end (puruṣārtha).
BG_C02_V64: But the self-controlled one, moving among the objects of sense with the senses freed from attraction and aversion and brought under his own command, attains lucidity of mind. (64)
BG_C02_V64::block-0: The root of every calamity has been declared to be brooding upon objects. Now, accordingly, the cause of liberation is being set forth.
BG_C02_V64::block-1: "Freed from attraction and aversion" — rāga and dveṣa together form the dvandva rāga-dveṣau; for the activity of the senses is naturally preceded by these two. He who is the seeker of liberation, moving among the unavoidable objects, that is, perceiving them, with the ear and the other senses that are freed from those two — "by the senses brought under his own command," meaning the senses that have become subservient (vaśya) to himself (ātmā), under his control — being one whose ātman, the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is amenable (vidheya) to his will — he attains prasāda. Prasāda is serene clarity (prasannatā), the wholesome poise of the mind (svāsthya). (64)
BG_C02_V65: In that lucidity all his sorrows are destroyed; for in one whose mind is serene the buddhi soon becomes firmly established. (65)
BG_C02_V65::block-0: When such lucidity has come about, what then results? It is being declared.
BG_C02_V65::block-1: "In that lucidity" of mind, all sorrows — adhyātmika and the rest — meet their destruction (hāni), their utter ruin, for this striver (yati). Furthermore — "of the one whose mind is serene," of him whose inner organ has attained wholesome poise, "soon," that is, swiftly, the buddhi becomes wholly established (paryavatiṣṭhate) — like the sky, abiding everywhere, all around. The meaning is: it becomes immovably fixed in the very form of the Self (ātma-svarūpa).
BG_C02_V65::block-2: Since the one whose mind is serene and whose buddhi is thus established has fulfilled all that is to be done (kṛta-kṛtyatā), the upshot of the whole passage is this: with senses freed from attraction and aversion, joined to objects that are unavoidable and not opposed to the śāstra, let him conduct himself — yoked. (65)
BG_C02_V66: There is no buddhi for the unyoked; nor for the unyoked is there meditative dwelling; for one who does not so dwell there is no peace; and to the peaceless, whence happiness? (66)
BG_C02_V66::block-0: This very lucidity is now praised.
BG_C02_V66::block-1: "There is not" — that is, does not exist, does not arise — buddhi whose object is the form of the Self (ātma-svarūpa-viṣayā) for the "unyoked" (ayuktasya), one whose inner organ is unsteadied (asamāhita-antaḥkaraṇa). Nor is there for such an unyoked one bhāvanā — that is, settled adherence to the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna-abhiniveśa). Likewise — for one who does not so dwell, who does not engage in such adherence to Self-knowledge, there is no peace (śānti), no inward stilling. And to the peaceless, whence happiness? For the cessation of the senses' thirst for the enjoyment of objects — that alone is happiness; not thirst whose object is sense-objects. That thirst, indeed, is sheer suffering. While craving persists, not even a trace of happiness can come to be — this is the meaning. (66)
BG_C02_V67: When the mind runs after the wandering senses, it carries away his prajñā as the wind carries away a boat upon the waters. (67)
BG_C02_V67::block-0: Why is there no buddhi for the unyoked? It is being declared.
BG_C02_V67::block-1: "For the senses, indeed," — that is, since for the senses that are wandering, engaged each in its own object, the mind which "follows after" (anuvidhīyate), which moves along with them, that mind, having become active by way of fashioning the sense-objects, robs this striver's prajñā — the discernment born of the discrimination between Self and not-Self — and destroys it. How? "As the wind a boat upon the waters" — when men wish to go forward upon the water, the wind, lifting the boat off its course and turning it onto a wrong path, drives it astray; even so the mind, having stolen away the prajñā whose object is the Self, makes it the prajñā whose object is sense-objects. (67)
BG_C02_V68: Therefore, O mighty-armed, he whose senses are restrained on every side from their objects — his prajñā is firmly established. (68)
BG_C02_V68::block-0: Having shown in many ways the establishment of the matter put forward in "yatato hi" (Bh. Gītā 2.60), and having confirmed that very point, he now winds up the discussion.
BG_C02_V68::block-1: Since the fault in the activity of the senses has been established, therefore, of that yati, O mighty-armed (mahābāho), whose senses are "restrained on every side" — by all kinds of restraint, mental and the rest — from the objects of the senses, sound and so on, his prajñā stands firmly established. (68)
BG_C02_V69: What is night for all beings, in that the self-restrained one is awake; that wherein beings are awake — that is night for the seeing sage. (69)
BG_C02_V69::block-0: This worldly and Vedic transaction (vyavahāra) — of one in whom discriminative knowledge has arisen, of the sthita-prajña, since it is the effect of avidyā, ceases when avidyā ceases; and avidyā's cessation comes from its opposition to vidyā. Making this very point clear, he says —
BG_C02_V69::block-1: "That which is night," the night that, by virtue of being of the nature of darkness, brings about non-discrimination of all things — for all beings, that is, for all creatures. What is that? It is the supreme reality (paramārtha-tattva), the object of the sthita-prajña. Just as for night-rovers, what is their day is for others nothing but night, so likewise the supreme reality, for all beings who stand in the place of night-rovers — the ignorant — is, as it were, night, since it lies beyond the range of those whose buddhi is not turned to it. In that night which is of the form of the supreme reality, awakened from the slumber of ignorance, the saṁyamī, the man of restraint — that is, the yogī of conquered senses — keeps awake. And that, on the other hand, in which beings, fast asleep as it were, are said to be awake — that night which has the form of avidyā characterized by the distinction of grasper and grasped, in which they are like dreamers — that, being of the form of avidyā, is night for the muni who beholds the supreme reality.
BG_C02_V69::block-2: Hence rites are enjoined only in the state of avidyā, never in the state of vidyā. For when vidyā has arisen, avidyā perishes like the dark of night when the sun has risen. Prior to the rise of vidyā, avidyā, being apprehended through the buddhi that takes it for valid (pramāṇa-buddhi) and figuring as the threefold distinction of action, agent, and fruit, becomes the cause of all karma. There is no possibility of its being a cause of karma when it is apprehended through a buddhi that does not take it as valid; for it is on the conviction "this rite is enjoined upon me as duty by the Veda which is itself pramāṇa" that the agent engages in the rite — not on the conviction "all this is mere avidyā, like night." But for him who has the knowledge "all this assemblage of distinctions is, like night, mere avidyā," for that knower of the Self there is qualification only for renunciation of all karma, never for engagement in it. And so it will be shown — by such words as "tad-buddhayas tad-ātmānaḥ" (Bh. Gītā 5.17) — that his qualification is solely for jñāna-niṣṭhā, abiding in knowledge.
BG_C02_V69::block-3: If it be objected: even there, in the absence of any pramāṇa to set him going, engagement is not possible — we reply: not so; because Self-knowledge has the Self itself for its object. The Self does not stand in need of any prompting pramāṇa with regard to its own self, by the very fact of its being the Self; and because all pramāṇas terminate in It as the limit of their being pramāṇa. For once the Self's own form is reached, the transaction of pramāṇa and prameya cannot recur. The final pramāṇa, indeed, dispels the Self's status as a knower (pramātṛtva); and in dispelling it, it itself becomes no-pramāṇa — like the pramāṇas of the dream-state when one wakes. And in the world it is not seen that pramāṇa is a cause of activity once the thing has been ascertained. Therefore it is established: the knower of the Self has no qualification for karma. (69)
BG_C02_V70: As waters flow into the brimming sea that abides unmoved in its own bed, so do all desires enter him — he attains peace; not the desirer of desires. (70)
BG_C02_V70::block-0: Showing by an illustration that liberation is gained only by the wise one who has cast off the threefold longing — the sthita-prajña, the yati — and not by the non-renunciate, the desirer of desires, he says —
BG_C02_V70::block-1: "Filled" by waters, "unmoved in its station" — that whose station, that is, abiding, is by way of immovability, the immovably-poised sea — into that the waters, gone there from every quarter, enter, while the sea remains established in itself, undergoing no transformation: just as that. Even so, all desires (kāmas) — that is, the various longings — though objects are at hand, from every side, enter into that man — like the waters into the sea — without producing any transformation, dissolving in the Self alone, and do not bring him under their sway: he attains peace, that is, mokṣa. Not the other, the kāma-kāmī. "Kāmas" are the desirable things — the sense-objects; he whose disposition is to desire them is kāma-kāmī; he, the meaning is, by no means attains it. (70)
BG_C02_V71: Casting off all desires, that man who walks free of longing, free of "mine," free of egoism — he attains peace. (71)
BG_C02_V71::block-1: "Casting off," relinquishing, "desires," — he who, the saṁnyāsī, the man, casts off all of them, exhaustively, in their entirety, and "walks" — the meaning is, with mere bodily living as the residual activity, he wanders about. "Free of longing" (niḥspṛhaḥ) — he from whom longing has departed even with regard to the bare maintenance of the body, he being niḥspṛha; "free of mine" (nirmamaḥ) — even in the case of those few possessions which the bare maintenance of the body itself enforces, devoid of the obsession "this is mine"; "free of egoism" (nirahaṅkāraḥ) — that is, free of the self-conceit that arises from such grounds as being learned and so forth. Such a one, the sthita-prajña, the knower of Brahman, attains śānti — that is, the cessation of all the sufferings of saṁsāra, designated nirvāṇa; he comes to be Brahman itself: this is the meaning. (71)
BG_C02_V72: Such, O Pārtha, is the Brāhmī state; having attained it, one is no more deluded. Standing firm in it even at the moment of death, one attains Brahma-nirvāṇa.
BG_C02_V72::block-0: This very same jñāna-niṣṭhā is now praised:
BG_C02_V72::block-1: "This" — the state already described — is brāhmī, that which arises in (or pertains to) Brahman; "this state" (sthitiḥ) means abiding in the very form of Brahman after renouncing every action. O Pārtha, having attained — that is, having gained — this state, one does not become deluded; one does not fall into delusion. Standing firm in this brāhmī state, in the manner already taught, even at the antakāla — even in the final span of life — one attains brahma-nirvāṇa, the quietude that is Brahman, that is mokṣa; one reaches it. What need then to mention the case of one who, renouncing from the very stage of brahmacarya, abides in Brahman alone all life long? Such a one most surely attains Brahma-nirvāṇa.
BG_C03_V01::block-0:
Two distinct kinds of buddhi (intellectual conviction) — corresponding to the spheres of pravṛtti and nivṛtti, the two domains of scripture — have been pointed out by the Lord, namely the buddhi of the Sāṅkhya path and the buddhi of the Yoga path. Of these, beginning with "When one casts off all desires" (BhG 2.55) and continuing to the close of the chapter, the renunciation incumbent upon those who have taken to the Sāṅkhya-buddhi was declared, and their fulfilment was said to lie in steadfastness in that very stand alone — "Such is the Brāhmī state" (BhG 2.72). To Arjuna, however, taking his stand on the yoga-buddhi, He said, "Thy right is to action alone… Let not thy attachment be to inaction" (BhG 2.47), enjoining only action; nor did He say that the highest good is reached from action by itself. Marking this very point, Arjuna, his mind thrown into confusion, spoke. How could the Lord, after first making him hear of jñāna-niṣṭhā rooted in Sāṅkhya-buddhi as the direct means to the highest good for a devotee who seeks that good, then yoke him — me — to action which is shot through with many visible evils and which, even mediately, has only a non-decisive promise of welfare? Such confusion in Arjuna is fitting; the question that follows it — "If… more excellent" (BhG 3.1) etc. — fits, and the Lord's answer to that question fits the scripture according to the division of provinces just stated.

Objection: Some, however, fabricate a different sense for Arjuna's question and so describe the Lord's reply contrary to that, just as they have, in a so-called "connecting tract" of their own, set forth a meaning for the Gītā at variance with what they themselves now propound here regarding the question and reply.

Reply: How so? In their connecting tract they laid it down that the meaning settled by the Gītā-śāstra is the conjoint pursuit (samuccaya) of jñāna and karma by all members of all āśramas; and they further specified that the doctrine "liberation is gained from knowledge alone after abandoning the actions enjoined by the lifelong (yāvajjīva) Vedic injunction" stands wholly forbidden. Yet here, while showing the option of āśramas, they say that the actions enjoined by that very lifelong Vedic injunction are to be relinquished. How could the Lord pronounce so contradictory a doctrine to Arjuna, or how could the listener accept what is contradictory?

Objection: Perhaps it might be said: "Liberation through knowledge alone, by abandoning Vedic action, is forbidden only for householders, not for the other āśramas."

Reply: This too is mutually contradictory with their earlier and later statements. How? Having proclaimed that the conjoint pursuit of jñāna and karma by members of all āśramas is the settled meaning of the Gītā-śāstra, how can they then declare, contrary to that, liberation from knowledge alone for the other āśramas?

Objection: Suppose the view be: this statement is made with reference to Vedic (śrauta) action — "For householders liberation through knowledge alone, devoid of śrauta action, is forbidden"; thus, even though smārta action does exist for householders, it is set aside as if non-existent and the words "from knowledge alone" are spoken.

Reply: This too is contradictory. How so? How can the discerning settle that liberation is forbidden for the householder from knowledge conjoined with smārta action only — and not for the other āśramas? Further, if smārta actions are held to be conjoined as means to liberation for those who have ascended to perpetual continence (ūrdhva-retas), let the conjunction for the householder also be with smārta actions only, and not with śrauta actions.

Objection: Then perhaps: for the householder, the conjunction of both śrauta and smārta is the means to liberation, while for the ūrdhva-retas, liberation is from knowledge conjoined with smārta action alone.

Reply: That being so, owing to the householder's exceeding burden, both śrauta and smārta — action which is in great measure painful — would be heaped upon his head.

Objection: Then suppose: just because of this very abundance of toil, liberation belongs to the householder alone, and not to the other āśramas, since they are devoid of obligatory śrauta action.

Reply: This too is unsound, for in all the Upaniṣads, in the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas and the Yoga-śāstras, the renunciation of all action by the seeker of liberation is enjoined as a limb of knowledge; and in śruti and smṛti the option among, or conjunction of, the āśramas is also taught.

Objection: Then it stands established that all members of all āśramas must conjoin jñāna and karma.

Reply: No — for the renunciation of all action by the mumukṣu is enjoined: "Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worldly attainment, they go forth as mendicants" (Bṛ.U. 3.5.1); "Therefore they declare nyāsa (renunciation) as the highest of all austerities" (Tai.Nār. 79); "Renunciation alone surpassed" (Tai.Nār. 78); "Not by action, not by progeny, not by wealth — by renunciation alone did certain ones attain Immortality" (Tai.Nār. 12); and "Let one go forth from the very stage of brahmacarya" (Jāb.U. 4) and the like. So too: "Cast off dharma and adharma, cast off both truth and falsehood; and casting off both truth and falsehood, cast off that by which thou castest them off" (Mokṣadharma 329.40); and Bṛhaspati's verse, "Seeing this very saṃsāra as essenceless, in their longing to behold the essence, they go forth without ever marrying, having taken refuge in supreme dispassion"; and Śuka's instruction, "By action the creature is bound, by knowledge it is loosed; therefore the yatis who see the further shore perform no action" (Mokṣadharma 241.7). Here too: "Mentally renouncing all actions…" (BhG 5.13) and the like.

Moreover, since liberation is no thing-to-be-produced, action is purposeless for the seeker of liberation. Objection: But the obligatory rites are for the avoidance of demerit (pratyavāya). Reply: No — the incurring of demerit pertains only to the non-renunciate. For the saṃnyāsin, demerit cannot be supposed to arise from non-performance of the agnihotra and the like, as it can for brahmacārins and other non-renunciate karmins. Indeed, a positive entity called demerit cannot be supposed to spring up from the mere absence of nityakarmas, for the śruti "How could what is be born from what is not?" (Chā.U. 6.2.2) denies the birth of being from non-being. If the Veda were to declare an unaccountable demerit from the non-performance of the enjoined, then the Veda would be pronounced productive of harm, and so itself of no authority — for what is enjoined would, whether done or not done, yield only suffering. Hence the scripture would have to be construed as kāraka (an injunctive maker), not jñāpaka (a revealer), an unintelligible position. And this is not accepted. Therefore actions are not for the saṃnyāsins. Hence the conjunction of jñāna and karma is unsustainable; and Arjuna's question, "If thou holdest the buddhi to be more excellent than action" (BhG 3.1), would also be unintelligible on the conjunction view.

For had the Lord, in the second chapter, said "Thou must perform jñāna and karma conjointly," Arjuna's question — "If thou holdest the buddhi to be more excellent than action" (BhG 3.1) — would not arise. Once it had been told to Arjuna himself that buddhi and karma both are to be carried out by him, and the buddhi which is more excellent than karma was in that very statement included, the reproach or the question "Why then dost thou yoke me to fearsome action, O Keśava?" (BhG 3.1) could in no way fit. Nor is it reasonable to suppose that the Lord had earlier said to Arjuna alone, "The more excellent buddhi is not to be performed by thee," so as to make the question "If more excellent" arise from a discrimination on Arjuna's part.

If, alternatively, the Lord had previously said that, owing to the contradiction between jñāna and karma, simultaneous performance by one and the same person is impossible, and that they are therefore to be performed by different persons — then the question "If more excellent" etc. would fit. Even granting that the question be supposed to spring from non-discrimination, the Lord's reply, distributing jñāna-niṣṭhā and karma-niṣṭhā to different persons, would not fit; nor can one suppose that the Lord's reply rests on ignorance. From this very fact, that the Lord's reply distributes jñāna-niṣṭhā and karma-niṣṭhā to different persons, the conjunction of jñāna and karma is untenable. Therefore, the meaning settled in the Gītās and in all the Upaniṣads is this: liberation is from knowledge alone.

Further, the prayer "Tell me one, having determined" (BhG 3.2) — a prayer asking for one alone of jñāna and karma — would itself be unintelligible were conjunction of the two possible. And by "Therefore do thou perform action" (BhG 4.15) He will hereafter show, by a definite restriction, the impossibility of jñāna-niṣṭhā for Arjuna at this stage.
BG_C03_V01::block-1: "More excellent" — superior — "if thou holdest, O Janārdana, that buddhi (knowledge) is more excellent than action." If buddhi and karma were intended as conjointly to be performed, then, since both together would be one means to the highest good, the singling out of buddhi as superior to karma — making it something over and above karma — would, on Arjuna's part, be unintelligible: for the very same thing cannot, in the matter of fruit, be over and above itself. Likewise, the very form of the reproach in his words — "The buddhi has been declared by the Lord as more conducive to the highest good than action; yet He directs me to perform action which is less conducive to the good — for what reason then?" — and "Why then, O Keśava, dost thou yoke me to fearsome action, cruel and marked by violence?" — would not fit. For if the Lord had taught the conjunction of all members with smārta action alone, and Arjuna had so understood, how could it be fitting for him to say, "Why dost thou yoke me to fearsome action?" etc.
BG_C03_V02: With seemingly entangled speech thou dost, as it were, bewilder my understanding. Tell me one, having determined it, by which I shall attain the highest good.
BG_C03_V02::block-1: "As if entangled" — though the Lord speaks with sharp distinction, yet to me, of dull intellect, His speech appears as if entangled. By that thou dost, as it were, bewilder my understanding; thou hast set out to remove the bewilderment of my understanding — how, then, dost thou bewilder it? Hence I say: thou dost, as it were, bewilder my understanding. If thou holdest that simultaneous performance by one and the same person of jñāna and karma — which have different agents — is impossible, then in such a case, having ascertained which of the two, buddhi (knowledge) or karma, is fitting for Arjuna in the present condition of his intellectual capacity, declare that one alone, by which, by either knowledge or action, I may attain the highest good. Even what was thus said does not fit, on the conjunction view.
BG_C03_V02::block-2: For if knowledge had been spoken of by the Lord as a subordinate factor in the niṣṭhā of action, how could Arjuna's wish to be told be confined to one alone of the two — "Tell me one"? The Lord did not say earlier, "I shall declare only one of jñāna and karma, never both," so that Arjuna, judging both to be unattainable for himself, should pray for one alone.
BG_C03_V03::block-0: The Blessed Lord gave a reply suited precisely to the question:
BG_C03_V03::block-1: "In this world" — among those of the three twice-born varṇas qualified for the performance of what the scriptures enjoin — "a twofold (dvividhā) niṣṭhā" — that is, a state, the directing of conduct toward what is to be performed — "was, of yore" — in former times, at the very beginning of creation — "declared by Me" — the all-knowing Lord — when, after creating the creatures, I made manifest the tradition of the Vedic meaning, the means for them to attain temporal welfare and the highest good — "O sinless one." What is that twofold niṣṭhā? He says: "by jñāna-yoga" — knowledge itself is yoga — by that, the niṣṭhā was declared for the Sāṅkhyas, those endowed with the discriminative knowledge of Self and non-Self, who, having renounced from the very stage of brahmacarya, who have made their goal certain through the knowledge of the Vedānta, who are paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas standing in Brahman alone. "By karma-yoga" — action itself is yoga — by that karma-yoga the niṣṭhā was declared for yogins, the karmins. This is the meaning. If the Lord's intention had been, or were going to be expressed in the Gītā or in the Vedas, that one and the same person should perform jñāna and karma conjointly for one and the same human end, how could He, here, to the dear Arjuna who has approached Him, speak of jñāna-niṣṭhā and karma-niṣṭhā as severally pertaining to particular distinct persons? If, again, it were imagined that the Lord meant, "Arjuna, having heard both jñāna and karma, will himself perform both; but to others I shall say that they are to be performed by different persons," then the Lord would be assumed to be partial and unauthoritative — which is not allowable. Therefore, by no device whatever can the conjunction of jñāna and karma be sustained.
BG_C03_V03::block-2: What was said by Arjuna — namely, the superiority of buddhi over action — stands established, since it has not been refuted; and that jñāna-niṣṭhā is to be performed by saṃnyāsins alone follows from the Lord's own assigning of the two niṣṭhās to different persons. It is to be understood that the Lord himself approves precisely this view.
BG_C03_V04: Not by abstaining from action does a man attain the state of action-transcendence (naiṣkarmya); nor by mere renunciation does he reach perfection.
BG_C03_V04::block-0: Marking that Arjuna, dejected at heart with the thought "Thou yokest me to action that is the cause of bondage," was minded "Then I shall not undertake action," the Lord said: "Not by abstaining from action…" Or, alternatively — since, owing to the mutual contradiction of jñāna-niṣṭhā and karma-niṣṭhā, simultaneous performance by one person is impossible, and so each, independent of the other, would be a means to the human end, the conclusion would have to be drawn that karma-niṣṭhā is a means to the human end mediately, that is, by being the means to attaining jñāna-niṣṭhā, and not in its own right, while jñāna-niṣṭhā, having for its very being the goal attained through karma-niṣṭhā as its means, is a means to the human end in its own right, independent of anything else; setting forth this very point the Lord says —
BG_C03_V04::block-1: "Of actions" — that is, of acts such as sacrifices, performed in this birth or in another, which become causes of the purification of being (sattva-śuddhi) by destroying the demerit hitherto accumulated, and which thereby, by giving rise to knowledge, become causes of jñāna-niṣṭhā — as the smṛti says, "Knowledge arises in men by the destruction of the action that is sin, as one beholds the Self in the self when the surface of a mirror is bright" (Mokṣadharma 204.8) — "by anārambha" — by non-performance — "naiṣkarmya" — the state of being free from action, of being void of action, that is, niṣṭhā by way of jñāna-yoga, abiding in the very form of the actionless Self — "the man does not attain." That is the meaning.
BG_C03_V04::block-2: From the statement "By the non-performance of actions one does not attain naiṣkarmya," the converse is understood: by their performance one attains naiṣkarmya. Why, again, does one not attain naiṣkarmya by the non-performance of actions? It is said: because the very undertaking of action is the means to naiṣkarmya. There is no attainment of the end-to-be-attained without the means. And karma-yoga's being the means to jñāna-yoga, characterised as naiṣkarmya, is established in the śruti and here. In the śruti, with reference to the Self-world to be known: "Him, this very one, the brāhmaṇas seek to know by recitation of the Veda, by sacrifice…" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.22) and so on — there karma-yoga is set forth as the means to jñāna-yoga. And here too: "But, O mighty-armed, renunciation is hard to attain without yoga" (BhG 5.6); "Yogins perform action giving up attachment, for the purification of self" (BhG 5.11); "Sacrifice, gift and austerity are purifiers of the wise" (BhG 18.5) — and the like will be set forth.
BG_C03_V04::block-3:
Objection: Now, in passages such as "Having given fearlessness to all beings, let one practise naiṣkarmya" (Aśva. 46.18), the attainment of naiṣkarmya is shown even from the renunciation of obligatory actions. And in common use it is even more familiar that "naiṣkarmya is from the non-performance of actions." Therefore for the seeker of naiṣkarmya, what need is there of undertaking action?

Reply: Hence He says: "Nor by mere renunciation." Nor, again, by mere renunciation alone — by the bare abandonment of action, devoid of knowledge — does one attain siddhi, which is jñāna-yoga-niṣṭhā characterised as naiṣkarmya.
BG_C03_V05: No one ever, not even for a moment, remains without performing action; for everyone is helplessly made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti.
BG_C03_V05::block-0: When the question arises why, by mere renunciation of action devoid of knowledge, one does not attain the siddhi characterised as naiṣkarmya, He says —
BG_C03_V05::block-1: "For not" — since — even "for a moment" of time, "ever" — at any time — does anyone remain without performing action. Why? Because — "is made to act" — is impelled — for, helplessly indeed, dependent and not free, every living being is yoked to action by the guṇas born of prakṛti — by sattva, rajas and tamas, sprung from prakṛti. "By the ignorant" — this is the supplement to be added; for He will hereafter say, "He whom the guṇas do not move" (BhG 14.23). Through this very setting apart of the Sāṅkhyas, karma-yoga is for the ignorant alone, not for the knowers. For the knowers, who are not moved by the guṇas, there is no movement of their own; therefore karma-yoga is unintelligible for them. So has it been explained on "Know that to be indestructible" (BhG 2.21).
BG_C03_V06: He who, restraining the organs of action, sits dwelling in mind upon the objects of the senses — that deluded one is called a hypocrite.
BG_C03_V06::block-0: What was said — that the non-knower of the Self does not undertake the enjoined action — is plainly false; this He shows:
BG_C03_V06::block-1: "The organs of action" — hands and the rest — "having restrained" — having drawn them in — he who "sits" — remains — "recollecting in mind" — pondering — the "sense-objects" — the objects — that deluded one, his inner organ utterly bewildered, is a false-conduct one, a feigner, an evil-doer —
BG_C03_V07: But he, O Arjuna, who, restraining the senses with the mind, undertakes by the organs of action karma-yoga, unattached — he excels.
BG_C03_V07::block-0: But he, again, who is qualified for action, an ignorant one, having restrained the buddhīndriyas (organs of cognition) with the mind, undertakes, O Arjuna, with the karmendriyas — the organ of speech, the hands, and so on — what does he undertake? He says: karma-yoga, being unattached — devoid of any aiming at fruits — he excels above the other, the one of false conduct.
BG_C03_V08: Perform you the enjoined work, for action is superior to inaction; even the bare maintenance of your body would not be accomplished through inaction.
BG_C03_V08::block-1: ‘Niyatam’ — that which is constant, prescribed by the śāstra; the work for which one is qualified by birth-station and which is enjoined without reference to any specific fruit — that is ‘niyata-karma’; perform that, you, O Arjuna. For action (karma) is superior — that is, more excellent in result — to inaction, that is, to non-performance, to non-undertaking. How so? Because the very maintenance of the body — śarīra-yātrā, the bodily subsistence — would not be accomplished, would not come to fulfilment, for you, were you to remain in inaction, in non-doing. Hence the distinction between action and inaction is plainly seen in ordinary life as well.
BG_C03_V09: This world is bound by action, save for action performed for the sake of yajña; therefore, O son of Kuntī, free from attachment, perform action for that purpose alone.
BG_C03_V09::block-0: And as to your further opinion that, since action results in bondage, action ought not to be performed — that too is wrong. How so? —
BG_C03_V09::block-1: By the śruti ‘yajño vai viṣṇuḥ’ (Tai. Saṃ. 1.7.4), ‘yajña verily is Viṣṇu,’ ‘yajña’ here means the Lord (Īśvara); the work which is undertaken for His sake is ‘yajña-artham karma.’ Apart from that work — through any other work — this world, that is, the qualified agent who performs work, becomes ‘karma-bandhana,’ one whose bondage is constituted by his work; but it does not become so when the work is for yajña’s sake. Therefore, for that purpose, for the sake of yajña, perform action, O son of Kuntī; ‘mukta-saṅgaḥ’ — being one who is wholly rid of attachment to the fruit of action — undertake it, accomplish it.
BG_C03_V10: Having created the creatures together with yajña in the beginning, the Lord of creatures (Prajāpati) said: ‘By this shall you propagate yourselves; let this be unto you the milker of desired wishes.’
BG_C03_V10::block-0: And for this further reason action ought to be performed by one who is qualified —
BG_C03_V10::block-1: ‘Saha-yajñāḥ’ — accompanied by yajña — the creatures, namely the three varṇas (twice-born), having ‘sṛṣṭvā,’ created, brought forth, ‘purā,’ formerly, at the beginning of the creation, ‘uvāca,’ spoke, did Prajāpati, the creator of creatures: ‘by this yajña you shall propagate yourselves’ — ‘prasava’ means increase, generation; ‘bring that about.’ ‘Let this yajña be unto you (vaḥ) the iṣṭa-kāma-dhuk’ — that which milks forth, like a wish-cow, the desired wishes, that is, the specific fruits aimed at; hence ‘iṣṭa-kāma-dhuk.’
BG_C03_V11: Nourish the gods by this yajña; let those gods nourish you. Thus mutually nourishing one another, you shall attain the supreme good.
BG_C03_V11::block-1: ‘Devān’ — the gods, namely Indra and the rest — ‘bhāvayata,’ make them prosper, increase them, by this yajña. ‘Te devāḥ’ — those gods — ‘bhāvayantu,’ may they make you flourish, namely satiate you (āpyāyayantu) by rain and the like, ‘vaḥ,’ that is, you. Thus, ‘paras-param’ — mutually, one with the other — ‘bhāvayantaḥ,’ nourishing one another, ‘śreyaḥ paramavāpsyatha’ — you shall attain the supreme good, that is, that whose mark is mokṣa, by the gradation of the rise of true knowledge (jñāna-prāpti-krama). Or else, you shall attain heaven (svarga) as the supreme good.
BG_C03_V12: Nourished by yajñas, the gods will give you the desired enjoyments. He who enjoys what is given by them without offering back to them — he is verily a thief.
BG_C03_V12::block-1: ‘Iṣṭān’ — desired, aimed-at — ‘bhogān,’ enjoyments, certainly, ‘vaḥ,’ to you, the gods ‘will give,’ will bestow — namely wife, cattle, sons and so forth — being ‘yajña-bhāvitāḥ,’ that is, augmented, gratified, by yajñas: this is the meaning. The enjoyments given by those gods, not having offered them back, that is, not having paid the debt to these gods, he who eats — that is, who satisfies merely his own body and senses — is verily a thief (steno hi); he is one who steals what belongs to the gods and the rest.
BG_C03_V13: The good, who eat the leavings of yajña, are released from all sins; but those wicked ones who cook for their own sake — they consume sin.
BG_C03_V13::block-0: But those who, on the contrary —
BG_C03_V13::block-1: Having accomplished the deva-yajña and the rest, those whose habit it is to eat the remainder of those — that food called ‘amṛta’ — they are ‘yajña-śiṣṭa-aśinaḥ.’ Being such, the good (santaḥ) ‘mucyante,’ are released, ‘sarva-kilbiṣaiḥ,’ from all sins — from those produced by the five household ‘sūnās’ (slaughter-spots), namely the hearth and the rest, and from others arising from injuries committed through inadvertence and the like. But those self-fillers (ātmam-bharayaḥ) — they, on the contrary, eat sin (agham); themselves wicked (pāpāḥ) — those who cook, that is, who carry out cooking, ‘ātma-kāraṇāt,’ for the sake of their own self alone.
BG_C03_V14: Beings come into being from food; food has its origin in rain; rain comes from yajña; yajña arises from action.
BG_C03_V14::block-0: And for this further reason action ought to be performed by one who is qualified, since action is the cause for the turning of the world-wheel (jagac-cakra-pravṛtti). How so? It is said —
BG_C03_V14::block-1: ‘Annāt’ — from food which has been eaten and digested into blood and seed — beings ‘bhavanti,’ come into being, are born, manifestly. ‘Parjanyāt,’ from rain, is the production of food, ‘anna-sambhavaḥ.’ ‘Yajñāt bhavati parjanyaḥ’ — rain comes from yajña — by the smṛti, ‘The oblation properly cast in the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born; from rain food; thence creatures’ (Manu 3.76). ‘Yajñaḥ’ here is the apūrva (the unseen potency). And that yajña is ‘karma-samudbhavaḥ’: the activities of the ṛtvik and the yajamāna are karma; that yajña — namely the apūrva — whose origin (samudbhava) is that, that yajña is ‘karma-samudbhava.’
BG_C03_V15: Know action to spring from Brahman (the Veda); Brahman has its origin in the Imperishable. Therefore Brahman, the all-pervading, is ever established in yajña.
BG_C03_V15::block-0: And whence has such an action arisen? He says —
BG_C03_V15::block-1: ‘Karma brahma-udbhavam’ — ‘Brahman’ here is the Veda; that work whose ‘udbhava,’ that is, whose cause, whose revealer, is the Veda — that action, know to be ‘brahma-udbhava’; understand it thus. And the Brahman, namely the Veda, is itself ‘akṣara-samudbhavam’: the akṣara (the imperishable), the supreme Self (paramātman), is its samudbhava, its origin; therefore ‘akṣara-samudbhavam.’ Brahman here means Veda. Since immediately from the Imperishable, named the supreme Self, the Veda has come forth, as it were, like the breath of the Puruṣa, therefore — by reason of its revealing all objects — it is ‘sarvagatam,’ all-pervading. Yet, even being all-pervading, it is ever, perpetually, ‘yajñe pratiṣṭhitam,’ established in yajña, since the injunctions concerning yajña are its principal content.
BG_C03_V16: He who, in this world, does not follow the wheel thus set in motion — sinful in life, revelling in the senses — O Pārtha, he lives in vain.
BG_C03_V16::block-0:
“Evam” — in this manner, with the Veda and the sacrifice as its starting-point, the wheel of the world has been set in motion by the Lord. He who, being qualified for action, does not follow it round here in this world is “aghāyuḥ” — “agha” means sin, “āyuḥ” means life; he whose very life is sin is aghāyuḥ, that is, one whose living is sinful. “Indriyārāmaḥ” — “ārāma” is sporting, recreation, play among objects through the senses; he whose recreation is with the senses among sense-objects is indriyārāmaḥ. O Pārtha, that man lives “mogham” — uselessly, in vain.

Therefore the purport of this section is that the ignorant qualified man must indeed perform action. Until the fitness for steadfastness in Self-knowledge is attained, the practice of karma-yoga, undertaken for the sake of that fitness, is obligatory upon the qualified man who does not yet know the Self — this has been established beginning with “Not by abstention from actions” (Bg. 3.4) and going up to “Even bare bodily maintenance would not be accomplished for thee without action” (Bg. 3.8); and again, beginning with “Save action done for sacrifice” (Bg. 3.9) and going up to “in vain, O Pārtha, does he live” (Bg. 3.16), many reasons, incidentally, have been stated by the text for the performance of action by the qualified man who does not know the Self. And the faults of not performing it have also been declared.
BG_C03_V16::block-1: Therefore the meaning of the section is that action must indeed be done by the ignorant qualified man. Before fitness for steadfastness in Self-knowledge is attained, the qualified non-knower of the Self must, with that very fitness as the goal, undertake karma-yoga — this has been propounded beginning with “Not by abstention from actions” (Bg. 3.4) up to “Even bodily maintenance would not be accomplished for thee without action” (Bg. 3.8); and likewise, beginning with “Save action done for the sake of sacrifice” (Bg. 3.9) up to “in vain, O Pārtha, does he live” (Bg. 3.16), many supporting reasons have, in passing, been stated for the performance of action by the qualified non-knower of the Self; and the censure of its non-performance has also been pronounced.
BG_C03_V17: But that man whose delight is in the Self alone, who is satisfied with the Self, and contented in the Self alone — for him there is nothing to be done.
BG_C03_V17::block-0: When this is so, is the wheel thus set in motion to be followed by everyone, or is steadfastness in jñāna-yoga alone — to be observed by the Self-knowing Sāṅkhyas — to be reached only by him who has not yet attained it through the means of the previously stated practice of karma-yoga, by the non-knower of the Self? Anticipating such a question on Arjuna’s part, or even of his own accord, in order to bring out clearly the discrimination of the meaning of the scripture, the Lord — making manifest in this Gītā-śāstra the very purport of the Śruti, namely: “Having known this Self, the Brāhmaṇas, with false knowledge ceased, rise above the desires for sons and the rest, which are necessarily to be performed by those who possess false knowledge, and wander forth in the life of mendicancy, undertaken merely for the maintenance of the body; for them there is no duty whatever apart from steadfastness in Self-knowledge” (Bṛ. Up. 3.5.1) — speaks:
BG_C03_V17::block-1: But the Sāṅkhya, the one steadfast in Self-knowledge, is “ātma-rati” — he whose delight is in the Self alone, not in objects; such a one is ātma-ratiḥ. He is also “ātma-tṛpta” — content with the Self alone, not by food, drink and the like; that human being, the saṃnyāsin. And he is contented in the Self alone. Contentment indeed arises in everyone upon the gain of an external object; but he, irrespective of any such, is contented in the Self itself — that is, he is wholly free from craving on every side. For such a knower of the Self, “kāryam” — what is to be done — “na vidyate” — does not exist; this is the meaning.
BG_C03_V18: For him there is no purpose to be served by what is done, nor any by what is left undone here; nor has he any need that depends, in the case of any being, upon any creature whatsoever.
BG_C03_V18::block-1: For that knower delighting in the supreme Self, “kṛtena” — by action done — there is no “artha,” no purpose. “Then let there at least be, by the not-doing, ‘akṛtena,’ the demerit known as pratyavāya, the calamity” — no, even by what is left undone, here in this world, there is for him not the slightest pratyavāya in the form of incurred sin, nor anything of the nature of loss to the Self. And for him, among all beings — beings ranging from Brahmā down to the immobile — there is no “artha-vyapāśraya,” no leaning whatsoever upon any being for the sake of any object accomplishable through purposive action; that is, taking refuge in any particular being, there is no end to be accomplished, on account of which an action for that end need be performed. But thou dost not stand in this fully-flooded all-engulfing right-vision (samyag-darśana), comparable to a place inundated by waters on every side.
BG_C03_V19: Therefore, unattached, perform always the action that is to be done; for the man who, unattached, performs action, attains the Supreme.
BG_C03_V19::block-1: “Tasmāt” — therefore — being “asaktaḥ” — devoid of attachment — perform “satatam” — always — the action that is the duty, the obligatory work, “samācara” — accomplish it. For he who, unattached, performing action, doing the work for the sake of the Lord, attains “param” — the Supreme — that is, mokṣa: “pūruṣaḥ,” the man — by way of the purification of the inner sense (sattva-śuddhi); this is the meaning.
BG_C03_V20: By action alone Janaka and others reached perfection; even with a view to the maintenance of the world, thou shouldst act.
BG_C03_V20::block-1: By action alone, indeed — “karmaṇaiva hi” — for, the kṣatriyas of old, the wise, “āsthitāḥ” — were established in, set forth toward, “saṃsiddhim” — the attainment of mokṣa. Who? Janaka and the rest — Janaka, Aśvapati and the like. If they were possessed of right vision attained, then for the sake of the maintenance of the world, since their initiated action was already in progress (prārabdha-karman), they reached perfection together with action itself, without renouncing it; this is the meaning. But if Janaka and the rest had not attained right vision, then they reached perfection through action which serves as the means to purification of the inner sense, gradually — thus is the verse to be expounded. Now, if you think: “By the ancients, by Janaka and others themselves not yet knowing, the obligatory action was performed; that does not necessarily mean another, the possessor of right vision who has accomplished his end, must also perform it” — even so, dependent as thou art upon the action already begun, beholding “loka-saṅgraha” itself — the prevention of the world from going astray on the wrong path is loka-saṅgraha — beholding that very purpose, thou oughtst to act.
BG_C03_V21: Whatever the great man does, that very thing other people also do; whatever standard he sets up, the world follows it.
BG_C03_V21::block-0: Why must loka-saṅgraha be done? In answer it is said —
BG_C03_V21::block-1: Whatever action “śreṣṭhaḥ” — the foremost, the principal one — performs, that very action does “itaraḥ janaḥ” — the other person — perform, following him. Further, whatever standard — be it worldly or Vedic — that great one upholds, the world follows; that is, takes that very thing for its standard. This is the meaning.
BG_C03_V22: There is, O Pārtha, no duty for Me whatsoever in the three worlds; nothing unattained that is to be attained — and yet I am engaged in action.
BG_C03_V22::block-0: If, herein, thou hast still some confusion regarding the duty of loka-saṅgraha, why then dost thou not look at Me? —
BG_C03_V22::block-1: “Na me” — for Me, O Pārtha, “na asti” — there does not exist — “kartavyam” — anything to be done — in any of the three worlds — “kiñcana” — anything whatsoever. From what cause? Because there is nothing unattained, nothing yet to be obtained — “anavāptam avāptavyam” — and yet, even so, I am engaged in action.
BG_C03_V23: For if I were not, ever unwearied, to engage in action, men would in every way follow My path, O Pārtha.
BG_C03_V23::block-0: For, if I were ever — at any time, “jātu” — not to engage, “atandritaḥ” — being unwearied, free from sloth, in action — being the foremost as I am, men would follow “mama vartma” — My path, My track — O Pārtha, “sarvaśaḥ” — in every way, by all means.
BG_C03_V24: These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action; and I should become the agent of confusion of castes (saṅkara) and would destroy these creatures. (24)
BG_C03_V24::block-0: Utsīdeyuḥ — would perish, would be destroyed; ime — these; sarve lokāḥ — all these worlds; would suffer ruin from the absence of action which is the cause for the maintenance of the world, na kuryāṁ karma cet aham — should I not perform action. Further, saṅkarasya ca kartā syām — and I should also become the maker of the intermixture of castes. By that cause, upahanyām imāḥ prajāḥ — I should ruin these creatures. The meaning is: though engaged for the favour of the creatures, I should accomplish their undoing, their destruction. Such conduct would be unbefitting of Me, the Lord.
BG_C03_V25: As the unwise, attached to action, perform action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man, unattached, act, desiring the maintenance of the world. (25)
BG_C03_V25::block-0: But if, even as I, you have the conviction that the goal is already attained — being a knower of the Self — or if any other such Self-knower exists, even for him, though there is no duty for his own sake, the favour of others alone remains his duty. Hence the Lord says —
BG_C03_V25::block-1: Saktāḥ karmaṇi — attached to action, with the thought ‘the fruit of this action will accrue to me’; thus do certain avidvāṁsaḥ — the unlearned, the non-knowers — act, O Bhārata; kuryāt vidvān — let the wise man, the knower of the Self, act tathā — likewise, while remaining asaktaḥ — unattached. Then for what purpose does he act? Hear that: cikīrṣuḥ — desiring to bring about; lokasaṅgraham — the gathering and upholding of the world.
BG_C03_V26: Let him not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action; the wise man, himself acting in concert with concentration, should make them perform all actions. (26)
BG_C03_V26::block-0: Thus, for one who desires the upholding of the world, no duty remains for Me the knower of the Self, nor for any other such, save the upholding of the world. Therefore this teaching is given to that knower of the Self —
BG_C03_V26::block-1: Buddher bhedaḥ — splitting of the understanding; buddhi-bhedaḥ — the disturbance, the unsettling, of the firm conviction in the form ‘I must do this; the fruit of this action is for me to enjoy’ — that he should not janayet, not produce, in ajñānām — the non-discriminating; karma-saṅgināṁ — those clinging to action, possessed of attachment to it. What then should he do? Joṣayet — let him cause them to engage in; sarva-karmāṇi — all actions; vidvān — the wise man; while himself, yuktaḥ — being abhiyuktaḥ, well applied, samācaran — diligently performing that very same action of the unlearned.
BG_C03_V27: Actions are wrought in every way by the guṇas of primal nature; he whose self is deluded by ahaṅkāra thinks ‘I am the doer.’ (27)
BG_C03_V27::block-0: How does the unlearned, the ignorant, become attached to actions? The Lord says —
BG_C03_V27::block-1: Prakṛteḥ — of prakṛti, that is, pradhāna, the state of equilibrium of the guṇas sattva, rajas and tamas; by the guṇaiḥ — the modifications of that prakṛti, in the form of the body and the organs (kārya-karaṇa); kriyamāṇāni karmāṇi — actions worldly and scriptural that are being wrought; sarvaśaḥ — in every manner. Ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā — the ahaṅkāra is the cognition of selfhood with respect to the aggregate of body and organs; the man whose ātman, that is, antaḥkaraṇa, is variously and manifoldly deluded by that ahaṅkāra; he, possessing the qualities of body and organs, identifying with body and organs through avidyā, attributing to the Self actions which belong to them, thinks of the various actions: ‘I am the doer.’
BG_C03_V28: But the knower of the truth, O mighty-armed, of the divisions of guṇas and karmas, knowing that ‘the guṇas operate amid the guṇas,’ does not become attached. (28)
BG_C03_V28::block-0: But the one who is wise —
BG_C03_V28::block-1: Tattvavit tu — yet the knower of the truth, O mighty-armed. Knower of the truth of what? The meaning is: the knower of the truth of guṇa-karma-vibhāgayoḥ — of the division of the guṇas and the division of the actions. Guṇāḥ — the guṇas in the form of the organs (karaṇa); guṇeṣu — in the guṇas in the form of objects (viṣaya); vartante — operate; not the Ātman. Knowing thus, na sajjate — he does not become attached, he forms no clinging.
BG_C03_V29: Those wholly deluded by the guṇas of primal nature become attached to the actions of the guṇas; the knower of the whole should not unsettle those dull-witted ones who know only in part. (29)
BG_C03_V29::block-1: Prakṛteḥ guṇaiḥ — by the guṇas of primal nature; samyak mūḍhāḥ — being thoroughly deluded, beguiled; they sajjante — become attached; guṇānāṁ karmasu — to the actions of the guṇas, that is, guṇa-karmasu — saying ‘we perform action for the sake of the fruit.’ Those clingers to action, the akṛtsna-vidaḥ — those who see only the fruit of action and not the whole, the mandān — the dull-witted; the kṛtsna-vit — the knower of the whole, that is, the knower of the Ātman, himself na vicālayet — should not unsettle. The very generating of buddhi-bheda is that ‘unsettling’ — that he should not do, is the meaning.
BG_C03_V30: Surrendering all actions to Me, with mind set on the Self, free from desire and from the sense of ‘mine,’ fight, with thy fever gone. (30)
BG_C03_V30::block-0: But how is action to be performed by the unlearned, qualified for action, who seeks liberation? The reply is given —
BG_C03_V30::block-1: Mayi — in Me, in Vāsudeva, the supreme Lord, the all-knowing, the Self of all; sarvāṇi karmāṇi — all actions; saṁnyasya — depositing, casting; adhyātma-cetasā — with the discriminative understanding ‘I am the agent acting for the Lord, like a servant for his master’ — with this conception. Further, nirāśīḥ — the one in whom desire is forsaken; nirmamaḥ — the man from whom the sense of ‘mine’ has departed — being such, do thou bhūtvā yudhyasva — fight, vigata-jvaraḥ — having torment gone, having grief gone, is the meaning.
BG_C03_V31: Those men who constantly follow this teaching of Mine, full of faith and free from cavil, they too are released from actions. (31)
BG_C03_V31::block-0: This teaching of Mine, that action is to be performed, has been declared along with its proof. Such being so —
BG_C03_V31::block-1: Ye — those who; me — Mine, this; idaṁ matam — this teaching; nityam — constantly; anutiṣṭhanti — practise, follow after; mānavāḥ — men; śraddhāvantaḥ — possessed of faith, putting their trust in it; anasūyantaḥ — not bearing cavil, not finding fault with Me, the supreme Guru, Vāsudeva — being such, mucyante te’pi — they too are released; karmabhiḥ — from actions named dharma and adharma.
BG_C03_V32: But those who, finding fault with this teaching of Mine, do not put it into practice — know them to be deluded in respect of all knowledge, lost, and devoid of discrimination. (32)
BG_C03_V32::block-0: But those who are the very opposite of these — finding fault with (abhyasūyantaḥ), that is, censuring this teaching of Mine — do not put it into practice (na anutiṣṭhanti), do not conform to My doctrine. They are deluded in many ways with respect to every kind of knowledge (sarveṣu jñāneṣu vividhaṃ mūḍhāḥ). Know them (viddhi, jānīhi) — these who are deluded in all knowledge (sarva-jñāna-vimūḍhān) —
BG_C03_V32::block-1: to be lost (naṣṭān), gone to ruin, devoid of mind (acetasaḥ), that is, lacking discrimination. (32)
BG_C03_V33: Even one possessed of knowledge acts in conformity with his own primal nature (prakṛti); beings follow their nature — what will repression accomplish? (33)
BG_C03_V33::block-0: Leading bhāṣya — Objection: For what reason, then, do they not follow Your teaching, but follow the duties of others (para-dharma) and not their own (sva-dharma)? Being thus opposed to You, why are they not afraid of the fault of transgressing Your command? — To this He replies:
BG_C03_V33::block-1: Every being, even one possessed of knowledge (jñānavān api), behaves (ceṣṭate) — performs effort — in a manner conformable (sadṛśam, anurūpam) to its own (svasyāḥ, svakīyāyāḥ) primal nature (prakṛteḥ). What is called 'prakṛti' is the residual impression (saṃskāra) of dharma, adharma and the rest acquired in former lives, which becomes manifest at the beginning of the present birth; that is prakṛti. To that nature alone every creature, even the man of knowledge, conforms in his action — how much more the fool! Therefore beings (bhūtāni), that is, living creatures (prāṇinaḥ), follow (yānti, anugacchanti) their nature. What will repression (nigrahaḥ), in the form of prohibition, accomplish — whether Mine or another's? (33)
BG_C03_V34: Attachment and aversion are seated in regard to each sense's object; one should not come under their sway, for they are his way-blockers. (34)
BG_C03_V34::block-0: Leading bhāṣya — Objection: If every creature acts only in conformity with its own nature, and there is no one devoid of nature, then since there is no scope for human effort (puruṣakāra), the scriptures (śāstra) would be rendered useless. To meet this objection it is said:
BG_C03_V34::block-1: In the object (arthe) of each and every sense (indriyasya indriyasya) — that is, in the objects of all the senses, sound and the rest — toward what is desired there is attachment (rāga), toward what is undesired there is aversion (dveṣa). Thus, with respect to each sense-object, attachment and aversion are inevitable. Here lies the field for human effort and for the purport of the śāstra. One who is engaged in what the śāstra enjoins should at the very outset refuse to come under the sway of attachment and aversion. For the nature (prakṛti) of a person impels him into his own action only when preceded by attachment and aversion; then there comes about abandonment of one's own dharma and the practice of another's dharma. But when one restrains attachment and aversion by their opposites, then a person becomes one whose vision is solely the vision of the śāstra, not one under the sway of nature. Therefore one should not come under the sway of those two, attachment and aversion, since they are this person's way-blockers (paripanthinau) — obstructors of the path of the highest good, like robbers on the road. This is the meaning. (34)
BG_C03_V35: Better is one's own dharma though deficient in merit than another's dharma well performed; better is death in one's own dharma — another's dharma is fraught with fear. (35)
BG_C03_V35::block-0: Leading bhāṣya — There, prompted by attachment and aversion, one might construe even the meaning of the śāstra otherwise, thinking, 'Even another's dharma, being a dharma, is to be performed.' That is wrong:
BG_C03_V35::block-1: Better (śreyān), more praiseworthy, is one's own dharma (sva-dharmaḥ), even though deficient in merit (viguṇaḥ api, vigata-guṇaḥ api), even when performed, than another's dharma (para-dharmāt) — even when well performed (svanuṣṭhitāt), accomplished with the requisite merits. For one established in his own dharma, even death (nidhanam, maraṇam api) is better than the life of one established in another's dharma. Why? Because another's dharma is fraught with fear (bhayāvahaḥ) — it brings fear in the form of hell and the like.
