BG_C03_V35::block-2: Although it has been said that the source of all evil is described in 'For one who dwells on sense-objects' (BG 2.62) and in 'For attachment and aversion are his way-blockers' (BG 3.34), this was stated in a scattered manner and was not made definite. Wishing to know it concisely and definitely as 'just this is the source,' Arjuna spoke — for, 'Once it is known, I would strive to root it out.' (35)
BG_C03_V36: Arjuna said: But by what is a man impelled to commit sin, even against his own wish, O Vārṣṇeya, as if compelled by force? (36)
BG_C03_V36::block-0: But — by what cause as the impelling factor, propelled by which (kena hetu-bhūtena prayuktaḥ san) — like a servant by a king — does this man (puruṣaḥ) commit (carati, ācarati) sinful action (pāpaṃ karma) himself, even unwilling (svayam anicchan api), O Vārṣṇeya (born in the family of Vṛṣṇi), as though compelled by force (balāt iva niyojitaḥ) — 'like by a king' is the simile given.
BG_C03_V36::block-1: Hear thou of him, that enemy who works all evil, of whom you ask — thus the Lord said: (36)
BG_C03_V37: The Blessed Lord said: This is desire, this is wrath, born of the rajo-guṇa — the great devourer, the great evil-doer; know this to be the foe here. (37)
BG_C03_V37::block-0: 'Of complete sovereignty, of dharma, fame, prosperity, dispassion, and of liberation — of these six is the term bhaga used' (Viṣṇu-purāṇa 6.5.74). The aggregate of the six, sovereignty and the rest, exists in Vāsudeva eternally, without obstruction, and in its entirety. 'He knows the origin and the dissolution, the coming and going of beings, knowledge and ignorance' (Viṣṇu-purāṇa 6.5.78) — and one in whom this knowledge concerning origin and the rest abides — that Vāsudeva is to be denominated 'Bhagavān.'
BG_C03_V37::block-1: Desire (kāma) is this — the enemy of the whole world — by reason of which all evil befalls beings. This very desire, when obstructed by something, transforms itself into wrath (krodha). Therefore wrath too is none other than this. Born of the rajo-guṇa (rajo-guṇa-samudbhavaḥ) — rajaḥ which is also a guṇa, that is the rajo-guṇa; the desire whose origin (samudbhava) is that — alternatively, that which is the source of rajo-guṇa: for desire when arisen, by setting rajaḥ in motion, sets the man in motion. The lament of those engaged in service and the like — the work of rajaḥ — is heard: 'I have been forced to it by craving!' Mahāśanaḥ — 'his eating (aśana) is great (mahat)' — therefore mahāśanaḥ; and for that very reason mahā-pāpmā, the great evil-doer; for, urged on by desire (kāma), the creature commits sin. Therefore know this — kāma — to be the foe here, in saṃsāra. (37)
BG_C03_V38: As fire is enveloped by smoke, as a mirror by dirt, as the embryo is enveloped by the womb-membrane, so is this enveloped by that. (38)
BG_C03_V38::block-0: Leading bhāṣya — How is it the foe? He makes this clear by examples:
BG_C03_V38::block-1: By the smoke (dhūmena) co-born with it (sahajena), fire — which is luminous in nature — is enveloped by what is non-luminous in nature; or as a mirror is enveloped by dirt; or as the embryo (garbhaḥ) is enveloped (āvṛtaḥ), covered, by the womb-membrane (ulbena, jarāyuṇā) — that which envelopes the embryo — so is this enveloped by that. (38)
BG_C03_V39: Knowledge is enveloped, O son of Kuntī, by this constant foe of the knower, in the form of desire, an insatiable fire. (39)
BG_C03_V39::block-0: Leading bhāṣya — But what is that, denoted by the word 'this' (idam), which is said to be enveloped by desire? —
BG_C03_V39::block-1: Knowledge is enveloped (āvṛtam) by this — by the constant foe (nitya-vairiṇā) of the knower (jñāninaḥ); for the man of knowledge knows from the very outset, 'I have been engaged in evil by this'; and he is unceasingly afflicted. Hence this one is the constant foe of the knower, but not so of the fool. For the fool, in the time of craving, sees desire as a friend, as it were; only when its consequence — pain — has come does he know,
BG_C03_V39::block-2: 'I have been brought to misery by craving' — and not before. Therefore it is the constant foe of the man of knowledge alone. In what form? In the form of desire (kāma-rūpeṇa) — desire whose form is craving (icchā), so 'kāma-rūpa,' by that. Insatiable (duṣpūreṇa) — its filling is by suffering (duḥkhena pūraṇam), hence duṣpūra. A fire (analena) — for it 'no sufficiency (alam) exists,' hence anala. (39)
BG_C03_V40: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat. Through these it deludes the embodied one by veiling his knowledge.
BG_C03_V40::block-0: Now, what is the seat of this kāma which, by acting as the veil over knowledge, has become the enemy of every being? In response to this expectation, the Lord speaks; for once the seat of the foe is known, the slaying of him can be accomplished with ease —
BG_C03_V40::block-1: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be the seat (adhiṣṭhāna), the resting-place (āśraya), of this kāma. By means of these — the senses and the rest, taken as its bases — this kāma deludes (vimohayati = mohayati in many ways) the embodied one (dehinam = the bearer of the body) by covering up (āvṛtya = ācchādya) his knowledge.
BG_C03_V41: Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, having first restrained the senses, slay this evil one — the destroyer of jñāna and vijñāna.
BG_C03_V41::block-1: Therefore (tasmāt), thou (tvam), O bull of the Bharatas (Bharatarṣabha), having at the very outset (ādau = pūrvam eva) restrained (niyamya = vaśīkṛtya) the senses, cast off (prajahihi = parityaja) this kāma — the perpetrator of sinful conduct (pāpmānam = pāpācāram), the very enemy that has been under discussion (enaṃ prakṛtaṃ vairiṇam) — the destroyer of jñāna and vijñāna. Here jñāna is the apprehension of the Self and the rest as taught by śāstra and the ācārya, while vijñāna is the particular, direct experience of that very same. Of these two — jñāna and vijñāna — which are the means to the attainment of the highest good, this kāma is the destroyer, the annihilator. Therefore cast it off; that is, banish it from oneself.
BG_C03_V42: They say the senses are higher; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; and that which is higher than the intellect is He.
BG_C03_V42::block-0: It has been stated, "Having first restrained the senses, slay this enemy kāma." Now, taking what as one's resort should one slay kāma? In answer to this it is said —
BG_C03_V42::block-1: The senses — the five beginning with the ear — relative to the body, which is gross, external and limited, are, in respect of being subtler, more inward and pervasive and so forth, declared by the wise to be higher (parāṇi = prakṛṣṭāni). Higher than the senses, likewise, is the mind, whose nature is saṅkalpa and vikalpa. Higher than the mind, again, is the intellect, whose nature is determination (niścaya). And that which, more inward than every object of perception culminating in the buddhi, the dehin (the bearer of the body), the one whom kāma — joined with the senses and the rest as its seats — has been said to delude by way of the veiling of knowledge — "and He is higher than the buddhi" — He is the witness (draṣṭā) of the buddhi, the supreme Self (para Ātman).
BG_C03_V43: Thus, having known that which is higher than the intellect, having steadied the self by the Self, slay, O mighty-armed one, the enemy in the form of kāma — hard to assail.
BG_C03_V43::block-1: Thus, having known (buddhvā = jñātvā) the Self that is higher than the buddhi, and having well steadied (saṃstabhya = samyak stambhanaṃ kṛtvā) the self (ātmānam) by the self itself (ātmanā) — that is, by the mind well refined, having well composed it in samādhi — slay (jahi) this enemy, O mighty-armed one (Mahābāho), this enemy in the form of kāma, the hard-to-assail (durāsadam) — that whose āśadana, that is, attainment, is achieved only with difficulty (duḥkhena āsadaḥ); thus durāsada, meaning marked by manifold particulars that are very hard to discern.
BG_C04_V01::block-0: This yoga which has been taught in the two preceding chapters, characterised by jñāna-niṣṭhā together with renunciation, having karma-yoga as its means, in which the meaning of the Veda has come to its consummation — both the meaning marked by pravṛtti and that marked by nivṛtti — and which alone is intended by the Bhagavān throughout the entire Gītā: regarding the meaning of the Veda as having reached its completion in this, Śrī Bhagavān now extols it by recounting the lineage in which it was handed down —
BG_C04_V01::block-1: This yoga that has been declared in the two chapters I myself proclaimed at the beginning of creation to Vivasvān, the sun, for the purpose of imparting strength to the kṣatriyas, the protectors of the world; endowed with that yoga-strength they become competent to safeguard the brahman (the priestly order and the Veda). When the brahman and the kṣatra are both well guarded, they are able to maintain the world. Imperishable (avyayam), because its fruit is imperishable; for the fruit of this yoga, characterised by ṣteadfastness in right vision, namely that which is called liberation, never decays. And that Vivasvān declared it to Manu. Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku, his own son, the foremost king.
BG_C04_V02: Thus received in succession, the royal sages knew this. By the lapse of long time, that yoga has been lost here, O scorcher of foes.
BG_C04_V02::block-0: Thus received through an unbroken succession of kṣatriyas, the rājarṣis — those who were both kings (rājānaḥ) and seers (ṛṣayaḥ) — knew this yoga. That yoga, by the lapse of long time here, has been lost — that is, has come to have its tradition (sampradāya) severed. "O Parantapa" — those who are hostile to oneself are termed "para"; he who, by the rays that are valour and splendour, scorches them as the sun scorches by its beams, is parantapa, that is, scorcher of foes.
BG_C04_V03: That very same ancient yoga has now been declared by Me to thee, since thou art My devotee and friend; for this is the supreme secret.
BG_C04_V03::block-0: Encountering men who are weak and have not conquered the senses, perceiving that this yoga has thereby been lost, and seeing the world as one no longer connected with the highest goal of man —
BG_C04_V03::block-1: That very same yoga, ancient as it is, has now been declared by Me to thee. Thou art My devotee and friend
BG_C04_V03::block-2: — and so on. "For this is supreme" — since this is the supreme secret, the meaning being: the yoga, that is, jñāna.
BG_C04_V04::block-0: Lest anyone form the notion that the Lord has uttered something self-contradictory, and as if raising an objection for the sake of removing such a thought, Arjuna said —
BG_C04_V04::block-1: Later (aparam = arvāk) — that is, recent — is Thy birth, here in the house of Vasudeva. Earlier (param = pūrvam) — at the very beginning of creation — is the birth, the coming forth, of Vivasvān the sun. How then am I to understand this without contradiction in meaning, namely that Thou Thyself, who didst at that beginning declare this yoga, art the very same who hast now declared it to me?
BG_C04_V05::block-0: In order to dispel the doubt of fools who suspect Vāsudeva of being non-īśvara and non-omniscient, the Blessed Lord spoke; for it is precisely with that aim that Arjuna's question was put —
BG_C04_V05::block-1: "Many" (bahūni) — past, gone by — births of mine (me) and of yours too, O Arjuna. All of them I (aham) know (vedmi); but you do not know (na tvaṁ vettha), because your power of knowledge stands obstructed by dharma, adharma and the rest. I, on the other hand, know them, since by my very nature I am eternally pure, awakened and free, and my power of knowledge is therefore unveiled — thus do I know, O scorcher of foes (parantapa).
BG_C04_V06: Though birthless, though of imperishable Self, though Lord of all beings, yet, presiding over my own primal nature, I come into being by my own māyā.
BG_C04_V06::block-0: How then, when you, the eternal Īśvara, are devoid of dharma and adharma, can there be birth for you? — to this it is replied:
BG_C04_V06::block-1: Though birthless (ajaḥ api), that is, although bereft of birth, and though of unwasting Self (avyayātmā) — that is, even though my essential nature is one of undiminishing power of knowledge — and though Lord (īśvaraḥ) of beings (bhūtānām), from Brahmā down to the tuft of grass, that is, though by nature one whose function is to rule, yet, taking my support upon my own primal nature (prakṛtim svām) — my Vaiṣṇavī māyā, made up of the three guṇas, under whose sway the entire world stands, deluded by which the world does not know its own Self, Vāsudeva — presiding over (adhiṣṭhāya), bringing under control, that primal nature of mine, I come into being (sambhavāmi), that is, I become as though embodied, as though born, by my own māyā (ātmamāyayā), the māyā that is mine — not really, as in the case of ordinary folk.
BG_C04_V07: Whenever, O Bhārata, there is a decline of dharma and an upsurge of adharma, then I send forth myself.
BG_C04_V07::block-0: And when, and for what purpose, that birth occurs is now told —
BG_C04_V07::block-1: Whenever, O Bhārata, there is a decline (glāniḥ) — that is, an impairment — of dharma, of that dharma whose mark is the system of varṇa, āśrama and the rest, which is the means of both worldly prosperity and supreme good for living beings, and there is an upsurge (abhyutthānam) — that is, a rising up — of adharma, then and then again I send forth (sṛjāmi) myself, by my māyā.
BG_C04_V08: For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evildoers, and for the firm establishing of dharma, I come into being age after age.
BG_C04_V08::block-1: For the protection (paritrāṇāya) — that is, for the safeguarding — of the good (sādhūnām), of those who stand on the right path; and for the destruction (vināśāya) of the evildoers (duṣkṛtām), the perpetrators of sin; and further, for the firm establishing of dharma (dharma-saṁsthāpana-arthāya) — that is, for the proper establishing of dharma — I come into being (sambhavāmi) age after age (yuge yuge), in every yuga.
BG_C04_V09: He who thus knows, in truth, my divine birth and action — he, having relinquished the body, comes not to a fresh birth; he comes to me, O Arjuna.
BG_C04_V09::block-1: Birth (janma), which is of the form of māyā, and action (karma), which is the protection of the good and the rest, that are mine (me), are divine (divyam) — that is, non-natural, pertaining to the Lord. He who in this manner, just as it has been declared, knows them in truth (tattvataḥ) — that is, exactly as they are — having relinquished (tyaktvā) this body (deham), does not come (na eti) to fresh birth, that is, does not attain re-arising; he comes (eti) to me (mām) — that is, he reaches me. He is liberated, O Arjuna.
BG_C04_V10: Freed from passion, fear and anger, absorbed in me, taking refuge in me, many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have come to my state of being.
BG_C04_V10::block-0: This path of liberation has not arisen only now; rather, even of old —
BG_C04_V10::block-1: Vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhāḥ — those from whom rāga (passion), bhaya (fear) and krodha (anger) have departed, have gone away — they are vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhāḥ. Manmayāḥ — knowers of Brahman, those who see no difference from the Lord. Mām eva ca — having taken refuge precisely in me, the Supreme Lord — that is, devoted solely to jñāna-niṣṭhā: such is the meaning. Bahavaḥ — many. Jñāna-tapasā — by jñāna itself, jñāna whose object is the supreme Self, which is therefore tapas — by that jñāna-tapas pūtāḥ, having attained supreme purity, they have come (āgatāḥ) — that is, fully arrived at — mad-bhāvam, the state of being of the Lord, that is, mokṣa. The qualifying word "jñāna-tapasā" is the mark indicating that this is jñāna-niṣṭhā independent of any other tapas.
BG_C04_V11: In whatever manner men resort to me, in just that manner I requite them; men follow my path, O Pārtha, in every way.
BG_C04_V11::block-0: But then, attachment and aversion exist in you, since it is to certain people only that you grant the state of being your Self, and not to all — to this it is replied:
BG_C04_V11::block-1: In whatever manner (ye yathā) — that is, by which mode, with what motive, with the desire for what fruit — they resort to (prapadyante) me, those very ones I requite (bhajāmi) — that is, I favour (anugṛhṇāmi) — in just that manner (tathā eva), namely by bestowing the corresponding fruit. This is the meaning. Because they have no desire for liberation. For one and the same person cannot at the same moment be a seeker of liberation and a desirer of fruit. Hence those who are seekers of fruit, them I favour by giving the fruit; those who act as enjoined and yet are non-fruit-seekers, that is, mumukṣus, them I favour by giving knowledge; those who are jñānins, sannyāsins, mumukṣus, them I favour by giving liberation; and the afflicted, by removing their affliction — thus, in whatever way they resort to me, even so do I requite them. This is the meaning. But never do I favour anyone out of attachment, aversion, or delusion. In every way, in every state, men follow the path (vartma), the road, of me, the Lord — those men, that is, who, with desire for some fruit, undertake some action for which they are eligible: such men are here referred to. O Pārtha, sarvaśaḥ — by every kind of mode.
BG_C04_V12: Desiring the fruition of works, men here worship the gods; for in the human world success born of action is swift.
BG_C04_V12::block-0: If, in your case as the Lord, since the defects of attachment and the rest are absent, your favour towards all beings is equal, and you are competent to bestow every kind of fruit, then why do not all, becoming mumukṣus, resort precisely to you alone with the knowledge "Vāsudeva is everything"? Hear the reason for that —
BG_C04_V12::block-1: Desiring (kāṅkṣantaḥ) — that is, longing for, praying for — the fruition of works (karmaṇāṁ siddhim), the ripening of fruit, men here, in this world, worship (yajante) the gods (devatāḥ), Indra, Agni and the rest; according to the śruti, "Now, he who worships another deity thinking 'He is one and I am another,' he does not know; he is like a beast for the gods" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10). For those who, sacrificing to various gods and seeking fruit, are such, swiftly (kṣipram) — that is, quickly — for the reason that the qualification for the śāstras lies precisely in the human world (mānuṣe loke), success comes about. By the qualifying "swiftly in the human world" the Lord intimates that the fruition of action takes place in other realms as well. The peculiarity of the human world is that the actions of varṇa-āśrama and the rest belong to it, and for those entitled to such varṇa-āśrama actions, the success comes about swiftly. Karmajā — born of action.
BG_C04_V13: The four-fold order of varṇas has been brought forth by Me through the distribution of guṇas and karmas. Though I am the agent of that, know Me as a non-agent, immutable.
BG_C04_V13::block-0: If the question be raised — by what reason is it laid down that adhikāra for the karmas of varṇa and āśrama belongs only to the human realm and not to other worlds? — or, alternatively, when it has been said (in the previous verse) that men endowed with the divisions of varṇa and āśrama follow My path in every way, why is the rule so specific that they follow Your path alone and not anyone else's? — to this it is replied:
BG_C04_V13::block-1:
The four-fold order — the four varṇas and nothing else — chāturvarṇyam mayā, by Me the Lord, sṛṣṭam, has been produced; this stands on the authority of the śruti 'brāhmaṇo'sya mukham āsīt' (Ṛg-Veda 10.8.91) and the like. guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ — by the distribution of guṇas and by the distribution of karmas. The guṇas are sattva, rajas, and tamas. Among these, for the brāhmaṇa who is sāttvika, in whom sattva predominates, the karmas are 'śamo damas tapaḥ' (Bhagavad-Gītā 18.42) and the rest; for the kṣatriya in whom rajas predominates with sattva subordinate, the karmas are valour, splendour and so on; for the vaiśya in whom rajas predominates with tamas subordinate, the karmas are agriculture and the like; for the śūdra in whom tamas predominates with rajas subordinate, the karma is service alone — thus by this distribution of guṇas and karmas the four-fold order has been brought forth by Me. This is the meaning. And this four-fold order does not exist in other worlds; hence the qualification 'in the human realm.'

Then surely, since You are the agent of the karma of producing the four-fold order and so on, You become connected with its fruit; therefore You are not eternally liberated, nor the eternal Lord. To this it is replied: although in the dealings carried on through māyā I am indeed the agent of that karma, in the highest sense know Me as a non-agent. Precisely on this account, know Me also as immutable, as not subject to saṁsāra.
BG_C04_V14: Karmas do not stain Me; nor do I have any longing for the fruit of karma. He who knows Me thus is not bound by karmas.
BG_C04_V14::block-0: But of those karmas of which you take Me to be the agent in the highest sense — of those I am verily the non-agent, since:
BG_C04_V14::block-1: Those karmas do not, lipanti, stain Me by way of being initiators of body and the like, because of the absence of ahaṅkāra. Nor have I, in regard to the fruits of those karmas, spṛhā — thirst. As to those saṁsārins who have the conceit 'I am the agent' towards the karmas, and the longing for their fruits — concerning them it is fitting to say that the karmas stain them; since this conceit is absent in Me, karmas do not stain Me. Thus also any other person who recognizes Me as identical with the Self, knowing 'I am not the agent, I have no longing for the fruit of karma' — saḥ, he, karmabhiḥ na badhyate, is not bound by karmas; for him too karmas which initiate body and the rest do not arise. This is the meaning.
BG_C04_V15: Karma was performed even by the ancients who sought liberation, knowing thus. Therefore do you also do karma alone, just as the ancients did in earlier times.
BG_C04_V15::block-0: Knowing thus, that 'I am not the agent, I have no longing for the fruit of karma' —
BG_C04_V15::block-1: Karma — knowing thus — was performed by the ancients also, by those mumukṣus who passed away long ago. Therefore do you, kuru, perform karma alone; one is not to remain silent, nor is renunciation to be undertaken — for the very reason that it has been practised even by the ancients. If you are not a knower of the Self, then karma is for the purpose of self-purification (sattva-śuddhi); if, however, you are one who knows the truth, then it is for the sake of loka-saṅgraha. As was performed pūrvataram, in earlier times, by the ancients such as Janaka and the rest — not in the manner now newly fabricated.
BG_C04_V16: What is karma, what is akarma — over this even the wise have been deluded. That karma I shall declare to thee, knowing which thou shalt be released from the inauspicious.
BG_C04_V16::block-0: Now (one might object): if karma is to be done, I shall do it merely on Your word; what is the need of qualifying it as 'pūrvaiḥ pūrvataraṁ kṛtam' — 'as performed by the ancients in earlier times'? Because there is great unevenness with respect to karma. How? —
BG_C04_V16::block-1: kim karma kim ca akarma iti — 'what is karma and what is akarma' — kavayaḥ, the wise, the discerning, api, even they, atra, here in this matter of karma and the rest, mohitāḥ, have come into delusion. Therefore te, to you, I, aham, shall declare karma and akarma, knowing which — having understood karma and the rest — you shall be released, mokṣyase, from aśubha, from saṁsāra.
BG_C04_V17: For one must understand the nature of karma, one must understand also the nature of vikarma, and one must understand the nature of akarma; impenetrable is the way of karma.
BG_C04_V17::block-0: Nor should you think this — 'karma is the activity of the body and so forth, well known in the world; akarma is the cessation of that, sitting silently; what is there to be understood in this?' Why not? It is replied:
BG_C04_V17::block-1: karmaṇaḥ — of karma, that is, of what is enjoined by the śāstra — hi api, indeed, asti boddhavyam, there is something to be understood; and likewise there exists something to be understood viṣakarmaṇaḥ, of vikarma, of what is forbidden; and so too akarmaṇaḥ ca, of akarma, of remaining silent (tūṣṇīm-bhāva), there is something to be understood. Thus the supplementary phrase 'must be understood' has to be carried over to all three. Because gahanā, deep, uneven, hard to know — 'karmaṇaḥ' here functioning by upalakṣaṇa to denote karma and the rest — is the gatiḥ, the true nature, the tattva, of karma, akarma, and vikarma. This is the meaning.
BG_C04_V18: He who sees akarma in karma, and karma in akarma — he is the wise one among men; he is the yogin, the doer of all karma in its entirety.
BG_C04_V18::block-0: What then is the truth of karma and the rest, which You promised to declare must be understood? It is said:
BG_C04_V18::block-1:
karmaṇi — karma being mere activity, that which is done — in that very karma, akarma, the absence of karma, who would see; and akarmaṇi, in the absence of karma — since pravṛtti and nivṛtti depend upon an agent, and it is solely on the ground of avidyā that the entire activity of action, instrument, and the like proceeds without ever attaining the (real) thing — who would see, paśyet, karma, action: he is buddhimān, the wise, among men; he, saḥ, is yuktaḥ, the yogin, and saḥ, kṛtsna-karma-kṛt, the doer of all karma in its entirety. Thus the seer of the mutual interpenetration of karma and akarma is praised.

Well — is not this a contradiction that is being uttered, 'who would see akarma in karma' and 'karma in akarma'? For karma cannot be akarma, nor can akarma be karma. How then would the seer see the contradictory? — No: in truth it is akarma alone, being existent, that appears as if karma to the deluded vision of the world; and likewise it is karma itself that appears like akarma. Therefore, in order to bring about the seeing of things as they really are, the Lord says, 'who sees akarma in karma' and so on. Hence there is no contradiction. And this is borne out by the appropriateness of one's being called wise and so forth. The word 'boddhavyam' (4.17) speaks of seeing as it really is. And from a perverse cognition there cannot be release from the inauspicious; whereas it has been said, 'knowing which you shall be released from the inauspicious' (4.16). Therefore karma and akarma have been grasped by living beings under reverse aspects, and to remove that reverse grasp the Lord's words 'karmaṇi akarma yaḥ' and the rest are uttered. Nor is there in this case akarma residing in karma as a substratum, the way jujube fruits lie in a basin; nor is there karma residing in akarma as a substratum, since akarma is the very absence of karma. Hence it is only by the lokic minds that karma and akarma are reversely grasped, just as water is grasped in a mirage or silver in mother-of-pearl. Well — is not karma simply karma to all, never deviating from itself anywhere? — No: from the fact that for one in a moving boat, mountains on the bank, themselves motionless, are seen to move in the contrary direction; and that for distant objects not directly close to the eye, while moving, an absence of motion is seen — even so here, the seeing of karma in akarma, and of akarma in karma, is reverse seeing; in order to refute that, it is said, 'who sees akarma in karma' and so on.

This very reply, though uttered repeatedly, is not retained, for the world being thoroughly steeped in extreme reverse vision is again and again deluded; having heard the truth more than once, it forgets and forgets, and, repeatedly bringing in the false issue, raises objections; therefore the Lord answers again and again, observing also the difficulty of cognition concerning the reality. By 'avyaktaḥ ayaṁ acintyaḥ ayam' (Bhagavad-Gītā 2.25), 'na jāyate mriyate' (Bhagavad-Gītā 2.20) and so on, the absence of karma in the Self has been stated and will be stated, established by śruti, smṛti, and reasoning. In that Self, where karma is absent, the reverse seeing of karma in akarma is utterly entrenched; whence, 'kim karma kim akarma iti kavayo'py atra mohitāḥ' (Bhagavad-Gītā 4.16). Superimposing on the Self karma which has the body and so on as its support — saying 'I am the agent, this karma is mine, by me the fruit of this karma is to be enjoyed,' and again, 'I shall remain silent so that I may be effortless, free of karma, happy,' — and superimposing on the Self the cessation of activity which has the bodily organism as its support, together with the happiness arising from it, the world fancies, 'I do nothing, I sit silent and happy.' To remove this perverse seeing of the world, the Lord says, 'who sees akarma in karma' and the rest.

And here karma, being only karma, having the bodily organism as its support, is by all superimposed on the karma-less, immutable Self; whence even the learned think, 'I do.' Hence in karma, well known to the entire world as inhering in the Self, just as motion in trees on a riverbank in the contrary direction, who sees akarma — the absence of karma — as it really is, like the absence of motion in trees; and in akarma — the cessation of activity of the bodily organism, when it has been superimposed on the Self as karma, since that very 'sitting silent without doing, I rest happy' is the cause of the egoistic resolve — in that akarma, who sees karma; whoever knows in this way the distinction of karma and akarma — saḥ buddhimān, he is the wise, the learned, among men; saḥ yuktaḥ, he is the yogin and the doer of all karma in its entirety; he, released from the inauspicious, becomes one whose work is done. This is the meaning.

This verse has been explained otherwise by some. How? The nityakarmas, when performed for the sake of the Lord, have, it is said, no fruit; therefore they are called akarma by a secondary usage. And the non-performance of these is akarma; that, since it bears the fruit of demerit, is called karma — again by a secondary usage. Thus, in nitya-karma, who would see akarma — that is, by reason of absence of fruit, just as a cow that does not yield milk is called 'no cow'; and likewise, in the non-performance of the nitya — namely, in akarma — who would see karma, since it yields the fruit of hell and the like.

This explanation is not proper. Because by such knowledge release from the inauspicious would not be possible, and the Lord's statement 'knowing which you shall be released from the inauspicious' (4.16) would be contradicted. How? Release from the inauspicious might come from the performance of the nityas, but not from knowing their fruitlessness. The knowledge of the fruitlessness of the nityas has nowhere been enjoined as having release from the inauspicious as its fruit, nor has knowledge of the nitya-karma; nor has it been so stated by the Lord here. By this also, the seeing of karma in akarma is rebutted: for here the seeing of 'karma' in akarma is not enjoined as something to be done — only the duty of doing the nitya. Nor would any fruit accrue from the cognition that 'from the omission of the nitya there arises demerit.' Nor has the omission of the nitya been enjoined as something to be known. Nor from the false cognition 'karma is akarma' would release from the inauspicious, the state of being wise, the state of being yoked, the doership of all karma and the like, accrue as fruit; nor would the praise be applicable. False knowledge itself is directly the inauspicious form. Whence release from another, distinct, inauspicious? For darkness is not the dispeller of darkness.

Well, the seeing of akarma in karma, or of karma in akarma, is not false knowledge; what then? — it is secondary, occasioned by the absence and presence of fruit — No: because from this secondary cognition of karma and akarma also, no fruit is heard of in scripture. Nor in such abandonment of what is heard and fabrication of what is unheard is any distinction perceived. By a direct word too it could have been said: 'the nitya-karmas have no fruit, and from non-performance of them there will be falling into hell.' What then is the use of the device having the form of misleading another, 'karmaṇi akarma yaḥ paśyet' and so on? In that case the Lord's utterance, on this such explanation, would clearly turn out to be a contrivance for the deluding of the world. And this is not a thing to be guarded by an utterance of the form of disguise; nor would it become well understood by being uttered repeatedly in different words — to say so is not fitting. In 'karmaṇi eva adhikāras te' (Bhagavad-Gītā 2.47) the meaning has been declared with great clarity; it does not need to be restated. And everywhere what is praiseworthy and to be understood is precisely what is to be done; nothing useless is enjoined to be understood.

Nor is false knowledge a thing to be understood; nor is the appearance of an object presented by it. Nor, from the omission — the non-being — of the nityas does there arise a being of demerit; for by the saying 'nāsato vidyate bhāvaḥ' (Bhagavad-Gītā 2.16) and 'kathaṁ asataḥ saj jāyeta' (Chāndogya-Upaniṣad 6.2.2) it has been shown that the production of the existent from the non-existent is denied. One who maintains the production of the existent from the non-existent must be saying that what is non-existent itself becomes existent, and what is existent likewise becomes non-existent; and that is improper, being contrary to all means of knowledge. Nor would the śāstra enjoin a fruitless karma, since it is of the nature of pain, and pain, when intentional, cannot fittingly be a thing to be performed; and from accepting that there is hell-falling on its non-performance, harm follows in either case — both in performance and in non-performance — and the śāstra would turn out to be made fruitless. There is also contradiction with one's own admission: having accepted 'the nitya is fruitless karma,' to say 'for the fruit of mokṣa.' Therefore the meaning is just as it is heard from 'karmaṇi akarma yaḥ' onwards. And so the verse has been explained by us.
BG_C04_V19: He whose every undertaking is devoid of desire and resolve, whose karmas are burnt by the fire of knowledge — him the wise call a paṇḍita.
BG_C04_V19::block-0: Now this very seeing of akarma in karma is praised:
BG_C04_V19::block-1: yasya — of him, of one having the seeing as stated — sarve, all, however many, samārambhāḥ, undertakings — that which is begun is samārambha, hence all karmas — are kāma-saṅkalpa-varjitāḥ, devoid of desires and the resolves which are their cause; they are simply performed as mere outward exertions; if he is among the engaged (pravṛtta), it is for the sake of loka-saṅgraha; if among the withdrawn (nivṛtta), it is for the sake of mere maintenance of life. Him — jñānāgni-dagdha-karmāṇam — the seeing of akarma and the rest in karma and the rest is jñāna; that very thing is fire; he whose karmas marked as auspicious or inauspicious have been burnt by that fire of knowledge — him, in the highest sense, paṇḍitam, learned, the budhas, knowers of Brahman, āhuḥ, declare him to be.
BG_C04_V20: Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of karma, ever content, dependent on nothing, even when engaged in karma he does nothing whatever.
BG_C04_V20::block-0: But he who is the seer of akarma and the rest, by the very fact of seeing akarma and the rest becomes one without karma, a saṁnyāsin, exerting himself only for the sake of life's maintenance, and does not engage in karma — even though, prior to discrimination, he was engaged. The one who is one of prārabdha-karma, however, and in whom afterwards there arises perfect Self-cognition, seeing no purpose in any karma, abandons even the karma along with its instruments. When, due to some occasion, abandonment of karma is impossible, then, being unattached to that karma and to its fruit, having no purpose of his own, he engages in karma as before for the sake of loka-saṅgraha, and yet does nothing at all; his karma, since his karma is burnt by the fire of knowledge, becomes nothing but akarma. To bring out this point He says:
BG_C04_V20::block-1: tyaktvā, having abandoned, conceit in karmas and attachment to fruit, by the said knowledge, nitya-tṛptaḥ, ever content, niranākāṅkṣaḥ, free from craving with regard to objects — this is the meaning. niraśrayaḥ, dependent on nothing — āśraya, namely, that on dependence upon which one wishes to accomplish the human end; free from any support of the means of bringing about a desired fruit visible or invisible — this is the meaning. The karma performed by the wise is, in the highest sense, only akarma, since he is endowed with the seeing of the actionless Self. Therefore, when in such a one, since he has no personal purpose, the karma along with its instruments would seem proper to be abandoned, then, since departure from karma is not possible, with the desire to make loka-saṅgraha or with the desire to avoid being censured by the cultivated, he, although engaged in karma as before, since he is endowed with the seeing of the actionless Self, does nothing at all.
BG_C04_V21: Free of expectation, with mind and self restrained, having relinquished every possession, performing only bodily action, he incurs no taint. (21)
BG_C04_V21::block-0: But the man who is the opposite of the one previously described — in whom, even before the undertaking of action, the vision of the Self has arisen with respect to Brahman, the inmost Self of all, which is actionless — being thus wholly devoid of any longing for objects, seen or unseen, and seeing no purpose in action aimed at seen or unseen ends, renounces action together with its accessories. As an ascetic (yati), whose activity is restricted to mere bodily maintenance, established in knowledge (jñāna-niṣṭha), he becomes liberated. To set forth this very meaning the Lord proceeds —
BG_C04_V21::block-1: Nirāśīḥ — he from whom expectations (āśiṣaḥ) have departed (nirgatāḥ) is nirāśīḥ. Yata-citta-ātmā — citta is the inner organ; ātman here is the outer aggregate of the body and senses; the one by whom both these are restrained (yatau saṃyatau) is yata-citta-ātmā. Tyakta-sarva-parigrahaḥ — he by whom every possession (parigraha) has been relinquished. Śārīram — that whose sole purpose is the maintenance of the body. Kevalam — and even there, devoid of the conceit "I do." Performing such action, he does not attain (na āpnoti) kilbiṣa, that is, undesirable form — both demerit (pāpa) and merit (dharma). Even merit (dharma) is, for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), nothing but kilbiṣa, since it too brings about bondage. Hence he becomes free from both, that is, freed from saṃsāra — this is the meaning.
BG_C04_V21::block-2:
Objection: Concerning the phrase "performing only śārīra (bodily) action," what is meant by śārīra karma — is it action accomplished by the body (śarīra-nirvartya), or is it action whose sole purpose is bodily maintenance (śarīra-sthiti-mātra-prayojana)? And what difference does it make whether it is the one or the other?

Reply: Were śārīra to mean "action done by the body," then the saying "performing with the body action which has seen or unseen ends, even when prohibited, he incurs no taint" would amount to a self-contradiction; and likewise, were one to say "performing with the body any scriptural action of seen or unseen purpose, he incurs no taint," one would be prohibiting what was never enjoined as wrong. Moreover, by the qualification "performing śārīra action" together with the use of the word kevala (only), it would be implied that one performing action accomplished by speech and mind — action falling within injunction or prohibition, designable as dharma or adharma — does incur the taint. There again, on the alternative that what is performed by speech and mind is enjoined practice, the statement that taint is incurred would itself become contradictory; and on the alternative that it is the indulgence in what is prohibited, it would be a mere restatement of the obvious, hence pointless.

But when śārīra karma is taken to mean action whose sole purpose is the maintenance of the body, then — refraining from any other action of seen or unseen aim, falling within injunction or prohibition, accomplished by body, speech, or mind, and performing through these very same body, etc., only what serves bodily maintenance, and that too (because of the word kevala) shorn of the conceit "I do," merely going through bodily motions in the eyes of the world — he does not attain kilbiṣa. For one of this nature, the attainment of what is properly called pāpa being impossible, he does not attain kilbiṣa in the sense of saṃsāra; rather, since all his karmas are burnt up in the fire of knowledge, he is, without any obstruction whatsoever, simply liberated. This is no more than the restatement of the fruit of right vision (samyag-darśana) already declared. Thus, on this construal of "performing only śārīra action," the verse stands free of objection. (21)
BG_C04_V22: Content with whatever comes unsought, transcending the pairs of opposites, free from envy, even-minded in success and failure — though acting, he is not bound. (22)
BG_C04_V22::block-0: Since the ascetic who has relinquished every possession lacks even food and the like — the means of bodily maintenance — and would consequently be obliged to keep up the body by begging and similar means, the Lord, displaying the door through which food etc. for the maintenance of the ascetic's body is sanctioned by the text "Whatever, unsolicited, unprepared, comes by chance" (Aśv. 46.19) and so on, says —
BG_C04_V22::block-1: Yadṛcchā-lābha-santuṣṭaḥ — yadṛcchā-lābha is gain unasked-for that comes of itself; content (sañjāta-alaṃ-pratyaya — feeling "that suffices") with such gain. Dvandva-atītaḥ — though smitten by the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, he whose mind does not become depressed is called dvandva-atīta. Vimatsaraḥ — vigata-matsara, of mind devoid of enmity. Samaḥ — equal, the same, in the obtaining and not obtaining of what comes by chance. Such an ascetic, equal in gain and loss of food etc. — the means of bodily maintenance — devoid of joy and sorrow, who in respect of action and the like sees actionlessness and is established in seeing the Self as it truly is, while engaged in begging-rounds and the like — actions of which the sole purpose is the maintenance of the body and which are accomplished by the body and so on — constantly reflects, "I do nothing whatever" (Bh. Gītā 5.8) and "the guṇas operate among the guṇas" (Bh. Gītā 3.28), and seeing thus the absence of agency in the Self, performs no begging-round or other action whatever; only by the common perception of worldly conduct is he, in begging-rounds etc., made into an agent through agency superimposed by people. By his own experience, however, born of scriptural authority and the like, he is the non-agent alone. He, having had agency thus superimposed on him by others, even when he performs begging-rounds and other action whose sole purpose is the maintenance of the body, is not bound; for the karma which is the cause of bondage, together with its causes, has been burnt up in the fire of knowledge. Hence this too is but a restatement of what has been already declared. (22)
BG_C04_V23: For one whose attachments have departed, who is liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, who acts for the sake of sacrifice — his action, in its entirety, dissolves away. (23)
BG_C04_V23::block-0: By the verse "Having relinquished attachment to the fruits of action" (Bh. Gītā 4.20), it has been shown that one who, while engaged in works already commenced (prārabdha-karman), comes to possess the vision of the Self as the actionless Brahman, perceives in the Self the absence of agent, action, and purpose; hence the renunciation of action would naturally follow. But when, on account of some cause, that renunciation is not feasible, and he continues, as before, engaged in that very action, still — "He does nothing whatever" (Bh. Gītā 4.20) — the absence of action has been pointed out. Of him alone, in whom the absence of action has thus been shown —
BG_C04_V23::block-1: Gata-saṅgasya — of him whose attachment has wholly ceased on every side. Muktasya — of him from whom the bondage of dharma, adharma and the rest has departed. Jñāna-avasthita-cetasaḥ — he whose cetas (mind) is established (avasthita) in knowledge (jñāna) alone is jñāna-avasthita-cetāḥ; of such a one. Yajñāya — for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice. Ācarataḥ — of him who carries it out. Karma samagram — "samagra" because it stands together (sam-) with its tip (agra), namely the fruit; such karma in its entirety. Pravilīyate — vanishes; this is the meaning. (23)
BG_C04_V24: Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation; into the fire of Brahman, by Brahman, is the oblation poured. Brahman alone is to be reached by him whose absorption is in Brahman as the act. (24)
BG_C04_V24::block-0: But for what reason is it said that the action being performed, not initiating any effect of its own, dissolves entirely? Because —
BG_C04_V24::block-1: Brahma arpaṇam — the instrument by means of which the knower of Brahman pours the oblation into the fire — that he sees as Brahman alone; he sees no existence in it apart from the Self, just as on the mother-of-pearl one sees the absence of silver. This is what is meant by "Brahman alone is the arpaṇa" — just as that which is the silver is the mother-of-pearl alone. "Brahma arpaṇam" is here a non-compounded pair of words. What in the world is taken with the notion "this is the offering-instrument" — that, for this knower of Brahman, is Brahman alone: such is the meaning. Brahma haviḥ — likewise, what is taken with the notion of haviḥ is also for him Brahman alone. So too "Brahma-agnau" is a compounded word: even the fire wherein the offering is made is itself Brahman, the agent (kartṛ) being Brahman; that is, Brahman alone is the agent. Whatever is offered (hutam) by him — the very act of offering — is Brahman alone. And what is to be reached by him as fruit, that too is Brahman alone — by him whose samādhi is brahma-karma, that is, the very karma is Brahman, on which his samādhi is fixed; by such a one, possessed of brahma-karma-samādhi, Brahman alone is to be attained.
BG_C04_V24::block-2: Thus, the action performed by him too — even though he undertakes it with a view to setting an example to the world (loka-saṅgraha) — is, in truth, no action at all, since the conception of it as karma is wholly dissolved by the conception of Brahman. This being so, even for the renouncer of all karma, who has ceased from action, the construing of (his) jñāna as a yajña — for the purpose of extolling samyag-darśana — becomes very fitting; for whatever arpaṇa and the rest is well-known on the adhi-yajña side, that, for one who sees the supreme truth, is, on the adhyātma side, Brahman alone. Otherwise, when all is Brahman, the special declaration that arpaṇa and the rest in particular are Brahman would be meaningless. Hence, for the wise man who recognises "this all is Brahman alone," there is the absence of karma. And because the conception of karaka (the agency-categories) is also absent. For nowhere is the action called yajña ever observed devoid of the conception of the kārakas: every karma whatever — the agnihotra and the rest — is observed as informed by the conceptions of the particular deities offered to (sampradāna) and the other kārakas as designated by the Vedic word, accompanied by the agent's conceit and the longing for fruit; never as devoid of the conception of the differentiation of action, kārakas and fruit, devoid of the agent's conceit, and devoid of longing for fruit. But this karma here is one in which the conception of the differentiation of arpaṇa and the rest of the kārakas, the action and the fruit, is dissolved by the brahma-buddhi. Therefore it is just non-action. And so it has been shown by "He who sees actionlessness in action" (Bh. Gītā 4.18), "Even though engaged in action, he does nothing at all" (Bh. Gītā 4.20), "The guṇas operate upon the guṇas" (Bh. Gītā 3.28), "The knower of truth, equipped (in yoga), should think 'I do nothing at all'" (Bh. Gītā 5.8), and so on. While so showing, in place after place, he effects the dissolution of the conception of the differentiation of action, kārakas and fruit. And it is observed that in the kāmya agnihotra and the like, by the dissolution of the desire (kāma), the kāmya agnihotra and the rest themselves cease to be. So too the productive efficacy of intentional and unintentional acts is observed only with reference to a particular result. Likewise here also, where the conception of the differentiation of arpaṇa and the rest of the kārakas, action and fruit is dissolved by the brahma-buddhi, the karma of the wise man, by mere outer motion, becomes non-karma. Hence it has been said "It is dissolved entirely" (Bh. Gītā 4.20).
BG_C04_V24::block-3: Objection: Some here say — what is Brahman, that is the arpaṇa and the rest. Brahman alone, indeed, established as the fivefold kāraka in the form of arpaṇa and so on, performs that very karma. There the conception of arpaṇa and the rest is not removed; rather, the conception of Brahman is superimposed upon arpaṇa and the rest — as the conception of Viṣṇu and the like is superimposed upon an image, or as the conception of Brahman is placed upon the syllable, the name and the like.
BG_C04_V24::block-4: Reply: True, this would be so were it not that this section is for the praise of the jñāna-yajña. Here, however, samyag-darśana is termed jñāna-yajña; and after introducing several special activities styled yajña, He extols knowledge with "Better than the sacrifice of substance is the sacrifice of knowledge" (Bh. Gītā 4.33). Here too the present passage "Brahmārpaṇam" and the rest is competent to constitute knowledge as a yajña; otherwise, when all is Brahman, the special declaration that arpaṇa and the rest in particular are Brahman would be meaningless. As for those who say that on arpaṇa and the rest the conception of Brahman is to be projected, like the conception of Viṣṇu on an image, or like the conception of Brahman on syllable, name and the like — by them no brahma-vidyā is being intended here, but only knowledge having arpaṇa and the rest for its sphere. And by the knowledge that consists of mere superimposition of a (different) view, the fruit of liberation is not attained, whereas it is said "Brahman alone is to be reached by him." That through such (mere superimposition) the fruit of liberation should be attained, without samyag-darśana, is contradictory. There is also contradiction with the prakaraṇa: the topic at hand is samyag-darśana — at "He who sees actionlessness in action" (Bh. Gītā 4.18) — and at the close also samyag-darśana, since the conclusion is of that itself. The chapter, with "Better than the sacrifice of substance is the sacrifice of knowledge" (Bh. Gītā 4.33), "Having attained knowledge, he attains supreme peace" (Bh. Gītā 4.39) and so on, is occupied entirely with the praise of samyag-darśana, and so culminates. To suddenly speak there, out of context, of a brahma-dṛṣṭi superimposed upon arpaṇa etc. — like the viṣṇu-dṛṣṭi on an image — is unwarranted. Hence the meaning of this verse is just as has been expounded. (24)
BG_C04_V25: Some yogins assiduously perform sacrifice to the gods. Others, in the fire of Brahman, offer the sacrifice itself by the sacrifice. (25)
BG_C04_V25::block-0: There, having now constituted samyag-darśana as a yajña, in order to praise it, other yajñas as well are introduced —
BG_C04_V25::block-1: Daivam eva — the sacrifice by which the gods (devāḥ) are worshipped is the daiva yajña; that very yajña some others, the yogins — namely the karmins — paryupāsate, that is, perform: such is the meaning. Brahma-agnau — by Brahman is here meant that which is set forth in such texts as "Truth, knowledge, infinite is Brahman" (Tait. Up. 2.1.1), "Knowledge, bliss is Brahman," "That which is direct, immediate, Brahman, the Self that is inmost in all" (Bṛ. Up. 3.4.1) — devoid of every saṃsāric attribute such as hunger and the like, with all particularity wholly negated by "not this, not this" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22). And that very Brahman, with a view to designating it as the locus of the homa, is called Brahma-agni. In that Brahma-agni some others, the knowers of Brahman, offer the yajña — the Self designated by the word yajña, since the word yajña is listed among the names of the Self — that is, that very Self which is yajña, in truth nothing other than the supreme Brahman, but conjoined with the limiting adjuncts of buddhi etc. and bearing all the superimposed attributes of the upādhis, in the form of the oblation, by means of yajña — by the Self alone, of the character described, they offer up (upajuhvati), that is, cast in. The realisation of the Self that is conjoined with upādhis as nothing but the supreme Brahman, the upādhi-less, is itself the homa upon It. The renouncers (sannyāsins), established in seeing the oneness of Brahman and the Self, perform that homa: such is the meaning. (25)
BG_C04_V26: Some offer the senses, beginning with hearing, into the fires of restraint; others offer the objects, beginning with sound, into the fires of the senses. (26)
BG_C04_V26::block-0: This very yajña, characterised as samyag-darśana, is being introduced among the daiva-yajña and other yajñas; commenced by the verses beginning "Brahmārpaṇam," it is for the sake of praise, by such words as "Better than the sacrifice of substance is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes" (Bh. Gītā 4.33) —
BG_C04_V26::block-1: Śrotrādīni — the senses beginning with hearing — these other yogins (offer) into the fires of restraint (saṃyama-agni). Because restraint differs with each sense, the plural is used. The restraints themselves are the fires; into them they offer (juhvati) — that is, they merely effect the restraint of the senses: such is the meaning. Śabdādīn viṣayān — others (offer) the objects, beginning with sound, into the fires of the senses; the senses themselves are fires, and into those sense-fires they offer; they regard the apprehension of objects, not contrary (to scripture), through hearing and the rest, as a homa. (26)
BG_C04_V27: Others again offer all the activities of the senses and the activities of the prāṇa into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge. (27)
BG_C04_V27::block-1: Sarvāṇi indriya-karmāṇi — all the activities of the senses (indriya-karmāṇi); likewise prāṇa-karmāṇi — prāṇa is the inner (ādhyātmika) breath; its actions are contraction, expansion and the like; these too others offer into ātma-saṃyama-yoga-agni — restraint with respect to the Self is ātma-saṃyama; that very ātma-saṃyama is the fire of yoga; into that ātma-saṃyama-yoga-agni they offer, that is, cast in. Jñāna-dīpite — into one inflamed, as a lamp by oil, with brightness produced by the discriminative knowledge (viveka-vijñāna); into such a fire they offer — that is, they cause to dissolve away: such is the meaning. (27)
BG_C04_V28: Others, again, are sacrificers by substance, sacrificers by austerity, sacrificers by yoga; and likewise sacrificers by recitation and by knowledge — ascetics, of vows keenly sharpened. (28)
BG_C04_V28::block-0: Dravya-yajñāḥ — those who, at sacred fords (tīrthas), apply substance with the conception of yajña, are dravya-yajñas. Tapo-yajñāḥ — those tapasvins whose yajña is tapas are tapo-yajñas. Yoga-yajñāḥ — those whose yajña is yoga, characterised by prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra and the rest, are yoga-yajñas. Likewise others — svādhyāya-jñāna-yajñāḥ: those whose yajña is svādhyāya — recitation of the Ṛk and the rest, according to rule — are svādhyāya-yajñas. Jñāna-yajñāḥ — those whose yajña is jñāna, the thorough understanding of the meaning of the śāstra, are jñāna-yajñas. And these are yatayaḥ — striving by nature; saṃśita-vratāḥ — those whose vows are saṃyak śitāni, well sharpened, made fine, made keen, are saṃśita-vratas. (28)
BG_C04_V29: Others offer the prāṇa (out-breath) as oblation into the apāna (in-breath), and likewise others offer the apāna into the prāṇa; restraining the courses of prāṇa and apāna, they are wholly devoted to prāṇāyāma. (29)
BG_C04_V29::block-1: Into the apāna — that is, into the function of the apāna — they offer, that is, cast, the prāṇa, the function of the prāṇa: the meaning is that they perform the prāṇāyāma known as pūraka (filling-in inhalation). And others, in like manner, offer the apāna into the prāṇa: that is, they perform the prāṇāyāma known as recaka (exhalation). The courses of prāṇa and apāna — the going-out of the wind through the mouth and nostrils is the course of the prāṇa, and the contrary downward going is the course of the apāna; restraining, that is, completely arresting, these two courses of prāṇa and apāna, they are wholly devoted to prāṇāyāma, intent upon prāṇāyāma — meaning that they perform the prāṇāyāma known as kumbhaka (retention). (29)
BG_C04_V30: Others, of regulated diet, offer the prāṇas into the prāṇas. All these too are knowers of sacrifice, whose stains have been consumed by sacrifice. (30)
BG_C04_V30::block-1: Others, of regulated diet — those whose food (āhāra) is regulated, that is, measured (parimita), are called niyatāhārāḥ — being so, offer the prāṇas, that is, the various forms of vital air, into the prāṇas themselves: when the conquest (jaya) of any one of the airs is being effected, they offer the other vital airs into that one, and these become as it were merged (praviṣṭa) within it. All these too are knowers of sacrifice, whose stains have been consumed by sacrifice — they are those whose stain (kalmaṣa) has been worn away, that is, destroyed, by the sacrifices set forth above; therefore they are called yajñakṣapitakalmaṣāḥ. (30)
BG_C04_V31: Those who feed on the nectar that remains from the sacrifice attain the eternal Brahman. This world is not for him who performs no sacrifice — how then any other, O best of the Kurus? (31)
BG_C04_V31::block-0: Thus, having accomplished the sacrifices set forth above —
BG_C04_V31::block-1: Yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujaḥ — what is left over (śiṣṭa) of the sacrifices is yajñaśiṣṭa; that yajñaśiṣṭa is itself the nectar (amṛta), hence yajñaśiṣṭāmṛta; those who eat (bhuñjate) that are yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujaḥ. Having performed the sacrifices set forth above, they eat in the time remaining thereafter the food enjoined by rule, called amṛta — therefore they are yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujaḥ. They go, that is, attain, the eternal (sanātana) — the ancient — Brahman, provided they are seekers of liberation; this is gathered by implication, taking into account the lapse of time (i.e. crama-mukti, gradual liberation). For him who performs no sacrifice — he who has not even one of the sacrifices set forth above is the ayajña — there is not even this world, common though it be to all living beings; how then any other (loka), attainable only by some special means, O best of the Kurus? (31)
BG_C04_V32: Thus manifold are the sacrifices spread out at the mouth of Brahman (the Veda). Know them all to be born of action; knowing thus, you shall be liberated. (32)
BG_C04_V32::block-0: Thus the manifold sacrifices set forth above, of many kinds, are spread out (vitata) — extended — at the mouth of Brahman: of the Veda, that is, at its door (dvāra); being made known through the door of the Veda, they are said to be spread out at the mouth of Brahman. Such, for instance, are passages like 'Into speech, indeed, we offer the prāṇa' (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.2.6), and the rest. Born of action — arising from bodily, vocal, and mental action — know them all to be such, and not born of the Self (anātmajān); for the Self is actionless (nirvyāpāra). Therefore, knowing thus, you shall be liberated from the inauspicious. 'These are not My doings; I am actionless, indifferent (udāsīna)' — knowing thus, by this right vision (samyagdarśana) you shall be liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra: this is the meaning. (32)
BG_C04_V33: Better than the sacrifice of material substance is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes. All action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge. (33)
BG_C04_V33::block-0: By the verse beginning 'Brahman is the offering' (Bhagavad-Gītā 4.24), the character of right vision (samyagdarśana) as itself a sacrifice was established. Many sacrifices have also been taught. By these, whose purpose — the highest human end — has been thus accomplished, knowledge is now extolled. How? —
BG_C04_V33::block-1: Better (śreyān) than the sacrifice of substance — that which is accomplished by material means — is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes. For the sacrifice of substance initiates a result (phala-ārambhaka); the sacrifice of knowledge initiates no result; therefore it is better, that is, more praiseworthy. How so? Because all action, the entirety, the totality, without obstruction, O Pārtha, culminates — that is, becomes wholly included — in knowledge, the means to liberation, which is comparable to a body of water flooded on every side; this is the meaning. As the śruti says: 'As, when one has won the throw called Kṛta, the lower throws are subsumed within it, so does whatever good creatures do come together within him; whoever knows that which he knows' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.4). (33)
BG_C04_V34: Know that (knowledge) by prostration, by repeated questioning, and by service. The wise, the seers of truth, will instruct you in that knowledge. (34)
BG_C04_V34::block-0: Then, by what means is this distinguished knowledge attained? — this is now stated —
BG_C04_V34::block-1: That — know it, that is, understand by what method it is attained. Approaching teachers (ācāryas), by prostration — pra (intensely) + nipāta (falling low) is praṇipāta, a prolonged salutation — by that; by repeated questioning, such as 'How does bondage arise? How is liberation? What is true knowledge (vidyā)? What is avidyā?' — by such inquiry; and by service — the attendance upon the guru — and by the like. The teachers, won over by such humility, will instruct, that is, will declare, to you the knowledge having the qualifications stated. The seers of truth (tattvadarśinaḥ): for some, though learned, do not see things as they are, while others do; therefore He distinguishes them by the qualifier 'seers of truth'. Knowledge imparted by those who have right vision becomes effectual (kāryakṣama); not the other — such is the Lord's teaching. (34)
BG_C04_V35: Knowing which, you shall not again fall into delusion thus, O Pāṇḍava; by which you shall see the whole of beings without exception in the Self, and then in Me. (35)
BG_C04_V35::block-0: And in that case, this further utterance is also pertinent —
BG_C04_V35::block-1: Knowing which — having attained, having reached, the knowledge instructed by them — you shall not again, a second time, fall into delusion as you have just now fallen into delusion, O Pāṇḍava. Furthermore — by which knowledge you shall see directly all beings without exception, from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass, in the Self, in the inner Self (pratyagātman), as 'these beings are situated in Me'; and likewise also in Me, in Vāsudeva, the supreme Lord, as 'these too are in Me'. The meaning is: you shall see the unity of the kṣetrajña (the knower of the field) and the Lord (Īśvara), well-established in all the Upaniṣads. (35)
BG_C04_V36: Even if you should be the most sinful of all sinners, you shall cross over the whole sea of evil simply by the boat of knowledge. (36)
BG_C04_V36::block-0: Furthermore, the greatness of this knowledge —
BG_C04_V36::block-1: Even if (api cet) you are, of all evildoers, the most evildoer in the highest degree (atiśayena pāpakṛt = pāpakṛttamaḥ), you shall, by knowledge alone made into a raft (plava), cross over the whole — the ocean of evil (vṛjina-arṇava), the sea of sins. Even dharma is here called pāpa for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu). (36)
BG_C04_V37: As a kindled fire reduces fuel-sticks to ashes, O Arjuna, even so does the fire of knowledge reduce all karmas to ashes.
BG_C04_V37::block-0: How does knowledge destroy sin? An illustration is now stated —
BG_C04_V37::block-1:
Just as edhāṃsi — fuel-sticks of wood — when samiddhaḥ — well kindled, brightly blazing — the fire reduces to bhasmasāt, that is, into the state of ash, so too, O Arjuna, knowledge itself being a fire — the fire of knowledge — reduces all karmas to ashes; the meaning is, it renders them seedless. For verily the fire of knowledge cannot, like ordinary fire with kindling, directly burn karmas to ashes. Therefore the import is that right vision is the cause of the seedlessness of all karmas.

By implication, that karma by which this body has already been initiated, since its fruit has commenced, is exhausted only through experience. Hence, those karmas whose fruits have not yet commenced — those done before the rise of knowledge, those done concurrent with knowledge, and those done in many past lives — all of these alone does the fire of knowledge reduce to ashes.
BG_C04_V38: Verily there exists in this world no purifier equal to knowledge. He who has been perfected by yoga finds that knowledge of himself, in time, within his own Self.
BG_C04_V38::block-1: Verily, no thing equal — tulyam — to knowledge, that is, purifying — pavitram, śuddhi-karam — exists in this world. That knowledge — the seeker of liberation himself, having become saṃsiddhaḥ — perfected, refined, brought to fitness — by yoga, namely by karma-yoga and by the yoga of samādhi, in the course of much time finds, that is, attains, in his own Self. This is the meaning.
BG_C04_V39: The man of faith, devoted to it, with senses restrained, attains knowledge. Having attained knowledge, he reaches the supreme peace without delay.
BG_C04_V39::block-0: The means by which the attainment of knowledge becomes assured — that means is now taught —
BG_C04_V39::block-1:
The man possessed of faith — the śraddhālu — attains knowledge. Yet even one who has faith may at times be slack in pursuit; therefore the Lord adds — tatparaḥ, devoted, fully engaged in the means of obtaining knowledge such as approaching the teacher and the like, while remaining a man of faith. Even one who is thus devoted may yet have unsubdued senses; therefore the Lord further adds — saṃyatendriyaḥ: he whose senses are restrained, that is, withdrawn from sense-objects, is the saṃyatendriya. He who is such — possessed of faith, devoted to that, and with senses restrained — he assuredly attains knowledge.

Mere prostration and the like, being external, may also prove inconclusive, since deceit and the like are possible there; not so in the case of being endowed with faith and so on. Hence this is the unfailing means for the attainment of knowledge.

What then comes about from the gaining of knowledge? It is said: having gained knowledge, he reaches without delay — that is, swiftly — the supreme peace called liberation, namely cessation. That liberation results swiftly from right vision is the firmly established conclusion well known throughout the entire reasoning of the śāstras.
BG_C04_V40: The ignorant man, the man without faith, the man whose self is filled with doubt — he perishes. For the doubting self there is neither this world, nor the world beyond, nor happiness.
BG_C04_V40::block-0: Here doubt must not be entertained, for doubt is the most sinful of all; how that is so is now stated —
BG_C04_V40::block-1: The ajña — the one ignorant of the Self — and the aśraddadhāna — the one without faith in the words of the teacher and the śāstras — and the saṃśayātmā — the one whose mind is given over to doubt — perish. Although the ignorant and the faithless do indeed perish, they do not perish in the same manner as the doubting self does. The doubting self is the most sinful of all. How? For him there is not even this ordinary world, nor likewise the world beyond, nor is there happiness — since with regard to that too doubt arises in the saṃśayātman, the one of doubting mind. Therefore doubt must not be entertained.
BG_C04_V41: Him who has renounced karmas through yoga, whose doubt is severed by knowledge, who is poised in the Self — karmas do not bind, O Dhanañjaya.
BG_C04_V41::block-1: Yoga-saṃnyasta-karmāṇam — him by whom, the seer of the supreme Reality, all karmas called dharma and adharma have been renounced through yoga which has the characteristic of paramārtha-darśana, the vision of the supreme Truth — him whose karmas have been thus renounced through yoga. How is it that his karmas are renounced through yoga? The Lord says — jñāna-sañchinna-saṃśayam: he whose doubt is severed by knowledge, namely the knowledge characterised by the vision of the oneness of the Self and the Lord, is the jñāna-sañchinna-saṃśaya. Him who is thus one whose karmas are renounced through yoga, ātmavantam — possessed of the Self, ever vigilant — karmas seen as the play of the guṇas do not bind: they do not produce any fruit of the form of the desired, undesired, and so on, O Dhanañjaya.
BG_C04_V42: Therefore, having severed with the sword of knowledge this doubt of your own — born of ignorance, seated in the heart — take to yoga; arise, O Bhārata!
BG_C04_V42::block-0: Since the man whose doubt has been severed by the knowledge born of the destruction of impurity through karma-yoga is not bound by karmas — for his karmas have already been burnt by the fire of knowledge — and since the man who entertains doubt with regard to the performance of jñāna-yoga and karma-yoga perishes, therefore —
BG_C04_V42::block-1:
Therefore, this most sinful doubt — born of ignorance, that is, of non-discrimination — seated in the heart, namely lodged in the buddhi — sever with the sword of knowledge: that knowledge is right vision which removes the defects of grief, delusion and the like; that very knowledge, being a sword, a khaḍga — by that sword of knowledge, of the Self — that is, of one's own self; for the doubt belongs to the Self.

Not indeed has another's doubt come up to be cut by another, that it should require the qualification 'one's own.' Therefore, even though it has the Self as its object, it is one's very own. Having severed this doubt — the cause of one's own destruction — take to yoga, the means of right vision, namely the performance of karmas: that is, perform it. And arise now for the battle, O Bhārata!
BG_C05_V01::block-0:
Beginning with 'He who sees inaction in action' (BG 4.18), continuing through 'He is yoked, the doer of all karmas' (BG 4.18), 'him whose karmas have been burnt by the fire of knowledge' (BG 4.19), 'performing only bodily karma' (BG 4.21), 'content with whatever comes by chance' (BG 4.22), 'Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation' (BG 4.24), 'know all those to be born of karma' (BG 4.32), 'all karma in its entirety, O Pārtha' (BG 4.33), 'the fire of knowledge — all karmas' (BG 4.37), and 'him whose karmas have been renounced through yoga' (BG 4.41) — by these utterances the Lord enjoined the renunciation of all karmas. By the statement 'having severed this doubt, take to yoga' (BG 4.42) he enjoined that one should also engage in yoga, characterized by the performance of karma.

Now, of these two — performance of karma and renunciation of karma — since they stand in mutual contradiction, like standing and going, they cannot both be undertaken by one and the same person; nor is there any prescription for them by division of time. Hence, since by implication only one of them is to be undertaken, considering 'whichever of these two — performance of karma or renunciation of karma — is the more praiseworthy, that should be done, not the other,' Arjuna, with the desire to know which is the more praiseworthy, said: 'Renunciation of karmas, O Kṛṣṇa…' and so on.
BG_C05_V01::block-1:
Pūrvapakṣa: But surely, with the desire to teach the niṣṭhā in jñāna-yoga of the knower of the Self, the Lord by the previously cited utterances enjoined renunciation of all karmas, and that not for the one who does not know the Self. And since therefore the performance of karma and renunciation of karma have different persons as their domain, this question — born of the desire to know which of the two is the more praiseworthy — does not stand to reason.

Siddhānta: True, the question does not stand to reason on your supposition; but on the questioner's own supposition the question is indeed coherent. We answer thus. How? Because by the cited statements the Lord intended renunciation of karma to be the duty enjoined; and since without principal status — namely, an agent — its being a duty is not possible, even the one not knowing the Self, taken as an alternative agent, is restated in passing; it is not that the renunciation has been intended as belonging exclusively to the knower of the Self. Holding this view, Arjuna thinks that the performance of karma and the renunciation of karma may both have for their agent the man not yet possessed of knowledge. Hence, since by the manner already stated they mutually contradict each other, when by implication only one of them is to be undertaken, the more praiseworthy alone should be undertaken, not the other. Hence the question, born of the wish to know the more praiseworthy, is not without ground.
BG_C05_V01::block-2:
By the analysis of the meaning of the answering verse also, the questioner's intention is understood to be just this. How? The reply is: 'Renunciation and karma-yoga, both bring about the highest good; but of these two, karma-yoga excels' (BG 5.2). This must be examined. Is it the case that, having stated that the renunciation and karma-yoga of the knower of the Self bring about the highest good, of those very two, on some specific ground, the excellence of karma-yoga over renunciation of karma is being declared? Or is this twofold statement made of the renunciation and karma-yoga of the one who does not know the Self?

Moreover — if it be of the renunciation of karma and karma-yoga of the knower of the Self that the bringing-about of the highest good is being stated, and of those two the excellence of karma-yoga over renunciation of karma — or if it be of the renunciation and karma-yoga of the one who does not know the Self that this twofold statement is made — Here it is replied: in the case of the knower of the Self, since both renunciation and karma-yoga are impossible, the statement that they bring about the highest good and the assertion that karma-yoga excels their renunciation of karma — both these are unsustainable. If for the one not knowing the Self the renunciation of karma and the karma-yoga which is its opposite, characterized by the performance of karma, were both possible, then the statement that they bring about the highest good and the declaration of karma-yoga's excellence over renunciation of karma — both these would stand. But for the knower of the Self, since both renunciation and karma-yoga are impossible, the statement that they bring about the highest good and the assertion that karma-yoga excels renunciation of karma — both these are untenable.
BG_C05_V01::block-3: Here it is asked: Is it that for the knower of the Self both renunciation and karma-yoga are impossible? Or is it that one of the two is impossible? And when one of them is impossible, which is it — renunciation of karma, or karma-yoga? And the reason for the impossibility must also be stated. Here it is replied: For the knower of the Self, since false knowledge has ceased, karma-yoga, whose root is the cognition of the contrary, becomes impossible. He who knows as the Self the Self that is actionless — devoid of all transformation such as birth and so on — for him, the knower of the Self, whose false knowledge has been cast off by right vision, the Lord, having taught the renunciation of all karmas characterised by abiding in one's own actionless Self-nature, declares throughout this Gītā-śāstra, in the various passages dealing with the determination of the Self's nature, the absence of the karma-yoga which is its opposite — namely, that which is preceded by the conceit of agency rooted in false knowledge and consists in abiding in an active Self-nature — on the ground of the contradiction between right knowledge and false knowledge together with their effects. Therefore, for the knower of the Self, whose false knowledge has ceased, the karma-yoga rooted in the cognition of the contrary is not possible: it would be appropriately said.
BG_C05_V01::block-4: In which passages dealing with the determination of the Self's nature is the absence of karma for the knower of the Self set forth? Here it is said — beginning with 'But that is indestructible' (BG 2.17), and 'He who knows this as the slayer' (BG 2.19), 'Know that as imperishable, eternal' (BG 2.21), and so on, in various places the absence of karma for the knower of the Self is declared.
BG_C05_V01::block-5: Pūrvapakṣa: But surely karma-yoga too is being set forth in those very passages dealing with the determination of the Self's nature; for example: 'Therefore fight, O Bhārata' (BG 2.18), 'And considering also one's own dharma' (BG 2.31), 'Your right is only to action' (BG 2.47), and so on. How then is karma-yoga impossible for the knower of the Self? Here it is replied: Because of the contradiction between right knowledge and false knowledge together with their effects; because by the statement 'through the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas' (BG 3.3) the niṣṭhā in the yoga of knowledge — characterised by abiding in one's actionless Self-nature — has been set apart for the Sāṅkhyas, the knowers of the truth of the Self, from the niṣṭhā in karma-yoga whose agent is the one not knowing the Self; because for the knower of the Self, having achieved all that was to be achieved, no further purpose remains; because of the statement 'For him there is nothing to be done' (BG 3.17), declaring the absence of any further duty; because of injunctions like 'Not by abstention from karmas' (BG 3.4) and 'Renunciation, O mighty-armed, is hard to attain without yoga' (BG 5.6), prescribing karma-yoga only as a means to knowledge of the Self; because by 'For one who has ascended yoga, śama is said to be the cause' (BG 6.3) the absence of karma-yoga for one in whom right vision has arisen is declared; because by 'performing only bodily karma, he incurs no sin' (BG 4.21) any karma beyond what is needed for bodily maintenance is forbidden; and because by 'Yoked, the knower of Truth should think — I do nothing at all' (BG 5.8) the upadeśa is given that, even with respect to the karmas of seeing, hearing and so on which are merely occasioned by bodily existence, the cognition 'I act' is, for the knower of the true nature of the Self with composed mind, never to be entertained at all — for the knower of the Self the karma-yoga rooted in false knowledge, contradictory to right vision, cannot be conceived even in a dream.
