Therefore, the statement that they bring about the highest good is made only of the renunciation and karma-yoga whose agent is the one not knowing the Self, and the declaration of karma-yoga's excellence — over that renunciation of karma which is distinct from the previously mentioned renunciation of all karmas whose agent is the knower of the Self — refers, when the cognition of agency still subsists, to a renunciation pertaining only to one portion of karmas, attended by yamas and niyamas, hard to perform; whereas karma-yoga, being easy to practise, is declared excellent. Thus, by the analysis of the answering verse also, the questioner's intention as already stated is established. So it stands.
BG_C05_V01::block-6: On 'If, in your view, knowledge is superior to karma' (BG 3.1) — when knowledge and karma cannot coexist — having been asked by Arjuna with 'Tell me which one of these is the better' (BG 3.2), the Lord delivered the conclusion that for the Sāṅkhyas, the renunciants, the niṣṭhā is by the yoga of knowledge, and again for the yogins the niṣṭhā is by karma-yoga. From the statement 'Nor does he reach perfection by mere renunciation' (BG 3.4), the means to perfection accompanied by knowledge is desired; and karma-yoga is enjoined. Now: Is renunciation, devoid of knowledge, superior, or is karma-yoga superior? With the desire to know the distinction between these two —
BG_C05_V01::block-7: Saṃnyāsa, the relinquishment of the karmas — those particular ones to be performed which are prescribed in the śāstras — you praise, you commend, you teach: this is what is meant. Again, yoga, that is, the very performance of those karmas as something necessarily to be done, you also praise. Hence, my doubt: Which of these is the better — is the performance of karma the better, or the abandonment of it? And the more praiseworthy alone should be undertaken. Therefore, that which is the better, the more praiseworthy, of these two — renunciation of karma and karma-yoga — by the practice of which you think the attainment of welfare would be mine, that one alone — only one of the two — since the practice of both by a single person at the same time is impossible — that, tell me, with full certainty, in accordance with your own intention.
BG_C05_V02::block-0: Declaring his own intention to settle the matter, the Blessed Lord said —
BG_C05_V02::block-1: Saṃnyāsa, the relinquishment of karmas, and karma-yoga, their performance — both alike are bringers of the highest good: they bring about liberation, by being causes for the rise of knowledge. Although both are bringers of the highest good, yet of these two causes of the highest good, karma-yoga excels mere renunciation of karma. Thus he praises karma-yoga.
BG_C05_V03: He should be known as a perpetual saṁnyāsin who neither hates nor longs for anything; for, free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, he is easily released from bondage.
BG_C05_V03::block-1: He is to be known — that is, recognised — as a perpetual saṁnyāsin: that very karma-yogin who neither hates anything nor longs for anything, neither pain and pleasure nor their causes. One of this description, although engaged in action, must be understood as a perpetual saṁnyāsin; this is the sense. For (hi) being free from the pairs of opposites — devoid of the dualities (such as cold and heat, gain and loss) — O mighty-armed one, he is released from bondage easily, without strain.
BG_C05_V04: Children, not the wise, declare Sāṅkhya and Yoga to be different; one who has rightly resorted to even one of them obtains the fruit of both.
BG_C05_V04::block-0: An objection presents itself thus: saṁnyāsa and karma-yoga, being to be undertaken by different persons and being mutually opposed, must surely also yield opposed fruits; it is not reasonable that both alike confer the highest good. To this the Lord replies —
BG_C05_V04::block-1: Children — that is, the unwise — declare Sāṅkhya and Yoga to be distinct, with mutually contrary fruits; not the wise. The wise, the men of knowledge, hold that the fruit of both is one and unopposed. How? He explains: one who has rightly resorted to — that is, has rightly practised — even one of the two, Sāṅkhya or Yoga, obtains the fruit of both. For the fruit of both is one and the same, namely the highest good (niḥśreyasa); hence there is no contradiction in their fruits.
BG_C05_V04::block-2: Objection: having opened the discussion with the words saṁnyāsa and karma-yoga, how is it that here he speaks instead of the unity of fruit of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, which were not the topic? There is no fault here. Although Arjuna, intending only saṁnyāsa and karma-yoga in their bare form, had put the question, the Lord, without abandoning those very topics, joined to them his own intended specification and gave the reply by designating them with other terms — namely, Sāṅkhya and Yoga. It is the Lord's view that those very two — saṁnyāsa and karma-yoga — when joined with knowledge (and with the means thereto, such as evenness of mind), are denoted by the words Sāṅkhya and Yoga. Therefore the procedure is not foreign to the topic at hand.
BG_C05_V05: The state attained by the Sāṅkhyas is reached by the Yogins also; he who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one, he sees indeed.
BG_C05_V05::block-0: How, by the right practice of even one of them, does he obtain the fruit of both? This is now stated —
BG_C05_V05::block-1: That state, called liberation, which is attained by the Sāṅkhyas — those established in knowledge, the saṁnyāsins — is reached also by the Yogins, namely those who, taking action as a means to the attainment of knowledge, dedicate their works to the Lord and perform them without aim at any personal fruit; by them too it is reached, through arriving at the saṁnyāsa that is true knowledge of the supreme reality. This is the purport. Therefore, he who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one — by reason of unity of fruit — he indeed sees, that is, sees rightly.
BG_C05_V05::block-2: If so, then saṁnyāsa stands distinguished above Yoga; how then was it said, 'Of these two, karma-yoga is distinguished above the renunciation of action' (Bh. Gītā 5.2)? Hear the reason. You questioned with reference only to bare renunciation of action and bare karma-yoga, asking which of the two is the better; in conformity with that question my reply was given — that karma-yoga is distinguished above the renunciation of action — without taking knowledge into account. But the saṁnyāsa that presupposes knowledge is what I intend by 'Sāṅkhya'; and that itself is the supreme Yoga. Whereas that karma-yoga which is Vedic is figuratively called Yoga and saṁnyāsa because it is undertaken for the sake of that. How is it 'for the sake of that'? This is being explained.
BG_C05_V06: But saṁnyāsa, O mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without Yoga; the Yoga-yoked sage attains Brahman without delay.
BG_C05_V06::block-0: But saṁnyāsa — that is, the supreme one (the renunciation joined with knowledge) — O mighty-armed one, is hard to attain — to reach — without Yoga, that is, without the (preliminary) Yoga. The Yoga-yoked one — he who is yoked by the Vedic karma-yoga that is offered to the Lord and performed without expectation of fruit — being a 'muni' (because he reflects, manana, on the nature of the Lord), reaches Brahman. Here Brahman means the saṁnyāsa under discussion, which is characterised by abiding firm in the knowledge of the supreme Self; for this is called Brahman in the śruti, 'Renunciation indeed is Brahmā, and Brahmā is the supreme' (Tai. Nā. 78). Brahman — that is, the supreme renunciation, marked by abiding firm in supreme knowledge — he attains, na cireṇa, swiftly indeed. Therefore I have said, 'karma-yoga is distinguished above' (Bh. Gītā 5.2).
BG_C05_V07: Yoked in Yoga, of purified inner being, conqueror of the body, conqueror of the senses, his Self being the Self of all beings — though he acts, he is not tainted.
BG_C05_V07::block-0: When, on the other hand, he (the karma-yogin) is taken as a means to the attainment of right knowledge —
BG_C05_V07::block-1: Yoked in Yoga, that is, joined with Yoga, of purified inner being — of pure sattva —, conqueror of the body (vijita-ātmā = vijita-deha), and conqueror of the senses, and one whose Self has become the Self of all beings — that is, he whose Self, the inner conscious one, has become the Self of all beings, from Brahmā down to the clump of grass — meaning, one of right vision (samyag-darśin); such a one, abiding thus, even while doing action for the welfare of the world (loka-saṁgraha), is not tainted, that is, is not bound by works. This is the sense.
BG_C05_V08: 'I do nothing at all' — thus would the yoked one, the knower of truth, hold, while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, going, sleeping, breathing,
BG_C05_V08::block-0: And in truth he does not act at all (paramārthataḥ) — therefore —
BG_C05_V09: speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, closing the eyes — holding firm that 'the senses are functioning among the sense-objects.'
BG_C05_V09::block-0: 'I do nothing whatever' — thus would the yoked one, that is, the composed one (samāhita), hold, that is, reflect; the knower of truth — he who knows the true nature (yāthātmya) of the Self — being the seer of the supreme reality, this is the meaning.
BG_C05_V09::block-1: When and how, fixing the truth firmly in mind, would he hold this view? He answers — 'while seeing,' etc. The construction is to be made with 'would hold,' from the previous verse. For one who is thus a knower of truth — a seer of the right — in all the activities of the sense-organs and the body, in all works there is no work at all; for such a one of right vision, the qualification (adhikāra) lies only in the renunciation of all works, since for him there is the perception of the absence of action. For one who has set out to drink, taking what is mirage to be water, does not, even after coming to know that there is no water there, persist in setting forth toward that very place for the purpose of drinking.
BG_C05_V10: He who, having placed his actions in Brahman and abandoned attachment, acts — he is not tainted by sin, even as a lotus-leaf is not by water.
BG_C05_V10::block-0: But he who is not yet a knower of truth and is engaged in karma-yoga —
BG_C05_V10::block-1: Having placed his works in Brahman — that is, in the Lord — depositing them with the thought, 'I do this work for His sake,' as a servant does for his master's sake; and having abandoned attachment to the fruit, even to liberation, in regard to all works, he who acts — that is, performs all works — he is not tainted by sin, that is, is not connected with it, even as a lotus-leaf is not by water. The fruit of his work will be only the purification of the inner being (sattva-śuddhi), nothing more.
BG_C05_V11: With body, mind, intellect, or even with the senses alone, the yogins perform action, abandoning attachment, for the purification of the self. (11)
BG_C05_V11::block-1: With the body — that is, with the physical frame — and with the mind, and with the intellect, and even with the senses that are kevala, that is, devoid of the sense of "mine," empty of the notion of mineness because the resolve is, "I perform action only for the Lord, not for any fruit of mine" — the word kevala is to be construed individually with the body and the rest as well, in order to bring out the abandonment of mineness in every operation. The yogins, the doers of action, perform action, having abandoned attachment with respect to the fruit, for the purification of the self — that is, for the purification of the inner being (sattva-śuddhi). Therefore, since your authority lies precisely there, perform action itself.
BG_C05_V12: The yoked one, abandoning the fruit of action, attains peace that is rooted in steadfastness; the unyoked one, attached to the fruit through the impulse of desire, becomes bound. (12)
BG_C05_V12::block-1: The yoked one — being collected with the resolve, "I perform actions for the Lord, not for any fruit of mine" — having abandoned, that is, completely renounced, the fruit of action, attains the peace called liberation, which is naiṣṭhikī, that is, born of niṣṭhā (steadfast establishment). The completion of the sentence is: through the sequence of purification of the inner being, the rise of knowledge, the renunciation of all action, and steadfastness in knowledge (jñāna-niṣṭhā). But the other, the unyoked one — the uncollected — through kāmakāra (kāra means doing; the doing of desire is kāmakāra), that is, propelled by desire, with the resolve, "I do this action for my own fruit," thus attached to the fruit, becomes bound. Therefore the import is: be you the yoked one.
BG_C05_V13: Renouncing all actions by the mind, the embodied one — self-controlled — sits happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing to act. (13)
BG_C05_V13::block-0: But the one who is the seer of the highest truth — he —
BG_C05_V13::block-1:
All actions — sarva-karmāṇi (the dissolution of the compound: "all" + "actions") — the daily, the occasional, the optional, and the prohibited: all these actions, having renounced, that is, having relinquished by the mind — by the discriminating intellect — through the seeing of non-action in action and the rest (as taught in IV.18), the import being "having abandoned them by the recognition of action's emptiness" — sits, that is, abides, happily. Having let go of activity of speech, mind, and body, free of strain, of tranquil mind, with all external purposes other than the Self ceased — for that reason it is said, "sits happily." Vaśī means one who has conquered the senses. Where, and how, does he sit? He answers: in the city of nine gates. The seven openings in the head are gates of perception for the embodied one, and below there are two more for the discharge of urine and faeces; on account of these gates the body is called the "city of nine gates," a city as it were, having the Self alone as its sole sovereign, and inhabited as if by townsmen by the senses, mind, intellect, and objects which are its servants and which produce manifold cognitions of fruits. In that city of nine gates the embodied one sits, having renounced all action.

What purpose is served by such a qualification? Every embodied being, whether a renouncer or not, sits in the body alone; therefore the qualification is meaningless. Reply: It is said — the ignorant embodied one who takes his self to be merely the aggregate of body and senses, that one thinks, "I sit in the house, on the ground, on the seat"; for in one who sees the self as nothing more than the body the cognition "I sit in the body" as one sits in a house cannot arise. But for one who sees the Self as distinct from the aggregate of body and the rest, the cognition "I sit in the body" does fit. And the renunciation, by the mind through the discriminative knowledge, of others' actions falsely superimposed by avidyā upon the Self, who is other, is intelligible. Even for the one in whom discriminative knowledge has arisen and who has renounced all actions, the sitting in the body itself, as in a house, in the city of nine gates is on account of the residual continuance of the impressions of the prārabdha-karman whose fruit has begun, since particular cognitions arise in the body alone. Hence "sits in the body itself" — the qualification does have its purpose, since it depends upon the difference between the cognitions of the wise man and the ignorant man.
BG_C05_V13::block-2:
Although it has been said, "having renounced and sitting," with reference to the activities of body, organs, and actions superimposed by avidyā upon the Self, still — apprehending that agency and the causing of action might inhere in the Self itself — the Lord says: neither himself acting, nor causing the body and senses to act, that is, prompting them into operations.

Is it that the agency and causing-to-act, though inherent in the Self of the embodied one, do not occur because of renunciation — just as the going of one walking would cease upon the abandonment of the activity of walking? Or is it that they are not in the Self at all by its very nature? To this it is replied: by its own nature the Self has neither agency nor the causing of action. For it has been said, "This is declared to be without modification" (Bh.G. II.25), and "Even though abiding in the body, He neither acts nor is tainted" (Bh.G. XIII.31), and the Śruti, "As if meditating, as if moving" (Bṛ.U. IV.3.7).
BG_C05_V14: The Lord-Self creates neither agency nor the actions for the world, nor union with the fruit of action; it is one's own innate nature that operates. (14)
BG_C05_V14::block-1: Neither agency — "act of yourself" — nor actions such as chariots, pots, palaces, and the rest, the most desired of all, does the prabhu, the Self, create or produce for the world. Nor does He create for one who has made a chariot or the like the union with its fruit — that is, no "union with the fruit of action." If the embodied one neither does anything of himself nor causes anything to be done, who then is it that, doing and causing to be done, sets things in motion? It is said: but svabhāva — one's own state, sva-bhāva — that is, prakṛti characterized by avidyā, māyā — operates; the very māyā which is to be spoken of further as "For this divine māyā of mine…" (Bh.G. VII.14) and so on.
BG_C05_V15: The all-pervading Self takes neither the sin of anyone nor even the merit; knowledge is veiled by ignorance — by that, creatures are deluded. (15)
BG_C05_V15::block-1: He does not take, that is, does not accept, the sin even of any devotee. Nor indeed does the all-pervading One accept the merit offered by devotees. For what purpose, then, is the merit characterized by worship and the like — sacrifices, gifts, oblations and so on — offered by devotees? He says: knowledge — that is, discriminative cognition — is veiled by ignorance; by that, creatures are deluded — undiscerning saṃsārins fall into the delusion, "I do, I cause to do, I shall enjoy, I shall feed."
BG_C05_V16: But for those whose ignorance of the Self has been destroyed by knowledge, that knowledge — like the sun — illumines the supreme reality. (16)
BG_C05_V16::block-0: But by knowledge — by which ignorance, being veiled, the creatures are deluded — that ignorance, in those creatures whose ignorance of the Self has been destroyed by discriminative knowledge having the Self as its object, in those creatures, like the sun — just as the sun reveals every form of thing — so does knowledge reveal the entire knowable: the supreme, the truth-of-the-highest-import (paramārtha-tattva).
BG_C05_V17: Those whose intellect is fixed on That, whose Self is That, who are steadfast in That, whose supreme resort is That — they go to non-return, their stains shaken off by knowledge. (17)
BG_C05_V17::block-0: What that supreme knowledge that has been illumined is —
BG_C05_V17::block-1: Tad-buddhayaḥ: those whose intellect has gone to that Brahman are tad-buddhayaḥ. Tad-ātmānaḥ: those whose Self is that very supreme Brahman are tad-ātmānaḥ. Tan-niṣṭhāḥ: niṣṭhā means absorption, the highest aim; those who, having renounced all actions, abide in that Brahman alone — they are tan-niṣṭhāḥ. Tat-parāyaṇāḥ: those whose supreme resort, the supreme goal, is That — they are tat-parāyaṇāḥ; the import is, they have their delight in the Self alone. Those whose ignorance of the Self has been destroyed by knowledge, such ones go to apunarāvṛtti, that is, to non-resumption of any further connection with a body, jñāna-nirdhūta-kalmaṣāḥ — those whose kalmaṣa, the defect of sin and the rest which is the cause of saṃsāra, has been shaken off and destroyed by the knowledge as described — they, the strivers (yatis), are intended.
BG_C05_V18: In a brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant, and even in a dog and in a dog-eater, the wise are equal-seers. (18)
BG_C05_V18::block-0: Those whose ignorance of the Self has been destroyed by knowledge — these wise ones, how do they see the truth? It is said —
BG_C05_V18::block-1: Vidyā-vinaya-sampanne: vidyā and vinaya, that is, learning and humility — vinaya being inner calm — endowed with these, that is, both learned and well-trained, is the brāhmaṇa; in that brāhmaṇa, in a cow, in an elephant, in a dog, and even in a śva-paca (dog-cooker, the lowest outcaste), the paṇḍitas are equal-seers. In the brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility — of supreme refinement, of the sāttvika (nature) — and in the middling, the rājasic, namely the cow, and in the utterly devoid of refinement, the wholly tāmasic, namely the elephant and the rest — those whose nature it is to see that one Brahman, untouched and homogeneous and changeless, utterly unaffected by the qualities sattva and the rest and by the impressions born of them, by the rājasic and tāmasic ones too, are the wise — the equal-seers.
BG_C05_V19: Even here is the round of birth conquered by those whose mind stands established in evenness; for Brahman is flawless and equal, and therefore they too are established in Brahman.
BG_C05_V19::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: But surely such men, whose food may not be eaten, are tainted with fault, on the strength of the Smṛti, "By honouring the unequal as equal and the equal as unequal" (Gautama Dharma-sūtra 2.8.20; 17.18). Siddhānta: They are not tainted with fault. How so? — He answers:
BG_C05_V19::block-1: Even here itself, that is, even while still living, by these same wise ones who see equally the round of birth — sarga, that is, birth — has been conquered, brought under their sway: namely those in whose mind, the inner instrument, stands fixed and unmoving in sameness, in the equal abiding in Brahman that pervades all beings. Brahman is flawless: although among the faulty — outcastes and the like — the deluded fancy It as though stained by their faults, yet, being untouched by those faults, It is flawless, free from defect; for so it is. Nor is It differentiated by distinctions of any qualities of Its own, since Consciousness is without guṇas. The Lord too will declare that desire and the rest are properties of the kṣetra (the field), and will say, "because It is beginningless, because It is without guṇas" (BG 13.31). Nor are there ultimate particulars (antya-viśeṣas, as the Vaiśeṣikas hold) that distinguish one Self from another, since no proof can be furnished for their existing one in each body. Therefore Brahman is the same, and one. Hence they stand established in Brahman alone. So not even the faintest scent of fault touches them, because they have no conceit of taking the aggregate of body and the rest as the Self. The sūtra "By honouring the unequal as equal and the equal as unequal" (Gautama 2.8.20) has its scope precisely in those who do entertain the conceit of the body-aggregate as Self, since it is qualified by reference to honouring. For it is observed that, in the matter of honour, gifts and the like, the connection with particular qualities — "a knower of Brahman," "a knower of the six aṅgas," "a knower of the four Vedas" — is the determining cause. But Brahman is free of all connection with quality and fault; hence "they stand established in Brahman" is fitly said. The text "By honouring the unequal as equal and so on" applies to the domain of action; whereas the present teaching, beginning with "having mentally renounced all actions" (BG 5.13) and continuing to the end of the chapter, has for its theme the renunciation of all action.
BG_C05_V20: He should not exult on obtaining the pleasant, nor recoil on obtaining the unpleasant; with steady understanding, undeluded, the knower of Brahman stands firm in Brahman.
BG_C05_V20::block-0: Since Brahman, the Self, is flawless and equal, therefore —
BG_C05_V20::block-1: He should not exult — should not give way to elation — on obtaining what is pleasant, the desired. Nor should he recoil on obtaining the unpleasant, the undesired. For it is they who see the body alone as the Self in whom the obtaining of the pleasant and the unpleasant produces elation and dejection; not in him who sees the bare Self alone, since for him the very obtaining of pleasant and unpleasant is impossible. Further — he in whom the understanding is steady, free from doubt, namely "the one Self, equal and flawless, abides in all beings," he is sthira-buddhi, of steady understanding; he is also asaṃmūḍha, free from confusion. Such a knower of Brahman as has been described stands established in Brahman; the meaning is that he performs no action, being the renouncer of all action.
BG_C05_V21: He whose mind is unattached to outer contacts finds within the Self the joy that is there; with his mind firmly yoked in the union with Brahman he attains imperishable bliss.
BG_C05_V21::block-0: Further, of the one established in Brahman —
BG_C05_V21::block-1: In bāhya-sparśas — "outer contacts," namely the contacts that are external; or, by etymology, those things which are touched, that is, the objects beginning with sound — in these outer contacts he whose ātman, the inner instrument, is unattached, devoid of fondness for objects, is asakta-ātman; he, being such, finds — that is, obtains — that joy which is in the Self; this is the meaning of vindati. He, sa, brahma-yoga-yukta-ātmā: brahma-yoga is yoga, samādhi, in Brahman; he whose ātman, the inner instrument, is yukta — concentrated, engaged — in that brahma-yoga, is brahma-yoga-yukta-ātmā; he reaches — pervadingly attains — sukham akṣayam, imperishable bliss. Therefore, the meaning is: one who desires imperishable bliss in the Self should withdraw the senses from the fleeting fondness for outer objects.
BG_C05_V22: Those enjoyments that are born of contact are themselves the wombs of pain, having a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī; the wise man does not delight in them.
BG_C05_V22::block-0: And on this further account he should withdraw —
BG_C05_V22::block-1: For — yasmāt, since — those enjoyments which are saṃsparśa-jāḥ, born of the contact between sense-objects and senses, those bhogas, experiences of enjoyment, are themselves wombs of pain, since they are wrought by avidyā. For one observes the pains belonging to body, mind, etc., to be caused by them. As in this world, so too in the next: this is conveyed by the word "eva." Knowing that there is not even the trace of a scent of joy in saṃsāra, he should withdraw the senses from the mirage of objects. Not only are they wombs of pain, they are also āḍy-antavantaḥ — having a beginning and an end: the beginning of enjoyments is the conjunction of object and sense, and the end is precisely the disjunction of these; therefore, having beginning and end, they are non-eternal, the meaning being that they exist only for the moment in between. O son of Kuntī, in those enjoyments the wise man — the discriminating one who has reached the supreme reality — does not delight; for delight in objects is observed only in the utterly deluded, like beasts and the rest.
BG_C05_V23: He who, even here, is able to bear, before the dropping of the body, the surge that springs from desire and anger — he is the yogin, he is the happy man.
BG_C05_V23::block-0: And this — desire and anger — opposed to the path of the highest good, the cruellest of faults, the cause of every calamity, and exceedingly hard to ward off; therefore the utmost effort should be exerted to expel it. Thus the Lord says —
BG_C05_V23::block-1: He is able — utsahate — even here, that is, even while still alive, to bear, to withstand, prāk — before — śarīra-vimokṣaṇāt, before the casting off of the body, that is, until death, this being the meaning. The fixing of death as the limit is given because, while one lives, the surge of desire and anger is bound to occur — it has innumerable occasions; until death, therefore, no relaxation in this is to be admitted, that is the sense. Kāma is that yearning, that thirst, which is for an object of enjoyment present to the senses, or heard of, or remembered, when it is the cause of pleasure — that is kāma. And krodha is that aversion which arises towards what is contrary to oneself, towards what is the cause of pain, when seen, heard of, or remembered — that is krodha. The surge of which kāma and krodha are the source is kāma-krodha-udbhava-vega. The surge born of desire is marked by signs such as horripilation, gleaming eyes and face, and consists in the agitation of the inner instrument; the surge born of anger is marked by signs such as trembling of limbs, perspiration, biting of the lips, reddening of the eyes, and the like. Whoever is able, withstands, to bear that surge born of desire and anger — he is the yogin, the yoked one, and a happy man here in this world.
BG_C05_V24: He whose joy is within, whose delight is within, whose light too is within — that yogin, having become Brahman, attains the absolute peace that is Brahman.
BG_C05_V24::block-0: And of what nature is the one established in Brahman who attains Brahman — this the Lord declares —
BG_C05_V24::block-1: He whose sukha is within — antaḥsukhaḥ, that is, in whose Self the joy is — is antaḥ-sukhaḥ; likewise, he whose ārāma — sporting, play — is within, in the Self alone, is antarārāmaḥ; likewise, he whose jyotis, light, is within, in the Self itself, is antarjyotis. He who is such a yogin, having here itself become Brahman even while living, attains brahma-nirvāṇa — extinction in Brahman, liberation.
BG_C05_V25: The seers attain absolute peace in Brahman, those whose taints are worn away, whose dualities are sundered, whose selves are restrained, who delight in the welfare of all beings.
BG_C05_V25::block-1: They attain — labhante — brahma-nirvāṇa, liberation, those ṛṣis, the right-seers, the renouncers, whose kalmaṣa — sin — is worn away, who are sinless, flawless; chinna-dvaidhāḥ — those whose doubts are sundered; yatātmānaḥ — those whose senses are restrained; sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ — those who delight in the welfare, the friendliness, towards all beings, that is, the non-injurers.
BG_C05_V26: For the renouncers, free from desire and anger, with mind subdued, who have known the Self, the absolute peace of Brahman is present on every side.
BG_C05_V26::block-1: Of those who are kāma-krodha-viyukta — kāma and krodha are kāma-krodhau, freed from these are the kāma-krodha-viyuktas — of those yatis, renouncers, of yata-cetasas, those whose inner instrument is restrained, abhitaḥ — on both sides, both while living and after death — the brahma-nirvāṇa, liberation, is present; of the vidita-ātmans, those by whom the Self has been known, hence vidita-ātmans, that is, of the right-seers — that is the meaning.
BG_C05_V27: Having cast outside all external contacts (with sound and the rest), and fixing the gaze between the two eyebrows, equalising the prāṇa and the apāna currents that move within the nostrils — (28).
BG_C05_V27::block-0: For those who are firmly grounded in right knowledge and have taken to renunciation, immediate liberation has already been declared. And karma-yoga, performed by offering every act to the Lord — placing it in the Lord, in Brahman — leads to liberation through the sequence of purification of the inner being (sattva-śuddhi), the attainment of knowledge, and the renunciation of all works; this the Bhagavān has stated step by step, and will state again. Now, however, with the words "I shall expound at length the dhyāna-yoga which is the inner means (antaraṅga-sādhana) of right knowledge," he proceeds to teach those verses which stand in the place of aphorisms (sūtra-sthānīya) for that yoga —
BG_C05_V28: The muni whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained, who is wholly intent on liberation, from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed — he is verily ever-liberated.
BG_C05_V28::block-0:
"Casting the contacts — sound and the rest — outside": the objects of sense, sound and the rest, that have been admitted inwards into the buddhi through the gateways of the ear and the like, become "thrown outside" (bahir-kṛta) for him who ceases to dwell upon them; sound and the rest then remain only externally. Having thus cast them outside, "the eye between the two eyebrows" — the verb "having made" (kṛtvā) is to be supplied. Likewise, having equalised the prāṇa and apāna currents that move within the nostrils, the "yatendriyamanobuddhiḥ" — he by whom the senses, mind, and intellect have been restrained (yata, fully held in) is the yatendriya-mano-buddhiḥ; "muni" — the renunciant, so called from his mananam (deep reflection); "mokṣa-parāyaṇaḥ" — he whose supreme resort, whose highest goal (parā gatiḥ), is liberation alone, having so disposed his bodily posture; such a one becomes the muni intent on mokṣa.

"Vigatecchābhayakrodhaḥ" — he from whom desire, fear, and anger (icchā ca bhayam ca krodhaś ca, the dvandva icchā-bhaya-krodhāḥ) have all departed. Whoever, being a renunciant, abides ever in this manner — "he is verily already liberated" (mukta eva saḥ): for him there remains no other thing to be done for the sake of mokṣa.
BG_C05_V29: Knowing Me as the enjoyer of yajñas and tapas, the great Lord of all the worlds, the friend of all beings, he attains peace.
BG_C05_V29::block-0: What, then, is to be known by such a one of composed mind? It is now stated —
BG_C05_V29::block-1: "The enjoyer of yajñas and tapas" — of sacrifices and austerities, both as the agent (kartṛ-rūpeṇa, indwelling the doer) and as the deity (devatā-rūpeṇa, the recipient); "the great Lord of all the worlds" — the great Īśvara of all the lokas; "the friend (suhṛd) of all beings" — He who confers benefit upon all creatures without expecting any return; who lies in the heart of every being; the overseer of the fruits of all karmas; the witness of every cognition (sarva-pratyaya-sākṣin) — having known Me, Nārāyaṇa, in this manner, one attains "śānti," the cessation of all transmigration (sarva-saṃsāra-uparati).
BG_C06_V01:
The Blessed Lord said —
He who, without depending upon the fruit of action, performs the action that ought to be done — he is the saṃnyāsin and he is the yogin; not the one who is merely without sacred fires and without rites.
BG_C06_V01::block-0: At the close of the immediately preceding chapter, those verses beginning with "sparśān kṛtvā bahiḥ" (BG 5.27) — which stand as aphorisms (sūtra-bhūtāḥ) for the dhyāna-yoga that is the inner instrument (antaraṅga) towards right knowledge — were taught. As the commentary upon them (vṛtti-sthānīya), this sixth chapter is now begun. Therein, since karma is the outer instrument (bahiraṅga) of dhyāna-yoga, and since for the householder duly entitled (adhikṛta), action remains a duty so long as he is competent to ascend to dhyāna-yoga, the Lord praises that karma — "anāśritaḥ . . ."
BG_C06_V01::block-1: Objection: Why posit any limit at all to the ascent to dhyāna-yoga, since the prescribed action is to be performed lifelong (yāvajjīvam)? — Not so; for there is the qualification "of the muni who is desirous of ascending to yoga, action is said to be the means" (BG 6.3), and for one who has already ascended, association is made only with quiescence (śama). Were both śama and karma intended as obligatory equally for the ascender and the ascended, then the differentiation by qualifications ("ārurukṣoḥ" and "ārūḍhasya") and the partitioning by separate domains (śama and karma) would be purposeless.
BG_C06_V01::block-2: If it be said: "Among those in the āśramas some are seekers of the ascent (ārurukṣu), some have ascended (ārūḍha), and others are neither; the qualification and partitioning hold good with reference to such persons" — not so. For the words "tasyaiva" ("of him alone") and the repeated mention of yoga as "yogārūḍhasya" show that the very same person who was formerly an aspirant becomes, on having ascended, one for whom śama alone is enjoined as the means towards the fruit of yoga. Hence no act whatsoever is enjoined on anyone as obligatory throughout life. Furthermore, from the statement about the yoga-vibhraṣṭa: if in the sixth chapter yoga were ordained for the karmin-householder, then since even one fallen from yoga "attains the goal of works, the fruit of works," the doubt of his ruin (nāśa-āśaṅkā) raised therein would be groundless. For karma — whether kāmya or nitya — once performed inevitably yields its own fruit; and as for nityakarma, since mokṣa is eternal and therefore not something to be commenced (anārabhya), nityakarma must yield some fruit, since it is laid down by the authority of the Veda — else the Veda would lapse into futility, as we have already said. Nor can the apprehension of "falling from both" hold while karma still subsists, for there is no cogent ground for the lapse of meaningful karma.
BG_C06_V01::block-3: If it be said: "Action having been renounced into the Lord, the agent's karma yields him no fruit" — not so; for renunciation in the Lord is itself the cause of an even greater fruit.
BG_C06_V01::block-4: If it be said: "That renunciation is for the sake of mokṣa alone — when one's actions are surrendered into the Lord, it is for mokṣa alone, joined with yoga, and not for any other fruit; and one falls from yoga; therefore the doubt of his ruin is fitting" — not so. For there is the prescription of karma-saṃnyāsa in the words "alone (ekākī), with mind and self restrained, free from desire and free from possessions" (BG 6.10), "established in the vow of brahmacarya" (BG 6.14). Nor can there be in the time of dhyāna any apprehension of needing a wife as helpmate, on account of which solitude (ekākitvam) would be enjoined. Nor are statements such as "free from desire and free from possessions" suitable for a householder. And the question about "falling from both" then becomes itself untenable.
BG_C06_V01::block-5: If it be objected: "By the word 'anāśritaḥ' the saṃnyāsin-hood and yogin-hood of the karmin alone are affirmed, and the saṃnyāsin-hood and yogin-hood of him who is without fires (niragni) and without rites (akriya) are denied" — not so. For the verse aims at praising the renunciation of attachment to the fruit of action on the part of one whose karma is itself the outer instrument towards dhyāna-yoga. It is not that the man without sacred fires and without rites alone is the saṃnyāsin and the yogin — but the karmin too, in renouncing attachment to the fruit of action and undertaking karma-yoga for the purification of his sattva, is praised by "saḥ saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca bhavati." One single sentence cannot at once praise the renunciation of fruit-attachment and prohibit the fourth āśrama. Nor does the Bhagavān prohibit that saṃnyāsin-hood and yogin-hood of the absolute renunciant — without fires, without rites — which is well known and ordained throughout the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Yoga-śāstras. There would, moreover, be self-contradiction with His own words: "Mentally renouncing all karmas . . . he sits, neither doing nor causing to do" (BG 5.13); "silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, of steady mind" (BG 12.19); "casting off all desires, the man moves about free from craving" (BG 2.71); "renouncer of all undertakings" (BG 12.16) — these declarations of His own are shown by the Bhagavān at place after place, and a prohibition of the fourth āśrama would conflict with them. Therefore: for the muni who is an aspirant towards yoga, abiding in householdership, the agnihotra and the rest, performed without dependence on fruit, become the means of ascending to dhyāna-yoga through purification of the sattva — and so he is praised as "saḥ saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca."
BG_C06_V01::block-6: "Anāśritaḥ" — not depending upon: not depending. On what? On the fruit of action — karma-phalam — that is, free from craving for the fruit of action. For he who craves the fruit is one who depends upon it; this man is the very opposite, hence "not depending on the fruit of action." Being such, whoever performs the action that ought to be done (kāryam) — namely the regularly enjoined (nitya) and not its opposite the kāmya, such as the agnihotra — accomplishes it: any such karmin is distinguished from other karmins; and to convey this the Lord says, "saḥ saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca." "Saṃnyāsa" is renunciation; he in whom that exists is the saṃnyāsin. "Yoga" is concentration of the mind (citta-samādhāna); he in whom that exists is the yogin. He who is endowed with these qualities is to be regarded thus, and not he alone who is without fires and without rites. "Niragni" — he from whom the fires that constitute the limbs of action have departed; "akriya" — he in whom even the actions not requiring fire — austerity, gift, and the like — are absent.
BG_C06_V02: What they call saṃnyāsa, know that, O Pāṇḍava, to be yoga; for none becomes a yogin who has not renounced the saṅkalpa.
BG_C06_V02::block-0: Objection: But in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Yoga-śāstras the saṃnyāsin-hood and yogin-hood of the man without fires and without rites alone are well established. How here is the saṃnyāsin-hood and yogin-hood of one with fires and with rites — which is unestablished — being declared? — There is no fault: the two are being made to come together by a certain figurative usage (gauṇa-vṛtti). How so? Through the renunciation of the saṅkalpa for the fruit of action there is saṃnyāsin-hood; and through the performance of action as a limb of yoga, while renouncing that fruit-saṅkalpa which is the cause of distraction of the mind, there is yogin-hood. Both, therefore, are figurative; and not the principal saṃnyāsin-hood and yogin-hood are intended. To show this very meaning he says —
BG_C06_V02::block-1: "That paramārtha-saṃnyāsa — characterised by the renunciation of all karmas and their fruits — which the knowers of Śruti and Smṛti call saṃnyāsa, know that, the karma-yoga that consists in the performance of action, to be that paramārtha-saṃnyāsa, O Pāṇḍava." One may ask: between karma-yoga which is of the nature of pravṛtti and paramārtha-saṃnyāsa which is its opposite, of the nature of nivṛtti, on the basis of what common ground is identification (tad-bhāva) being asserted? — and so this is being said: there is indeed similarity with paramārtha-saṃnyāsa for karma-yoga, through the door of the agent. For he who is a paramārtha-saṃnyāsin, having abandoned all means of all action, renounces the saṅkalpa concerning all karmas and their fruits — that saṅkalpa which is the cause of desire that prompts pravṛtti. So too this karma-yogin, even while doing karma, renounces the saṅkalpa concerning the fruit. To show this he says: "na hi" — for not, since one whose saṅkalpa concerning the fruit is not renounced (asaṃnyasta — not abandoned), no karmin whatsoever becomes a yogin, that is, one possessed of samādhi; it is not possible — because the saṅkalpa for fruit is the cause of distraction of the mind. Therefore, whichever karmin has renounced the saṅkalpa for the fruit, he becomes a yogin, possessed of samādhi, his mind undistracted, since the cause of mental distraction — the saṅkalpa for fruit — has been renounced. This is the import.
BG_C06_V03: For the muni who is desirous of ascending to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that very same one, when he has ascended to yoga, quiescence (śama) is said to be the means.
BG_C06_V03::block-0: Thus, with reference to the saṃnyāsa-hood common to both — paramārtha-saṃnyāsa and karma-yoga — through the door of the agent, the saṃnyāsa-hood of karma-yoga has been spoken of, by way of praise, in "yaṃ saṃnyāsam iti prāhur yogaṃ taṃ viddhi pāṇḍava." Karma-yoga, performed without expectation of fruit, is the outer means (bahiraṅga-sādhana) of dhyāna-yoga; having so praised it as saṃnyāsa, he now shows that karma-yoga is the means to dhyāna-yoga —
BG_C06_V03::block-1: "Of the ārurukṣu" — of him desirous of ascending; of the not-yet-ascended; that is, of one who is not yet able to abide in dhyāna-yoga. Of which such ārurukṣu? "Of the muni" — of the renouncer of the fruit of action. Desirous of ascending what? "Yoga." "Karma is said to be the cause" — the means. "Of him who has ascended to yoga, however, of that very same one (tasyaiva), śama" — quietude, cessation from all actions — "is said to be the cause" — the means of the yogārūḍha; this is the meaning. The more one ceases from action, the more, being free from exertion and having mastered the senses, one's mind becomes concentrated. So being, he becomes ārūḍha in yoga in no time. Likewise, Vyāsa has said: "There is no such wealth for the brāhmaṇa as oneness, evenness, truthfulness, śīla, steadfastness, the laying down of the rod, uprightness, and turning away from one action after another" (Mokṣa-dharma 175.37).
BG_C06_V04: When indeed one becomes attached neither to the objects of sense nor to actions, having renounced all saṅkalpas — then he is said to be ascended in yoga (yogārūḍha).
BG_C06_V04::block-0: Now, then, when does one become yogārūḍha? It is being said —
BG_C06_V04::block-1:
When the yogin whose mind is being concentrated does not, with the conviction of their pointlessness (prayojana-abhāva-buddhyā), become attached either to the indriya-arthas — sound and the rest, the objects of the senses — or to actions, namely the nitya, the naimittika, the kāmya, and the prohibited (pratiṣiddha); that is, he does not form an attachment to them as duties to be done — "sarva-saṅkalpa-saṃnyāsī" — he by whose nature it is to renounce all saṅkalpas, namely those that are causes of all desires for objects in this world and the next; "yogārūḍhaḥ" — one who has attained yoga: at that time he is so called.

By the very phrase "sarva-saṅkalpa-saṃnyāsī" the meaning is that one should renounce all desires and all actions. For all desires are rooted in saṅkalpa — "Desire is rooted in saṅkalpa, sacrifices spring from saṅkalpa" (Manu 2.3); "O Desire, I know thy root: from saṅkalpa thou art born; I will not henceforth saṅkalpa thee, and so thou shalt not be unto me" (Mokṣa-dharma 177.25), and other Smṛti texts. And in the renunciation of all desires, the renunciation of all actions stands accomplished — "as is one's desire, such is one's resolve (kratu); as is one's resolve, so does one perform action" (Bṛhad. Up. 4.4.5) and the like Śruti texts; "whatsoever the creature performs, that is the prompting of desire" (Manu 2.4) and similar Smṛti texts; and by reasoning too — for upon the renunciation of all saṅkalpas no one is even able to stir. Therefore, by the words "sarva-saṅkalpa-saṃnyāsī" the Bhagavān causes one to give up all desires and all actions.
BG_C06_V05: Let one raise the self by the Self; let one not let the self sink. For the Self alone is the friend of the self; the Self alone is the enemy of the self.
BG_C06_V05::block-0: When one becomes yogārūḍha thus, then by him the self has been raised up out of the entire host of evils that constitute saṃsāra. Hence —
BG_C06_V05::block-1: "Let him raise up" — by the Self, the self that lies sunk in the ocean of saṃsāra; "ud" — upward; "haret" — let him raise; that is, let him bring it to yogārūḍha-hood. "Let him not let the self sink" — let him not bring it downward, let him not cause it to descend. "For the Self alone is the friend of the self" — for there is no other friend who avails for liberation from saṃsāra. Even the friend, after all, is opposed to mokṣa, being the very seat of attachment and the like bondages. Therefore the emphatic limitation is well placed — "the Self alone is the friend of the self." "The Self alone is the enemy" — the foe. Whatever other external enemy there is who does harm, even he is set on by the self alone; therefore, the emphatic limitation is well placed — "the Self alone is the enemy of the self."
BG_C06_V06: For the one by whom the very Self has been conquered by the Self, to him the Self is a friend; but for one whose Self is unconquered, the Self alone would remain in the position of an enemy, like a foe.
BG_C06_V06::block-0: It has been declared that the Self alone is the friend of the Self, and the Self alone is the foe of the Self. With reference to that, the question now arises: of what description is the Self that becomes the friend of the Self, and of what description the Self that becomes the foe of the Self? It is in answer to this that the verse follows.
BG_C06_V06::block-1: The Self is the friend of that Self by whom the Self itself has been conquered; that is, of him by whom the aggregate of body and sense-organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta), which is here called "the self," has been brought under control — meaning, of him who has subdued his senses (jitendriya). But for the un-self, that is, for one whose self has not been conquered, the Self itself would abide in the relation of an enemy, just as a foe does. The sense is: just as the un-self in the form of an external enemy works to the harm of one, so too does this very Self engage in working harm against itself.
BG_C06_V07: Of one who has conquered the self and is fully tranquil, the supreme Self stands wholly collected — equally amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise in honour and dishonour.
BG_C06_V07::block-0: Of the jitātmā — of him by whom the aggregate of body and sense-organs called the "self" has been conquered — and who is praśānta, that is, of clear and serene inner organ, being a saṃnyāsin, the supreme Self stands samāhita: it abides directly as his very Self-nature. Such is the meaning. Furthermore, in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise in honour and dishonour — that is, in being worshipped and being slighted — he should be the same.
BG_C06_V08: He whose inner being is satisfied through knowledge and direct realisation, who stands unmoved as the immovable summit, whose senses are wholly subdued — such a yogin is declared yukta, one for whom clod, stone, and gold are alike.
BG_C06_V08::block-0: Jñāna-vijñāna-tṛptātmā — here jñāna is the thorough understanding of the entities expounded in the śāstra, while vijñāna is the making of those very entities, learnt from śāstra, into one's own direct experience (svānubhava-karaṇa). By these two — knowledge and realisation — he in whom the inner organ has become satisfied, in whom the conviction "this suffices, nothing more is wanting" (alaṃ-pratyaya) has arisen — such a one is jñāna-vijñāna-tṛptātmā. He becomes kūṭastha, that is, unshakable; and is one whose senses are wholly conquered. He who is of such a description is called yukta — composed, gathered into samādhi. That yogin is sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcana — one for whom clod, stone, and gold stand on a level: for him to whom these are equal, he is sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcana.
BG_C06_V09: Among well-wishers, friends, foes, neutrals, mediators, those who are hateful, kinsmen, and even among the virtuous and the sinful — he who is of equal vision excels above all.
BG_C06_V09::block-1: Beginning with "suhṛt," the half-verse forms a single compound expression. Suhṛt is one who renders benefit without expecting any return; mitra is one bound by affection; ari is the foe; udāsīna is one who takes no side; madhyastha is he who, between two opposed parties, wishes the welfare of both; dveṣya is one disagreeable to oneself; bandhu is the kinsman. Among these, and likewise among the sādhus — those who follow the śāstra — and even among pāpas — those who do what is forbidden — among all of them his understanding stays equal: that is, his mind is not engaged in calculations such as "who is this, and what does he do for me?" Viśiṣyate — "he excels." There is also the alternative reading vimucyate, "he is liberated." The sense is: among all those who are mounted upon yoga, this one is the foremost.
BG_C06_V10: The yogin, established in solitude, alone, with mind and body restrained, free from longing and free from possessions, should constantly yoke the inner self in concentration.
BG_C06_V10::block-0: Hence, for the attainment of that highest fruit —
BG_C06_V10::block-1: The yogin — the meditator — should yoke, that is, gather into samādhi, the ātman — here the inner organ — sa-tatam, always; rahasi sthitaḥ, dwelling in a solitary place such as a mountain-cave; ekākī, without a companion. By the qualifications "dwelling in solitude" and "alone," it is implied that he should do so after taking up saṃnyāsa. Yata-cittātmā — he by whom both the citta, that is, the inner organ, and the ātman, that is, the body, are subdued, is yata-cittātmā; nirāśīḥ — free from longing; aparigrahaḥ — free from accumulated possessions. The meaning is: even though a saṃnyāsin, having abandoned every form of possession, he should yet engage himself in this yoking.
BG_C06_V11: Having set up for himself in a clean place a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, covered over with cloth, deer-skin, and kuśa grass —
BG_C06_V11::block-0: Now, since for one who is undertaking yoga, a regulation must be stated regarding seat, food, recreation and the like as accessories of yoga, and also the marks of one who has attained yoga together with its fruit — therefore that exposition is now begun. Among these, the seat alone is first taken up:
BG_C06_V11::block-1: In a śuci, that is, a clean and secluded place — clean either by its own nature or by purification through ritual saṃskāra — having set up for himself a steady, immovable āsana, neither too high nor too low; and that āsana is caila-ājina-kuśa-uttara, that is, an āsana upon which cloth, deer-skin, and kuśa grass are spread as the upper covering. Here the order of the items caila and the rest is the reverse of the order of mention — in actual arrangement the kuśa is placed lowest, the deer-skin upon it, and the cloth uppermost.
BG_C06_V12: Seated upon that seat, having made the mind one-pointed and having restrained the activities of mind and senses, let him practise yoga for the purification of the inner being.
BG_C06_V12::block-0: Having set it up — what then?
BG_C06_V12::block-1: There, upon that seat, having sat down, let him practise yoga. How? Withdrawing the mind from all sense-objects and making it one-pointed; being yata-citta-indriya-kriya, that is, he by whom the activities (kriyās) of the citta and the indriyas are subdued, is yata-citta-indriya-kriya. For what purpose should he engage in this yoga? To this it is said: ātma-viśuddhaye — for the purpose of the purification of the inner organ; just this, and nothing else.
BG_C06_V13: Holding body, head, and neck erect and motionless, steady, gazing as it were at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in the directions —
BG_C06_V13::block-0: The external seat has been spoken of; now how the body itself is to be held is set forth —
BG_C06_V13::block-1: Samaṃ kāya-śiro-grīvam — the kāya (trunk), the śiras (head), and the grīvā (neck) — together kāya-śiro-grīvam — these one should hold sama, evenly, and acalam, motionless. For one who only holds them evenly, movement is still possible; therefore He further qualifies it with acalam. Sthiraḥ — having become firm, this is the meaning. Having sam-prekṣya, that is, having performed, as it were, a thorough looking at the tip of his own nose. The word "as it were" (iva) is to be understood as elided. For the actual gazing at one's own nose-tip is not what is here enjoined. What then? The convergence of the eye's vision; and that, too, is intended only as something subordinate to the steadying of the inner organ. For if the gazing at the nose-tip itself were what was intended, the mind would be settled there alone, not in the Self; whereas He will go on to declare the settling of the mind in the Self with the words "having made the mind abide in the Self" (Bh. Gī. 6.25). Therefore, with the elision of the word iva, what is called sam-prekṣya is just the convergence of the gaze of both eyes. And not looking about at the directions: that is, not making any glancing about at the various quarters.
BG_C06_V14: With the inner being thoroughly tranquil, free from fear, established in the vow of the brahmacārin, restraining the mind, with thought fixed on Me, integrated in yoga, let him sit, holding Me as the supreme.
BG_C06_V14::block-1:
Praśāntātmā — he whose ātman, that is, whose inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is exceedingly (prakarṣeṇa) tranquil (śānta); such a one is praśāntātmā. Vigatabhīḥ — one from whom fear has departed. Brahmacāri-vrate sthitaḥ — established in the vow of the brahmacārin, namely brahmacarya, which consists of service to the guru, subsisting on alms-food, and the like; established in that, meaning he should be a practitioner of it.

Further: manaḥ saṃyamya — having drawn back the modifications (vṛtti) of the mind; this is what is meant. Maccittaḥ — he whose thought (citta) is fixed on Me, the supreme Lord; such a one is maccittaḥ. Yuktaḥ — being collected (samāhita), āsīta — he should sit. Matparaḥ — he to whom I am the supreme (para); such a one is matparaḥ.

A certain attached man may have his thought set upon a woman, yet he does not take that very woman as his supreme; rather, he takes some king, or Mahādeva, as supreme. But this yogin is both maccitta and matpara — fixed on Me in thought and holding Me as the highest goal.
BG_C06_V15: Thus ever uniting the self in yoga, the yogin of restrained mind attains the peace whose culmination is nirvāṇa and which abides in Me.
BG_C06_V15::block-0: Now next the fruit of yoga is stated —
BG_C06_V15::block-1:
Yuñjan — performing samādhāna; evam — by the manner already prescribed; sadā ātmānam — the self always; the yogin niyatamānasaḥ — he whose mind (mānasa) is restrained, well-controlled (saṃyata); such a one is niyatamānasaḥ.

Śāntim — the cessation (uparati); nirvāṇa-paramām — that peace whose ultimate (paramā) culmination (niṣṭhā) is nirvāṇa, that is, mokṣa; such a peace is nirvāṇa-paramā. Matsaṃsthām — abiding under My sovereignty, dependent upon Me. Adhigacchati — he reaches, attains.
BG_C06_V16: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor at all for one who does not eat; nor for one given to excess of sleep, nor for one who keeps awake too much, O Arjuna.
BG_C06_V16::block-0: Now the rule for the yogin regarding food and the rest is stated —
BG_C06_V16::block-1:
Na atyaśnataḥ — for one who eats beyond the measure of food suited to himself (ātma-saṃmita), thus eating to excess, there is no yoga. Nor again is there yoga for one who does not eat at all (ekāntam anaśnataḥ). For the śruti says: "That food which is suited to one's measure protects one and does not injure one; what exceeds, injures; what is less than the proper food does not protect" (cf. Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa).

Therefore the yogin should eat neither more nor less than the food suited to his own measure. Or alternatively: for the yogin who eats more than the quantity laid down in the yoga-śāstra, there is no yoga. For it has been said: "Half [the stomach] with food and condiments, the third part with water, and the fourth let him leave empty for the movement of the vital air" — and similar prescriptions of measure.

Likewise, yoga does not arise for one who is given to excessive sleep (atisvapnaśīla); nor again does it come about for one who keeps awake (jāgrat) beyond measure, O Arjuna.
BG_C06_V17: For him whose food and recreation are measured, whose movements in actions are measured, whose sleep and waking are measured, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
BG_C06_V17::block-0: How then does yoga arise? It is said —
BG_C06_V17::block-1:
Yuktāhāra-vihārasya — āhāra (āhriyate iti) is what is taken in, namely food; vihāra is roaming about, the placing of the feet; both being yukta — that is, of fixed measure (niyata-parimāṇa) — for him who has them so, he is yuktāhāra-vihāra; for such a one. So too, yuktaceṣṭasya — for one whose activity (ceṣṭā) in actions is measured (niyatā). So also, yuktasvapnāvabodhasya — for one whose sleep (svapna) and waking (avabodha) are at fixed times.

For such a yogin — of measured food and recreation, of measured activity in actions, of measured sleep and waking — yoga arises as duḥkha-hā: that which slays (hanti) all sorrows is duḥkha-hā; the meaning is that yoga becomes the destroyer of all the sorrow of saṃsāra.
BG_C06_V18: When the well-restrained mind comes to rest in the Self alone, then, free from longing for any of the objects of desire, he is said to be 'integrated in yoga'.
BG_C06_V18::block-0: Now then, when does he become 'integrated in yoga'? It is said —
BG_C06_V18::block-1:
Yadā — when the citta, viniyatam — specifically restrained, well-controlled, having attained one-pointedness, abandoning all thought of external objects, comes to abide in the Self alone (ātmany eva kevale), that is, finds its standing in its own Self — this is the meaning.

Niḥspṛhaḥ sarva-kāmebhyaḥ — the yogin from whom longing (spṛhā), thirst (tṛṣṇā) for both seen and unseen objects has utterly gone forth — such a one, being collected (samāhita), is said to be yukta, at that time.
BG_C06_V19: 'As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker' — this is the simile remembered for the yogin of restrained citta who is practising the yoga of the Self.
BG_C06_V19::block-0: The simile for that yogin's collected citta is now stated —
BG_C06_V19::block-1:
Just as a lamp (dīpa, pradīpa) niavātasthaḥ — standing in a place free from wind — na iṅgate, does not move, does not flicker: that simile (upamā — by which a thing is likened) is smṛtā, has been pondered and recorded by knowers of yoga who have observed the movements of the citta.

For the yogin of yatacitta — of restrained inner organ — who is yuñjat, performing the yoga, that is, practising the samādhi of the Self (ātmanaḥ samādhim anutiṣṭhataḥ) — for such a one, this is the upamā. The meaning is: he is one who is performing the samādhi of the Self.
BG_C06_V20: When the citta, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and when, beholding the Self by the self, he finds contentment in the Self —
BG_C06_V20::block-0: Thus, the citta — having become one-pointed by the strength of the practice of yoga, like a lamp in a windless place —
BG_C06_V20::block-1: Yatra — at which time — the citta uparamate — comes to cessation (uparati), being niruddham — its outward going checked on every side — by yoga-sevā, the practice of yoga; and yatra ca eva — at which time — by ātman, that is, by the inner organ purified through samādhi, beholding ātman — the supreme Caitanya whose nature is light — perceiving It, he is content in his own Self alone (sve eva ātmani tuṣyati), that is, attains contentment.
BG_C06_V21: — that absolute happiness which is grasped by the buddhi alone, beyond the senses, he experiences; established in which, this knower never wavers from the truth.
BG_C06_V21::block-1:
Sukham — happiness; ātyantikam — that which is utterly so, hence ātyantika, meaning endless (ananta); yat tat — which is buddhi-grāhyam, grasped by buddhi alone, independent of the senses, hence buddhi-grāhya; atīndriyam — beyond the range of the senses, that is, not produced by any sense-object, this is the meaning.

Vetti — he experiences such happiness; yatra — at which time. And further, this knower (vidvān), being established in the very nature of the Self, does not from there waver — tattvataḥ, from the very svarūpa of the truth, he does not fall away. This is the meaning.
BG_C06_V22: Having gained which, he reckons no other gain higher than that; and abiding in which, he is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.
BG_C06_V22::block-1: "Having gained which" — having gained, having attained, that gain of the Self; he does not consider, does not entertain the thought, that there is any "other" gain, any further gain, "higher than that." Moreover, abiding "in which" Self-reality he is not shaken even by sorrow of the form of weapon-strokes and the like, however great and heavy.
BG_C06_V23: Let one know that disjunction from union with sorrow as that which goes by the name of yoga; that yoga is to be practised with resolve and with a mind not despondent.
BG_C06_V23::block-0: From "yatropararamate" (Bh. Gītā 6.20) onward, by however many qualifying clauses the particular state of the Self has been described as yoga —
BG_C06_V23::block-1: "Let one know that" — let one understand — as "the disjunction from union with sorrow": union with sorrows is duḥkha-saṁyoga; disjunction from that is duḥkha-saṁyoga-viyoga; let him know that very disjunction from union with sorrow precisely as designated by the name "yoga" — by an inverted characterisation, that is the meaning. Having concluded with the fruit of yoga, by way of fresh resumption the duty of practising yoga is again declared, in order to enjoin resolve and freedom from despondency as the means to yoga. "That" yoga, having such a fruit as has been stated, "is to be practised" with "resolve" — with firm determination — "with a mind not despondent": that which is not despondent is anirviṇṇa. Not despondent — what? The mind: with that mind, with that intellect free from despondency, is the meaning.
BG_C06_V24: Forsaking wholly all the desires that have their origin in saṅkalpa, and restraining the whole troop of senses on every side by the mind alone —
BG_C06_V24::block-1: "Saṅkalpa-prabhavān" — those desires whose source (prabhava) is saṅkalpa are saṅkalpa-prabhava-kāmāḥ; "forsaking," wholly relinquishing, those desires "in entirety," without residue. Furthermore, by the mind alone — endowed with discrimination — "restraining," putting under control, the troop of senses, the aggregate of the senses, "on every side," all around.
BG_C06_V25: Little by little let him cease, by the intellect held with steadfastness; having made the mind established in the Self, let him think of nothing whatever.
BG_C06_V25::block-0: "Little by little" — not all at once — "let him cease," let him bring about cessation. By what? "By the intellect." Of what kind? "Held with steadfastness" — held by dhṛti, that is, by firmness; dhṛti-gṛhītayā — endowed with firmness, is the meaning. Having made the mind "established in the Self" — abiding in the Self in this manner: "the Self alone is the All; apart from That, nothing else whatever exists" — having so made the mind established in the Self, let him think of nothing whatever. This is the supreme injunction of yoga.
BG_C06_V26: Whensoever the mind, fickle and unsteady, wanders forth, from that very cause let him restrain it and lead it back to be subject to the Self alone.
BG_C06_V26::block-0: There, the yogin who has set out to make the mind thus established in the Self —
BG_C06_V26::block-1: "From whatever" cause — sound and the like — the mind, by reason of its inherent defect, "wanders forth," goes out — being "fickle," exceedingly mobile, and for that very reason "unsteady" — "from that very" cause, namely sound and the rest, "having restrained" it, having reduced that very cause to a mere appearance through ascertainment of its true nature and through the cultivation of dispassion, let him "lead" this mind "to be subject to the Self alone," let him bring it under the Self's mastery. Thus, by the strength of yoga-practice, the yogin's mind comes to rest in the Self alone.
BG_C06_V27: For unto this yogin, of mind utterly stilled, with the dust of passion laid to rest, become Brahman, free from blemish, the highest happiness draws near.
BG_C06_V27::block-0: "Of mind utterly stilled" — he whose mind is stilled in supreme degree is praśānta-manāḥ; "unto this" praśānta-manas, this yogin, indeed — happiness, "the highest," the unsurpassable, "draws near," approaches; "with passion stilled" — with the dust of the afflictions, delusion and the rest, worn away, that is the meaning; "become Brahman" — the one liberated while living, possessed of the firm conviction "Brahman alone is the All" — become Brahman; "free from blemish" — devoid of dharma, adharma and the like.
BG_C06_V28: Thus ever yoking himself, the yogin freed from blemish gains with ease the boundless happiness whose touch is Brahman.
BG_C06_V28::block-0: "Thus ever yoking" — by the order described, the yogin, free from impediments to yoga, ever, at all times, "yoking himself," "freed from blemish," devoid of sin, "with ease," effortlessly, gains the happiness whose touch is Brahman: that whose touch is with the supreme Brahman is brahma-saṁsparśa; "boundless" — that which extends past the limit, hence boundless, supreme, unsurpassable — he "reaches," pervades, that happiness.
BG_C06_V29: He whose self is yoked in yoga, of equal vision everywhere, beholds the Self abiding in all beings and all beings abiding in the Self.
BG_C06_V29::block-0: Now is set forth that fruit of yoga, namely the realization of the oneness of Brahman, which is the cause of severance of the entire round of saṁsāra —
BG_C06_V29::block-1: "Abiding in all beings" — abiding in all beings — his own Self; and "all beings" — from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass — abiding "in the Self," come to oneness in the Self — does "he behold," he sees, "whose self is yoked in yoga," whose inner instrument is fully composed; "of equal vision everywhere" — he whose vision, that is, knowledge, having for its object the oneness of Self and Brahman, is equal — undifferenced — in all beings, dissimilar though they be, from Brahmā down to that which is immobile, he is "of equal vision everywhere."
BG_C06_V30: He who sees Me everywhere, and sees all in Me — for him I do not vanish, and he does not vanish from Me. (30)
BG_C06_V30::block-0: The fruit of this vision of the Self's oneness is now declared —
BG_C06_V30::block-1:
He who sees Me, Vāsudeva, the Self of all, everywhere — that is, in all beings — and sees all, the entire array of beings beginning with Brahmā, in Me, the Self of all — for him, the seer of the Self's oneness in this manner, I, the Lord, do not vanish, that is, I do not become indirect or remote.

And he too does not vanish from Me: that knower does not vanish from Me, Vāsudeva — does not become remote — because of the oneness of his Self with Mine. For one's own Self is by very nature dear to oneself, and because I Myself am the seer of the oneness of the Self of all.
BG_C06_V31: Established in oneness, he who worships Me as abiding in all beings — that yogin, in whatever way he conducts himself, abides in Me. (31)
BG_C06_V31::block-0: Restating the import of the previous verse — namely, perfect knowledge — its fruit, liberation, is now declared —
BG_C06_V31::block-1: Conducting himself in every way, in every manner whatsoever, the yogin who possesses perfect knowledge abides in Me, in the supreme Vaiṣṇava state. He is ever-liberated indeed; he is not obstructed by anything in the matter of liberation — this is the meaning.
BG_C06_V32: He who, by the analogy of his own self, sees the same everywhere — be it pleasure or pain, O Arjuna — he is held to be the supreme yogin. (32)
BG_C06_V32::block-1:
Ātmaupamya: ātmā svayameva upamīyate anayā — that by which the self itself is taken as the standard of comparison is upamā; the state of being such an upamā is aupamya; thus 'by the analogy of one's own self.' He who, O Arjuna, sees the same — that is, equally — in all beings everywhere. And what is it that he sees as the same? It is told: just as pleasure is desired by me and is favourable, so too pleasure is favourable to all living beings.

The word vā is in the sense of 'and.' Or — yad vā — whatever pain is unfavourable, undesired by me, just so is pain unfavourable and undesired to all living beings. Thus, by the analogy of one's own self, he sees pleasure and pain — the favourable and the unfavourable — as the same in all beings; he does not act adversely toward anyone — that is, he is non-injurious. He who is thus non-injurious and steadfast in perfect knowledge — that yogin is held, that is, regarded, as paramaḥ, the highest, the most excellent, among all yogins.
BG_C06_V33::block-0: Observing that the yoga that has the character of perfect knowledge, as just described, is hard to attain, Arjuna, eager to learn the certain means of attaining it, said —
BG_C06_V33::block-1: This yoga which has been declared by you, O Madhusūdana, as marked by sameness — by even-mindedness — of this yoga I do not see, do not perceive, a steady, unshaking sthiti, on account of the fickleness of the mind. What is it that he does not see? — sthirām, firm; acalām, unmoving — sthiti, abidance.
BG_C06_V34: For the mind is fickle, O Kṛṣṇa, agitating, mighty and tenacious; its restraint, I deem, is exceedingly hard to achieve — like the wind's. (34)
BG_C06_V34::block-1:
For the mind is fickle. The word 'Kṛṣṇa' is the form derived from the root 'kṛṣ,' meaning 'to draw or scrape.' Because He draws away the faults — sins and the rest — of His devotees, He is Kṛṣṇa; the vocative thereof is 'O Kṛṣṇa.' Hi — because — the mind is cañcalam, fickle: not merely exceedingly fickle, but pramāthi as well — of an agitating nature; agitating the body and the senses, by tossing them about, it brings them under another's sway.

Further, balavat — strong, mighty: it cannot be controlled by anyone, being hard to ward off. Further still, dṛḍham — firm, like the snake-cord, impossible to cut. Of such a mind I deem the niggraha, the restraint, the curbing, to be — as of the wind: just as the restraint of the wind is hard to accomplish, so I deem this still harder than that — such is the import.
BG_C06_V35::block-0: The Blessed Lord said: 'It is just so as you say' —
BG_C06_V35::block-1:
Beyond doubt, there is no doubt that 'the mind is hard to restrain and unsteady,' in this matter, O mighty-armed one. But, however — abhyāsena tu — abhyāsa is the repeated turning of the mind, on some one chosen ground, to a single uniform cognition. Vairāgyena — vairāgya is freedom from craving, born of repeated contemplation of the defects in the seen and the unseen objects of enjoyment.

And by that vairāgya, the wandering of the mind, in the form of distraction, is checked. Thus is that mind taken hold of — that is, restrained, curbed — this is the meaning.
BG_C06_V36: By one whose self is unsubdued, yoga, I deem, is hard to attain; but by one of subdued self, striving, it can be attained through the means. (36)
BG_C06_V36::block-0: But for him whose self is unsubdued —
BG_C06_V36::block-1:
Asaṃyatātmanā — by one whose antaḥkaraṇa, the inner organ, is unsubdued by abhyāsa and vairāgya: he is asaṃyatātmā; by such a one, yoga is duṣprāpa, hard to attain — that is, attained only with difficulty. Such is My judgement.

But he whose ātman, that is, mind, has been brought into mastery by abhyāsa and vairāgya — such a one is vaśyātmā; by him, vaśyātmā, however — striving, that is, making strenuous and repeated effort — yoga can be attained: by the means, that is, through the means already declared.
BG_C06_V37::block-0: Therein, by undertaking the practice of yoga, the works that are the cause of attaining this world and the next have been renounced; and yet the fruit of the perfection of yoga — perfect knowledge, the means to liberation — has not been attained. Apprehending the destruction of such a yogin who has fallen away from the path of yoga, his mind grown unsteady at the time of death, Arjuna said —
BG_C06_V37::block-1: Ayatiḥ — he who does not strive — though endowed with śraddhā, with the conviction of belief, on the path of yoga; whose mind, at the moment of the end, has fallen away — calita-mānasa — whose memory is shattered — he, not having attained the consummation of yoga, the fruit of yoga, namely perfect knowledge — what course, O Kṛṣṇa, does he go to?
BG_C06_V38: Fallen from both, without support, perplexed on the path of Brahman, does he not perish, O mighty-armed one, like a riven cloud? (38)
BG_C06_V38::block-0: kaccit — is it not so? — n'obhayavibhraṣṭaḥ — fallen from both, that is, fallen away both from the path of works (karma-mārga) and from the path of yoga (yoga-mārga) — chinnābhram iva naśyati, perishes like a riven cloud; or does he not perish? apratiṣṭhaḥ, without support, lacking any resting-place, O mighty-armed one (mahābāho), being viṃūḍhaḥ, deluded, brahmaṇaḥ pathi, on the path of Brahman, that is, on the road that leads to the attainment of Brahman.
BG_C06_V39: This doubt of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, You alone are competent to cut away without remainder; for, other than You, no one capable of severing this doubt can be found. (39)
BG_C06_V39::block-0: etat me, this doubt of mine, kṛṣṇa, You are fit to cut away (chettum arhasi), to remove it aśeṣataḥ, leaving no remainder. tvad-anyaḥ, other than You — that is, any seer or even a deity apart from Yourself — cannot stand forth as the severer (chettā), the destroyer, of this doubt; for such a one na hi upapadyate, simply does not come into being, is not possible. The purport, therefore, is: You alone are competent to cut it away.
BG_C06_V40:
The Lord said:

O Pārtha, neither here nor hereafter is there destruction for him; for never, dear one, does any doer of good come to a base course. (40)
BG_C06_V40::block-0: O Pārtha, na eva iha loke — not in this world — na amutra, nor in the other, the higher world — does any vināśaḥ, destruction, exist for him; there is none. What is here called "destruction" is the obtaining of a birth lower than the previous one; that does not befall the one fallen from yoga. For — na hi — no kalyāṇa-kṛt, doer of auspicious deeds, ever comes to a durgatim, an evil course, a despicable goal. He addresses him as tāta, dear one: he who extends himself (tanoti ātmānaṁ) in the form of his son is called pitā, and so tāta. Reciprocally, the father himself appearing as the son, the son too is addressed as tāta; and the disciple too, being like a son, is addressed as tāta. Such a one does not go (na gacchati) to an evil course.
BG_C06_V41: Having attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and dwelt there for unending years, the one fallen from yoga is born in the home of the pure and the prosperous. (41)
BG_C06_V41::block-0: But what then becomes of him? —
BG_C06_V41::block-1: The renunciate (saṁnyāsin) who has set out upon the path of yoga, by the strength of that very practice, prāpya — having attained, having gone to — puṇya-kṛtām lokān, the worlds of those who have performed meritorious rites such as the Aśvamedha; and there uṣitvā, having dwelt, having enjoyed his sojourn for śāśvatīḥ samāḥ, eternal — that is, very long — years, then on the exhaustion of that enjoyment, śucīnām — of those who act as the scriptures enjoin, that is, the pure — śrīmatām — of those endowed with prosperity and lordly fortune — gehe, in the household, the yoga-bhraṣṭa abhijāyate, takes birth.
BG_C06_V42: Or else he is born in the very family of yogins, of the wise. Such a birth as this is exceedingly hard to obtain in the world. (42)
BG_C06_V42::block-0: Or else (athavā), apart from the families of the prosperous, he comes to be born — bhavati, jāyate — in the very household of yogins, even of indigent ones, of the wise (dhīmatām), the intelligent. Such a birth as this — namely, in the family of poor yogins — is durlabha-taram, far harder to obtain, far more difficult to win, even compared to the former; for such a birth as this, in the very kind of family just described, is exceedingly rare in the world.
BG_C06_V43: There he regains that union with the discriminative faculty acquired in his former body, and from that he strives further toward perfection, O joy of the Kurus. (43)
BG_C06_V43::block-1: tatra, there, in the family of yogins, he obtains taṁ buddhi-saṁyogam — the saṁyoga, conjunction, with that very buddhi, the discriminative awareness; this conjunction is pauradehikam, that which had arisen in the former body (pūrva-deha-bhavam). And, ttaḥ, from that, namely from the saṁskāra acquired in the previous birth, yatate, he exerts himself, makes effort, bhūyaḥ — yet more abundantly — toward saṁsiddhi, the cause of perfect attainment, O joy of the Kurus (kuru-nandana).
