BG_C06_V44: By that very former practice he is borne onward, even though without will of his own. Even the mere seeker after yoga transcends the Veda's word-Brahman. (44)
BG_C06_V44::block-0: How does this conjunction with the buddhi of the former body come about? That is being told —
BG_C06_V44::block-1: The abhyāsa, practice, performed in the former birth — this is pūrva-abhyāsa; by that very pūrva-abhyāsa, being powerful, he is borne (hriyate) toward perfect attainment (saṁsiddhi); for, even avaśaḥ — without volition, helplessly — saḥ, that one fallen from yoga, is so carried. If there has not been performed any deed of the nature of adharma and the like, more powerful than the saṁskāra arising from the practice of yoga, then he is borne by the saṁskāra produced from yoga-practice itself. If, however, an adharma stronger than that has been done, by it the saṁskāra born of yoga is indeed overpowered; yet on the exhaustion of that adharma, the yoga-born saṁskāra of itself begins its work — for there is no destruction of that saṁskāra even after a long lapse of time. This is the meaning. Therefore, jijñāsuḥ api yogasya — even one who merely wishes to know the very nature of yoga — that is, the saṁnyāsin who has set out on the path of yoga, the yoga-bhraṣṭa — by the very strength of his having so set forth, even he atikrāmati, transcends, casts beyond, the śabda-brahman, the fruit yielded by the performance of works enjoined in the Veda; how much more, then, the one who, having understood, is established in yoga and pursues its practice.
BG_C06_V45: But the yogin striving with effort, his impurities thoroughly washed away, perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal. (45)
BG_C06_V45::block-0: On what further ground, then, is the state of being a yogin the higher good? —
BG_C06_V45::block-1: prayatnāt yatamānaḥ — striving with effort, that is, exerting himself with redoubled diligence. Among such, the yogin, the man of knowledge (vidvān), saṁśuddha-kilbiṣaḥ — one whose impurities are thoroughly purified, whose sins are altogether washed away — aneka-janma-saṁsiddhaḥ — across many births accumulating one after another some little impression of saṁskāra, and through that accumulated mass, wrought across many births, brought to perfection — thereupon (tataḥ), having attained right vision (samyag-darśana), proceeds, yāti, to the parā gati, the supreme, the most excellent goal.
BG_C06_V46: The yogin is greater than ascetics, and is held to be greater even than men of knowledge; the yogin is greater than men of works as well — therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogin.
BG_C06_V46::block-1: The yogin is greater than ascetics. "Even than men of knowledge" — knowledge here means proficiency in the meaning of scripture (śāstrārtha-pāṇḍitya); even than those endowed with that, he is held, that is, known, to be higher, more excellent. "Than men of works" — that is, than those who perform works such as the agnihotra and the like; than those endowed with such works also, the yogin is greater, distinguished. Since this is so, become a yogin, O Arjuna.
BG_C06_V47: Among all yogins, he who, with his inner self gone unto Me, full of faith, worships Me — he is held by Me to be the most steadfastly united.
BG_C06_V47::block-0: Among all yogins — that is, even among those devoted to meditation upon Rudra, the Ādityas and the like — he who, with his inner self, his inner organ (antaḥ-karaṇa), gone unto Me, that is, gathered into Me, Vāsudeva, being full of faith, possessed of śraddhā, worships, serves Me — he, in My estimation, is the most steadfastly united (yukta-tama), supremely yoked; that is My settled view.
BG_C07_V01::block-0: Having set forth the seed of the question — "Of all yogins, he who, with his inner self gone unto Me, full of faith, worships Me, is held by Me to be the most steadfastly united" (BG 6.47) — the Blessed Lord Himself, wishing to declare "Such is My true nature; thus would one be one whose inner self is fixed on Me," speaks —
BG_C07_V01::block-1: He whose mind is fastened on Me — on the Supreme Lord, qualified by the attributes about to be set forth — is "one with mind fastened on Me" (mayy-āsakta-manāḥ); O Pārtha, practising yoga, that is, accomplishing the gathering together of the mind in samādhi; "having Me as resort" (mad-āśraya) — he whose resort is Myself, the Supreme Lord alone, is "one resorting to Me." For whoever desires some object of human pursuit takes recourse to some means for accomplishing it — works such as the agnihotra, austerity, gift-giving, or the like — but this yogin takes recourse to Me alone as his resort; abandoning every other means whatsoever, he becomes one whose mind is fastened on Me alone. How thou, being such, shalt know Me, the whole, the entire, the One endowed with the attributes of glory, strength, power, sovereignty, and the rest, without doubt — that is, by what manner thou shalt know Me beyond the shadow of doubt, with the certitude "thus indeed is the Blessed Lord" — that hear, as it is being declared by Me.
BG_C07_V02: I shall declare to thee, in its entirety, this knowledge together with realization, knowing which there remains nothing else here yet to be known.
BG_C07_V02::block-1: I shall declare to thee this knowledge "together with vijñāna" — accompanied by direct personal experience (sva-anubhava-yukta) — entirely, in its fullness. He extols the knowledge He intends to declare, in order to turn the listener's mind toward it: knowing which knowledge, here in this world there does not remain again any other thing yet to be known as the means of human attainment; that is, it does not remain unaccomplished. The meaning is: he who knows the truth concerning Me becomes all-knowing. Hence, on account of its yielding so distinguished a fruit, this knowledge is rare to obtain.
BG_C07_V03: Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; even of those who strive and are accomplished, scarcely one knows Me in truth.
BG_C07_V03::block-1: Among many thousands of men, scarcely one makes effort, that is, exertion, for the sake of accomplishment (siddhi). Of those making effort and accomplished — for they alone are the truly accomplished who strive for liberation — among those, scarcely one indeed knows Me in truth, just as I am.
BG_C07_V04: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and egoity — thus is My nature divided eightfold.
BG_C07_V04::block-0: Having turned the listener's face toward it by enticement, He says —
BG_C07_V04::block-1: "Earth" — by this is meant the subtle element (tan-mātra) of earth, not the gross element, on the strength of the statement "My nature divided eightfold." In the same way, water and the rest also are spoken of as the very subtle elements — water, fire, air, ether. By "mind" the cause of the mind, namely the ahaṅkāra, is taken. By "intellect" the great principle (mahat-tattva), the cause of the ahaṅkāra. By "ahaṅkāra" is taken the unmanifest (avyakta) conjoined with avidyā. Just as food conjoined with poison is called "poison," even so the unmanifest, the root cause, being scented through with the latent impression of egoity (ahaṅkāra-vāsanā), is here called "ahaṅkāra," because of the ahaṅkāra's being the prime mover in initiating activity. For in the world it is the ahaṅkāra alone that is observed to be the seed of all engagement (pravṛtti-bīja). "Thus, this" — the nature spoken of as above — "is Mine," the sovereign māyā-power belonging to Me, the Lord, divided eightfold, that is, having come to division.
BG_C07_V05: This is the lower; but other than this, know My higher nature, the very Jīva, O mighty-armed, by which this universe is upheld.
BG_C07_V05::block-0: "Lower" — not higher, debased, impure, productive of ill, of the very nature of the bondage of saṃsāra — such is this. But other than this, that is, other than the one just spoken of, know thou My pure nature, that which is My very Self, as higher, more excellent, of the form of the Jīva, having the characteristic of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), serving as the cause of the upholding of the vital breaths — O mighty-armed — by which nature, having entered within, this universe is upheld.
BG_C07_V06: Bear in mind that all beings have these as their womb. I am the origin of the entire universe, and likewise its dissolution.
BG_C07_V06::block-0: "Having these as womb" — these two natures, the lower and the higher, characterized as the Field and the Knower of the Field, are the womb, the source, of which beings — they are "having these as womb" — that is, all beings; thus apprehend, know thou. Inasmuch as My two natures are the womb, the cause, of all beings, therefore I am the origin, the arising, of the entire, the whole universe, and its dissolution, its destruction, likewise. The meaning is that, by way of the pair of natures, I, the omniscient Lord, am the cause of the universe.
BG_C07_V07: There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya. All this is strung on Me, like rows of gems on a thread.
BG_C07_V07::block-1: There is no other cause, none whatsoever, higher than Me — than the Supreme Lord; the meaning is, I alone am the cause of the world, O Dhanañjaya. Because it is thus, in Me, the Supreme Lord, all beings — this entire world — is strung (protam), that is, threaded, pervaded, interwoven, knotted together, as cloth is upon long warp-threads, and as rows of gems are upon a thread.
BG_C07_V08: I am the taste in waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun; the syllable Om in all the Vedas, sound in space, and manhood in men.
BG_C07_V08::block-0: By which qualifying attributes is it said that all this is strung in You? —
BG_C07_V08::block-1: I am taste — what is the essence of water, that is taste; the meaning is that in Me, who am of the nature of taste, the waters are strung. So in every case. As I am taste in waters, so am I the radiance (prabhā) in the moon and the sun. The syllable Om (praṇava) is in all the Vedas; in Me, who am of the nature of the praṇava, all the Vedas are strung. So too, in space (kha, ākāśa) the essence is sound; in Me, who am that sound, space is strung. Likewise, manhood (pauruṣam) — being-a-puruṣa is pauruṣam, that on account of which the cognition "this is a man" arises in regard to men; in Me, who am that, men are strung.
BG_C07_V09: I am the holy fragrance in earth, and the brilliance in fire; the life in all beings, and the austerity in ascetics.
BG_C07_V09::block-0: I am the holy fragrance — the sweet-smelling fragrance — in earth; in Me, who am of the nature of fragrance, the earth is strung. The naturally holy character of fragrance is shown with reference to earth in order to imply, by the same token, the holy character of taste and the rest in waters and the other elements. The unholy character, on the other hand, of fragrance and the rest, accruing to transmigratory beings on the basis of avidyā-laden attributes and the like, comes about through their contact with particular elemental conditions. And I am brilliance, that is, blazing radiance, in fire (vibhāvasu). So too, the life in all beings — that by which all beings live is "life." And I am austerity in ascetics; in Me, who am that austerity, the ascetics are strung.
BG_C07_V10: Know Me, O Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings; I am the intellect of the intelligent, the splendour of the splendid.
BG_C07_V10::block-0: Know Me, O Pārtha, as the seed — the cause of sprouting — of all beings, sanātana, that is, perennial. Further: I am the intellect — the discriminative power of the inner organ — of the intelligent, that is, of those who possess such discriminative power; and I am splendour — boldness, vigour — of the splendid, those who possess that.
BG_C07_V11: I am the strength of the strong, devoid of desire and passion; in beings I am desire that is not opposed to dharma, O bull of Bharatas.
BG_C07_V11::block-0: I am the strength — capacity, vigour — of the strong; and that strength is devoid of desire and passion. Desire (kāma) and passion (rāga) together are kāma-rāgau — desire is craving for objects not yet at hand, passion is the relishing colouration in regard to objects already obtained. The strength, the sattva, that is bereft of these two — kāma and rāga — and is meant only for the sustaining of the body and the like, that strength I am; not the kind that, for transmigrating beings, is the cause of craving and passion. Further — that desire (kāma) which, in living beings, is not opposed to dharma — that is, not opposed to the meaning of the scripture — for instance, the desire for food, drink and the like meant only for the sustaining of the body, that desire I am, O bull of the Bharatas.
BG_C07_V12: Whatever sāttvika states there are, and whatever rājasa and tāmasa, know that they proceed solely from Me; yet I am not in them — they are in Me.
BG_C07_V12::block-1: Those states (bhāvas) — entities — that are sāttvika, brought forth from sattva; rājasa, brought forth from rajas; and tāmasa, brought forth from tamas; whichever of these states arise in living beings on account of their own karma — know all of them, the entire lot, as arising from Me alone. Although they arise from Me, yet I am not in them, am not subordinate to them, not under their sway, as transmigrating beings are. Rather, they are in Me, under My sway, dependent on Me.
BG_C07_V13: Deluded by these three states made of the guṇas, this whole world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and immutable.
BG_C07_V13::block-0: Even though He is thus — the Supreme Lord, of the nature of eternal purity, awareness and freedom, the Self of all beings, devoid of guṇas, the cause of burning up the seed of the defects of saṃsāra — yet the world does not recognize Me. Such is the compassion the Lord shows. And what is the cause of the world's ignorance? That is now told —
BG_C07_V13::block-1: By these three guṇa-modifications — these states or entities of the form of attachment, aversion, delusion and the like — by these aforesaid states, all this — the entire host of living beings, the world — has been deluded, that is, brought into a condition of non-discrimination, and so does not recognize Me, who am beyond, that is, distinct and disparate from these aforesaid guṇas, and immutable (avyaya), free from waning, devoid of every modification of state such as birth and the rest. That is the meaning.
BG_C07_V14: For this divine māyā of Mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross over; those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this māyā.
BG_C07_V14::block-0: How then does one cross over this divine māyā, of the nature of the three guṇas, that belongs to Viṣṇu? It is now told —
BG_C07_V14::block-1: Divine — for it is the innate nature of the Deva, that is, of Me, the Lord, Viṣṇu — for this aforesaid māyā of Mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross (duratyayā): she whose crossing-over, whose passing beyond, comes only with great pain, is duratyayā. That being so, those who, abandoning all dharmas, take refuge with their entire being in Me alone — the wielder of māyā, the very Self of theirs — they cross over, they pass beyond, this māyā that deludes all beings; they are released from the bondage of saṃsāra. That is the meaning.
BG_C07_V15: The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in Me; their knowledge has been carried off by māyā, and they cling to the demoniac mode of being.
BG_C07_V15::block-0: If those who take refuge in You cross over this māyā, then why is it that not all take refuge in You alone? In answer to this it is said —
BG_C07_V15::block-1: Me, the supreme Lord, Nārāyaṇa, the evil-doers — those who perform sinful deeds — the deluded, the lowest of men — that is, the most degraded and despicable among men — do not take refuge in. And they have their knowledge carried off by māyā, their discernment thoroughly stolen away; and they cling to the demoniac mode of being, marked by violence, falsehood, and the like.
BG_C07_V16: Four kinds of meritorious men worship Me, O Arjuna — the afflicted, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of knowledge, O bull of the Bharatas.
BG_C07_V16::block-0: But those who are the noblest of men, the doers of meritorious deeds —
BG_C07_V16::block-1: Of four kinds, of four sorts, do they worship — that is, serve — Me, the people who are meritorious doers of pious deeds, O Arjuna. The afflicted (ārta) is one seized by affliction, overcome and beset by thieves, tigers, disease, and the like; the seeker of knowledge (jijñāsu) is one who desires to know the true nature of the Lord; the seeker of wealth (arthārthī) is one who desires riches; and the man of knowledge (jñānī) is the knower of the reality of Viṣṇu, O bull of the Bharatas.
BG_C07_V17: Among them, the man of knowledge, ever-yoked, of single-pointed devotion, stands out; for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me.
BG_C07_V17::block-0: Among those four, the man of knowledge — the knower of the truth — is, by virtue of his knowing the truth, ever-yoked (nityayuktaḥ) and of single-pointed devotion (ekabhaktiḥ), since he sees no other worthy of being worshipped. Hence, that one of single-pointed devotion stands out — that is, attains pre-eminence, surpasses the others; this is the meaning. "For I am dear" — since I am the very Self of the man of knowledge, therefore I am exceedingly dear to him; for it is well known in the world that "the Self is dear." Hence, by virtue of being the very Self of the man of knowledge, Vāsudeva is dear to him — this is the sense. And he, the man of knowledge, being verily My — that is, Vāsudeva's — own Self, is exceedingly dear to Me.
BG_C07_V18: All these are indeed noble; but the man of knowledge is My very Self — this is My judgement. For he, with his self firmly fixed (in Me), is established in Me alone as the unsurpassable Goal.
BG_C07_V18::block-0: Are not, then, the afflicted and the other three not dear to Vāsudeva? Not so. Then what? —
BG_C07_V18::block-1: Noble — that is, exalted — are all these without exception; the meaning is that all three of them too are dear to Me. For no devotee of Mine is unloved by Me, Vāsudeva. The man of knowledge, however, is exceedingly dear — this is the distinction. Why so? It is therefore said: but the man of knowledge is My very Self, no other than Myself — this is My judgement, My settled conclusion. "Established" — that is, who has set himself to ascend — that man of knowledge, since (he holds) "I am verily Bhagavān Vāsudeva, and none other," being thus yuktātmā — of well-collected mind — has set out to attain Me alone, the supreme Brahman, the unsurpassable Goal that is to be reached. This is the meaning.
BG_C07_V19: At the end of many births, the man endowed with knowledge takes refuge in Me, (realizing) "Vāsudeva is all"; such a great soul is exceedingly hard to find.
BG_C07_V19::block-0: The man of knowledge is praised yet again —
BG_C07_V19::block-1: At the end — at the completion — of many births that have served as receptacles for the saṃskāras conducive to knowledge, he who is endowed with knowledge — whose knowledge has reached its full ripening — takes refuge in Me, Vāsudeva, the inmost Self, by direct realization. How? "Vāsudeva is all" — thus. He who in this manner realizes Me, Nārāyaṇa, the Self of all, is the great soul (mahātmā); none equal to him exists, nor any superior. Hence he is exceedingly hard to find — for it has been said, "Among thousands of men…" (BG 7.3).
BG_C07_V20: Those whose knowledge has been carried off by this or that desire take refuge in other deities, adopting this or that observance, constrained by their own (inborn) nature.
BG_C07_V20::block-0: The cause of one's not realizing "the Self alone is the all, is Vāsudeva" is now stated —
BG_C07_V20::block-1: Those whose knowledge has been carried off by this or that desire — for sons, cattle, heaven, and the like — that is, those whose discriminative knowledge has been thoroughly stolen away, take refuge in other deities — they reach deities other than the Self, who is Vāsudeva. Adopting — resorting to — this or that observance, the particular regimen well-established for the propitiation of (each) deity, constrained — that is, regulated — by their own nature, by the particular saṃskāra acquired in former births and that has now become their disposition.
BG_C07_V21: Whatever form any devotee desires to worship with faith, that very faith of his I render unwavering.
BG_C07_V21::block-1: Whichever desire-laden person, endowed with faith and being a devotee, desires to worship — that is, to do pūjā to — whichever form of a deity, that very faith of that desire-laden one I render unwavering, that is, I make firm and steady.
BG_C07_V22: Endowed with that faith, he engages in the propitiation of that (deity), and from it obtains those desires, which have indeed been ordained by Me alone.
BG_C07_V22::block-0: He who, by force of his prior tendency arising from his innate nature, sets out to worship some deity-form with faith —
BG_C07_V22::block-1: He, endowed with that faith ordained by Me, engages — that is, exerts himself — in the propitiation, the worship, of that form of the deity. And from that — that is, from that propitiated deity-form — he obtains the desired objects, namely, those desires that have been ordained, fashioned, by Me alone, the omniscient supreme Lord, by virtue of My knowing the apportionment of the fruits of action; for since those desires have been ordained by Bhagavān, he therefore necessarily attains them — this is the meaning. If the word-division is taken as 'hitān' ("beneficial"), the beneficial-ness of desires must be construed in a figurative sense; for desires are not, in truth, beneficial to anyone.
BG_C07_V23: But finite is the fruit that accrues to those of small understanding; the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, while My devotees come to Me alone.
BG_C07_V23::block-0: Since the very means employed by these undiscriminating, desire-laden persons are themselves finite in their operation, therefore —
BG_C07_V23::block-1: The fruit which accrues to them — those of small understanding, that is, those whose discernment is meagre — is antavat, perishable, finite. Devān devayajo yānti: those who worship the gods are devayajaḥ, sacrificers to the gods; they go to the gods. Mad-bhaktā yānti mām api: My devotees come to Me alone. Thus, even though the exertion is equal in both cases, these worshippers do not take refuge in Me alone for an unending fruit, but, alas, persist in great hardship — in this way the Lord shows His compassionate concern.
BG_C07_V24: The unintelligent, not knowing My higher nature — imperishable and unsurpassed — think that I, the Unmanifest, have come into manifestation.
BG_C07_V24::block-0: On what account, then, do they not take refuge in Me alone? — that is now stated.
BG_C07_V24::block-1: Avyaktam — unmanifest, unrevealed; vyaktim āpannam — having come into the manifest, having attained visibility, just now. Manyante mām: they think of Me, though I am the ever-established Lord, in this manner. Abuddhayaḥ — the unintelligent, those without discernment. Param bhāvam — the supreme nature, the very Self-form of the Paramātman. Ajānantaḥ — being ignorant. Mama avyayam — My imperishable, exempt from decline; anuttamam — unsurpassed, beyond which there is none higher; not knowing this nature that is Mine, they think thus — such is the meaning.
BG_C07_V25: I am not manifest to all, being veiled by My yoga-māyā; this deluded world does not recognise Me, the unborn, the imperishable.
BG_C07_V25::block-0: What is the cause of that ignorance? — that is now stated.
BG_C07_V25::block-1:
I am not the prakāśa — not manifestly known — to all, that is, to the world at large; the implication is that I am manifest only to some, namely, My devotees. Yoga-māyā-samāvṛtaḥ: yoga is the conjunction or fitting together of the guṇas; that very combination is māyā — hence yoga-māyā; veiled by that yoga-māyā, that is, concealed — such is the meaning. Therefore this deluded world does not recognise Me, the unborn (aja), the imperishable (avyaya).

Though this world, veiled by yoga-māyā, does not recognise Me, that yoga-māyā, being Mine — belonging to Me, the Lord, the Wielder of māyā — does not obstruct My own knowledge, just as another magician's māyā does not obstruct his own knowledge of his māyā.
BG_C07_V26: I know, O Arjuna, the beings that are past, those that are present, and those that are yet to come; but no one knows Me.
BG_C07_V26::block-1: I, however, do know — comprehend — the beings that are samatītāni, fully past and gone, those vartamānāni that are present, O Arjuna, and those bhaviṣyāṇi that are yet to come; all these I know. But Me, no one knows — except the one who is My devotee, who has taken refuge in Me. It is precisely because of the absence of knowledge of My true nature that the rest do not worship Me.
BG_C07_V27: By the delusion of the pairs of opposites born of desire and aversion, O scorcher of foes, all beings come to utter bewilderment at birth, O Bhārata.
BG_C07_V27::block-0: By what obstacle to the knowledge of My true nature, then, are all beings, when they come to be born, hindered, so that they do not know Me? — in answer to this expectation, He says —
BG_C07_V27::block-1: Icchā-dveṣa-samutthena: icchā and dveṣa are desire and aversion; that which arises from these two is icchā-dveṣa-samuttha — by that. Anticipating the question 'by what specifically?', He says: dvandva-mohena — the delusion caused by the pairs (dvandva-nimittaḥ mohaḥ = dvandva-mohaḥ); by that. Those very desire and aversion — like cold and heat, mutually opposed, having for their objects pleasure and pain and their causes, becoming connected with all beings according to the season — are designated by the term dvandva. Wherever and whenever desire and aversion attain their reality through the encounter with pleasure and pain and their causes, then these two, by drawing the discernment of all beings under their own sway, generate that delusion which is the cause obstructing the rise of knowledge concerning the truth of the supreme Self. For one whose mind is overpowered by the defects of desire and aversion, true knowledge of objects does not arise even with respect to outer things; how much less, then, need it be said that for one whose intellect is invaded and bewildered by them, knowledge of the inner Self — surrounded as it is by many obstructions — does not arise. Therefore, by that delusion of the pairs born of desire and aversion, O Bhārata, scion of the line of Bharata, all beings, becoming utterly bewildered, attain saṃmoha — utter delusion — sarge, at birth, that is, at the time of coming forth, O scorcher of foes (parantapa). The intent is that all beings, on coming to be born, are born only under the sway of delusion. Since this is so, therefore, all beings, their understanding obstructed by that delusion of the pairs and thus utterly bewildered, do not know Me as their very Self; and precisely on that account they do not adore Me as the Self.
BG_C07_V28: But those persons of meritorious deeds whose evil has reached its end — they, freed from the delusion of the pairs, worship Me, firm in their vow.
BG_C07_V28::block-0: Who, then, are they that, freed from this delusion of the pairs, having known Thee, worship Thee with the conviction that Thou art their very Self, in accordance with the scripture? — to display this expected meaning, it is said —
BG_C07_V28::block-1: But those — yeṣām — whose pāpa, sin, has reached its end (anta-gatam), nearly exhausted, worn out; jananām, of those persons, puṇya-karmaṇām, who possess meritorious action, that is, action serving as the cause of purification of the inner instrument (sattva-śuddhi) — they are called puṇya-karmāṇaḥ. They, freed from the aforesaid delusion of the pairs, worship Me, the supreme Self, dṛḍha-vratāḥ — firm in their vow. Those whose discernment is settled with the resolve, 'Thus alone is the supreme Truth, not otherwise,' through the vow of total renunciation, are termed dṛḍha-vratāḥ — firm in their vow.
BG_C07_V29: Those who, taking refuge in Me, strive for liberation from old age and death — they know that Brahman, the entire adhyātma, and karma in its fullness.
BG_C07_V29::block-0: For what purpose do they worship? — that is now stated.
BG_C07_V29::block-1: Jarā-maraṇa-mokṣāya — for the sake of liberation from old age and death — taking refuge in Me, the supreme Lord, with their minds firmly fixed upon Me (mat-samāhita-cittāḥ), those who strive (yatanti) — they know that supreme Brahman; they know the entire (kṛtsnam, samastam) adhyātma — the reality pertaining to the inner Self (pratyag-ātma-viṣayam vastu); and they know karma also in its entirety (akhilam, samastam).
BG_C07_V30: Those who know Me as together with the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva, and together with the adhiyajña — they, with mind firmly poised, know Me even at the hour of departure.
BG_C07_V30::block-0: Sādhibhūtādhidaivam: adhibhūta and adhidaiva together are adhibhūtādhidaivam; that which exists together with the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva is sa-adhibhūtādhidaivam — those who know Me thus; and sādhiyajñam — accompanied by the adhiyajña — those who know Me thus also; at the hour of departure, that is, even at the time of death (maraṇa-kāla), they know Me — yukta-cetasaḥ, they whose minds are firmly composed and concentrated. Such is the meaning.
BG_C08_V01::block-0: By the Lord, in passages such as 'They know that Brahman in its entirety' (Bh. Gī. 7.29), the seeds of Arjuna's questions have been sown. Therefore, in order to ask about those very topics, Arjuna spoke —
BG_C08_V02:
What is that Brahman? What is the Self (adhyātma)? What is action (karma), O most excellent of men? What is said to be 'over the elements' (adhibhūta), and what is called 'over the divinities' (adhidaiva)?

Who here, in this body, is the 'lord of sacrifice' (adhiyajña), and how, O Madhusūdana? And how, at the time of departure, are You to be known by those of disciplined Self?
BG_C08_V03::block-0: For the determination of these questions in due order, the Blessed Lord spoke —
BG_C08_V03::block-1:
'That which does not perish (na kṣarati) is akṣara' — hence akṣara is the supreme Self (Paramātman), as the śruti declares: 'Verily, O Gārgī, under the rule of this Imperishable…' (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.9). And the syllable Oṁ is excluded here because it is separately specified later as 'Oṁ, the one-syllabled Brahman' (Bh. Gī. 8.13). The qualifier 'supreme' (paramam) too is most fittingly applied to the unsurpassable Brahman, the Imperishable.

The very being of that supreme Brahman as the inner Self in each body — that is its 'own state' (svabhāva); and svabhāva (sva-bhāva, the vigraha being 'one's own being'), pertaining to the embodied self, is what is termed adhyātma. The reality which, taking the body-self as its locus, presents itself as the inner Self and culminates in the supreme Brahman — that 'own being' is called adhyātma; it is designated by the word adhyātma.

Bhūta-bhāvodbhava-karaḥ: 'bhūta-bhāva' is the becoming of beings; its arising (udbhava) is bhūta-bhāvodbhava; that which produces this is bhūta-bhāvodbhava-kara — meaning the cause of the genesis of the substance of beings. Visarga is visarjana, the relinquishing of substance such as caru, puroḍāśa, etc., aimed at a deity; this very act characterised by visarga is the sacrifice (yajña), and it is what is denoted by the term karma. From this, indeed, as from a seed, through the sequence of rain and so forth, beings stationary and moving spring forth.
BG_C08_V04: Adhibhūta is the perishable being; the Puruṣa is adhidaiva; and the adhiyajña, here in this body, is I Myself, O best of the embodied!
BG_C08_V04::block-0:
Adhibhūta — that which exists with reference to (adhikṛtya) the host of living beings. What is it? Kṣaraḥ — 'kṣaratīti kṣaraḥ', that which perishes, the perishable; bhāvaḥ — any born thing whatsoever, that is the meaning. Puruṣa — 'pūrṇam anena sarvam', that by which all is filled; or, from 'lying in the citadel (puri śayanāt)' — He is Hiraṇya-garbha residing within the orb of the sun, the gracious sustainer of the organs of all living beings; He is adhidaivata.

Adhiyajña is the deity called Viṣṇu, the presiding consciousness of all sacrifices, as the śruti says: 'Verily, the sacrifice is Viṣṇu' (Tai. Sa. 1.7.4). And that very Viṣṇu is I Myself; here, in this body, of the sacrifice that is performed, I am the adhiyajña. For the sacrifice, being something accomplished through the body and inhering in it, has the body as its locus — O best of the embodied!
BG_C08_V05: And he who, at the final hour, departs casting off the body, remembering Me alone — he attains My state; here there is no doubt.
BG_C08_V05::block-0: Antakāle — at the time of death — and remembering Me alone, the supreme Lord Viṣṇu, casting off (parityajya) the body, he who departs, that is, goes — he attains My state, the Vaiṣṇava reality. Nāsti — there does not exist — in this matter any doubt as to 'whether he attains it or not'.
BG_C08_V06: Whatever state a man remembers when, at the end, he casts off the body — that very state he attains, O son of Kuntī, having always been imbued with the contemplation of that state.
BG_C08_V06::block-0: This rule is not confined to Me alone. Then what? —
BG_C08_V06::block-1: Yaṁ yaṁ vāpi — whatsoever state, that is, whatsoever particular deity, one remembers, contemplates, when at the end — the time of the departure of the breath — he relinquishes the body — that very remembered state alone he attains, and no other, O son of Kuntī. Sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ — 'bhāvaḥ in that' is tad-bhāva, and one by whom this has been bhāvita, that is, repeatedly practised through constant remembrance, is tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ; being such, he attains it.
BG_C08_V07: Therefore, at all times remember Me, and fight; with mind and intellect offered up in Me, you shall, without doubt, come to Me alone.
BG_C08_V07::block-0: Since the final thought is in this manner the cause of attaining another body —
BG_C08_V07::block-1: Therefore, at all times remember Me in accordance with the teaching of the scriptures. Yudhya ca — and engage in battle, that is, fulfil your own duty (svadharma). With mind and intellect offered up in Me, in Vāsudeva — being such — you, with mind and intellect surrendered in Me, shall come to Me, that is, attain Me, in the very manner in which I am remembered. Asaṁśayaḥ — there is no doubt in this matter at all.
BG_C08_V08: With a mind united by the yoga of repeated practice and not wandering elsewhere, contemplating Him, one attains, O Pārtha, the supreme, divine Puruṣa.
BG_C08_V08::block-1: Abhyāsa-yoga-yuktena cetasā: in Me, the one object set forth as the locus for surrender of the mind, the unbroken repetition (āvṛtti) of one and the same cognition, uninterrupted by cognitions of other kinds — that is abhyāsa; and this very abhyāsa is the yoga; with the mind that is yoked by it, the yogī's mind that is engaged in That alone — by such a mind. Nānya-gāmin — that mind which has not the habit of going elsewhere, into any other object — by such a mind not wandering elsewhere. Paramaṁ — unsurpassable; puruṣaṁ; divyam — born in heaven, that is, residing in the orb of the sun — one attains, O Pārtha, anucintayan — meditatively pondering, in accordance with the teaching of the scriptures and the teacher.
BG_C08_V09: Whoever constantly meditates upon the Seer, the Ancient One, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, of inconceivable form, of the colour of the sun, beyond the darkness — (he reaches that supreme Puruṣa).
BG_C08_V09::block-0: And of what nature is the Puruṣa whom one reaches — that is now stated.
BG_C08_V09::block-1: Kavi — the seer with penetrating vision, the omniscient. Purāṇa — ancient, eternal. Anuśāsitāra — the ruler, the governor of the entire world. Aṇor aṇīyāṁsam — subtler even than the subtle (aṇu); that is, finer than the most minute. Yaḥ anusmaret — whoever continually meditates upon, contemplates Him; the Sustainer (dhātāram) of every kind of fruit of action — that is, the apportioner who distributes them in their manifold variety to living beings; and of inconceivable form (acintya-rūpam), since although His form does in fact exist, it cannot be conceived by anyone — hence acintya-rūpaḥ; Him; ādityavarṇam — He whose colour is like that of the sun, namely the radiance of eternal consciousness; Him of the sun's colour; tamasaḥ parastāt — beyond the darkness of delusion characterised by ignorance — Him, contemplating thus, one reaches: this is the connection with the previous verse.
BG_C08_V10: At the time of departure, with an unmoving mind, endowed with devotion and with the power of yoga, having properly fixed the prāṇa between the two eyebrows, he reaches that supreme, divine Puruṣa.
BG_C08_V10::block-1: Prayāṇa-kāle — at the time of death; manasā acalena — with a mind devoid of motion, unwavering; bhaktyā yuktaḥ — bhajana is bhakti, endowed with that; yoga-balena ca eva — and indeed by the power of yoga: yoga-bala is the steadiness of mind characterised by the accumulated impressions born of samādhi — endowed with that as well, this is the meaning. First having subjugated the mind in the lotus of the heart, and then through the upward-going channel, by the gradual conquest of the (bodily) regions, having placed (āveśya) — having established — the prāṇa in the middle of the two brows, properly (samyak), being undistracted — such a knowing yogin reaches (upaiti), attains, that supreme Puruṣa described in "Kavim purāṇam" (BG 8.9) etc., divine, of the nature of luminosity.
BG_C08_V11: That which the knowers of the Veda call the Imperishable, that into which the dispassionate ascetics enter, and desiring which they practise the discipline of brahmacarya — that goal I shall declare to you in brief.
BG_C08_V11::block-0: Once again the Lord, by means of the upāya about to be expounded, sets forth the description of Brahman — the very thing intended to be reached — qualifying it by such epithets as "that which the Veda-knowers declare" —
BG_C08_V11::block-1: Yat akṣaram — that which does not perish (na kṣarati), hence akṣara, the imperishable; vedavidaḥ — those who know the meaning of the Veda; vadanti — declare, as per the śruti "That, indeed, O Gārgī, the brāhmaṇas call the akṣara" (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8); they declare it as that which excludes all (limiting) particularities — "not gross, not subtle" and so forth. Furthermore — viśanti — enter into; yat — which; yatayaḥ — those given to striving, the saṁnyāsins; vīta-rāgāḥ — those from whom rāga (attachment) has departed (vīta = vigata), they are vīta-rāgāḥ; (they enter into it) when right vision is attained. And that akṣara desiring (yat icchantaḥ) — "to know," supplying the implied word — they practise (caranti = ācaranti) brahmacarya at the feet of a teacher: that pada — that goal known as akṣara, the destination — for you (te = tava) saṅgraheṇa — saṅgraha is brevity, by such brevity — pravakṣye — I shall declare, expound.
BG_C08_V12: Having restrained all the gates (of the senses), having confined the mind in the heart, having placed his own prāṇa in the head, established in the firm hold of yoga —
BG_C08_V12::block-0: Beginning with "Now then, Bhagavan, whichever man among men shall meditate upon this Oṁkāra until the end of life, which world does he conquer thereby?" (Pra. Up. 5.1) and "To him He said: Verily this, O Satyakāma, is the higher and the lower Brahman, namely the Oṁkāra" (Pra. Up. 5.2), and continuing with "He, again, who meditates upon the supreme Puruṣa with this very syllable Oṁ in its three measures — he is led upward by the Sāman verses to the brahma-loka" (Pra. Up. 5.5) and so forth; and beginning with "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (Ka. Up. 1.2.14) and continuing with "That goal which all the Vedas extol, which all austerities declare, desiring which men live the life of brahmacarya — that goal I shall tell you in brief: it is Oṁ" (Ka. Up. 1.2.15) and so on — by these scriptural utterances, the upāsanā of the Oṁkāra has been taught for those of dull and middling intellect, as a means to the realisation of the supreme Brahman, either in the manner of a name (vācaka-rūpeṇa) of the supreme Brahman, or in the manner of a symbol (pratīka-rūpeṇa, like an image), having mukti at a later time as its fruit. That very same upāsanā of the Oṁkāra, which is the means to the realisation, in the manner already explained, of the supreme Brahman set forth here too in "Kavim purāṇam anuśāsitāram" (BG 8.9) and "Yad akṣaraṁ vedavido vadanti" (BG 8.11) — that upāsanā together with yogic dhāraṇā, having mukti at a later time as its fruit, must now be expounded, along with whatever else is connected and consequentially relevant; with this purpose the following passage is begun —
BG_C08_V12::block-1: Sarva-dvārāṇi — all those (avenues) which are the gates for cognition; saṁyamya — having restrained, having performed restraint of all of them; manaḥ — the mind; hṛdi — in the lotus of the heart; nirudhya — having confined, having brought it to non-roaming; with the mind thus subjugated there, having ascended upward from the heart through the upward-going channel, having placed (ādhāya) the prāṇa of oneself (ātmanaḥ) in the head (mūrdhni), being established (āsthitaḥ), engaged, in upholding the dhāraṇā of yoga.
BG_C08_V13: Uttering the single syllable Brahman, namely Oṁ, and remembering Me — whoever, abandoning the body, departs, he attains the supreme goal.
BG_C08_V13::block-0: And while holding (the dhāraṇā) right there —
BG_C08_V13::block-1: Om iti — Oṁkāra, which is the syllable expressive of Brahman, the one-syllabled Brahman; vyāharan — uttering it; mām — Me, the Lord, who am the meaning of that syllable; anusmaran — contemplating; yaḥ prayāti — whoever departs, dies; saḥ tyajan — abandoning, relinquishing; deham — the body — the phrase "abandoning the body" qualifies the act of going, indicating that the going of the Self is by way of relinquishing the body, not by way of the destruction of His own essential nature, that is the meaning — saḥ — such a one; yāti — goes; paramāṁ gatim — the supreme, the highest goal.
BG_C08_V14: He whose mind is fixed on no other, who constantly remembers Me daily — to that yogin ever joined (in yoga), I am easy of attainment, O Pārtha.
BG_C08_V14::block-1: Ananya-cetāḥ — he whose cetas (mind) is on no other object, this one is ananya-cetāḥ; the yogin who, satatam — always; yaḥ — who; mām — Me, the supreme Lord; smarati — remembers; nityaśaḥ — daily. "Satatam" expresses uninterruptedness; "nityaśaḥ" expresses long duration. Not for six months or a year — what then? — for as long as one lives, uninterruptedly, he who remembers Me, this is the meaning. To that yogin I am sulabhaḥ — easy to obtain — O Pārtha — to the yogin who is nitya-yuktaḥ — whose mind is ever-collected. Since this is so, therefore one should, being ananya-cetāḥ, ever remain collected in Me.
BG_C08_V15: Having reached Me, the great souls who have attained the supreme perfection do not return to rebirth — that abode of sorrow, that impermanent state.
BG_C08_V15::block-0: What is gained by Your being easy of attainment? That is now told. Hear what comes about by My being easy of attainment —
BG_C08_V15::block-1: Mām upetya — having reached Me, the Lord, having attained My state; punar-janma — rebirth, fresh origination; na āpnuvanti — they do not obtain. Of what nature is the rebirth they do not obtain? — to specify it He says: duḥkhālayam — janma which is the abode (ālaya) of sufferings, namely the ādhyātmika and the rest — that in which sufferings come to rest (ālīyante) is duḥkhālayam, viz. birth. And not merely the abode of suffering, but also aśāśvatam — non-eternal, of an unsteady essential nature. The mahātmānaḥ — the yatis, the great souls — who have attained (gatāḥ) the supreme — saṁsiddhim — the perfection known as mokṣa, the most exalted — they do not obtain such rebirth. Those, on the other hand, who do not reach Me, return again.
BG_C08_V16: Up to the world of Brahmā, all the worlds are subject to return, O Arjuna; but having reached Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
BG_C08_V16::block-0: But do those who reach anywhere other than You return again? It is now stated —
BG_C08_V16::block-1: Ā brahma-bhuvanāt — bhavanti asmin bhūtāni iti bhuvanam (that in which beings come to be is bhuvana); the bhuvana of Brahmā is brahma-bhuvana, that is, the brahma-loka; up to brahma-bhuvana, including the brahma-bhuvana — all the worlds are punar-āvartinaḥ, of the nature of returning, O Arjuna. But on reaching Me, the One, O son of Kuntī, there is no punar-janma — no fresh origination.
BG_C08_V17: They who know that the day of Brahmā has the limit of a thousand yugas, and that the night too ends with a thousand yugas — those people are the knowers of day and night.
BG_C08_V17::block-0: Why, then, are the worlds — together with Brahmaloka — subject to return? Because they are bounded by time. How so? Hence the verse —
BG_C08_V17::block-1: Sahasra-yuga-paryantam — that day whose end, whose terminus, is a thousand yugas: such is the day, namely sahasra-yuga-paryanta, of Brahmā, that is, of Prajāpati Virāj. They know it; and the night too they know to end with a thousand yugas, having the same measure as the day. Who know this? He says — those people who are knowers of day and night, that is, knowers of the reckoning of time. Since, then, they are thus circumscribed by time, the worlds are subject to return.
BG_C08_V18: At the coming of day all manifestations issue forth from the Unmanifest; at the coming of night they dissolve into that very same — termed the Unmanifest.
BG_C08_V18::block-0: What occurs in Prajāpati's day and night is now told —
BG_C08_V18::block-1: Avyaktāt — the Unmanifest, which is Prajāpati's state of sleep; from that Unmanifest the vyaktayaḥ — those that are made manifest, hence vyaktayaḥ, all the creatures characterized as the immobile and the mobile — issue forth, that is, become manifested. Ahrāgame — at the coming of day, namely at the time of Brahmā's awakening. Likewise rātryāgame, at the time of Brahmā's sleep, all manifestations dissolve back there itself, in that very same previously mentioned Unmanifest by name.
BG_C08_V19: This very same multitude of beings, coming into being again and again, dissolves at the coming of night, helpless, O son of Pṛthā; it issues forth at the coming of day.
BG_C08_V19::block-0: In order to remove the defects of an effect arising without its cause and of a deed perishing unrequited, in order to display the fruitfulness of the activity of the scriptures concerning bondage and liberation, and because, owing to the deposit of karma rooted in the afflictions beginning with avidyā, the multitude of beings, helpless, comes into being again and again only to dissolve — and in order to engender dispassion towards saṃsāra — He says this —
BG_C08_V19::block-1: The bhūta-grāma, the aggregate of beings characterized as immobile and mobile, which existed in the previous kalpa, is this very same and no other. Coming into being again and again at the coming of day, it dissolves repeatedly at the coming of night, at the close of the day, helpless, that is, not at all independent. O son of Pṛthā, it issues forth, is born, again helpless indeed, at the coming of day.
BG_C08_V20: But beyond that Unmanifest there is another Being, unmanifest and eternal, who, when all beings perish, does not perish.
BG_C08_V20::block-0: What was set forth as the Imperishable — the means of attaining it has been indicated by 'Om-iti-ekākṣaraṃ brahma' (BG 8.13) and the rest. Now, with the wish to indicate the very nature of the Imperishable itself, this is said — that, by this path of yoga, it is this that is to be reached —
BG_C08_V20::block-1: Paraḥ — separate, distinct. From what? From that previously mentioned. The word tu is for the purpose of distinguishing, by way of contrast, the Imperishable that is intended to be spoken of from the [other] Unmanifest. Bhāva — the supreme Brahman called the Imperishable. Even when there is distinctness, the contingency of similarity of characteristics could arise; to remove that, He says anyaḥ — other, of unlike character. And It is avyakta — not within the range of the senses. It was said 'parastasmāt'; but beyond what? Beyond the previously mentioned Unmanifest, which is the seed of the multitude of beings and is characterized as avidyā. The intent is: It is a Being other and unlike. Sanātanaḥ — ancient — that Being which, in all beings such as Brahmā and the rest when they perish, does not perish.
BG_C08_V21: What was spoken of as 'Unmanifest' and 'Imperishable' — that they call the supreme goal; having reached which they do not return — that is My supreme abode.
BG_C08_V21::block-0: That which was spoken of as the Unmanifest, the Imperishable — that very Unmanifest Being, called the Imperishable, they call the supreme, the most exalted, goal. That supreme Being, having attained, having reached which, they do not return for saṃsāra — that abode, that station, supreme, most exalted, is Mine; the meaning is, the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
BG_C08_V22: That supreme Puruṣa, O son of Pṛthā, is to be reached only by undivided devotion — He within whom all beings dwell, by whom all this is pervaded.
BG_C08_V22::block-0: The means of attaining Him is now told —
BG_C08_V22::block-1: Puruṣaḥ — so called from lying in the city (puri śayanāt), or from being all-full (pūrṇatvāt). He, paraḥ — supreme, beyond which there is naught surpassing — than which Puruṣa nothing is higher. He is to be reached only by devotion, of the nature of knowledge, undivided, having the Self for its sole object. Within whom — of which Puruṣa — antaḥsthāni, lying inside, are the beings, that is, the effects; for the effect always abides within the cause. By which Puruṣa all this universe is tatam — pervaded — as pots and the like are by space.
BG_C08_V23: That time at which yogins, departing, attain non-return, and likewise return — that time I shall declare to you, O bull of the Bharatas.
BG_C08_V23::block-0: For the yogins under discussion — those whose intellect is fixed on Brahman through the praṇava and who attain liberation only after a course of time (krama-mukti) — the further path leading to the realization of Brahman has to be set forth. Hence, in order to convey the intended sense, this beginning with 'yatra kāle' is uttered; the mention of the path of return is for the purpose of extolling the other path —
BG_C08_V23::block-1: Yatra kāle prayātāḥ — the connection holds across the intervening words. At what time — but anāvṛttim — non-return, that is, no rebirth — and also return, the contrary thereof. Yoginaḥ — by 'yoginaḥ' both yogins and karmins are meant; karmins, however, are called yogins only secondarily, by virtue of qualification, as in 'karma-yogena yoginām' (BG 3.3). At what time the yogins, having departed — that is, having died — attain non-return, and at what time, having departed, they attain return — that time I shall declare, O bull of the Bharatas.
BG_C08_V24: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course — going thereby, the people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
BG_C08_V24::block-1: Agni — the deity presiding over time. Likewise jyotis is also a deity, presiding over time. Or else, agni and jyotis are deities just as the words signify. The designation 'yatra kāle' and 'taṃ kālam', however, is on the basis of the major component, in the manner of 'mango grove' (āmra-vaṇa). Likewise ahaḥ — the deity presiding over the day; śuklaḥ — the deity of the bright fortnight; ṣaṇ-māsā uttarāyaṇam — there too it is the deity itself that is the path: this principle has been settled elsewhere. Tatra — by that path, those who, having departed — that is, having died — go to Brahman are the brahma-vidaḥ — those devoted to the upāsanā of Brahman, those people whose pursuit is meditation on Brahman. 'Gradually (krameṇa)' is the supplement to the sentence. For there is no going or coming anywhere for those who possess immediate liberation (sadyo-mukti) and who are established in perfect knowledge — as the śruti says, 'his prāṇas do not depart' (Br̥. Up. 4.4.6). Their prāṇas are absorbed in Brahman; they are made of Brahman; they have indeed become Brahman.
BG_C08_V25: Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern course of the sun — gaining the lunar light by these, the yogin returns. (25)
BG_C08_V25::block-0: Smoke and night are the deities that preside over smoke and over night respectively. So too 'dark' (kṛṣṇa) is the deity presiding over the dark fortnight. And 'the six months constituting the southern course' is, as before, just the deity. By 'tatra cāndramasaṁ jyotiḥ' is meant the light born in the moon (the result obtained there); having reached and enjoyed this fruit, the yogin — that is, the performer of works such as the iṣṭi, etc., the karmin — on the exhaustion of that fruit returns here once again.
BG_C08_V26: These two — the bright and the dark — are held to be the everlasting paths of the world; by the one a man goes to non-return, by the other he returns again. (26)
BG_C08_V26::block-0: 'Śuklakṛṣṇe' — bright (śuklā) and dark (kṛṣṇā), in the dvandva 'bright-and-dark': bright because it illumines through knowledge, dark from the absence of that. 'Of the world' (jagataḥ) means of those qualified for knowledge and works respectively — for these two paths cannot belong to the entire world; they are 'śāśvate', perpetual, since transmigration itself is beginningless and perpetual; 'mate' — held, intended. There, by the one, the bright, one goes to non-return; by the other, by the second, one returns again, repeatedly.
BG_C08_V27: Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever falls into delusion; therefore at all times be steadfast in yoga, O Arjuna. (27)
BG_C08_V27::block-0: Knowing these two aforesaid paths or routes, O Pārtha — knowing 'the one is for transmigration, the other for liberation' — no yogin falls into delusion, none whatsoever. Therefore, at all times be 'yogayukta' — concentrated, collected — O Arjuna.
BG_C08_V28: Whatever fruit of merit is declared in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities, and in gifts — the yogin, knowing this, transcends all that, and attains the supreme primordial Abode. (28)
BG_C08_V28::block-0: Hear the greatness of that yoga —
BG_C08_V28::block-1: In the Vedas thoroughly studied, in sacrifices duly performed with all their good qualities, in austerities well practised, and in gifts duly bestowed — whatever fruit of merit is declared by the śāstra in these, all that mass of fruits the yogin transcends, leaves behind. 'Knowing this' — having well ascertained, through the determination of the seven questions, the meaning that has been set forth, and having put it into practice — the yogin attains, reaches the supreme, the highest, divine Abode, 'ādyam' — that which exists from the beginning, namely the Cause, Brahman: this is the meaning.
BG_C09_V01::block-0: In the eighth chapter, the saguṇa dhāraṇā-yoga, by way of the cranial nāḍī, was set forth; and its fruit was indicated as the attainment of Brahman in due course through the gradation of the path of fire, light and the rest — a fruit of the nature of non-return. There, with a desire to dispel the apprehension that 'liberation is to be had only in this manner and not otherwise,' the Blessed Lord said —
BG_C09_V01::block-1: This Brahman-knowledge, which is about to be expounded and which has also been spoken of in the previous chapters,
BG_C09_V01::block-2: Bringing it to mind he says 'idam' (this). The word 'tu' (but) serves to single it out as something distinct. Just this — sound knowledge — is verily the direct means to the attainment of liberation, as is shown by such śruti and smṛti as 'Vāsudeva is all' (Bh.G. 7.19), 'this Self alone is all this' (Chā. Up. 7.25.2), 'one only, without a second' (Chā. Up. 6.2.1); and not anything else, as is shown by śruti such as 'Now those who know otherwise than this — they have other rulers and inhabit perishable worlds' (Chā. Up. 7.25.2). 'To you' — I shall declare, expound, this most secret of secrets, to one who is free from cavil. What is it? Knowledge. Of what kind? Joined with vijñāna, with experience, by knowing which — that is, by gaining which — you shall be released from the inauspicious, from the bondage of saṁsāra.
BG_C09_V02: This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, the supreme purifier; it is to be known by direct experience, in accord with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable. (2)
BG_C09_V02::block-1: 'Rāja-vidyā' — the king of sciences, since it possesses the highest splendour; for this Brahman-knowledge shines forth pre-eminently among all sciences. Likewise 'rāja-guhyam' — the king among secrets. 'Pavitram' — purifying; 'idam uttamam' — this Brahman-knowledge is the most excellent among all purifiers, the supremest cause of purification. Even karma — dharma, adharma and the rest — accumulated through many thousands of births along with its root, it reduces to ashes in the mere blink of a moment; what need then to speak of its power to purify? Further — 'pratyakṣāvagamam' — that of which the apprehension is direct, like that of pleasure, etc., is pratyakṣāvagama. It is observed that even what has many merits may turn out opposed to dharma; not so the knowledge of the Self — it is not opposed to dharma but 'dharmyam' — not deviating from dharma. Even granting all this, it might still be hard to attain; therefore he says 'su-sukhaṁ kartum' — very easy to bring about, like the discriminating knowledge of a gem. Now, of other works that are easy to perform with little exertion, the fruits are seen to be small, and of the difficult ones the fruits great; so it might be objected that this, being easy, would, like the fruits of works, perish on the exhaustion of its fruit; anticipating this, he says 'avyayam' — imperishable. Of this there is no expenditure of fruit as in works; hence 'avyayam'. Therefore Self-knowledge is to be reverenced with faith.
BG_C09_V03: Men devoid of faith in this dharma, O scorcher of foes, fail to attain Me and return to the path of death and transmigration. (3)
BG_C09_V03::block-0: Those, on the other hand, who —
BG_C09_V03::block-1: 'Aśraddadhānāḥ' — devoid of faith both in the very nature of this dharma of Self-knowledge and in its fruit, the nāstikas, doers of evil, who have espoused the upaniṣad of the asuras — namely, the view that takes the body alone to be the Self — the asutṛps, sinful men, faithless ones, O Parantapa, 'aprāpya mām' — without attaining Me, the supreme Lord; the meaning is that they fail to attain even so much as the path of devotion, mere bhakti as a means to attaining Me, of which there is no question that they would attain Me. They 'nivartante' — definitely turn back; where? — 'mṛtyu-saṁsāra-vartmani' — saṁsāra accompanied by death is mṛtyu-saṁsāra; its 'vartman' is the path leading to such states as hells and animal births; on that very path do they ply: such is the meaning.
BG_C09_V04: By Me, in My unmanifest form, all this world is pervaded; all beings rest in Me, and yet I do not abide in them. (4)
BG_C09_V04::block-0: Having turned Arjuna face-to-face by way of praise, He says —
BG_C09_V04::block-1: By Me — by My supreme Being — is this entire world pervaded, spread through. 'Avyakta-mūrtinā' — by Me whose mūrti, whose proper form, is unmanifest; that I am 'avyakta-mūrti', and by that Me, of unmanifest form — that is, of a nature that does not fall within the range of the senses, this is the meaning. In Me, the unmanifest in form, are 'mat-sthāni' — abiding, stationed — all beings, from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass. For no being, devoid of the Self, is fit for any dealings whatsoever. Hence 'mat-sthāni' — abiding through Me as the Self, by virtue of having Me as their Self; therefore they are said to abide in Me. Of those beings, since I alone am the Self, dull-witted ones imagine I am stationed in them; therefore I declare — and yet I do not abide in those beings, since, unlike a corporeal thing, I am free from contact, for I am inmost even of space. For a thing not given to contact does not, anywhere, abide as something held in something else.
BG_C09_V05: And yet beings do not abide in Me. Behold My sovereign yoga! Sustaining beings, yet not abiding in beings, is My very Self, the bringer-forth of beings.
BG_C09_V05::block-0: Precisely because of this non-association which is Mine —
BG_C09_V05::block-1:
"And yet beings — Brahmā and the rest — do not abide in Me." Behold My yoga, that is, the joining together, the contrivance, of Me, the Lord — this sovereign (aiśvara) yoga belonging to the Īśvara: meaning, the true nature of the Self. So too the śruti, displaying non-attachment because of the absence of association, declares: "For the unattached one is not entangled" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26).

Behold this further marvel: "Sustaining beings" — though He is unattached, He yet bears all beings; "and yet not abiding in beings," since by the reasoning already shown the very abiding-in-beings is impossible. But then how is it said, "this is My Self"? Distinguishing the aggregate of body and the rest, superimposing on it the I-notion, and following the conventional reckoning of the world, He uses the expression "My Self" — not, like the unknowing crowd, supposing that the Self has another Self apart from itself. Likewise, "the bringer-forth of beings" — He is bhūta-bhāvanaḥ because He brings beings into being, that is, produces and nourishes them.
BG_C09_V06: As the great wind, ever moving everywhere, abides in space, even so know that all beings abide in Me.
BG_C09_V06::block-0: Establishing by an illustration the meaning conveyed by the two preceding verses, He says —
BG_C09_V06::block-1: Just as in the world the wind, abiding in space — that is, situated in ākāśa — being everywhere-going since it moves in all directions, and great by reason of its measure, so too, in Me who am all-pervading like ākāśa, beings abide without any actual contact at all — thus determine and know.
BG_C09_V07: All beings, O son of Kuntī, return at the end of a kalpa to My primal nature; and again at the beginning of a kalpa I send them forth.
BG_C09_V07::block-0: Thus, like the wind in space, all beings abide in Me during the period of subsistence; and they —
BG_C09_V07::block-1: "All beings, O son of Kuntī, return" — at the time of dissolution, the dissolution at the end of a kalpa — "to My primal nature," Mine, which is constituted of the three guṇas, lower (aparā), inferior. "And again," once more, at the time of origination, at the beginning of a kalpa, "I send forth those beings" — produce them, even as before.
BG_C09_V08: Holding fast My own primal nature, I send forth again and again this entire host of beings, helpless under the sway of prakṛti.
BG_C09_V08::block-0: Thus the primal nature characterised by avidyā —
BG_C09_V08::block-1: "Holding fast" — bringing under control — "My own," My very own, primal nature, "I send forth again and again" the host of beings born of prakṛti, this present aggregate of all beings in its entirety — "helpless," not self-dependent, brought under the sway of another by the defects of avidyā and the rest, "by the sway of prakṛti," by the sway of their own innate disposition (svabhāva).
BG_C09_V09: And those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya, who am seated as if indifferent, unattached in those very actions.
BG_C09_V09::block-0: Objection: Then for that supreme Lord of His, when He fashions this uneven host of beings, there must arise some connection with the dharma and adharma occasioned by that. To this, the Blessed One replies —
BG_C09_V09::block-1: "And" those actions which are the cause of the uneven creation of the host of beings — "those actions do not bind Me," the Lord, O Dhanañjaya. As to the cause of His non-connection with actions, He states: "seated as if indifferent" — just as some indifferent one, an onlooker, sits unconcerned, even so seated, since the Self is changeless; "unattached," devoid of attachment to fruits, free of the conceit "I act," in those actions. Hence even for another, the absence of the conceit of agency and the absence of attachment to fruits is the cause of non-bondage; otherwise the deluded man, like the silkworm, is bound by his own actions — such is the import.
BG_C09_V10: Under My superintendence prakṛti gives birth to the moving and the unmoving; by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
BG_C09_V10::block-0: Objection: Here "I send forth this host of beings" (BG 9.8) and "seated as if indifferent" (BG 9.9) are stated as mutually contradictory. To remove that, He says —
BG_C09_V10::block-1: "By Me, the superintendent" — by Me, the superintendent who am of the very nature of mere seership in all directions and changeless in essence — "prakṛti," My māyā, constituted of the three guṇas and characterised by avidyā, "gives birth" — produces — "the world together with the moving and the unmoving." So too the mantra-utterance: "One God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings, the overseer of works, dwelling in all beings, witness, conscious, alone, devoid of guṇas" (Śvet. Up. 6.11). "By this cause," by this occasioning factor, namely, by superintendence, O son of Kuntī, "the world," together with the moving and the unmoving, manifest and unmanifest, revolves through all states. For the entire activity of the world has its occasion in falling into the position of being an object of seership: "I shall enjoy this; I see this; I hear this; I experience pleasure; I experience pain; for that purpose I shall do this; I shall know this" — all such cognitive currents are grounded in cognition and terminate in cognition alone. The mantras, "He who is its overseer in the highest heaven" (Ṛg. 10.129.7; Tai. Br. 2.8.9) and the like, exhibit this very meaning. And from this it follows that of the one God, who is mere consciousness presiding over all and who in absolute truth has no concern with any enjoyment, there is in fact no other separate enjoyer, since no other conscious being is found apart from Him. As to the question "What is the cause of this creation?" — both the question and its answer are unsustainable, as is shown by mantra-passages such as "Who indeed knows? Who shall here proclaim it? Whence has it sprung, whence is this projection?" (Ṛg. 10.129.6; Tai. Br. 2.8.9). And the Blessed One has shown it: "Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance; thereby creatures are deluded" (BG 5.15).
BG_C09_V11: The deluded slight Me, since I have taken on a human form, not knowing My higher being as the great Lord of beings.
BG_C09_V11::block-0: Thus Me, who am of the nature of the eternally pure, awakened, and free, the all-knowing, who am even the very Self of all creatures —
BG_C09_V11::block-1: "They slight," they treat with contempt, with insult, "Me" — the deluded, those without discrimination — who have "resorted to a human body," a body relating to a man, that is, who am transacting through a human body. Not knowing My higher, supreme being, the truth of the supreme Self, ākāśa-like — nay, more inward than even ākāśa — the great Lord of beings, the great Lord (Īśvara) of all beings, who am their own Self. Hence those wretched ones are smitten down by their attitude of slighting Me.
BG_C09_V12: Their hopes vain, their actions vain, their knowledge vain, devoid of right reflection, they have resorted to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras.
BG_C09_V12::block-1: "Vain are their hopes" — those whose hopes, whose aspirations, are fruitless, are mogha-āśāḥ. So too "of vain actions" — the actions of the agnihotra and the rest performed by them, on account of their slighting the Blessed One, on account of their disregard for Him who is their own Self, become mogha, fruitless; hence "of vain actions." Likewise "of vain knowledge" — those whose knowledge is mogha, fruitless; their knowledge too proves fruitless. "Devoid of right reflection" — they become bereft of discrimination — such is the import. Further: they become "resorting to" — relying upon — "the rākṣasa nature," the disposition of rākṣasas, "and the āsura," the disposition of asuras, "the deluding," causing delusion, that which propounds the doctrine that the Self is the body, given to saying "Cleave! Cut! Drink! Eat! Seize what belongs to another!" — they become doers of cruel deeds, in accordance with the śruti: "Demonic, verily, are those worlds" (Īśā Up. 3).
BG_C09_V13: But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine prakṛti, worship Me with undeviating mind, knowing Me as the imperishable Source of all beings.
BG_C09_V13::block-0: Whereas those who, endowed with śraddhā, have entered upon the path to liberation that consists in devotion to the Lord —
BG_C09_V13::block-1: the great-souled ones (mahātmānaḥ) — those whose minds are not petty (akṣudra-cittāḥ) — having resorted to (āśritāḥ santaḥ) the divine prakṛti, that is, the prakṛti of the gods, characterized by śama (control of the inner organ), dama (control of the outer senses), dayā (compassion), śraddhā (faith) and the like, do worship (bhajanti, sevante), O Pārtha, Me, the Lord, with mind directed to no other (ananya-manasaḥ, ananya-cittāḥ), having known Me as bhūtādi — the cause (ādi, kāraṇa) of all beings (bhūtānām), namely the elements beginning with ether (viyad-ādīnām) and the embodied creatures (prāṇinām) — and as imperishable (avyayam).
BG_C09_V14: Constantly glorifying Me, striving with firm vows, and bowing down to Me with devotion, ever steadfast they worship Me.
BG_C09_V14::block-1: Constantly (satatam, sarvadā) glorifying (kīrtayantaḥ) Me — the Lord whose very form is Brahman — and striving (yatantaḥ) by means of the dharmas characterized by withdrawal of the senses, by śama, dama, dayā, ahiṁsā and the rest; firm in vow (dṛḍha-vratāḥ) — those whose vow is firm, steady, unshakable; and bowing down (namasyantaḥ) to Me, the Self seated in the heart (hṛdaya-īśayam ātmānam), with devotion, ever steadfastly united (nitya-yuktāḥ santaḥ) — they worship, they serve.
BG_C09_V15: And others, sacrificing by the sacrifice of knowledge, worship Me as one, as distinct, and in many ways — as the Universe-faced.
BG_C09_V15::block-0: It is now stated by which several modes they worship —
BG_C09_V15::block-1:
By the sacrifice of knowledge (jñāna-yajñena) — knowledge itself, having the Lord for its object, is the sacrifice; with that jñāna-yajña, sacrificing (yajantaḥ), worshipping (pūjayantaḥ) Me, the Lord, others (anye), having abandoned every other mode of upāsanā, do worship.

And that knowledge is of three modes: by oneness (ekatvena) — that is, by the supreme insight that 'there is but one supreme Brahman' — sacrificing thus, they worship. Some, again, worship through distinctness (pṛthaktvena), holding that 'the very same Lord Viṣṇu abides distributed under the differences of sun, moon and the rest.' Some others worship Him in many ways (bahudhā) — as the universe-formed (viśva-rūpam), the all-faced (sarvato-mukham), thinking 'that very Lord stands manifold' — they thus worship Him as the universe-form, the all-faced, in many modes.
BG_C09_V16: I am the kratu, I am the yajña, I am the svadhā, I am the herb; I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, I am the oblation.
BG_C09_V16::block-0: If they worship in many modes, how is it that they worship Thee alone? — to this He says:
BG_C09_V16::block-1: I am the kratu — the variety of Vedic (śrauta) ritual; I myself. I am the yajña — the sacrifice that is smārta (enjoined by smṛti). Further, I am svadhā — the food (anna) that is offered to the manes (pitṛs). I am the auṣadha — that which is eaten by all living beings, denoted by the word 'auṣadha' and common to rice, barley and the like. Or else: svadhā is food common to all beings, while auṣadha is medicine (bhaiṣajya) for the quelling of disease. I am the mantra — by which the oblation is given to the manes and to the deities. I myself am the ājya, the clarified butter, and the oblation. I am the agni — that fire in which the oblation is offered, that fire am I. I am also the hutam, the very act of oblation.
BG_C09_V17: I am the father of this world, the mother, the disposer, the grandsire; I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om, and the Ṛk, Sāma and Yajus alone.
BG_C09_V17::block-1: I am the father (pitā) — the begetter (janayitā) — of this world; the mother (mātā), the begetress (janayitrī); the disposer (dhātā) — He who apportions to creatures the fruit of their action; the grandsire (pitāmaha) — the father of the father; that which is to be known (vedyam, veditavyam); the purifier (pavitra, pāvana); the syllable Om; and the Ṛk, the Sāma, and the Yajus alone.
BG_C09_V18: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend; the origin, the dissolution, the ground, the treasury, and the imperishable seed.
BG_C09_V18::block-1: Goal (gati) — the fruit of action; sustainer (bhartā) — the nourisher; master (prabhu) — the lord; witness (sākṣī) — of what creatures have done and have not done; abode (nivāsa) — that in which creatures dwell; refuge (śaraṇa) — for the afflicted, the remover of distress for those who have surrendered; friend (suhṛd) — one who does good without expectation of return; origin (prabhava) — the rising-forth of the world; dissolution (pralaya) — that into which it dissolves; likewise ground (sthāna) — that wherein it stands; treasury (nidhāna) — the deposit, that which is to be enjoyed by creatures at a later time; seed (bīja) — the cause of sprouting for things subject to sprouting; imperishable (avyayam) — imperishable because it persists for the entire duration of saṁsāra. For nothing without a seed sprouts; and since sprouting is seen perpetually, it is understood that the lineage of seeds does not perish.
BG_C09_V19: I give heat; I send forth and withhold the rain. I am both immortality and death, the existent and the non-existent, O Arjuna.
BG_C09_V19::block-1:
I give heat (tapāmi) — having become the sun, by certain fierce rays. I send forth (utsṛjāmi) the rain by certain rays. Having sent it forth, I again withhold it (nigṛhṇāmi) by certain rays — and after eight months I again pour it forth in the rainy season (prāvṛṣ). I am the amṛta of the gods, and the death (mṛtyu) of mortals. The sat — that which exists as related to anything; and its opposite, the asat — that also am I, O Arjuna. Yet the Lord is not absolutely non-existent (atyantam asat); rather, sat and asat are the effect and cause that are within Himself.

Those knowers of jñāna who, by the modes of nivṛtti previously stated — namely, the sciences of oneness, distinctness, and the rest — and by these (knowledge-)sacrifices, worship Me, attain Me alone, each in accordance with his own knowledge.
BG_C09_V20: The knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of soma, purified of sin, having worshipped Me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven; they, attaining the holy world of the lord of gods, taste in heaven the divine enjoyments of the gods.
BG_C09_V20::block-0: But those, on the other hand, who are ignorant (ajñāḥ) and desirers of objects of desire (kāma-kāmāḥ) —
BG_C09_V20::block-1: The knowers of the three Vedas (trai-vidyāḥ) — the knowers of the Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman — worship Me in the form of Vasu and the other deities; they are soma-drinkers (soma-pāḥ — those who drink soma); through that very drinking of soma their sins are purged (pūta-pāpāḥ — of cleansed defilement). Having sacrificed to Me by the agniṣṭoma and the rest, having worshipped, they pray for the way to heaven (svar-gati) — going to heaven — that is, the very svar (heaven) is the gati: that they pray for. And they, having attained (āsādya, samprāpya) the punya — the fruit of merit — namely the realm of Surendra, the abode of the hundred-sacrifice (Śatakratu, Indra), enjoy (aśnanti, bhuñjate) the divine, the heaven-born, the unworldly (aprākṛta) deva-bhogas — the enjoyments of the gods.
BG_C09_V21: Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven, when their merit is exhausted they enter the world of mortals. Thus, resorting to the dharma of the three Vedas, desirers of desires obtain only going-and-coming.
BG_C09_V21::block-0: "Te taṁ bhuktvā" — having enjoyed that vast, that is, extensive, world of heaven, when their merit is exhausted (kṣīṇe puṇye) they enter, that is, return into, the world of mortals. "Evam," in the manner just stated, those who resort to the trayī-dharma — that is, merely the Vedic ritual prescribed in the three Vedas — being kāma-kāmāḥ, namely those who desire desires (the vigraha is: kāmān kāmayante iti kāma-kāmāḥ), obtain only gata-āgatam — gatam ca āgatam ca, going and coming back. The purport is: they obtain only this round of going-and-coming and never anywhere obtain freedom (svātantrya).
BG_C09_V22: Those people who, undeviating, contemplate Me and worship Me wholly — for them, ever-united, I bear the yoga-kṣema (the gaining of what is unattained and the safeguarding of what is attained).
BG_C09_V22::block-0: But those who are desireless, the perfect knowers of truth —
BG_C09_V22::block-1: Those people, that is, the renunciants (saṁnyāsins), who contemplate Me undeviatingly — ananyāḥ, not separate from Me, having reached the supreme God Nārāyaṇa as their very Self — and who thus worship Me wholly: for them, the seers of the Highest Truth, the ever-united, the constantly devoted, I bear the yoga-kṣema. Yoga is the obtaining of what is not yet attained; kṣema is the safeguarding of that. Both these I bear, that is, I bring about. Since it has been said, "The man of knowledge is verily My very Self — that is My view" (Gītā 7.18) and "And he is dear to Me" (Gītā 7.17), therefore they are My very Self and dear to Me.
BG_C09_V22::block-2: Objection: But surely the Lord bears the yoga-kṣema even of other devotees too. True, He does bear it; yet this is the distinguishing feature — other devotees themselves also exert for their own yoga-kṣema for their own sake; whereas the seers-of-none-other do not exert for yoga-kṣema for their own sake; for they entertain no clinging towards their own life or death; they have taken refuge in the Lord alone. Therefore the Lord Himself bears their yoga-kṣema.
BG_C09_V23: Even those devotees of other deities who worship endowed with faith — they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, but in a manner not according to rule.
BG_C09_V23::block-0: Objection: But if other deities too are You alone, then their devotees too worship You alone. True, it is so —
BG_C09_V23::block-1: Even those who are devotees-of-other-deities — being devoted to other deities — worship them, that is, render them pūjā, endowed with faith, that is, with belief in the existence of the unseen (āstikya-buddhi); they too worship Me alone, O son of Kuntī, but avidhi-pūrvakam — avidhi means ignorance, and pūrvakam means preceded by; the meaning is: they worship preceded by ignorance.
BG_C09_V24: For I alone am the enjoyer and the very Lord of all sacrifices; but they do not know Me in truth — therefore they fall.
BG_C09_V24::block-0: Why is it said that they worship not according to rule? Because —
BG_C09_V24::block-1: I alone am the enjoyer and the very Lord of all sacrifices — of all the sacrifices, both śrauta (Vedic) and smārta (traditional) — being the Self of the deity (devatātman).
