Becoming vyapeta-bhīḥ, one whose fear has wholly departed, and prīta-manāḥ, one whose heart is gladdened, behold once again (punaḥ, bhūyaḥ) this very (tadeva) form of Mine—the four-armed form bearing conch, discus and mace, the form that is dear to you (tava iṣṭam rūpam)—pratipraśya, look upon it directly. ॥ 49 ॥
BG_C11_V50::block-0: Thus (iti, evam), having spoken to Arjuna in such a manner, Vāsudeva once more (bhūyaḥ, punaḥ) showed (darśayāmāsa = darśitavān) His own (svakam) form—the very form that had taken birth in Vasudeva’s house. And He reassured (āśvāsayāmāsa = āśvāsitavān) him who was frightened, that great-souled One (mahātmā) becoming again of gentle body (saumya-vapuḥ), of serene frame (prasanna-deha). ॥ 50 ॥
BG_C11_V51::block-0: ‘Having beheld this human (mānuṣa) form of Yours, my friend (mat-sakham), serene (prasannam), gentle (saumyam), O Janārdana, I have now (idānīm, adhunā) become (saṁvṛttaḥ, sañjātaḥ).’ Become what? ‘Sa-cetāḥ—of clear and serene mind—and I have come back to my prakṛti, my natural state (svabhāvam gataḥ).’ ॥ 51 ॥
BG_C11_V52::block-0: Su-durdarśam—the seeing of which is exceedingly difficult, attained only with great hardship—is this (idam) form of Mine which you have now beheld. Even the gods and the rest (devādayaḥ) are nityam, ever and always, longing to behold (darśana-kāṅkṣiṇaḥ) this form of Mine. Though desirous of this sight (darśanepsavaḥ api), they have not beheld it as you have beheld it; nor will they behold it (na drakṣyanti)—this is the import. ॥ 52 ॥
BG_C11_V53: Not by the Vedas, nor by tapas, nor by gift, nor again by sacrificial worship, can I be seen in such a form as you have now beheld Me.
BG_C11_V53::block-1: Not (na) by the Vedas—even by the four, Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman and Atharvan together; not by tapas, even by the severe Cāndrāyaṇa and the like; not by dānam, by gift of cattle, land, gold and so forth; nor by ijyā, by sacrifice or by ritual worship—am I able (śakyaḥ) to be seen (draṣṭum) in such a form (evaṁ-vidhaḥ), in the very manner just shown to you, as you (yathā tvam) have beheld Me. ॥ 53 ॥
BG_C11_V54: But by undivided devotion, O Arjuna, am I, in this form, capable of being known and beheld in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
BG_C11_V54::block-0: ‘How then is it possible?’—to this it is said: —
BG_C11_V54::block-1: By bhakti—but of what particular kind, He says: ananyayā, undivided, not separate from the Lord. That bhakti which never, in any condition, turns elsewhere apart from the Lord—that alone is ananyā bhakti. By any one of the senses (sarvaiḥ api karaṇaiḥ) nothing other than Vāsudeva is perceived: such is ananyā bhakti. By that bhakti am I, in this very form (evaṁ-vidhaḥ), of the Viśva-rūpa kind, O Arjuna, capable of being known (jñātum) through scripture (śāstrataḥ). And not merely known through scripture, but also beheld (draṣṭum), realised directly (sākṣāt-kartum) tattvena, in His very being; and finally entered (praveṣṭum), that is, attained as mokṣa, O scorcher of foes. ॥ 54 ॥
BG_C11_V55: He who performs work for Me, who has Me as the supreme goal, who is devoted to Me, who is free from attachment, who is without enmity towards any being—he, O Pāṇḍava, comes unto Me.
BG_C11_V55::block-0: Now the very essence of the entire Gītā-śāstra, the meaning that aims at the highest good (niḥśreyas), is gathered together (samuccitya) and stated, as that which is to be put into practice (anuṣṭheyatvena): —
BG_C11_V55::block-1: Mat-karma-kṛt: that work which is for Me (mad-artham karma) is mat-karma; and the one who does that (tat karoti) is mat-karma-kṛt. Mat-paramaḥ: a servant indeed performs his master’s work, but does not regard the master as his own supreme goal, the goal to be attained after death (paramā pretya gantavyā gatiḥ); this man, however, while performing My work, attains Me alone as the highest goal—hence mat-paramaḥ, ‘he whose supreme goal (paramā gatiḥ) is I Myself.’ Likewise mad-bhaktaḥ: he worships Me alone, by every means, with the whole self (sarvātmanā), with all enthusiasm—therefore mad-bhaktaḥ. Saṅga-varjitaḥ: free from saṅga, that is from prīti or sneha, attachment and affection, towards wealth, son, friend, wife and the host of kinsmen. Nirvairaḥ: nirgata-vairaḥ, one from whom enmity has wholly departed, towards all beings (sarva-bhūteṣu), devoid of all hostile attitude even toward those engaged in causing him extreme injury. Whoever is My devotee (mad-bhaktaḥ) of this description—he comes unto Me (māṁ eti); I alone am his supreme goal, no other goal whatsoever exists for him. This is the teaching dear to Me, taught by Me to you, O Pāṇḍava. ॥ 55 ॥
BG_C12_V01::block-0: From the second adhyāya onwards, up to the chapter on Vibhūtis, the upāsanā of the supreme Self—Brahman, the Akṣara, in which all upādhi-distinctions have been wholly dissolved—has been taught; and side by side, here and there, the upāsanā of the Lord (Īśvara) too has been taught—of Him whose upādhi is the sattva endowed with all yoga-aiśvarya and with all jñāna-śakti. In the Viśva-rūpa-adhyāya, however, the Lord’s primal (ādyam) form, embracing the entire universe (samasta-jagad-ātma-rūpam), the Viśva-rūpa belonging to You, has been shown by You—and that for the sake of upāsanā alone. And after showing it, You said, ‘He who performs work for Me…’ (Bhag. Gītā 11.55), and so on. Therefore, with a desire to know more distinctly which of these two paths is the more excellent, I ask You—thus Arjuna spoke: —
BG_C12_V01::block-1: By ‘evam,’ ‘thus,’ he gathers up (parāmṛśati) the meaning stated in the immediately preceding verse beginning ‘mat-karma-kṛt’ (Bhag. Gītā 11.55) and the rest. ‘Thus ever yoked’ (evaṁ satata-yuktāḥ)—that is, with unbroken continuity, fully composed and engaged in the work for the Lord and the rest, in the meaning already declared—they have set forth in such practice. Those bhaktas who, having taken refuge in none other (ananya-śaraṇāḥ santaḥ), worship and meditate (paryupāsate, dhyāyanti) on You as the Viśva-rūpa just shown; and those others (ye ca anye api) who, having renounced all longings (tyakta-sarva-eṣaṇāḥ) and laid down all karmas (saṁnyasta-sarva-karmāṇaḥ), worship the Akṣara Brahman characterised as already specified—Brahman which, by reason of being free from all upādhis, is avyaktam, beyond the range of the senses (akaraṇa-gocaram). For that which falls within the range of the senses is called vyaktam, since the root añj has the meaning of ‘that which has the senses for its sphere of manifestation’; this Akṣara, however, is the very opposite of that, and is qualified further by the distinguishing marks that are about to be stated—those also (ye ca api) who worship It thus: among these two classes (ubhayeṣāṁ madhye), which are yoga-vit-tamāḥ? Who are, in the highest degree, knowers of yoga?—this is the sense. ॥ 1 ॥
BG_C12_V02::block-0: The Blessed Lord said: Now, those devotees of the Imperishable (akṣara) who are perfect seers (samyag-darśins) and have completely renounced craving (niṣpṛha of the three eṣaṇās) — let them stand aside for the moment; what is to be said with regard to them we shall declare further on. As for the others —
BG_C12_V02::block-1: Fixing and steadying the mind on Me, the Supreme Lord whose form is the universe (viśva-rūpa), those who, being devotees, worship Me — Me, the over-Lord of all masters of yoga, the all-knowing One, whose vision is wholly free from the darkness of the afflictions such as attachment and the rest — being ever-yoked (nitya-yuktāḥ), that is, perpetually conjoined in accordance with the meaning of the verse declared at the close of the immediately preceding chapter, and worship Me endowed with faith that is supreme and eminent (parayā śraddhayā prakṛṣṭayā) — they, in My view (mama matāḥ), are the most-yoked (yukta-tamāḥ); for it is by sheer continuity that they pass day and night with their consciousness fixed on Me. Hence it is fitting to call them the most-yoked. ॥ 2 ॥
BG_C12_V03: But those who worship the Imperishable, the Indefinable, the Unmanifest, the All-pervading and Inconceivable, the Immutable (kūṭa-stha), the Unmoving, the Eternal — ॥ 3 ॥
BG_C12_V03::block-0: Objection: Are not those others, then, the most-yoked? Reply: Not so; rather, listen to what is to be said with regard to them —
BG_C12_V03::block-1:
But those who worship the akṣara — anirdeśya, that is, since being unmanifest it is not within the range of speech, it cannot be pointed out, hence anirdeśya; avyakta, since it is not made manifest by any pramāṇa whatsoever, hence unmanifest — they pari-upāsate, that is, they worship it from every side. Now upāsanā means: in accordance with scripture, drawing near to the object to be worshipped by making it the content of one's mind, and remaining seated for a long time in a continuous flow of one and the same cognition like an unbroken stream of oil — that prolonged abiding is what is called upāsanā.

He states the qualifying terms of the akṣara, the object of worship: sarva-traga — pervading everywhere like ākāśa; acintya — inconceivable, because of being unmanifest. For whatever falls within the range of the senses can also be conceived by the mind; the akṣara, being the opposite of that, is acintya. Kūṭa-stha — kūṭa is a thing whose visible quality is one but which inwardly conceals a defect; the word kūṭa is well known in the world in expressions such as 'kūṭa-rūpa' (counterfeit form), 'kūṭa-sākṣya' (false witness). Likewise, that which, being the seed of saṃsāra in many forms beginning with avidyā, harbours an inner defect, and is well known under the names māyā, avyākṛta, and the like — as in 'one should know māyā as primal nature (prakṛti), and the wielder of māyā as the great Lord' (Śvetāśvatara 4.10), and 'My māyā is hard to cross over' (Bhagavad-gītā 7.14) — that is the kūṭa; that which abides in this kūṭa as its overseer is kūṭa-stha. Or else, kūṭa-stha is that which abides motionless like a heap. For that very reason it is acala (unmoving). Because it is unmoving, it is dhruva — eternal; that is the meaning. ॥ 3 ॥
BG_C12_V04: Restraining well the host of the senses, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the welfare of all beings — they too attain Me alone. ॥ 4 ॥
BG_C12_V04::block-0: Restraining well — that is, controlling and drawing in completely — the host of the senses, the aggregate of all the indriyas; sarvatra, at all times, sama-buddhayaḥ — those whose buddhi is even, equal, in the obtaining of the agreeable and the disagreeable, are the even-minded. They, being of such a nature, attain Me alone, delighting in the welfare of all beings. There is nothing further that need be said to them — 'they attain Me' — for it has already been declared, 'But the jñānin I deem to be My very Self' (Bhagavad-gītā 7.18). For of those who are of the very nature of the Lord, no question of being 'most-yoked' or 'not most-yoked' can rightly be raised. ॥ 4 ॥
BG_C12_V05: Greater is the trouble of those whose mind is attached to the Unmanifest; for the goal that is unmanifest is reached with hardship by the body-bound. ॥ 5 ॥
BG_C12_V05::block-1: Their trouble is greater. Even though for those devoted to actions for My sake there is indeed trouble, the trouble is greater for those who take the akṣara as the Self and behold the Supreme Self, owing to the renunciation of the conceit of the body. Of those whose mind (cetas) is attached (āsakta) to the Unmanifest — they are avyakta-āsakta-cetasaḥ; for them. The goal (gati) that is in the form of the akṣara, being unmanifest, is reached with pain by the body-bound, those still possessed of the conceit 'I am the body'; hence the trouble is greater. ॥ 5 ॥
BG_C12_V06: But those who, renouncing all actions in Me and holding Me as the supreme, worship Me, meditating upon Me with undivided yoga — ॥ 6 ॥
BG_C12_V06::block-0: The conduct of the worshippers of the akṣara we shall declare further on —
BG_C12_V06::block-1: But those who, renouncing all actions in Me, the Lord, become mat-parāḥ — those for whom I am the supreme — and, by an undivided yoga (ananyena yogena) — that is, the One who has no other (ananya), there being no other support apart from the divine Self in the form of the universe; through that very ananya — by what? — by yoga, by samādhi, meditating upon Me, contemplating Me, they worship Me. ॥ 6 ॥
BG_C12_V07: For them, whose minds are entered into Me, I become without delay, O Pārtha, the rescuer from the ocean of mortal saṃsāra. ॥ 7 ॥
BG_C12_V07::block-1: Of those wholly given to the worship of Me, I, the Lord, am the rescuer (samuddhartā). Wherefrom? He says: from the ocean of mortal saṃsāra — saṃsāra conjoined with death (mṛtyu) is mṛtyu-saṃsāra; that itself is like an ocean (sāgara), being hard to cross over; from that ocean of mortal saṃsāra I become their rescuer not after long. Then when? Forthwith, O Pārtha — for those whose cetas (mind) is āveśita (entered, fixed, well-collected) in Me, in the viśva-rūpa; they whose mind is fixed in Me are mayy-āveśita-cetasaḥ; for them. ॥ 7 ॥
BG_C12_V08: Fix the mind on Me alone; lodge thy buddhi in Me. Hereafter thou shalt dwell in Me alone — there is no doubt. ॥ 8 ॥
BG_C12_V08::block-1: On Me alone — on Me, the Lord whose form is the universe — fix (ādhatsva, place) the mind, which has the nature of saṅkalpa and vikalpa. Lodge in Me the buddhi, which makes determinations, in Me alone; place it. Then, what shall come to pass for thee? Listen — niva-siṣyasi — thou shalt assuredly dwell, taking up thy abode in Me as one with My very nature, hereafter — that is, after the falling of the body. There is no doubt — no doubt whatsoever is to be entertained here. ॥ 8 ॥
BG_C12_V09: But if thou art unable to fix the mind firmly on Me, then by the yoga of repeated practice (abhyāsa-yoga) seek to attain Me, O Dhanañjaya. ॥ 9 ॥
BG_C12_V09::block-0: Atha — if, in the manner I have just said, thou art not able to fix (samādhātum, place) the cetas firmly and unmoving on Me, then thereafter, by the yoga of practice — abhyāsa is the repeated re-establishing of the mind, drawing it together from every side, again and again upon a single object of support; the yoga preceded by such abhyāsa, having the character of samādhāna, is abhyāsa-yoga. By that abhyāsa-yoga, desire — that is, pray — to reach (āptum, prāptum) Me, the viśva-rūpa, O Dhanañjaya. ॥ 9 ॥
BG_C12_V10: If you are unable even in repeated practice, be intent on works for My sake. Performing actions merely for My sake also, you shall attain perfection.
BG_C12_V10::block-0: If even in such repeated practice you are unable, that is, incapable, then become one whose supreme aim is works for Me — mat-karma is action done for My sake; he whose foremost concern (parama) is that is mat-karma-parama, meaning one for whom My works are the chief thing. Even without that practice, performing actions merely for My sake, you shall attain perfection (siddhi) by the gradual sequence of purification of the inner organ (sattva-śuddhi), yoga, and the rise of knowledge.
BG_C12_V11: If, however, you are unable to do even this, then, having taken refuge in My yoga, perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions, with the self well-controlled.
BG_C12_V11::block-0: If, again, you are unable to do even this — namely, the state of having My works as supreme that has just been spoken of — then, having taken refuge in My yoga: dedicating to Me the actions being performed and then carrying out their execution, that itself is My yoga; resorting to it, perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions, that is, the surrender of the fruits of every action whatsoever; do this thereafter, being yatātmā — meaning one whose mind is well restrained.
BG_C12_V12: Knowledge is indeed superior to practice; meditation excels knowledge; the renunciation of the fruits of action excels meditation; from such renunciation peace follows immediately.
BG_C12_V12::block-0: Now He extols the renunciation of the fruits of all actions —
BG_C12_V12::block-1: Knowledge is indeed praiseworthy — superior. Superior to what? To practice unaccompanied by discrimination. Even to that knowledge, meditation preceded by knowledge is superior. Then, even to the meditation of one possessed of knowledge, the renunciation of the fruits of action — "is superior" — must be supplied by carry-over. Thus, from the renunciation of the fruits of action, qualified by all the foregoing excellences, peace, that is, cessation of saṃsāra together with its cause, follows immediately and not after some interval of time.
BG_C12_V12::block-2: For one who is ignorant and engaged in action, when he is incapable of performing the means previously taught, the renunciation of the fruits of all his actions has been prescribed as the means to the highest good — not at the very outset. Therefore, by the gradient of progressive superiority indicated in "Knowledge is indeed superior to practice," the renunciation of the fruits of all actions is being eulogized; for it has been enjoined as something to be performed when one is unable to undertake the more accomplished means. By what common feature does this become a eulogy? In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad it is said, "When all are released" (Ka. Up. 2.3.14), where immortality is declared to follow upon the relinquishing of all desires; this is well known. And all desires are nothing other than the fruits of the actions enjoined in śruti and smṛti. Upon the renunciation of these, the knower established in meditation attains peace immediately. So the relinquishment of the fruits of action by the ignorant shares with the relinquishment of all desires this common feature; on the strength of that commonality, this eulogy of the renunciation of the fruits of all actions is offered for the sake of attractive recommendation. Just as the brāhmaṇas of today too are praised on the strength of the common attribute of brāhmaṇa-hood by reference to the brāhmaṇa Agastya having drunk up the ocean, so by reason of the renunciation of the fruits of action the karma-yoga is here said to be a means to the highest good.
BG_C12_V13: Hating no being, friendly and compassionate, free of mineness and egoism, even-minded in pain and pleasure, and forbearing —
BG_C12_V13::block-0: Here, on the basis of the distinction between the Self and the Lord, the yoga consisting in the steadying of the mind on the Lord in His Universal Form has been spoken of, together with the performance of action for the Lord's sake. By the words "If, however, you are unable even to do this" (BG 12.11), which intimate the operation of ignorance, He shows that karma-yoga does not fit one who, beholding non-difference, worships the Imperishable; and conversely, that meditation upon the Imperishable does not fit the karma-yogin. Having declared, in "They attain Me alone" (BG 12.4), the independence of those who worship the Imperishable in the attainment of kaivalya, He showed in "For these I am the deliverer" (BG 12.7) the dependence of the others upon the Lord, on account of their being subject to another. For if those worshippers were held to be of the very nature of the Lord on account of their seeing non-difference, they would themselves be of the form of the Imperishable, and the speech of "deliverance" applied to them would be inappropriate. And since the Lord is supremely intent on Arjuna's welfare, He instructs him in karma-yoga conjoined with the vision of difference and unaccompanied by the right vision; for no one who has known the Self as the Lord on the strength of valid means of cognition wishes to occupy a subordinate position to anyone, since this is contradictory. Therefore, He proceeds with the words "Hating no being" and so on, intending to declare a host of qualities that, in the case of worshippers of the Imperishable, samyag-darśana-niṣṭhas, who are renunciants having abandoned all the eṣaṇās, are the direct cause of immortality —
BG_C12_V13::block-1: Hating no being — he hates none, not even the cause of his own pain; for he sees all beings as his own Self. Maitra: friendliness is maitrī; one who behaves with the disposition of a friend is maitra. And karuṇa: karuṇā is compassion, mercy, sympathy toward those in suffering; he who is endowed with that is karuṇa — one who confers fearlessness on all beings, that is, the renunciant. Free of mineness — devoid of the notion "mine." Free of egoism — from whom the notion "I" has departed. Even-minded in pain and pleasure — he in whom pain and pleasure are equal, not provoking aversion or attachment, is samaduḥkha-sukha. Forbearing — endowed with kṣamā: when reviled or even struck, he remains unaltered.
BG_C12_V14: Always content, a yogin, self-controlled, of firm conviction, with mind and intellect surrendered to Me — that devotee of Mine is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V14::block-0: Always content — perpetually, in the gain or non-gain of the means of bodily sustenance, with the sense of "that is enough" arisen. Likewise content in the gain or absence of items of comfort. Always a yogin — one whose mind is collected. Self-controlled — of restrained nature. Of firm conviction — he whose conviction, that is, the determination concerning the truth of the Self, is firm and stable, is dṛḍha-niścaya. With mind and intellect surrendered to Me — the mind, characterized by saṅkalpa and vikalpa, and the intellect, characterized by determination — both deposited and established in Me alone — such a renunciant is mayy-arpita-mano-buddhi. Whoever is My devotee of this kind, he is dear to Me. What was hinted in the seventh chapter, "To the man of knowledge I am exceedingly dear, and he is dear to Me" (BG 7.17), is here being expanded.
BG_C12_V15: He from whom the world does not shrink and who does not shrink from the world, who is freed from elation, intolerance, fear and agitation — he too is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V15::block-0: He from whom — that is, from which renunciant — the world does not shrink, does not become agitated, is not pained, is not perturbed; and who likewise does not shrink from the world; he who is freed from elation, intolerance, fear and agitation — harṣa is the inner organ's exhilaration on gaining what is dear, marked by signs such as horripilation, tears and the like; amarṣa is non-endurance; bhaya is dread; udvega is unease; freed from these — he too is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V16: Without longing, pure, capable, indifferent, free of distress, having renounced all undertakings — that devotee of Mine is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V16::block-0: Anapekṣa — devoid of longing toward such objects of expectation as the connection of the body, sense-organs and sense-objects. Pure — endowed with both outer and inner cleanliness. Capable — able, in matters that arise on the spot, to grasp at once the right course of action. Indifferent — he who does not take the side of any friend or the like is the indifferent ascetic. Free of distress — devoid of fear. Having renounced all undertakings — "undertakings" are those things that are undertaken, namely, actions whose causes are desire and which are aimed at the enjoyment of fruits in this world or the next; he whose nature is to relinquish all such undertakings is sarva-ārambha-parityāgī; he who is My devotee of this kind, he is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V17: He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both good and evil, full of devotion — he is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V17::block-1: He who does not rejoice on attaining the desired, does not hate on getting the undesired, does not grieve at separation from what is dear, and does not yearn for the unobtained; he whose nature it is to relinquish both auspicious and inauspicious actions is śubhāśubha-parityāgī; he who is such a one, full of devotion, is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V18: Equal toward foe and friend, and likewise in honour and dishonour; equal in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, free from all attachment.
BG_C12_V18::block-0: He is equal (samaḥ) toward foe and toward friend; likewise in māna and apamāna — that is, in honour (pūjā) and in contempt (paribhava); equal in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain; and everywhere free from clinging (saṅga-vivarjitaḥ).
BG_C12_V19: To whom blame and praise are alike, who is silent, content with whatever comes, without fixed abode, steady in mind, full of devotion — that man is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V19::block-0:
Furthermore —

Tulya-nindā-stutiḥ — he to whom nindā (blame) and stuti (praise) are nindā-stutī, and to whom these two are alike (tulye), is tulya-nindā-stutiḥ. Maunī — endowed with mauna, with restrained speech. Santuṣṭaḥ yena kenacit — content with whatever serves merely as a means for sustaining the body. Thus too has it been declared: ‘Covered by whatever, fed by whatever, sleeping wherever — him the gods know to be a brāhmaṇa’ (Mokṣa-dharma 245.12). Furthermore, anikethaḥ — niketa means resort, settled dwelling; he in whom no fixed dwelling exists is anikethaḥ; this is supported by another smṛti, ‘Not in a house...’ Sthira-matiḥ — he whose mati (understanding), directed upon the supreme Reality, is sthirā (steady), is sthira-matiḥ. Such a man, full of devotion, is dear to Me.
BG_C12_V20: But those who, with faith and holding Me as the supreme goal, devoutly resort to this dharma-laden nectar as it has been declared — those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me.
BG_C12_V20::block-0:
Beginning with ‘He who hates no being’ (BhG 12.13), the dharma-cluster pertaining to the worshippers of the Imperishable — to the saṁnyāsins in whom every craving has ceased and who are established in the knowledge of the Supreme Reality — was set forth; that is now drawn together to a close —

Ye tu — ‘But those’ saṁnyāsins; dharmyāmṛtam — the immortal that is not separated from dharma, and is itself amṛta because it is the cause of immortality; idam yathoktam — ‘this, as declared’ beginning with ‘He who hates no being’ (BhG 12.13); paryupāsate — they perform it devoutly, śraddadhānāḥ santaḥ — being filled with faith; mat-paramāḥ — those for whom I, declared as the akṣara-ātman, the unsurpassed goal, am the supreme; mad-bhaktāḥ — and My devotees, having taken refuge in the highest devotion characterised by knowledge of the Supreme — they are exceedingly (atīva) dear to Me. What was indicated in ‘the wise man is exceedingly dear to Me’ (BhG 7.17) is here, after exposition, summed up as ‘those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me.’

Since one who practises this dharma-laden nectar as taught becomes exceedingly dear to the Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Īśvara, therefore this dharmyāmṛta is to be diligently practised by the seeker of liberation, by him who wishes to attain the supreme abode dear to Viṣṇu — such is the purport of the sentence.
BG_C13_V01::block-0:
In the seventh chapter, two prakṛtis of the Lord were indicated: the inferior (aparā), composed of the three guṇas and divided eightfold, the cause of saṁsāra; and the other, the higher (parā), constituting the jīva, of the nature of the kṣetrajña, the very Self of the Lord — by means of which two prakṛtis the Īśvara comes to be the cause of the production, sustenance and dissolution of the world. Now, by determining the pair of prakṛtis characterised as kṣetra and kṣetrajña, this kṣetra-chapter is begun in order to ascertain the true nature of the Lord who possesses them. And in the chapter just past, from ‘He who hates no being’ (BhG 12.13) up to its close, the niṣṭhā of the saṁnyāsins who know the Reality, and the manner in which they comport themselves, was declared. By what knowledge of Reality, then, are these endowed, so that, by practising the dharma there described, they become dear to the Lord? — for this purpose too this chapter is begun. The prakṛti, composed of the three guṇas, transformed in the form of all karyas (effects) and karaṇas (instruments) and viṣayas (objects), becomes consolidated, for the sake of the puruṣa’s experience and ultimate release, in the form of body, senses and the rest. This very aggregate is ‘this body.’ Of just this the Lord speaks —

The word ‘idam’ (this), a pronoun, is specified by the word ‘śarīram’ (body). O Kaunteya — because of warding off injury (kṣata-trāṇa), or because it perishes (kṣaya), or because it flows away (kṣaraṇa), or because, like a kṣetra (field), the fruit of action is produced in it — this is termed ‘kṣetra’; the word ‘iti’ here has the sense of ‘in this manner’; ‘kṣetra’ is the appellation. He who knows (vetti) — who fully cognises — this body which is the kṣetra, that is, who from foot to head makes it the object of knowledge by natural or by taught understanding, distinguishing it part by part — him, the knower, the knowers thereof call (prāhuḥ) ‘kṣetrajña’; here too ‘iti’ has the same sense as before, namely ‘in this manner’ they declare him to be ‘kṣetrajña.’ ‘Who?’ — the tad-vidaḥ, those who know the pair, kṣetra and kṣetrajña.
BG_C13_V02: Know Me also as the kṣetrajña in all kṣetras, O Bhārata. The knowledge of the kṣetra and the kṣetrajña — that is what I hold to be true knowledge.
BG_C13_V02::block-0:
Thus the kṣetra and the kṣetrajña have been spoken of. Are they to be known by just this much of knowledge? Not so, it is said —

Know Me, the Parameśvara, who am free from saṁsāra, also as the kṣetrajña, of the character described. The kṣetrajña who is in all the kṣetras, divided up by the many upādhis of kṣetras ranging from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass — Him, with all distinctions of upādhi removed, beyond the reach of words and concepts such as ‘sat’ and ‘asat,’ know to be Myself: this is the import. O Bhārata, since, apart from the true nature of the kṣetra, the kṣetrajña and the Īśvara, no other thing remains as object of knowledge, therefore that knowledge by which the kṣetra and the kṣetrajña, the things to be known, are made the objects of cognition — that is right knowledge: such is the conclusion of Me, the Lord Viṣṇu.

Objection: If in all kṣetras there is one Īśvara alone, and apart from Him no other experiencer (bhoktṛ) exists, then the Īśvara would become a saṁsārin; or, if apart from Īśvara no other saṁsārin exists, the absence of saṁsāra results. Both consequences are unwelcome, since the śāstra concerning bondage, liberation and their causes would be rendered purposeless, and there would be a contradiction with pratyakṣa and the other pramāṇas. By pratyakṣa, indeed, saṁsāra characterised by pleasure, pain and their causes is apprehended; and from observation of the variety of the world, saṁsāra caused by dharma and adharma is inferred. All this becomes inexplicable on the unity of Self and Īśvara.

Reply: Not so; for it is intelligible by reason of the difference between vidyā and avidyā — ‘Far apart and divergent are these two, what is known as avidyā and what as vidyā’ (Kaṭha 1.2.4). Likewise the difference of fruit pertaining to the spheres of vidyā and avidyā has been declared as opposed: ‘the better and the pleasant’ (Kaṭha 1.2.2) — śreyas pertains to the sphere of vidyā, while preyas is the effect of avidyā. So too Vyāsa: ‘These two are the paths’ (Mokṣa-dharma 241.6) and ‘These two indeed are the paths,’ and the rest. Here too two niṣṭhās have been spoken of. That avidyā together with its effect is to be removed is grasped from śruti, smṛti and reasoning. Among the śrutis: ‘If here he has known It, then there is truth; if here he has not known It, great is the loss’ (Kena 2.5); ‘Knowing Him thus one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going’ (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13); ‘The knower fears nothing whatsoever’ (Tai. Up. 2.9.1). Of the ignorant: ‘Then fear arises in him’ (Tai. Up. 2.7.1); ‘Living in the midst of avidyā’ (Kaṭha 1.2.5); ‘He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman’; ‘He who knows ‘He is one, I am another,’ does not know — he is like a beast for the gods’ (Bṛhad. Up. 1.4.10); the knower of Self ‘becomes all this’ (Bṛhad. Up. 1.4.10); ‘When like a hide…’ (Śvet. Up. 6.20) — and others by the thousand. And the smṛtis: ‘Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance, by which creatures are deluded’ (BhG 5.15); ‘Even here is creation conquered by those whose mind is poised in equanimity’ (BhG 5.19); ‘Seeing the same in all’ (BhG 13.28), and so on. By reasoning too: ‘Men, knowing serpents and tips of kuśa-grass and a well, avoid them; some, through ignorance, fall into them. See thus how the fruit of knowledge is signal’ (Mokṣa-dharma 201.17). Likewise it is understood that one who, ignorant, has the notion of self in the body and the rest, impelled by attachment, hatred, etc., performs dharma and adharma, is born and dies; while those who see the Self as distinct from body and the rest, by abandoning attachment, hatred and the rest and ceasing from the activity of dharma and adharma, are released — and this no one can deny by reasoning. That being so, of the kṣetrajña, who is the Īśvara himself, on account of differences of upādhi created by avidyā, there comes about an apparent state of being a saṁsārin — just as one’s being identical with the body and the rest. For of all beings the well-known firm conviction of selfhood in the body and the rest, which are non-self, is created by avidyā — like the determination of a man in a stump; and yet, on that account, no quality of the man becomes a quality of the stump nor a quality of the stump a quality of the man. Likewise the quality of consciousness is not a quality of the body, nor are the qualities of the body — pleasure, pain and delusion and the rest — qualities of the conscious Self. They cannot be; for, as both are created by avidyā, they stand on a par, like old age and death.

Objection: Not so, for the cases are not parallel. — The stump and the man, both being objects of knowledge (jñeya), are mutually superimposed by the knower (jñātṛ) through avidyā. But of body and Self, the superimposition is between jñeya and jñātṛ themselves; hence the example is not equivalent. Therefore the qualities of the body, though it is jñeya, may belong to the jñātṛ Self. — Reply: not so; for then unconsciousness and similar consequences would follow. If the qualities of the kṣetra, which is jñeya — body and the rest — namely pleasure, pain, delusion, desire, etc., belong to the jñātṛ, then a special reason must be stated for saying, ‘some qualities of the kṣetra, the jñeya — those superimposed by avidyā — belong to the Self, while old age, death and the rest do not.’ As for ‘they do not belong,’ there is the inference: because they are superimposed by avidyā, like old age, death and the rest; because they are to be discarded, and because what belongs to the Self is to be retained — and so on. That being so, saṁsāra characterised by agency and experiencership, residing in the jñeya, is superimposed by avidyā upon the jñātṛ; thereby nothing of the jñātṛ is impaired — just as space is not impaired by the surface-stains and the like superimposed upon it by children.

Thus, of the Lord, the kṣetrajña, who is in all kṣetras, not even the faintest trace of being a saṁsārin is to be apprehended. For nowhere in the world has any benefit or injury to anyone been observed from a quality superimposed by avidyā.

What was said — ‘The example is not equivalent’ — that is wrong. How? For only the bare fact of avidyā-superimposition is the common feature (sādharmya) intended between the dṛṣṭānta and the dārṣṭāntika. That common feature is not transgressed. As for what you suppose, namely that it is transgressed in respect of the jñātṛ — its inconclusiveness too has been shown by the case of old age and the rest.

Objection: The kṣetrajña’s being saṁsārin follows from his having avidyā. — Reply: not so; for avidyā is of the nature of tamas. The cognition pertaining to avidyā is tāmasa, since being of the nature of veiling, avidyā either presents things contrary to their truth, or produces doubt, or is itself the very absence of apprehension; for in the presence of the discriminative light, none of these is found, and only when the tāmasa veiling defect such as timira (eye-cataract) is present are the three forms of avidyā — non-apprehension and the rest — observed.

Here it is said: well then, avidyā is a quality of the jñātṛ. — Not so; for the timira-defect and the like are observed in the karaṇa (instrument), the eye. As for what you suppose, namely that avidyā is a quality of the jñātṛ, and that having such avidyā-quality constitutes the saṁsārin-ness of the kṣetrajña, and that what was said, ‘the Īśvara himself is the kṣetrajña, not a saṁsārin,’ is therefore unsound — that is not correct: just as the defect of grasping things contrary to fact and the rest is seen to belong to the karaṇa, the eye. The wrong apprehension and what is caused by it — the timira-defect — does not belong to the perceiver; for, when by treatment of the eye the timira is removed, it is no longer seen in the perceiver: hence it is not a quality of the perceiver. Likewise, in every case, non-apprehension, contrary apprehension and doubt-cognitions, and what is caused by them, can pertain only to some karaṇa, not to the jñātṛ kṣetrajña. And because they are objects of awareness — like the light of a lamp — they are not qualities of the jñātṛ; for being objects of awareness means being something other than one’s own Self that is grasped. And in kaivalya, when there is dissociation from all karaṇas, the possession of avidyā and other defects is not admitted by any disputant. If, like heat in fire, avidyā were a natural quality of the kṣetrajña Self, then there would never be dissociation from it. And of the changeless, all-pervading like ākāśa, formless Self, neither conjunction with nor separation from anything is intelligible — therefore established is the kṣetrajña’s eternal īśvara-hood; and the Lord’s own statement, ‘Because it is beginningless and devoid of guṇas’ (BhG 13.31), confirms it.

Objection: But then, with the absence of saṁsāra and the saṁsārin, the defect of the purposelessness of the śāstra and the rest would arise. — Reply: not so; for the difficulty is conceded by all. A defect admitted by all those who hold the existence of an ātman cannot be expected to be removed by one alone. How is it admitted? For in the case of liberated selves (mukta-ātman), the absence of the empirical usage of saṁsāra and saṁsārin is upheld by all the upholders of an ātman; and yet, in their case, the consequence of the purposelessness of śāstra etc. is not admitted by them. So with us: when in the unity of the kṣetrajña and the Īśvara, let there be purposelessness of śāstra; but in the sphere of avidyā, let there be purpose — just as for all the dualists the meaningfulness of the śāstra holds only in the state of bondage, not in the state of liberation; even so for us.

Objection: For all the dualists, the two states of the Self — bondage and liberation — are real entities (vastubhūta) in the highest sense. Therefore, given the existence of things to be discarded and to be obtained, and of their means, the meaningfulness of the śāstra holds. But for the non-dualists (advaitins), since duality is not real-in-the-highest-sense, being created by avidyā, and since the state of bondage of the Self too is unreal in the supreme sense, the śāstra is left without an object and so is purposeless. — Reply: not so; for difference of states cannot apply to the Self. If the two states, bondage and liberation, were to belong to the Self, they would be either simultaneous or successive. They cannot be simultaneous, owing to mutual contradiction, like staying-still and motion in one and the same body. If successive, then if without cause, there would follow non-liberation; if from another cause, then, since they would not be self-existent, the consequence would be their non-supreme-reality, and so the abandonment of your own postulate. Further, when one investigates the priority and posteriority of the two states, the state of bondage must be posited as prior, beginningless and yet ending; that is contrary to pramāṇa. Similarly, the state of liberation, with a beginning yet endless, when posited, is contrary to pramāṇa. Nor is it possible to maintain the eternality of one who, being in a state, passes to another state. And if, in order to avoid the defect of non-eternality, the difference of bondage and liberation is not posited, then for the dualists too the defect of the purposelessness of the śāstra and the like is unavoidable. Hence, the defect being common, the advaitin need not remove it.

Nor is the śāstra purposeless; for the śāstra has for its sphere the unenlightened person as he is commonly known. For the ignorant alone is there the perception of self in the non-Self — namely in fruit and cause — not for the wise; for the wise, when they see the Self as other than fruit and cause, cannot have the perception of self in those two as ‘I.’ Even the most deluded, even an unhinged man, does not see the unity of self in water and fire, or in shade and light; what to speak of the discriminating man. Hence the śāstra of injunction and prohibition does not pertain to him who sees the Self as other than fruit and cause. For when one is enjoined ‘Devadatta, do this!’ Viṣṇumitra, even when he stands by and hears the injunction, does not understand ‘I am enjoined.’ Comprehension is intelligible only when the discrimination of distinct spheres is not grasped; so it is in respect of fruit and cause too.

Objection: With reference to the natural relationship, comprehension of the meaning of the śāstra is intelligible — even though one perceives the Self as distinct from fruit and cause — namely, ‘I am enjoined toward what causes a desired fruit, and dissuaded from what causes an undesired one,’ just as for father and son and the like, even though they perceive each other as different selves, mutual comprehension of injunction and prohibition arises. — Reply: not so; for the conception of selfhood in fruit and cause is established prior to the comprehension of the Self as distinct. Only after he has comprehended injunction and prohibition does the man understand the Self as distinct from fruit and cause, not before. Hence it is established that the śāstra of injunction and prohibition has the unenlightened person for its sphere.

Objection: In texts such as ‘He who desires heaven should sacrifice’ and ‘He should not eat kalañja,’ those who see distinction from the Self do not engage; nor do those whose perception of self is confined to the body and the rest; and so, due to absence of an agent, the śāstra is purposeless. — Reply: not so; for engagement and disengagement are intelligible just on the level of common belief. He who sees the unity of Īśvara and kṣetrajña, the brahma-vit, does not engage. So too the nairātmya-vādin, holding that there is no other-world, does not engage. But on the level of common belief, one who, since the hearing of the śāstra of injunction and prohibition would otherwise be inexplicable, has inferred the existence of a Self, who is unaware of the special character of the Self, who has cravings born of fruits of action, and who is endowed with faith — he engages. This is matter of immediate evidence to all of us. Hence the śāstra is not purposeless.

Objection: From observing the non-engagement of the discriminating, those who follow them too will not engage, and so the śāstra would be purposeless. — Reply: not so;

because discrimination arises only in some. Among many beings only some are discriminating, as today; and the deluded do not follow the discriminating, because their engagement is governed by the defects of attachment and the rest, and because engagement in things like sorcery and the like is observed, and because engagement is itself natural — as has been said, ‘But nature acts’ (BhG 5.14).

Therefore saṁsāra is mere avidyā, of the very nature of what one experiences. There is no avidyā or its effect of the kṣetrajña standing alone. Nor can mithyā-jñāna injure the supremely real entity. The water of a mirage cannot reduce a saline tract to mire by its moisture; so too avidyā can do nothing whatsoever to the kṣetrajña. Hence too is it said: ‘Know Me also as the kṣetrajña’ (BhG 13.2), and ‘Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance’ (BhG 5.15).

Well then, what is this — ‘I am thus,’ ‘this is mine’ — found in the learned just as in the saṁsārins? Hear: this is what is meant by being learned, namely the perception of the Self in the kṣetra. Were they to perceive the kṣetrajña as actionless, they would not desire enjoyment or action under the notion ‘this should be mine.’ Enjoyment and action are themselves modifications. That being so, it is the unenlightened, owing to desire for fruit, who engages. Of the wise, who see the Self as actionless, on the lapse of activity-stoppage of the body-mind aggregate due to absence of desire for fruit and the consequent impossibility of engagement, ‘nivṛtti’ is metaphorically attributed.

Let others, again, hold this other ‘pāṇḍitya’: ‘The kṣetrajña is the Īśvara himself; the kṣetra is something else, the object only of the kṣetrajña. But I am a saṁsārin, happy and sorrowing; and the cessation of saṁsāra is to be brought about by me through the discrimination of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, and through dhyāna, by directly realising the Īśvara, the kṣetrajña, and standing in His own nature.’ ‘He who thus understands and he who teaches thus is not the kṣetrajña.’ He who thinks like this — that worst of pretender-paṇḍitas — saying ‘I confer meaningfulness on saṁsāra and liberation and on the śāstra’ — is a slayer of self, himself deluded, who deludes others, devoid of the true tradition of the meaning of the śāstra, dropping what is heard and inventing what is unheard. Therefore one not in the right tradition, even though knower of all śāstras, is to be set aside like a fool.

What was said — ‘On the unity of the Īśvara and the kṣetrajña, saṁsārin-ness accrues to the Īśvara; on the unity of the kṣetrajñas with the Īśvara, since there is no saṁsārin, the absence of saṁsāra arises’ — both these defects have been answered by ‘the difference between vidyā and avidyā being conceded.’ How? Because the supremely real thing in their sphere is not impaired by a defect imagined by avidyā. The example too has been shown: a saline tract is not turned into mire by mirage-water. So too the defect of the absence of saṁsāra by absence of the saṁsārin has been answered by holding that both saṁsāra and saṁsārin are constructed by avidyā.

Objection: But the very having of avidyā is the defect of saṁsāritva of the kṣetrajña; and the resultant happiness, sorrow and the rest are perceived directly. — Reply: not so; because what is jñeya pertains to the kṣetra, and a defect produced thereby cannot belong to the kṣetrajña, the jñātṛ. Whatever defect-class you would attach to the kṣetrajña, that, owing to its being jñeya, is verily a quality of the kṣetra, not a quality of the kṣetrajña. The kṣetrajña is not impaired by it; for between jñeya and jñātṛ no contact is intelligible. If indeed there were contact, jñeya-hood itself could not stand. If having avidyā and being a sufferer were qualities of the Self, how, sir, would they be perceived directly, or how qualities of the kṣetrajña? Once the determination is reached that ‘the entire kṣetra is jñeya, and the jñātṛ alone is the kṣetrajña,’ the assertion ‘avidyā, sorrow and the rest are qualifiers of the kṣetrajña, qualities of the kṣetrajña, and yet directly perceived’ is a contradiction uttered relying solely on bare avidyā.

Here it is said: ‘To whom does that avidyā belong?’ — To him in whom it is observed. ‘To whom is it observed?’ — To this is replied: the question ‘to whom is avidyā observed?’ is meaningless. How? If avidyā is observed, you also see its possessor. And when its possessor is apprehended, the question ‘to whom does it belong?’ is not appropriate. When a man with cows is observed, the question ‘to whom do the cows belong?’ is not meaningful. — Objection: The example is not parallel. The cows and their owner being directly perceived, their relation too is directly perceived; hence the question is meaningless. But avidyā and her possessor are not so directly perceived; hence the question is not meaningless. — Reply: When the relation of avidyā with a possessor of avidyā who is not directly perceived is known, what would you have? — Since avidyā is the cause of evil, it should be removed. — He to whom avidyā belongs will remove it. — But avidyā is mine. — Then you know avidyā and the Self that possesses it. — I know, but not by direct perception. — If you know it by inference, how is the relation grasped? For your relation as the jñātṛ with avidyā which is jñeya cannot, at the time, be grasped, because avidyā is appropriated to the jñātṛ only as an object. Nor is it possible that another jñāna should grasp the relation between the jñātṛ and avidyā — because that would entail infinite regress. If even by another jñātṛ the relation of the jñeya is known, another jñātṛ would have to be assumed, and another for him, and another again — infinite regress would be unavoidable. If, on the other hand, avidyā is jñeya, or whatever else is jñeya, it is jñeya only. So too the jñātṛ is jñātṛ alone, never jñeya. That being so, by avidyā, sorrow and the rest, no harm whatsoever befalls the jñātṛ kṣetrajña.

Objection: But this very thing is the defect — being the knower of a kṣetra that has defects; and not by metaphor of knowership applied to the very nature of consciousness which is changeless — like the metaphor of the action of heating attributed to fire merely on account of its heat. — Reply: just as here by the Lord himself the absence of agency, instrumentality and fruit-character in the Self has been shown to be by nature so — agency, instrumentality and the like being only superimposed by avidyā upon the Self — so it has been shown in passages here and there: ‘He who thus knows it as slayer’ (BhG 2.19), ‘Actions are everywhere wrought by the guṇas of prakṛti’ (BhG 3.27), ‘He takes upon Himself the sin of none’ (BhG 5.15), and so on. So have we explained throughout. And in the chapters that follow, we shall show it again.

Well then! since in the Self there is by nature no agency-instrumentality-fruit-character, but it is superimposed by avidyā, it follows that actions are to be performed only by the unenlightened, not by the wise. — True, that does follow; and we shall show this very thing at ‘For it is impossible for an embodied one’ (BhG 18.11). And in the recapitulatory passage at the close of all the meaning of the śāstra, namely ‘In brief, O Kaunteya, that supreme niṣṭhā of jñāna’ (BhG 18.50), we shall show it specifically. Enough of further extensive treatment here; it is concluded.
BG_C13_V03: What that kṣetra is, and what its nature, what its modifications, and from what it arises; and who He is, and what His powers — hear this from Me in brief.
BG_C13_V03::block-0:
Of the meaning of the kṣetra-chapter taught in the verse beginning ‘This body’ etc., this saṅgraha-verse is now set forth: ‘What that kṣetra is’ etc. — for it is fitting to give a saṅgraha-summary of a meaning that one intends to expound —

What was indicated as ‘this body’ — that He refers to by the word ‘tat.’ And this kṣetra that has been pointed out, what (yat) it is, of what kind (yādṛk) — that is, with what natural qualities; the word ‘ca’ is for conjunction. ‘Yad-vikāri’ — that whose modifications are such; ‘yataḥ ca yat’ — and from what cause what arises (the effect), ‘what is produced’ being the supplied predicate. And ‘He’ — the kṣetrajña who has been pointed out — what powers (yat-prabhāvaḥ): of what powers, that is, the powers conferred by upādhis, He is possessed. The true nature of the kṣetra and the kṣetrajña, with all the specifications stated, hear from Me — from My speech — in brief, in summary; having heard, fix it firm in mind: such is the meaning.
BG_C13_V04: It has been sung in many ways by ṛṣis, separately by the various Vedic chandases, and also by the well-reasoned, conclusive aphoristic words concerning Brahman.
BG_C13_V04::block-0:
He praises the desired truth of the kṣetra-kṣetrajña in order to kindle the listener’s eagerness —

By ṛṣis such as Vasiṣṭha, ‘bahudhā’ — in many ways, ‘gītam’ — sung, expounded. By the chandases — the Ṛk and the rest — these various, of differing import, of differing modes, ‘pṛthak’ — distinctly with discrimination — sung. Furthermore, ‘brahma-sūtra-padaiḥ ca eva’: brahma-sūtras are statements indicative of Brahman; the words by which it is reached, attained, made known, are called padas; and by these too the truth of the kṣetra-kṣetrajña is ‘sung’ — supplied from above. By the brahma-sūtra-padas like ‘One should worship It as the Self’ (Bṛhad. Up. 1.4.7), the Self is made known. ‘Hetumadbhiḥ’ — endowed with reasoning; ‘viniścitaiḥ’ — of the form of certainty, free from doubt; productive of definite cognition: that is the meaning.
BG_C13_V05: The great elements, the I-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest itself; the ten senses and the one, and the five objects of the senses —
BG_C13_V05::block-0:
To Arjuna, made eager by the praise, the Lord says —

Mahābhūtāni — the great elements; ‘great’ because they pervade all transformations; ‘bhūtāni’ — the subtle ones. The gross ones will be designated by the term ‘indriya-gocaras’ (objects of the senses). Ahaṅkāra is the cause of the great elements, of the nature of the I-cognition. The cause of ahaṅkāra is buddhi, of the nature of decision. The cause of that is avyakta itself — what is not manifest is avyakta, the unevolved (avyākṛta), the power of Īśvara, as said: ‘My māyā is hard to overcome’ (BhG 7.14). The word ‘eva’ here is for the limitation of prakṛti: of just this much, eightfold, is prakṛti divided. The word ‘ca’ is for the conjunction of differences. The ten indriyas — the ear and the rest, five, called buddhīndriyas because they produce cognition; speech, hands and the rest, five, called karmendriyas because they accomplish action — these ten. ‘And one’ — what is that? Mind, the eleventh, of the nature of saṅkalpa and so on. The five indriya-gocaras are the viṣayas, sound and the rest. These the Sāṅkhyas declare to be the twenty-four tattvas.
BG_C13_V06: Desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience, fortitude — this, in brief, is declared to be the field together with its modifications. (6)
BG_C13_V06::block-0: Now, at this point, those very items which the Vaiśeṣikas describe as 'qualities of the Self' — the Lord declares that these too are properties of the field alone and never of the knower of the field. Thus he says —
BG_C13_V06::block-1: Desire (icchā): one who has previously perceived an object of a certain kind as a cause of pleasure, on later perceiving an object of that same kind, desires to take it up under the conviction 'this is a cause of pleasure.' This desire is a property of the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa); since it is an object of cognition, it is the field. Likewise hatred (dveṣa): one who has experienced an object of a certain kind as a cause of pain, on later perceiving an object of that same kind, hates it. This hatred too, being an object of cognition, is verily the field. So also pleasure (sukha), which is favourable and consists in the lucidity of sattva, is the field, since it is an object of cognition. Pain (duḥkha), of an unfavourable nature — that too is the field, being an object of cognition. The aggregate (saṅghāta) is the conjoint mass of body and senses. Within that aggregate the modification of the inner organ becomes manifest, suffused with the reflection of the Self's consciousness — like fire in a heated lump of iron — and this is sentience (cetanā); it too is the field, being an object of cognition. Fortitude (dhṛti) is that by which body and senses, when they have lapsed into exhaustion, are sustained; it too, being an object of cognition, is the field. The mention of 'desire' and the rest is meant to indicate, by representative example, every property of the inner organ. Having said all this, he now sums it up — 'this, in brief, is the field together with its modification, that is, together with the modification beginning with mahat, declared, spoken of.' That field, the aggregate of all the differentiated forms of fields, of which it was earlier said, 'this body is the field' (Gītā 13.1) — that field has now been expounded as differentiated into the great elements (mahābhūtas) and so on, ending with fortitude. (6)
BG_C13_V07: Absence of self-conceit, absence of hypocrisy, non-injury, forbearance, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, restraint of the body-mind aggregate — (7)
BG_C13_V07::block-0: The knower of the field, with the attributes about to be set forth — that knower of the field, by the full understanding of whose nature together with its glory immortality is attained — him the Lord himself will set forth, with his distinguishing marks, in the passage beginning 'I shall declare that which is to be known' (Gītā 13.12). At present, however, he sets forth the cluster of means to that knowledge, characterized by absence of self-conceit and the rest, possessed of which one becomes fit and authorised for the knowledge of that to-be-known, and devoted to which one is called the renunciant established in jñāna-niṣṭhā. The Lord designates this cluster — 'absence of self-conceit' and the rest — by the term 'knowledge,' since it is the means to knowledge —
BG_C13_V07::block-1: Absence of self-conceit (amānitva): the state of the conceited (mānin) is conceit (mānitva), the lauding of oneself; the absence of that is amānitva. Absence of hypocrisy (adambhitva): parading one's own dharma is hypocrisy (dambhitva); the absence of that is adambhitva. Non-injury (ahiṃsā): not injuring, not harassing living beings. Forbearance (kṣānti): unperturbedness on encountering offences from others. Uprightness (ārjava): the straight disposition, freedom from crookedness. Service of the teacher (ācāryopāsana): the waiting upon — through service and the like — of the teacher who instructs in the means to liberation. Purity (śauca): the cleansing of the body's impurities by earth and water; and within, the removal of the impurities of attachment and the rest from the mind by cultivating their opposites. Steadfastness (sthairya): firmness of disposition, having one's resolve set on the path of liberation alone. Restraint of the self (ātma-vinigraha): the curbing of that aggregate of body and instruments which, being injurious to the Self, is yet called by the term 'self' — restraining what by its very tendency runs out in every direction, and confining it to the right path alone, is restraint of the self. (7)
BG_C13_V08: Dispassion towards sense-objects, and absence of egoism; perception of the evil in birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain — (8)
BG_C13_V08::block-1: Dispassion (vairāgya) towards sense-objects — towards sound and the rest, the seen and unseen enjoyments — is the dispassionate disposition. And absence of egoism (anahaṅkāra), the absence of the I-notion. The repeated perception of the evil and pain in birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain — birth, and death, and old age, and diseases, and pains — within these, beginning with birth and ending with pain, the repeated perception of the evil in each one severally. In birth, the evil is the dwelling in the womb and emerging through the birth-passage; the repeated perception, the contemplation, of that. So too in death, the repeated perception of the evil. So too in old age, the repeated perception of the evil consisting in the obstruction of the powers of intellect, vigour and lustre, and of being held in disregard by others. So too —
BG_C13_V08::block-2: in diseases such as headache and the rest, the repeated perception of the evil. So too in pains arising from the three causes — adhyātma (self-caused), adhibhūta (caused by other beings), and adhidaiva (caused by divine agencies). Or else, pains themselves are the evil — duḥkha-doṣa — and the repeated perception of that in birth and the rest, as before: birth is pain, death is pain, old age is pain, diseases are pain. Birth and the rest are pain because they are causes of pain, not that they are pain in their very form itself. Through such repeated perception of the evil of pain in birth and the rest, dispassion arises towards the enjoyments of body, senses and objects. Thence the instruments turn inward, towards the inner Self, for the realisation of the Self. Thus, being a cause of knowledge, the repeated perception of the evil and pain in birth and the rest is itself called knowledge. (8)
BG_C13_V09: Non-attachment, the absence of clinging to son, wife, house and the like; and constant evenness of mind on the occurrence of the desired and the undesired — (9)
BG_C13_V09::block-1: Non-attachment (asakti): attachment is mere fondness for the objects which occasion clinging; its absence is non-attachment. Anabhiṣvaṅga: the absence of abhiṣvaṅga. Abhiṣvaṅga is a particular kind of attachment, characterized by identifying with another as not different from oneself; as when, when another is happy or unhappy, one feels 'I alone am happy, I alone am unhappy,' or when, when another lives or dies, one feels 'I alone live, I alone shall die.' Where? He says — towards son, wife, house and so on; towards sons, wives, houses, and, by the word 'and the like,' towards other extremely cherished ones such as one's retinue of servants. Both of these — non-attachment and the absence of clinging — being conducive to knowledge, are called knowledge. And constant evenness of mind, equality of disposition. Where? On the occurrence of the desired and the undesired — of the obtainments of the agreeable and the disagreeable; in those occurrences of the desired and the undesired, constant equality of disposition. He neither rejoices on the occurrence of the desired, nor is incensed on the occurrence of the undesired. This very constant evenness of mind is knowledge. (9)
BG_C13_V10: And unswerving devotion to Me through undivided yoga; resort to solitary places, distaste for the assembly of common people — (10)
BG_C13_V10::block-1: And in Me, the Lord, through undivided yoga (ananya-yoga), through unalloyed concentration — the firm resolve 'there is none higher than the Lord Vāsudeva; therefore he alone is our refuge' — such an unwavering, unswerving conviction is undivided yoga; worship through that is devotion (bhakti); not given to swerving, that devotion is unswerving (avyabhicāriṇī). And that too is knowledge. Resort to solitary places (vivikta-deśa-sevitva): a vivikta place is one free from impurities and the like, free from snakes, tigers and the rest, whether by its very nature or by sanctification — such as forests, river-banks, sandy islets, temples; one whose habit (śīla) is to resort to such a place is a vivikta-deśa-sevin, and that condition is vivikta-deśa-sevitva. For in solitary places the mind becomes serene, whence contemplation of the Self and the like arises in solitude. Hence resort to solitary places is called knowledge. Distaste — non-delight — in the assembly of people, in jana-saṃsad: the assembly, the gathering, of common people, of those devoid of refinement, the unrefined; not the assembly of the cultivated and the disciplined, since that is conducive to knowledge. Hence, distaste for the assembly of common people, being conducive to knowledge, is called knowledge. (10)
BG_C13_V11: Constancy in the knowledge of the Self, perception of the goal of the knowledge of the Truth — this is declared to be knowledge; what is otherwise is ignorance. (11)
BG_C13_V11::block-1: Constancy in the knowledge of the Self (adhyātma-jñāna-nityatva): knowledge whose subject-matter is the Self and the rest is adhyātma-jñāna; the state of being constant therein is constancy. The fruit of the maturation of the contemplation of the means to knowledge — namely, absence of self-conceit and the rest — is the knowledge of the Truth (tattva-jñāna); and the goal of that is liberation, the cessation of saṃsāra; the perception of that is tattva-jñānārtha-darśanam. For only when one perceives the fruit of the knowledge of Truth does engagement in the practice of its means come about. This — that is, all that has been spoken from 'absence of self-conceit' down to 'the perception of the goal of the knowledge of Truth' — is declared to be knowledge, since it is conducive to knowledge. What is otherwise — that is, the contrary of what has been said — is ignorance: self-conceit, hypocrisy, injury, intolerance, crookedness and the like are to be known as ignorance, in order that they may be cast off, since they are causes of engagement in saṃsāra. (11)
BG_C13_V12: I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains the immortal: the supreme Brahman, beginningless; it is said to be neither sat nor asat. (12)
BG_C13_V12::block-0: When the question arises, 'By the knowledge thus described, what is to be known?' — he says 'that which is to be known,' and so on. But — it may be objected — the yamas and niyamas, namely absence of self-conceit and the rest, are not means by which the to-be-known is known. For absence of self-conceit and the rest are nowhere seen to determine any object. Everywhere it is only that knowledge whose object is a thing that is seen to determine that knowable. By a knowledge whose object is one thing, another thing is not apprehended — as fire is not apprehended by knowledge whose object is a pot. — That is no fault: we have already said that they are called 'knowledge' because they are causes of knowledge; and also because they are co-operative causes of knowledge —
BG_C13_V12::block-1: That which is to be known, that I shall declare — proclaim eminently, just as it is. With what fruit? — In order to allure the listener and turn him towards the teaching, he says: knowing which to-be-known, one attains the immortal — immortality; the meaning is, one no longer dies. Beginningless (anādimat): one which has a beginning is ādimat; that which is not ādimat is anādimat. What is that? The supreme Brahman, the unsurpassed; the term 'to-be-known' from before is to be supplied.
BG_C13_V12::block-2: Here some break the word as 'anādi mat-param,' on the ground that, since the bahuvrīhi compound already conveys the sense, the suffix matup would be otiose, which would be undesirable. And they show a special meaning: 'mat-param' meaning 'that of which I, the supreme Power named Vāsudeva, am the supreme.' True, it would on this reading not be redundant — if a meaning were possible. But no such meaning is possible, since Brahman is desired to be made known precisely by the negation of every distinction, in 'It is said to be neither sat nor asat.' To exhibit possession of a distinguishing power, and to negate every distinction, would be self-contradictory. Therefore, even though matup has the same sense as the bahuvrīhi, its use is for the metrical filling out of the verse.
BG_C13_V12::block-3: Having drawn the listener forward by the allurement, 'I am declaring the to-be-known whose fruit is immortality,' he goes on: that to-be-known is not said to be sat (existent), nor again is it said to be asat (non-existent).
BG_C13_V12::block-4: But — it may be objected — having proclaimed loudly, with such an elaborate preamble, 'I shall declare the to-be-known,' it is unbefitting to say 'It is called neither sat nor asat.' — Not so; what has been said is precisely befitting. How? Because in all the Upaniṣads, the to-be-known Brahman is pointed out only by the negation of distinctions — 'not thus, not thus' (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6), 'neither gross nor subtle' (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8), and the like — and not as 'It is this,' since it is not within the range of words.
BG_C13_V12::block-5: But — it may be urged — there is no thing whatever that is not denoted by the word 'is' (asti). If it be not denoted by the word 'is,' then that to-be-known does not exist. And further, it is self-contradictory to say 'It is to-be-known' and 'It is not denoted by the word is' together. — Not, in the first place, that it does not exist, since it is not the object of the cognition 'it is not.'
BG_C13_V12::block-6: But — it may be urged — all cognitions are pervaded by the cognitions 'it is' and 'it is not.' That being so, the to-be-known too must be the object either of the cognition pervaded by 'it is' or of that pervaded by 'it is not.' — Not so, because, being beyond the senses, it is not the object of cognitions pervaded by either kind of awareness. For a thing such as a pot, which is grasped by the senses, may be the object of the cognition pervaded by 'it is' or by 'it is not.' But this to-be-known, being beyond the senses, is to be apprehended only by śabda (scriptural revelation) as its sole means of valid cognition; it is not, like a pot and the like, the object of cognition pervaded by both these awarenesses. Hence it is said, 'It is neither sat nor asat.'
BG_C13_V12::block-7: As to the further objection — that what is said is contradictory, namely 'It is to-be-known' and 'It is said to be neither sat nor asat' — there is no contradiction, by the śruti, 'verily other than the known, and yet above the unknown' (Kena Up. 1.4). If it be said that the śruti too has a contradictory sense — for instance, like 'whether it exists in that other world or not' (Tai. Saṃ. 6.1.1.1) said in undertaking the building of the sacrificial hall — not so; for the śruti about its being other than both the known and the unknown is meant to convey what must necessarily be known, while 'whether it exists in that other world' and the like is a subsidiary praise (arthavāda) attached to an injunction. And by reasoning too: Brahman is not denoted by words such as sat, asat and the rest. For every word, employed for the purpose of revealing meaning, when heard by hearers, conveys its meaning by way of the relation of genus, action, quality, or relation, in dependence on the prior grasp of the convention; not otherwise, since no other way is observed. Thus: 'cow,' 'horse' — by way of genus; 'cooks,' 'recites' — by way of action; 'white,' 'black' — by way of quality; 'wealthy,' 'cattle-owner' — by way of relation. But Brahman is not possessed of a genus; hence it is not denoted by words like sat and the rest. Nor is it possessed of qualities, that it might be denoted by a quality-word, since it is without qualities. Nor is it denoted by an action-word, since it is actionless — by the śruti, 'partless, actionless, peaceful' (Śve. Up. 6.19). Nor is it possessed of relation, since it is one. Because of its non-duality, because it is no object, and because it is the very Self, it is not properly denoted by any word; this is fitting, and so the śrutis say, 'whence words turn back' (Tai. Up. 2.9.1) and the like. (12)
BG_C13_V13: With hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side, with ears on every side — That stands enveloping all in the world. (13)
BG_C13_V13::block-0: Apprehending the suspicion that, since it is not the object of the word and concept 'is,' it might be non-existent, he establishes its existence through the upādhis of the instruments of all living beings, in order to remove that suspicion, and says —
BG_C13_V13::block-1: 'With hands and feet on every side': that whose hands and feet are on every side is sarvataḥ-pāṇi-pādam — that to-be-known. The existence of the knower of the field is conceived through the upādhis of the instruments of all living beings. And the knower of the field is spoken of through the upādhi of the field. And the field is differentiated in many ways through hands, feet and the rest. The variety produced by the difference of upādhis of the field belongs only mistakenly to the knower of the field; hence, with the removal of that, his knowable nature has been declared in 'It is said to be neither sat nor asat.' Yet the false form occasioned by the upādhis is, in order to make his existence known, attributed as if it were a property of the to-be-known, and so it is said: 'with hands and feet on every side,' and so on. Thus indeed it is the saying of those who know the tradition: 'By the method of superimposition and rescission, that which is free from prapañca is shown forth' (anonymous). Hands, feet and the rest, perceived as members of bodies everywhere and at all times, are effects of their own, occasioned by the existence of the power of the to-be-known; hence they are inferential marks for the existence of the to-be-known, and are spoken of, by metaphorical extension, as belonging to 'the to-be-known.' The rest is to be explained likewise. 'With hands and feet on every side' — that to-be-known. 'With eyes, heads, and faces on every side': that whose eyes, heads, and faces are on every side is sarvato-akṣi-śiro-mukha. 'With ears on every side': śruti is the organ of hearing; that whose śruti is on every side is śrutimat. In the world — in the host of living beings — enveloping, pervading all, it stands — abides. (13)
BG_C13_V14: Shining through the qualities of every sense, yet devoid of every sense; unattached, yet sustaining all; without guṇas, and yet the experiencer of guṇas. (14)
BG_C13_V14::block-0: Lest, on account of the superimposition (adhyāropa) upon the Knowable of the senses such as hands and feet which are themselves only adjuncts (upādhi), one should suspect the Knowable to actually possess them — to ward off such a suspicion this verse is begun:
BG_C13_V14::block-1:
"Shining through the qualities of every sense" — "all the senses" means the senses such as the ear and the rest, which are termed the senses of cognition (buddhīndriya) and the senses of action (karmendriya), together with the inner organ in its twofold form, the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (manas); for, since they are equally adjuncts of the Knowable, they are all gathered up by the expression "all the senses." Moreover, since even the ear and the rest become adjuncts only through the medium of the inner organ as their adjunct, the meaning is that, by means of the qualities of all the senses — that is, by the functions of the inner and outer organs such as resolve (adhyavasāya), volition (saṅkalpa), hearing, speaking, and so forth — That, the Knowable, shines forth, as though engaged in the operations of all the senses; hence it is "shining through the qualities of every sense." The Śruti supports this: "It meditates as it were, it moves as it were" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7).

For what reason, then, is It not actually grasped as engaged in those operations? In answer he says: "Devoid of every sense" — that is, wholly without instruments. Therefore the Knowable is not really engaged in the activities of any organ. As for the well-known mantra, "Without hands and feet It moves swiftly and grasps; though eyeless It sees, though earless It hears" (Śve. Up. 3.19) and the like — that mantra is intended only to display that the Knowable possesses the power of conforming to the qualities of all sense-adjuncts, and not to declare that motion and the rest belong to It directly. Its meaning is to be understood like that of the mantra "The blind man found the gem" (Tai. Ār. 1.11) and similar passages.

Since the Knowable is destitute of every instrument, therefore It is "unattached" — devoid of every kind of conjunction. Although such is the case, yet It is also "verily sustaining all." For everything has Existence (sat) as its substratum, since in every place the cognition of "is" follows along. Even mirage-water and the like are not without a substratum. Hence as "sustainer of all" It bears all.

This too is another way of arriving at the existence of the Knowable: It is "without guṇas" — sattva, rajas and tamas are the guṇas; the Knowable is free from them. Even so, It is also "the experiencer of the guṇas" — that is, the experiencer, the apprehender, of the guṇas (sattva, rajas and tamas) when they have been transformed, by way of sound and the rest, into the forms of pleasure, pain and delusion. (14)
BG_C13_V15: Outside and inside of beings, unmoving and yet moving; on account of subtlety It is unknowable; far away, and yet near at hand. (15)
BG_C13_V15::block-1:
"Outside" — taking the body, extending up to the skin, which has been falsely posited as the Self through avidyā, and using just that as the limit, It is said to be "outside." Likewise, with reference to the inmost Self (pratyagātman), and using that very body as the limit, It is said to be "inside."

When "outside and inside" has been said, the absence of It in the middle would seem to follow; hence what is now said is: "unmoving and yet moving" — that very Knowable is also that which appears as the moving and unmoving body, just as the appearance of a snake (in a rope) is none other than the rope.

Objection: If It were both unmoving and moving, then the entire range of common transactions would be the object of knowledge; why then is It not known by all as "this"?

Reply: True, It does indeed appear as everything; yet, like ākāśa, It is subtle. Hence, on account of subtlety, although It is the Knowable, It is unknowable in Its own form to the unwise. To the wise, on the other hand, It is constantly known through such authoritative passages as "All this is verily the Self" (Chā. Up. 7.25.2) and "All this is verily Brahman." By reason of being unknown, It is "far away" — for It cannot be reached by the unwise even in tens of millions of years. And yet It is "near at hand," since to the wise It is the very Self. (15)
BG_C13_V16: Undivided, and yet existing as though divided in beings; That is to be known as the Sustainer of beings, the Devourer (at dissolution), and the Originator (at creation). (16)
BG_C13_V16::block-1: "Undivided" — in each body It is, like ākāśa, but one. "In beings" — in all living creatures, It is "as though divided" and abides therein; for It is conceived only with reference to the bodies. "And the Sustainer of beings" — That is the Knowable which sustains beings, hence "sustainer of beings" during the period of preservation. At the time of dissolution It is "the Devourer," of the nature of devouring. At the time of origination It is "the Originator," of the nature of bringing forth — just as a rope and the like is so with respect to the snake and the like that have been falsely imagined upon it. (16)
BG_C13_V17: It is called the Light of lights, beyond darkness; It is Knowledge, the object of knowledge, the goal to be reached by knowledge, seated in the heart of every one. (17)
BG_C13_V17::block-0:
Furthermore — Objection: If It exists everywhere yet is not perceived, then surely the Knowable must be only darkness?

Reply: No. Then what is It? —
BG_C13_V17::block-1:
Of the lights such as the sun and the rest, It is the Knowable Light. For the lights such as the sun and the rest shine forth only when kindled by the Light of Self-consciousness; as the Śrutis declare: "Kindled by whose effulgence the sun blazes" (Tai. Br. 3.12.9), "By Its lustre all this is illumined" (Mu. Up. 2.2.11), and the like; and the Smṛti — here itself — "That splendour which is in the sun" (BG 15.12) and so on.

"Beyond darkness" — It is said to be untouched by ignorance (tamas = ajñāna). To support him who has fallen into despondency through the thought that knowledge and the rest are hard to attain, the Lord says: "Knowledge" — humility and the rest (already enumerated); "the Knowable" — that which has been declared in "I shall now describe what is to be known" (BG 13.12) and so on; "the goal to be reached by knowledge" — the very Knowable, when it has been known, is the fruit of knowledge, and is hence called "that which is reached by knowledge," while "the Knowable" is what is being known.
