This entire triad is "seated in the heart" — in the buddhi — "of every one," of every class of living being, abiding there in a special way. For it is precisely there that the triad becomes manifest. (17)
BG_C13_V18: Thus the field, knowledge, and the Knowable have been declared in brief. My devotee, knowing this, attains to My state. (18)
BG_C13_V18::block-0: This verse is begun to recapitulate the matter already stated:
BG_C13_V18::block-1:
"Thus" — in this manner — "the field," beginning with the great elements and ending with steadfastness; "knowledge," beginning with humility and ending with the perception of the purpose of true knowledge of Reality; and "the Knowable," beginning with "That which is to be known I shall now declare" (BG 13.12) and ending with "It is said to be beyond darkness" (BG 13.17) — has been declared "in brief," concisely. For all this is the entire purport of the Veda and of the Gītā, gathered up and proclaimed in summary.

In this right vision (samyag-darśana), who is qualified? In answer he says: "My devotee" — one in whom the entire sense of self has been surrendered to Me, who am Īśvara, the Omniscient, the supreme Teacher, Vāsudeva — whose intellect has been so possessed by the conviction "All that he sees, hears, or touches is none other than Bhagavān Vāsudeva" — he is My devotee. He, having truly known this right vision as expounded, attains "My state" — "My-ness," the state of the supreme Self; to that My state he "becomes fit," that is, he attains liberation (mokṣa). (18)
BG_C13_V19: Know that primal nature (prakṛti) and puruṣa are both beginningless; know also that the modifications and the guṇas are born of prakṛti. (19)
BG_C13_V19::block-0: There, in the seventh chapter, two prakṛtis of Īśvara have been set forth, the higher and the lower, characterized respectively as the field-knower and the field; and it has been said, "All beings have these as their womb" (BG 7.6). How is it that beings have for their womb the dual prakṛti consisting of field and field-knower? — that very point is now being explained:
BG_C13_V19::block-1: "Prakṛti and puruṣa" — these prakṛtis of Īśvara, this prakṛti and this puruṣa — both "know to be beginningless" — those of which there is no beginning are "beginningless." Since Īśvara is eternal, it is fitting that His prakṛtis too should be eternal. Indeed, the very fact of His possessing this twofold prakṛti is what constitutes Īśvara's lordship (īśvaratva). The two prakṛtis by which Īśvara is the cause of the origination, preservation, and dissolution of the universe — those two, being beginningless, are the cause of saṃsāra.
BG_C13_V19::block-2:
Some interpret "anādī" as the tatpuruṣa compound "na ādī" ("not the first ones," hence not primary causes). For thereby, they say, the causality of Īśvara would be established. For if prakṛti and puruṣa themselves were eternal, then the world would be wrought by them alone and not by Īśvara as its agent.

Reply: That is wrong. Prior to the origination of prakṛti and puruṣa, since there would be nothing to be ruled, Īśvara would have to lapse from being Īśvara; and saṃsāra, being without cause, would entail non-liberation; the scriptures would become purposeless; bondage and liberation would not exist. If, on the other hand, both Īśvara and His prakṛtis are eternal, all this stands consistently. How? —
BG_C13_V19::block-3: "Modifications and guṇas" — the modifications about to be enumerated, beginning with the intellect and ending with the body and the senses; and the guṇas, which transform into the form of the cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion — "know," understand, to be "born of prakṛti." Prakṛti is Īśvara's power of bringing forth modifications, namely māyā, of the nature of the three guṇas; that which is the source of those modifications and guṇas. Therefore know those modifications and guṇas as "born of prakṛti" — as the transformations of prakṛti. (19)
BG_C13_V20: Prakṛti is said to be the cause in the production of the body and the organs; puruṣa is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasures and pains. (20)
BG_C13_V20::block-0: What, then, are these modifications and guṇas which are born of prakṛti? —
BG_C13_V20::block-1:
"In the production of the effect (kārya) and the instruments (karaṇa)" — the effect is the body; the instruments are the thirteen residing in it. The five elements which begin the body, and the (five) sense-objects, which are the modifications born of prakṛti previously enumerated, are here gathered up by the term "kārya." The guṇas born of prakṛti, of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, since they reside in the instruments, are gathered up by the term "karaṇa." Of these effect and instruments, that which is the producing — the bringing-forth — is called "the agency in respect of effect and instruments"; in this agency, prakṛti is said to be the cause, the source, by way of being the originator. Thus, by being the agent of effect and instruments, prakṛti is the cause of saṃsāra.

In the alternative reading, "in the agency of cause and effect (kārya-kāraṇa-kartṛtve)," the meaning is: "kārya" is that which is the transformation of something (the effect, the modification); "kāraṇa" is the modifying cause — that of which there is the modification; in the agency in respect of these — modification and modifier, effect and cause. Or else: the sixteen modifications constitute the effect; the seven that are both prakṛti and modification (prakṛti-vikṛti) constitute the cause; these are spoken of as "kārya-kāraṇa," effect and cause. In their agency prakṛti is said to be the cause, by way of being the originator alone.

Next, how puruṣa becomes the cause of saṃsāra is stated: "Puruṣa" — the jīva, the field-knower, the experiencer (these being synonyms) — "is said to be the cause in the experiencing," the apprehending, of pleasures and pains, the things to be experienced.
BG_C13_V20::block-2:
Objection: How, then, is the causality of saṃsāra ascribed to prakṛti and puruṣa through their being respectively the agent of effect and instruments and the experiencer of pleasures and pains?

Reply: This is now answered. If prakṛti did not transform itself, in the form of cause and effect, into effect, instruments, pleasure and pain, and if puruṣa, the conscious one, were not the apprehender thereof — whence could saṃsāra arise? But when prakṛti, having become the experienced, has transformed itself in the form of cause and effect as effect, instruments, pleasure and pain, and there is conjunction of the nature of avidyā between her and puruṣa as the experiencer (who is by nature opposed to her), then saṃsāra arises. Hence what was stated — that prakṛti and puruṣa, by their being respectively the agent of effect and instruments and the experiencer of pleasures and pains, are the cause of saṃsāra — is well established.

And what is this thing called saṃsāra? The experiencing of pleasures and pains is saṃsāra. And puruṣa's being the experiencer of pleasures and pains is what is called saṃsāritva (the state of being a transmigrator). (20)
BG_C13_V21: For puruṣa, abiding in prakṛti, experiences the guṇas born of prakṛti; attachment to the guṇas is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. (21)
BG_C13_V21::block-0: Now, of that experiencership of pleasures and pains — the saṃsāritva — which has been declared as belonging to puruṣa, the cause is being stated:
BG_C13_V21::block-1: "Puruṣa" — the experiencer — "abiding in prakṛti" — that is, abiding in prakṛti characterized as avidyā and transformed in the form of effect and instruments — "prakṛti-stha" means "having gone to prakṛti, taking it as one's Self"; "hi" — "because"; therefore he "experiences," apprehends — that is the meaning. "The guṇas born of prakṛti" — those born from prakṛti, manifested in the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion — thus: "I am happy, I am pained, I am deluded, I am wise." Even while avidyā is present, when the guṇas in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion are being experienced, that attachment which is the sense of self-identification (ātma-bhāva) toward them is the principal cause of saṃsāra, of birth — as per the Śruti, "As is his desire, so is his resolve" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.5). That itself the Lord declares: "the cause" — the reason — is "attachment to the guṇas" — the attachment in respect of the guṇas — "his" — of this puruṣa, the experiencer — "in births in good and evil wombs": "good and evil wombs" are real and unreal wombs respectively; births in those good-and-evil wombs are "sad-asad-yoni-janmas"; in respect of those births, taken as the object, the cause is attachment to the guṇas. Or else, in "births in good and evil wombs," attachment to the guṇas is the cause of "this saṃsāra" — the word "saṃsāra" being supplied from the context. "Good wombs" are wombs such as those of the gods; "evil wombs" are wombs such as those of beasts. By implication, the wombs of human beings are also to be regarded — without contradiction — as both good and evil.
BG_C13_V21::block-2: What is being said is this: prakṛti-sthatva, called avidyā, and attachment toward the guṇas, called desire (kāma), are the cause of saṃsāra. And this is being declared with a view to its being abandoned. The means for the cessation of this is well known in the Gītā śāstra to be knowledge and dispassion together with renunciation (saṃnyāsa). And that knowledge has been set forth previously, having for its sphere the field and the field-knower, in "Knowing which one attains the immortal" (BG 13.12); it has been set forth both by the negation of all that is other (anyāpoha) and by the rejection of the superimposition of properties not pertaining to It (atad-dharmādhyāropa). (21)
BG_C13_V22: The supreme Puruṣa within this body is called the Witness-near (upadraṣṭā), the Permitter (anumantā), the Sustainer (bhartā), the Experiencer (bhoktā), the Great Lord (maheśvara), and also the Supreme Self (paramātman). (22)
BG_C13_V22::block-0: Of that very Self a direct designation is now made once again —
BG_C13_V22::block-1: "Upadraṣṭā" — He who, while standing close by, is Himself the Seer yet remains uninvolved. Just as in a sacrifice, when the priests and the sacrificer are absorbed in the rites of the offering, there is some other person standing apart, uninvolved, skilled in the science of sacrifice, who scrutinises the merits and faults in the doings of the priests and the sacrificer — even so the Self is another, distinct in nature from those operations of body and organs, who, while remaining uninvolved in the activities of the body and the senses, witnesses, by sheer proximity, those very organs of action engaged in their work; therefore He is the upadraṣṭā. Or else, the body, the eye, the mind, the intellect, and the Self are all seers; among these the body is the outermost seer, and proceeding inward from it, the innermost (pratyak) seer, nearest at hand, is the Self — beyond whom there is no further inward seer; He, by reason of being the seer at the very closest proximity, is the upadraṣṭā. Or, like the supervisor at a sacrifice, He is the upadraṣṭā because He takes everything for His object. "And the Permitter" (anumantā) — anumodana, anumanana, is the satisfaction taken in the activities of those who are acting; he who does that is the anumantā. Or, the anumantā is He who, although Himself not engaged in the activities of body and senses, is yet conceived of as though engaged, as it were favourable to them — by virtue of which He is the Permitter. Or again, He is the Permitter because, being the witness of those engaged in their own operations, He never at any time hinders them. "Sustainer" (bhartā) — bharaṇa is the holding-together of body, senses, mind and intellect, which are themselves an aggregate, by means of the reflections of consciousness occasioned by their existing for the sake of the conscious Self; that holding-together of their proper form is itself the work of the conscious Self alone — hence the Self is called the Sustainer. "Experiencer" (bhoktā) — just as fire is by its very nature heat, so by His very nature as eternal consciousness, the cognitions of the intellect, marked by pleasure, pain and delusion, having every object whatsoever for their content, arise as though grasped by the conscious Self and are distinctly cognised; hence the Self is called the Experiencer. "Great Lord" (maheśvara) — being the Self of all and self-dependent, He is great and Lord; therefore the Great Lord. "Supreme Self" (paramātman) — being the Self characterised by the marks beginning with witness-nearness, He is the supreme one over the body and the rest, ending with the intellect, that have, through avidyā, been imagined as the inner self; hence the Supreme Self. He, accordingly, is also spoken of, declared, in Śruti by this very word "Paramātman." Where is He? "Within this body" — He is the Puruṣa, the Supreme, beyond the Unmanifest — the very same of whom it will presently be said, "But the Supreme Puruṣa is another, who is termed the Paramātman" (BhG 15.17), and who has been introduced in "Know Me also as the kṣetrajña" (BhG 13.2), expounded throughout, and gathered up at the conclusion. (22)
BG_C13_V23: He who thus knows the Puruṣa and primal Nature together with the guṇas — even though he should still be moving in every manner of conduct, he is not born again. (23)
BG_C13_V23::block-0: This very Self, with the marks already declared —
BG_C13_V23::block-1: He who, in the manner above set forth, knows the Puruṣa directly as "I am That," and knows primal Nature, of the character of avidyā as already described, together with the guṇas, that is, with its own modifications, as having been done away with — reduced to non-being — by true knowledge (vidyā), he, even though existing in every manner — that is, conducting himself in any way whatsoever — is not born again, that is, does not arise once more for the sake of another body when this body of the wise man falls; the meaning is that he does not take another body. By the word "even," the implication is that — what need be said? — one who is established in his own proper conduct is certainly not born again.
BG_C13_V23::block-2:
Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Although the absence of rebirth subsequent to the rise of knowledge has been declared, still, of the karmas done before the rise of knowledge, of those that arise after, and of those amassed in many bygone births, perishing without yielding their fruit is not justifiable; and so there should be three births, since the destruction of what has been done is not justifiable, just as in the case of those karmas, ripe for fruition, that have already initiated the present birth. Nor is any distinction among karmas made out. Therefore the karmas of all three classes should each initiate a birth — three births; or, all combined, should initiate one birth. Otherwise, with destruction of what has been done, there would arise universal want of confidence, and the scriptures would be rendered futile. Hence the statement "He is not born again" is unjustified.

Reply (siddhānta): Not so. From hundreds of Śruti texts such as "His karmas are exhausted" (Mu.Up. 2.2.9), "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Mu.Up. 3.2.9), "For him there is delay only that long" (Chā.Up. 6.14.2), "All his karmas are burnt up like the tip of a reed" (Chā.Up. 5.24.3), and the like, the burning up of all the karmas of the knower has already been declared. Here too, by the verse beginning "As fuel" (BhG 4.37) and the like, the burning up of all karmas has been declared, and it will be declared further. By reasoning also — for it is karmas that have for their seed-cause avidyā, desire and the afflictions that initiate the sprout of another birth; and here also it has been said by the Lord here and there: "Karmas accompanied by ego-sense and intent on results initiate fruit; not the others." Likewise: "Just as seeds burnt up by fire do not sprout again, so the Self is not joined again, the afflictions being burnt up by knowledge" (Mokṣadharma 211.17).

Let it be granted that, of karmas done after the rise of knowledge, the burning up by knowledge takes place because of their being co-existent with knowledge. But of those done in this very birth before the rise of knowledge, and of those done in past births, the burning up is not justifiable. Not so — because of the qualification "all karmas" (BhG 4.37). If it be said that this means only "all the karmas done after knowledge" — no; for there is no ground for that restriction. As to what was urged — that, just as karmas which have initiated the present birth are not destroyed, having already started yielding their fruit even when knowledge has arisen, so also, with respect to those karmas whose fruits have not yet begun, destruction is not justifiable — that is unsound. How? Because they, like a discharged arrow, have already started yielding their fruit. Just as an arrow, formerly discharged from the bow for the piercing of a target, even after the piercing of the target ceases only by falling, on the exhaustion of the impetus already started, even so the karma which has initiated the body, even when the purpose of the body's continuance has ceased, continues just as before until the exhaustion of the impetus of the saṃskāra. Just as that very arrow, when its prompting cause has not yet generated impetus and it is undischarged, can be withdrawn even when fitted to the bow, so the karmas that have not yet begun to yield fruit are, while still residing in their own seat, rendered seedless by knowledge. Hence, when the body of the wise man has fallen, "he is not born again" — this has rightly been said. Thus is established. (23)
BG_C13_V24: Some, by meditation, behold the Self in the self by the self; others, by the discipline of Sāṅkhya; and yet others, by the yoga of action. (24)
BG_C13_V24::block-0: Here are now declared the alternative means for the vision of the Self — meditation and the rest —
BG_C13_V24::block-1: "By meditation" — meditation (dhyāna) is the one-pointed contemplation that consists in withdrawing the senses such as the ear and the rest from the objects sound and the like into the mind, and the mind into the inner Conscious one, with full concentration; that is dhyāna. So too the figurative usages: "the heron meditates as it were," "the earth meditates as it were," "the mountains meditate as it were" — and from such similes one understands that meditation is a continuous, unbroken cognition like an unbroken stream of oil. By such meditation, in the self — that is, in the intellect — they behold the Self, the inmost Conscious one, by the self — that is, by their very own inmost Conscious one through the inner organ refined by meditation — these are some yogins. "Others, by the discipline of Sāṅkhya" — Sāṅkhya is the contemplation "these guṇas — sattva, rajas and tamas — are objects to be seen by me; I am other than them, the eternal witness of their workings, distinct from the guṇas, the Self"; this is the Sāṅkhya-yoga. By that, "they behold the Self by the self" — the construction continues. "By the yoga of action" — action itself is yoga, since, when performed in the spirit of dedication to the Lord and consisting in mere doing, it is, by virtue of being a means to yoga, secondarily called yoga. By that, through the door of purification of being and the rise of knowledge, others (behold the Self). (24)
BG_C13_V25: Yet others, not knowing thus, hearing from others, take to worship; even they too cross beyond death, being devoted to what they have heard. (25)
BG_C13_V25::block-0: But others, not knowing thus the Self, in the manner already declared, by means of even one of these alternatives, having heard from others — that is, from teachers — "contemplate this very thing," worship Him, with faith, contemplating Him. They too verily cross beyond death — that is, transcend the saṃsāra that is bound up with death. "Devoted to what they have heard" — those for whom hearing (śruti), that is, listening, is the supreme refuge, the supreme means in setting forth on the path of liberation, are "śruti-parāyaṇa"; the implication is, those whose only authority is the teaching of others, themselves devoid of discrimination. What need be said, then, of those who, independent in matters of authority, themselves possessed of discrimination, cross beyond death — this is the import. (25)
BG_C13_V26: Whatever being, moving or unmoving, comes into existence — know it, O foremost of the Bharatas, to be born from the conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña. (26)
BG_C13_V26::block-0: It was said, "By knowing which one attains immortality" (BhG 13.12), that the knowledge whose subject-matter is the oneness of the kṣetrajña and the Lord is the means of liberation. From what cause is this so? — to display that cause, this verse is begun:
BG_C13_V26::block-1: "Whatever" — whatsoever — "comes into existence," arises — "a being," a thing. Without distinction? No, says he — "moving or unmoving," both the moving and the unmoving — that is born from the conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña — thus know, O foremost of the Bharatas.
BG_C13_V26::block-2: But what conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña is intended here? Surely no special connection of the type that obtains by the conjoining of parts (as in the case of a pot with the rope), the joining-together of parts, is possible between kṣetra and kṣetrajña, since like ākāśa, the latter is partless. Nor again is it of the nature of inherence (samavāya), as between threads and cloth, since no relation of mutual cause and effect between kṣetra and kṣetrajña is admitted. Therefore it is said: the conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, the object and the subject of differing natures, is of the form of mutual superimposition (adhyāsa) of the properties of one upon the other; it is occasioned by the absence of discrimination of the proper natures of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, just as in the case of the rope, the mother-of-pearl and the like, owing to the absence of discriminative knowledge of those, there is the conjunction of the superimposed serpent, silver and the like. This conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, of the very form of adhyāsa, has the mark of false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna). For him who, in accordance with the scriptures, having first comprehended the distinction in the marks of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, separates out the kṣetrajña of the character already declared from the kṣetra whose form has been displayed before — like an īṣīkā-reed from a muñja-grass — and beholds the Knowable in its very form as Brahman, devoid of all upādhi-distinctions, by the words "It is not said to be sat or asat" (BhG 13.12); and who, with respect to kṣetra, is one of settled cognition: "What is mere unreal shines forth as though real," like an elephant fashioned by māyā, like an object seen in dream, or like the city of the gandharvas — for him, on account of contradiction with the right vision already declared, false knowledge departs. With the going of that cause of birth, what was said in "He who thus knows the Puruṣa and primal Nature with the guṇas" (BhG 13.23) — namely, "the wise man is not born again" — has rightly been said. (26)
BG_C13_V27: He who beholds the supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, undecaying among the perishing — he, indeed, beholds. (27)
BG_C13_V27::block-0: By "He is not born again" (BhG 13.23), the absence of birth, which is the fruit of right vision, was declared by way of the cessation of the seeds of saṃsāra — namely, avidyā and the rest. The cause of birth was likewise declared to be the conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, occasioned by avidyā. Therefore the right vision which is the dispeller of that very avidyā, although already declared, is now stated again in different words —
BG_C13_V27::block-1: "Equally" — without distinction — "abiding," remaining; where? "In all beings," in all the totality of living beings, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass; whom? "The supreme Lord" — He is the supreme Lord, the Paramēśvara, in respect of the body, senses, mind, intellect, the Unmanifest and the (individual) self; Him, abiding equally in all beings. He distinguishes those, by saying "among the perishing," and Him, the supreme Lord, by saying "undecaying," for the sake of displaying the absolute distinction between beings and the supreme Lord. How? For of all the changes of state (bhāva-vikāras), the change of state characterised by birth (jani) is the root; all the other changes of state — those that come into being subsequent to birth — culminate in destruction; beyond destruction there is no further change of state, since there is then no being whose change it would be. For only when there is a substratum (dharmin) do attributes (dharmas) exist. Therefore by the implication of the absence of the final change of state, all the prior changes of state, together with their effects, stand denied. From this is established the absolute distinction of the supreme Lord from all beings, and His non-difference and oneness. He who thus beholds the supreme Lord, in the manner declared, he indeed beholds.
BG_C13_V27::block-2: Objection: But everybody sees; what is the point of the qualification? Reply: True, he sees; yet he sees perversely. Hence he distinguishes — "He alone beholds." Just as one whose vision is afflicted with timira sees many moons, and is distinguished by reference to the seer of the one moon — "he alone sees" — so here too, he who beholds the one, undivided Self in the manner already declared is distinguished from those whose vision is the perverse one of seeing many divided selves — "he alone beholds." Others, even though seeing, do not behold, on account of their perverse vision, like the seers of many moons — such is the meaning. (27)
BG_C13_V28: Beholding the Lord abiding equally everywhere, he does not slay the Self by the self; thereupon he reaches the supreme goal. (28)
BG_C13_V28::block-0: Now, by way of declaring the fruit of the right vision already described, a verse is begun for its eulogy —
BG_C13_V28::block-1: "Beholding equally" — apprehending; for, since everywhere, in all beings, He abides equally, abides in equipoise — that is, the Lord, of the character described in the immediately preceding verse — "beholding equally," what then? "He does not slay" — does not commit injury — by the self, that is, by his very own self, his own Self. Thereupon, that is, on account of that non-slaying, he reaches the supreme — that is, the highest — goal, called liberation.
BG_C13_V28::block-2: Objection (pūrvapakṣa): But surely no living being slays his very own Self. How is that which is not the case stated, "he does not slay," as in "Fire is not to be set on the earth, nor in the air" (Tai. Saṃ. 5.2.7) and the like? Reply: This is no defect, since with the unwise the obscuring of the Self is well established. For every unwise person, having obscured the most well-known, immediate, non-mediate Self and grasped the not-Self as the Self, and having performed dharma and adharma upon that very Self that he has assumed, slays the Self he has assumed and takes up another Self — a new one — and slaying that one too in the same way, takes up yet another, and slaying even that, takes up another. Thus, slaying again and again the Self he has assumed, every unwise person is a slayer of the Self. As for the Self in its true reality, even He is, as it were, ever slain by avidyā, since the result of His existence is wanting; thus all the unwise are verily slayers of the Self. But the other one — the seer of the Self in the manner declared — he in either way does not slay the Self by the self, does not slay it. "Thereupon he reaches the supreme goal" — the fruit declared above accrues to him; this is the meaning. (28)
BG_C13_V29: He who beholds that actions, in every way, are wrought by primal Nature alone, and likewise that the Self is no doer — he, indeed, beholds. (29)
BG_C13_V29::block-0: It was said that, beholding the Lord abiding equally in all beings, "he does not slay the Self by the self." That, however, is not justifiable in selves divided by reason of the difference of guṇas, actions and characteristics, each from each — anticipating this objection, He says —
BG_C13_V29::block-1: "By Nature" — Nature is the māyā of the Lord, of the form of the three guṇas, as in the mantra-passage "But know māyā as primal Nature" (Śve.Up. 4.10) — by that Nature alone, and by no other, transformed into the form of cause and effect (mahat and the rest), "actions," undertaken with speech, mind and body, are being done — being accomplished — "in every way," in all manner; he who beholds — apprehends — and likewise beholds the Self, the kṣetrajña, as no doer, devoid of all upādhis — he beholds; he is the seer of the supreme reality — such is the meaning. For, with regard to a guṇaless, non-doing, distinctionless reality like ākāśa, no proof for difference is established — that is the import. (29)
BG_C13_V30: When one perceives the manifold existence of beings as resting in One, and likewise their expansion as proceeding from That alone, then one becomes Brahman.
BG_C13_V30::block-0: Once again, by other words, He elaborates that very same right vision —
BG_C13_V30::block-1: When — at whatever time — one beholds (anupaśyati) the manifold differentiation of beings (bhūta-pṛthag-bhāvam, viz. the pṛthaktva, the separateness of beings) as resting in one Self alone (eka-stham, abiding in the one Ātman), having been instructed by scripture and the teacher, and then sees the Self in the manner of direct perception, conformably (anu) to that teaching — "This whole is verily the Self alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2); and when, from that same Self, he beholds the expansion (vistāra), that is, the origination, the unfolding, in such modes as: "From the Self is prāṇa, from the Self is hope, from the Self is memory, from the Self is space, from the Self is fire, from the Self are the waters, from the Self are appearance and disappearance, from the Self is food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1) — when in this fashion he sees the expansion, then, at that time, he attains Brahman, i.e. he becomes Brahman itself. This is the meaning.
BG_C13_V31: Because of beginninglessness and being devoid of guṇas, this supreme Self is imperishable; though seated in the body, O son of Kuntī, It neither acts nor is tainted.
BG_C13_V31::block-0: When the consequence threatens — that, since the one Self is the inner Self of all bodies, the defects of those bodies must attach to It — this is now said —
BG_C13_V31::block-1: Because of beginninglessness (anāditvāt): the state of being without beginning is anāditva; ādi means cause; that of which there is no such cause is anādi. For whatever has a beginning perishes by its own nature; but this Self, being beginningless, is therefore (it being thus established) without parts, and so does not perish. So too "because of being free of guṇas" (nirguṇatvāt): for that which has guṇas perishes through the perishing of those guṇas; but this Self, being guṇa-less, also does not perish. Hence this supreme Self is avyaya — there is no perishing of It, therefore avyaya. Because of this, even though seated in the body — for the apprehension of the Self takes place in bodies, and so He is called "seated in the body" (śarīra-stha) — even so, He does not act. And since He does not act, He is not tainted by the fruit of action. For he who is the agent is tainted by the fruit of action; this Self, however, is no agent, and therefore is not tainted by the fruit. This is the meaning.
BG_C13_V31::block-2: But then, who is it that acts in the bodies and is tainted? If, on the one hand, some embodied being other than the supreme Self acts and is tainted, then what was declared regarding the unity of kṣetrajña and Īśvara — "Know Me also as the kṣetrajña" (Bhagavad-Gītā 13.2) and so on — becomes inconsistent. If, on the other hand, there is no embodied being other than Īśvara, then who acts and is tainted? — this must be answered. Or that there is no other (besides Īśvara) — this is altogether hard to grasp and hard to express; and on this very ground the Aupaniṣada vision proclaimed by the Lord has been forsaken by the Vaiśeṣikas, the Sāṃkhyas, the Ārhatas (Jainas), and the Bauddhas. The reply on this point has been given by the Lord Himself: "It is svabhāva that is set in motion" (Bhagavad-Gītā 5.14). For it is what has the nature of mere avidyā that gives rise to the conventional usage "acts and is tainted"; in absolute reality, however, that does not exist in the one supreme Self. Hence, for those who abide in this paramārtha-sāṅkhya-darśana — the jñāna-niṣṭhās, the paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas, in whom the avidyā-vyavahāra has been put away — there is no adhikāra in karma. This too has been shown by the Lord at place after place.
BG_C13_V32: Just as the all-pervading sky, by reason of its subtlety, is not tainted, so the Self, though seated everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
BG_C13_V32::block-0: To the question, "In what manner does It neither act nor become tainted?" — He brings forward an illustration —
BG_C13_V32::block-1: Just as space (ākāśa, kha), though all-pervading and reaching everywhere, by reason of its subtlety (sūkṣma-bhāva, fineness of being) is not tainted, is not contaminated by contact, even so the Self, situated everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
BG_C13_V33: As the one sun illumines this entire world, so does the kṣetrī (knower of the field) illumine the whole field, O Bhārata.
BG_C13_V33::block-1: As one sun (ravi, savitṛ, āditya) illumines, lights up, this entire world, even so the one kṣetrī illumines the whole kṣetra — beginning with the mahā-bhūtas and ending with dhṛti. Who? The kṣetrī, the supreme Self — this is the meaning. The illustration of the sun here serves a twofold purpose with respect to the Self: like the sun, the Self is one and the same in all kṣetras, and likewise unstainable.
BG_C13_V34: Those who thus, with the eye of knowledge, perceive the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, and the release from the primal nature of beings, attain the supreme.
BG_C13_V34::block-0: This verse is meant to summarize the entire purport of the chapter —
BG_C13_V34::block-1: The distinction (antara), that is, the mutual difference of character, between the kṣetra and the kṣetrajña as already explained — "thus," in the manner already shown — by the eye of knowledge (jñāna-cakṣus): the cakṣus is that ātma-pratyayika knowledge born of the teaching imparted by the grace of scripture and the teacher; by that eye of knowledge; and bhūta-prakṛti-mokṣa — the prakṛti of beings is the avyakta marked by avidyā; the release (mokṣaṇa, going to non-being) from that prakṛti of beings — those who thus know (viduḥ, vijānanti), they go (yānti, gacchanti) to the supreme, the supreme Self-reality, Brahman; they no longer take on a body. This is the meaning.
BG_C14_V01::block-0: It has been said that whatever comes into being arises from the conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña. To show how that is so, the chapter beginning "Param bhūyaḥ" is now commenced. Or else, the purport is this: it is kṣetra and kṣetrajña, both dependent upon Īśvara, that are the cause of the world — not, as the Sāṃkhyas hold, two independent (autonomous) entities. Again, it has been said that being seated in prakṛti, and attachment to the guṇas, is the cause of saṃsāra. In which guṇa is attachment, and how? What are the guṇas? In what way do they bind? How can release from the guṇas come about? And the marks of the released one must be told. With all this in view the Lord said —
BG_C14_V01::block-1: "The supreme jñāna" — the connection (anvaya) is established across the intervening words: bhūyaḥ, "again," although said many times in all the previous chapters, I shall yet declare. And it is param, supreme, because its viṣaya (object) is the supreme reality. What is that? Jñāna, the highest of all jñānas, by reason of its supreme fruit. By "jñānas" here is not meant amānitva and the rest; rather, the jñānas whose objects are knowable things such as yajña and the like. Those do not lead to mokṣa; this one alone leads to mokṣa — by the words "para" and "uttama" He praises it, in order to generate eagerness (rucy-utpādana) in the listener's intellect. "Knowing which" — having known, having attained, this knowledge, all the munis — saṃnyāsins, those given to manana — went upward, gone, attained, the supreme siddhi called mokṣa, beyond, that is, freed from this bondage of the body.
BG_C14_V02: Having taken refuge in this knowledge and attained sameness of nature with Me, they are not born again at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution.
BG_C14_V02::block-0: And He shows the absoluteness — the unfailing, single-issued character — of this siddhi —
BG_C14_V02::block-1: Having taken refuge in this knowledge as already declared — that is, having practised the means of that knowledge — they have come to mama sādharmya, the very nature of Mine, the supreme Lord; sādharmya here is not "sameness of properties," since in the Gītā-śāstra no difference is admitted between kṣetrajña and Īśvara. And this declaration of fruit is uttered by way of stuti (eulogy). Even at the time of creation (sarga) they are not born; they do not come into being. And at the pralaya — the time of destruction even of Brahmā — they do not suffer (vyathām na āpadyante), they do not fall away. This is the meaning.
BG_C14_V03: My womb is the great Brahman; in that I cast the seed; from this proceeds the birth of all beings, O Bhārata.
BG_C14_V03::block-0: He says that the conjunction of kṣetra and kṣetrajña, of just this character, is the cause of beings —
BG_C14_V03::block-1: Mine — belonging to Me, of My own being — is māyā, the prakṛti consisting of the three guṇas: she is the yoni, the cause, of all beings. Since she surpasses (mahattva) all effects and bears (bharaṇa) her own modifications, she is qualified by being the yoni precisely as "mahad-brahma" (great Brahman). In that — in the great Brahman, the yoni — I cast (dadhāmi, ni-kṣipāmi) the garbha, the seed of the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, which is the seed and cause of the birth of all beings. I, the Īśvara, possessed of the powers of both prakṛtis — the kṣetra-kṣetrajña duality — bring the kṣetrajña, who carries with him the upādhis of avidyā, kāma and karma, into conjunction with the kṣetra. This is the meaning. From that — that very impregnation of the garbha — proceeds (bhavati) the sambhava, the origination, of all beings, by way of the production of Hiraṇyagarbha, O Bhārata.
BG_C14_V04: Whatever forms come to be in all the wombs, O son of Kuntī, of those the great Brahman is the womb; I am the seed-giving father. (4)
BG_C14_V04::block-0: In all wombs—those of gods, manes, men, cattle, beasts and the rest—O son of Kuntī, the forms (mūrtayaḥ) that come to be, namely those whose distinguishing mark is the configuration of a body, whose limbs and members are compacted together (mūrcchitāṅgāvayavāḥ), of all those forms the great Brahman, that is, the great primal nature (prakṛti) which abides through every state, is the womb, the cause; while I, the Lord (Īśvara), am the seed-giver, the father, the agent of impregnation. (4)
BG_C14_V05: Sattva, rajas and tamas—these guṇas, born of primal nature, bind down in the body, O mighty-armed, the embodied one, who in himself is imperishable. (5)
BG_C14_V05::block-0: Which are the guṇas, and how do they bind? It is now told—
BG_C14_V05::block-1: Sattva, rajas, tamas—these are their proper names. "Guṇa" here is a technical term (pāribhāṣikaḥ śabdaḥ); it does not denote guṇas resident in a substance, of the kind colour and the rest are. Nor is the distinction between guṇa and guṇin meant to be conveyed here. Rather, since they are by nature avidyā in relation to the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), they, like guṇas, eternally dependent on another, bind, as it were, the kṣetrajña. By taking him as their resort they obtain a self for themselves, and on that account it is said that they bind. And these, born of primal nature—that is, born of the Lord's māyā—bind, as it were, O mighty-armed; he whose two arms, mighty and most capable, hang down to his knees, he is mahābāhu—O mighty-armed, in the body, the śarīra, they bind the embodied one (dehinam), the possessor of the body, who is imperishable (avyayam). His imperisability has already been declared by the verse beginning "Because of beginninglessness…" (Gītā 13.31). It may be objected: it has been said "the embodied one is not tainted" (Gītā 13.31); how then is something contrary said here, that they bind? It has already been parried by us through the word "as it were"—they bind, as it were. (5)
BG_C14_V06: Among them, sattva, being free from impurity, illumines and is free from affliction; it binds, O sinless one, through attachment to happiness and through attachment to knowledge. (6)
BG_C14_V06::block-0: Among these, of sattva and the rest, the characteristic of sattva alone is now first stated—
BG_C14_V06::block-1: Because it is free from impurity, like a crystal gem, it is illumining, and being free from affliction (anāmayam), free from disturbance, sattva—it binds him. How? Through attachment to happiness: the unreal (mṛṣā) clinging to happiness, that is, the bringing about of a conjunction, in the form of "I am happy," between happiness, which is an object, and the Self, which is the experiencer—this very thing is avidyā. For a property of the object cannot belong to the experiencer. And by the Lord himself it has been said that desire and the rest, ending with firmness, are properties of the field (kṣetra), the object, alone. Hence, by means of avidyā, which is one's own assumed property and whose mark is the lack of discrimination between the object and the subject, sattva makes one cling, as it were, to happiness, which is not one's own self; it makes the unattached appear as though attached, the non-experiencer of happiness appear as though happy. Likewise, through attachment to knowledge: "knowledge," since it is mentioned in company with happiness, is a property of the field, of the object, that is, of the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—not of the Self. For if it were a property of the Self, neither attachment nor bondage would be intelligible. Hence attachment to knowledge and so on is to be understood after the manner of attachment to happiness. O sinless one (anagha), free from affliction. (6)
BG_C14_V07: Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, arising from craving and clinging; that, O son of Kuntī, binds the embodied one through attachment to action. (7)
BG_C14_V07::block-0: Rajas is rāgātmaka, of the very nature of dyeing/colouring (rañjana)—rāga, like red ochre and the like, dyes; know it as such of the very nature of dyeing. Arising from tṛṣṇā and saṅga: tṛṣṇā is longing for what is not yet attained; āsaṅga is the conjoining of the mind, characterised by affection, in regard to an object already attained—the welling up of these two together is what is meant by tṛṣṇā-saṅga-samudbhavam. "Tan-nibadhnāti"—that rajas binds, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action: clinging to actions, both seen and unseen in their fruits, devotion to them, is karma-saṅga; through that, rajas binds the embodied one. (7)
BG_C14_V08: But know tamas to be born of ignorance, the deluder of all the embodied; through heedlessness, sloth and sleep it binds, O Bhārata. (8)
BG_C14_V08::block-0: Tamas, the third guṇa, is ajñāna-jam—born of ignorance—know it so. It is mohanam, productive of delusion, productive of non-discrimination, of all the embodied (sarva-dehinām), of all those who have a body. Through pramāda, ālasya and nidrā—heedlessness, sloth and sleep, taken together as pramādālasyanidrāḥ, by these, that tamas binds, O Bhārata. (8)
BG_C14_V09: Sattva attaches one to happiness, rajas to action, O Bhārata; but tamas, having veiled knowledge, attaches one to heedlessness. (9)
BG_C14_V09::block-0: Again, in brief, the operation of the guṇas is now stated—
BG_C14_V09::block-1: Sattva attaches—conjoins—to happiness; rajas, O Bhārata, attaches to action—the verb "attaches" continues. Tamas, however, having veiled, having covered, the knowledge produced by sattva, namely discrimination (viveka), attaches one, by its own veiling nature, to pramāda—and pramāda is the not-doing of what has come up as one's duty (prāpta-kartavya-akaraṇam). (9)
BG_C14_V10: Overpowering rajas and tamas, sattva prevails, O Bhārata; rajas overpowers sattva and tamas; and tamas overpowers sattva and rajas. (10)
BG_C14_V10::block-0: When do the guṇas perform the effect already mentioned? It is now told—
BG_C14_V10::block-1: When sattva, having overpowered both rajas and tamas, comes into being, that is, rises up and grows, then sattva, having gained its own footing, begins its own effect—knowledge, happiness and the like—O Bhārata. Likewise, when the guṇa rajas, having overpowered both sattva and tamas, grows, then it begins its own effect—action such as ploughing and the rest. When the guṇa called tamas, having overpowered both sattva and rajas, in the same way grows, then it begins its own effect—the veiling of knowledge and so on. (10)
BG_C14_V11: When in all the gateways in this body the light, namely knowledge, comes to be, then one should know that sattva has indeed grown abundant. (11)
BG_C14_V11::block-0: When any guṇa has become dominant, what is its mark at that time? It is now told—
BG_C14_V11::block-1: In all the gateways—the gateways for the Self's apprehension are the ear and the rest, all the instruments (karaṇāni)—in those, in all the gateways, the modification (vṛtti) of the inner organ, the buddhi, namely light, comes to be in this body. That itself is jñāna (knowledge). When such light, called knowledge, comes to be, then by this light-of-knowledge as mark one should know that sattva has indeed grown abundant—has come up. The word "uta" carries the sense of "indeed." (11)
BG_C14_V12: Greed, activity, undertaking of works, restlessness, longing — these arise, O bull of the Bharatas, when rajas has grown abundantly.
BG_C14_V12::block-0: This is the mark when rajas has come to manifest predominance —
BG_C14_V12::block-1: Lobha (greed) is the desire to grasp at another's wealth and the like; pravṛtti is engagement, general activity, exertion as such; ārambha — undertaking; of what? — of works (karma). Aśama is non-cessation, the unceasing surge of joy, attachment and the rest; spṛhā is thirst directed indiscriminately to every kind of object. When the guṇa called rajas has grown abundantly, these signs are produced, O bull of the Bharatas (bharatarṣabha).
BG_C14_V13: Non-illumination, inactivity, heedlessness and delusion — these arise, O delight of the Kurus, when tamas has grown abundantly.
BG_C14_V13::block-0: Aprakāśa is the absence of discrimination (aviveka); apravṛtti is utter non-engagement, the absence of activity; pramāda, its product, and moha as well — that is, aviveka, stupefaction; this is the meaning. When the guṇa called tamas has grown abundantly, these signs are produced, O delight of the Kurus (kurunandana).
BG_C14_V14: When the embodied one comes to dissolution while sattva has grown abundantly, then he attains the spotless worlds of those who know the highest.
BG_C14_V14::block-0: Showing that even the fruit which is reached through the door of death — being caused by attachment and craving — is itself wholly secondary, the Lord says —
BG_C14_V14::block-1: When sattva has grown, that is, has come into manifest predominance, then the embodied Self (dehabhṛt) attains pralaya, namely death; tadā — at that time — he reaches the worlds of the uttamavits, that is, those who know the principles beginning with mahat; he reaches the worlds amalān, free from impurity (mala-rahita) — this is the meaning.
BG_C14_V15: Going to dissolution in rajas, he is born among those attached to works; likewise, dissolved in tamas, he is born in deluded wombs.
BG_C14_V15::block-0: When the rajas-guṇa has grown abundantly, having reached pralaya, namely death, he is born among men who are joined to attachment for works (karmāsakti). Likewise — in just the same manner — having dissolved (pralīna), having died, when tamas has grown, he is born in deluded wombs, in the wombs of beasts and the like.
BG_C14_V16: Of well-done action they declare the fruit to be sāttvika and spotless; the fruit of rajas is suffering, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
BG_C14_V16::block-0: A summary of the meaning of the preceding verses is now stated —
BG_C14_V16::block-1: Of action that is sukṛta — that is, sāttvika — the wise (śiṣṭāḥ) declare the fruit to be sāttvika alone, namely spotless. But the fruit of rajas is suffering — that is, the fruit of rājasa action; since the action belongs to the sphere of compulsion (karmādhikāra), its fruit too is suffering alone, conformable to its cause, and is therefore rājasa itself. Similarly, the fruit of tamas — namely of tāmasa action, of adharma — is ignorance, just as before.
BG_C14_V17: From sattva is born knowledge; from rajas, greed; from tamas arise heedlessness, delusion, and ignorance as well.
BG_C14_V17::block-0: Furthermore, from the guṇas there arises this —
BG_C14_V17::block-1: From sattva, when it has come to its own established condition (labdhātmaka), is born — that is, comes to arise — knowledge. From rajas, greed alone. From tamas, both pramāda and moha come into being, and ignorance too comes into being.
BG_C14_V18: Those abiding in sattva go upward; the rājasas remain in the middle; the tāmasas, abiding in the way of the lowest guṇa, go downward.
BG_C14_V18::block-1: Those abiding in sattva — that is, established in the conduct of the sattva-guṇa — go upward; they take birth in the realms of the gods and the like. The rājasas stand in the middle; they are born among men. Jaghanya-guṇa-vṛtta-sthāḥ — the lowest is that guṇa which is jaghanya, namely tamas; its way of functioning is sleep, sloth and so on; those who stand in that, the deluded, the tāmasas, go downward — they are born among beasts and the like.
BG_C14_V19: When the seer beholds none other than the guṇas as the agent, and knows what is beyond the guṇas, he attains My state of being.
BG_C14_V19::block-0:
It was stated in summary in the preceding chapter that the puruṣa, joined with the false knowledge in the form of being seated in prakṛti, has, with regard to the enjoyable guṇas which are of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, that attachment of the form 'I am happy, I am wretched, I am deluded'; and that this is the cause of saṃsāra for the puruṣa — saṃsāra characterised by birth in good and bad wombs. Now, beginning from 'sattva, rajas, tamas — these guṇas, born of prakṛti' (Bh. Gī. 14.5), and onward, having declared at length the nature of the guṇas, the function of the guṇas, the bondage-power of the guṇas through their own functioning, and the destiny of the puruṣa bound by the operation of the guṇas — all this, rooted in false knowledge, being the cause of bondage — and all this having been told in detail, now liberation through right vision must be told. Hence the Lord says —

When the seer (draṣṭā), having become a knower (vidvān), no longer sees as agent any other than the guṇas — which have transformed into the shapes that are the field of the body, the senses and their objects — when he sees that the guṇas alone, in all their states, are the agents of all action; and when, further, he knows that which is beyond the guṇas — that which stands as the witness (sākṣin) of the operation of the guṇas — then that seer attains My state of being (madbhāva), namely My true nature.
BG_C14_V20: Having transcended these three guṇas which arise together with the body, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrows, attains the deathless. (20)
BG_C14_V20::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] How does one attain it? It is told —
BG_C14_V20::block-1: Having transcended — i.e. having gone beyond, while yet living — these three guṇas of the aforesaid description, which are the upādhis (limiting adjuncts) consisting of māyā; (the term) deha-samudbhavān is to be construed as 'which are the seed-causes of the arising of the body'; the embodied one (dehī), being thus the knower (vidvān), liberated even while living (jīvann eva vimuktaḥ) from birth, death, old age and the sorrows — i.e. by janma-mṛtyu-jarā-duḥkhāni is meant 'birth, and death, and old age, and the sorrows', the dvandva-samāsa being thus resolved — partakes of the deathless (amṛtam aśnute). Such, indeed, is the meaning: in this manner he attains to My state (mad-bhāvam adhigacchati).
BG_C14_V21::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] Having received the seed of (this) question — namely, that one transcends the guṇas while yet living and partakes of the deathless — Arjuna spoke:
BG_C14_V21::block-1: By what marks (liṅgaiḥ), what tokens (cihnaiḥ), does (a man) come to be one who has transcended these three guṇas already explained, O Lord (prabho)? Of what conduct is he — i.e. what is his ācāra? — this is the import of kim-ācāraḥ. And how, by what manner, does he go beyond (ativartate) these three guṇas — i.e. abide having transcended them?
BG_C14_V22::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] Asked by Arjuna concerning both the marks of him who has transcended the guṇas and the means of such transcendence, the Lord, in this and the following verses, gives the answer to the twofold question. As for the first — 'By what marks is he, who has transcended the guṇas, characterised?' — listen:
BG_C14_V22::block-1:
Brilliance (prakāśa), which is the effect of sattva, activity (pravṛtti), which is the effect of rajas, and delusion (moha) itself, which is the effect of tamas — these, when fully arisen, i.e. having become manifest as objects of cognition, he does not hate. (For one who is yet bound thinks thus:) 'A tāmasa cognition has arisen in me; through it I have become deluded; likewise, a rājasa activity, of the nature of pain, has sprung up in me, by which I, being moved by rajas, have been shaken from my own true nature; lamentable indeed is this lapse from abiding in my own essential form; and so too the sāttvika quality, of the nature of light, by impelling me to discrimination and at the same time attaching me to the joy (it brings), binds me' — thus he hates them owing to defective vision (asamyag-darśitvena). The transcender of the guṇas, however, does not so hate them when they have fully arisen. And just as a person of sāttvika and similar disposition desires the cessation of the products of sattva etc. once they have illumined the Self, so the transcender of the guṇas does not desire their cessation — this is the import. This (mark), however, is not a sign perceptible to others (na para-pratyakṣaṁ liṅgam). What then? Since it is perceptible only to one's own self, this characteristic is for one's own use alone. For another cannot perceive hatred or longing whose object is one's own self.

Thus the gunātīta does not hate the prakāśa, pravṛtti, and moha when they manifest, nor does he yearn for them when they cease — these being inwardly cognised marks, serving the aspirant himself as criterion of his own attainment.
BG_C14_V23: He who, seated as one indifferent, is not perturbed by the guṇas; who, thinking 'the guṇas merely operate', stays firm and does not waver. (23)
BG_C14_V23::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] Now He gives the answer to the (second) question, 'Of what conduct is the gunātīta?' —
BG_C14_V23::block-1: Like one indifferent (udāsīna-vat) — just as an indifferent person takes the side of none, so this knower of the Self (ātma-vit), seated upon the path which is the means to transcending the guṇas — i.e. that saṁnyāsin — is not shaken by the guṇas (guṇaiḥ na vicālyate) from the established condition of discriminative vision (viveka-darśanāvasthātaḥ). This very point He elucidates: knowing that 'the guṇas, transformed into the forms of effect, instrument, and object, function among themselves' (anyo'nyasmin vartante), he abides (so). The use of the parasmaipada (avatiṣṭhati instead of avatiṣṭhate) is (allowed) for fear of breaking the metre; the variant reading is yo'nutiṣṭhati. He does not waver (na iṅgate) — i.e. does not stir; the meaning is that he abides established only in his own true nature (sva-rūpāvastha eva bhavati).
BG_C14_V24: To whom pain and pleasure are alike, who is established in himself, to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are alike, who is the same towards the dear and the not-dear, steadfast, the same to blame and praise of himself. (24)
BG_C14_V24::block-1: Sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ — he to whom pain and pleasure are equal is sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ. Svasthaḥ — abiding in his own Self (sve ātmani sthitaḥ), serene. Sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcanaḥ — clod, stone, and gold (loṣṭa, aśmā, kāñcana) — these loṣṭāśma-kāñcanāni are equal (samāni) to him, hence sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcanaḥ. Tulya-priyāpriyaḥ — the dear and the non-dear, priya and apriya, i.e. priyāpriye, are equal — tulye, same — to him; thus he is tulya-priyāpriyaḥ. Dhīraḥ — endowed with discernment (dhīmān). Tulya-nindātma-saṁstutiḥ — censure (nindā) and self-praise (ātma-saṁstuti), i.e. nindātma-saṁstutī, are equal to whom — to that ascetic (yati) they are tulye, same; he is tulya-nindātma-saṁstutiḥ.
BG_C14_V25: The same in honour and dishonour, the same to the side of friend and foe, who has renounced all undertakings — he is said to have transcended the guṇas. (25)
BG_C14_V25::block-1: In honour and dishonour (mānāpamānayoḥ) he is the same — equal, unaffected (nirvikāra). The same to the sides of friend and foe (tulyo mitrāri-pakṣayoḥ) — although certain (saints) are, by their own intent, indifferent, yet, by the intent of others, they appear to belong, as it were, to the side of friend or foe; with this in view (the Lord) says he is 'the same to the sides of friend and foe'. Sarvārambha-parityāgī — undertakings (ārambhāḥ) are works begun for visible or invisible ends (dṛṣṭa-adṛṣṭa-arthāni karmāṇi); he whose nature it is to renounce all undertakings is sarvārambha-parityāgī — the meaning is that he renounces all karman save what is needed merely for the sustenance of the body (deha-dhāraṇa-mātra-nimitta-vyatirekena sarva-karma-parityāgī). He is said to be the gunātīta. From 'like one indifferent' (Bh. Gītā 14.23) up to 'he is said to have transcended the guṇas' (14.25) — whatever is to be accomplished by effort is the means of transcending the guṇas to be practised by the saṁnyāsin who is desirous of liberation (mumukṣu); and the same, when it has become firmly established and self-cognised (sva-saṁvedya), constitutes the mark (lakṣaṇa) of the ascetic who has (already) transcended the guṇas.
BG_C14_V26: And he who serves Me by the unswerving yoga of devotion — he, having fully transcended these guṇas, is fit to become Brahman. (26)
BG_C14_V26::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] Now He gives the answer to the question, 'And how does one transcend the three guṇas?' (Bh. Gītā 14.21) —
BG_C14_V26::block-1: And Me — Īśvara, Nārāyaṇa, residing in the heart of all beings — whoever, whether ascetic (yati) or man of action (karmin), serves with the unswerving yoga of devotion (avyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena) — that which never deviates, in which there is no time when it strays — bhakti is bhajana (worshipful resort), and that itself is the yoga, hence bhakti-yoga; he by that yoga of devotion serves — that man, having fully transcended these guṇas of the aforesaid description, becomes fit (kalpate) for brahma-bhūya. Bhavana is bhūya; brahma-bhūya is brahma-bhavana, i.e. liberation (mokṣa); the meaning is that he becomes capable (samartha) of (attaining) it.
BG_C14_V27: For I am the abode of Brahman — of the deathless and the immutable, of the eternal Dharma and of absolute bliss. (27)
BG_C14_V27::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] Whence is this so? It is told —
BG_C14_V27::block-1:
Of Brahman, the supreme Self (parama-ātman), I — for so it is — am the abode (pratiṣṭhā): pratitiṣṭhati asmin iti pratiṣṭhā, that in which it stands firm — that I, the inner Self (pratyag-ātman), am. Of what kind of Brahman? Of the deathless (amṛta), the indestructible; of the immutable (avyaya), the changeless; of the eternal (śāśvata) and abiding Dharma — Dharma here meaning dharma-jñāna, the knowledge of Dharma to be attained through the dharma of jñāna-yoga; of the bliss (sukha) which is of the nature of ānanda; of the absolute (aikāntika), the unswerving — i.e. of the supreme Self whose very nature is amṛta etc., the embodiment of the highest bliss; the inner Self is the abode — for it is by perfect knowledge that He is determined (niścīyate) as identical with the supreme Self. This itself is what was said by 'is fit to become Brahman' (Bh. Gītā 14.26).

Moreover, that power (śakti) of the Lord, by which Brahman 'stands firm' — i.e. functions — for the purpose of grace upon devotees and the like, that śakti is verily Brahman, and that I am, since power and the powerful are non-different (śakti-śaktimatoḥ ananyatvāt) — such is the import.

Or alternatively: since (the term) is denoted by the word brahman, here Brahman is sa-vikalpaka. Of that Brahman, I, the nirvikalpaka, am alone (eva) the abode (pratiṣṭhā), the support (āśraya), and none other. Of what kind? Of the amṛta, whose dharma is non-dying; of the avyaya, devoid of decay. Furthermore, the relation 'I am the abode' continues with respect to the eternal Dharma, characterised by the steady abiding in jñāna (jñāna-niṣṭhā-lakṣaṇa), and to the bliss born thereof, which is absolute (eka-anta-niyata).
BG_C15_V01::block-0:
Since the fruit of action for those engaged in works depends on Me, and likewise the fruit of knowledge for the knowers of the Self, those who serve Me through the yoga of devotion, by My grace, gradually attain knowledge, transcend the guṇas, and reach liberation. What need is there to speak separately of those who, through devotion, come to know rightly the very truth of the Self? Therefore the Lord, even though Arjuna had not asked, wishing to declare the truth of the Self, spoke beginning with "With its root above" (ūrdhvamūlam). There, first of all, by the figurative imagining of a tree, He describes the nature of saṃsāra in order to engender dispassion — for it is one who has become dispassionate towards saṃsāra alone who has the qualification for the knowledge of the truth of the Lord, and not another.

ūrdhvamūlam — "with its root above": that which, owing to its subtlety in respect of time, owing to its being the cause, owing to its eternity, and owing to its greatness, is "above" — namely, Brahman, the unmanifest (avyakta), endowed with the power of māyā — that is its root. Hence this tree of saṃsāra is "rooted above." And so also says the Śruti: "Its root is above, its branches below; this aśvattha is eternal" (Kaṭha Up. 2.3.1). And in the Purāṇa it is said —

"Springing from the unmanifest as its root, raised up by His very grace; having buddhi as its trunk, with the apertures of the senses for hollows; the great elements as its main branches, leafy with sense-objects; with dharma and adharma as its fragrant flowers and pleasure and pain as its fruits; affording sustenance to all beings, this eternal Brahma-tree, this very Brahma-grove, Brahmā ever frequents. Cleaving and cutting it through with the supreme sword of knowledge, and thereafter winning delight in the Self, one returns thence no more," and so on. That tree of saṃsāra, rooted above, made of māyā — "with branches below" (adhaḥ-śākham): mahat, ahaṅkāra, the tan-mātras and the rest, hang down from it like branches; hence it is "branched below." That which does not stand even till tomorrow (na śvaḥ sthātā) is aśvattha — that aśvattha which perishes in a moment, they call it (so).

avyayam — undecaying: the māyā of saṃsāra has been current from beginningless time, hence this tree of saṃsāra is undecaying; for it is well known as the support of the beginningless and endless succession of bodies and the like; that undecaying [tree]. And here is yet another distinguishing mark of that very tree of saṃsāra — "its leaves are the chandases": the chandases — namely, the Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman, so called because they cover (chādana) — are like leaves of this tree of saṃsāra, [as leaves are] of [an ordinary] tree. As the leaves of a tree serve for its preservation, so the Vedas serve for the preservation of the tree of saṃsāra, since they show forth dharma, adharma, and their causes and fruits. He who knows that tree of saṃsāra, as thus expounded, together with its root, he is the knower of the Veda — that is, knower of the meaning of the Veda. For there remains nothing further to be known, not even an atom apart from this tree of saṃsāra together with its root; therefore he is omniscient, the knower of the entire meaning of the Veda. Thus knowledge of the tree of saṃsāra together with its root is here extolled.
BG_C15_V02: Its branches spread downwards and upwards, nourished by the guṇas, with sense-objects as their tender sprouts; and below, [other] roots stretch forth, binding [the soul] to action in the world of men.
BG_C15_V02::block-0:
Of that very tree of saṃsāra, another imagining of its parts is now spoken —

"Below" — from man down to immobile beings; "and above" — up to the abode of Brahmā, the creator of the universe, that being the upper limit; in accordance with works and in accordance with what scripture prescribes, the fruits of knowledge and action — these, like branches, are spread forth (prasṛtāḥ) — gone forth — like the branches of that tree; "nourished by the guṇas" (guṇa-pravṛddhāḥ) — increased and made gross by the guṇas, namely sattva, rajas and tamas, which are their material constituents; "with sense-objects as their sprouts" (viṣaya-pravālāḥ) — the objects, sound and the rest, are like fresh sprouts that bud forth from the branches which are the fruits of action — body and the like; for that reason these branches have sense-objects for their sprouts. The supreme root, the material cause, of the tree of saṃsāra has already been told. Now, however, the impressions (vāsanā) of attachment, aversion and the like, born of the fruits of action, are like further roots — being subordinate causes of the engagement in dharma and adharma; these too are stretched forth below, that is, downwards as compared with the gods, having entered all about, "binding to action" (karmānubandhīni) — "karma" being dharma and adharma, and "anubandha" being that which follows after, that is, that on the rising of which they too rise; they are "karma-following" — and "in the world of men" especially. For here, in the human world, qualification for action is well known.
BG_C15_V03: Its form is not perceived here as such; it has neither end, nor beginning, nor any [stable] foundation. This aśvattha, with its roots so firmly grown, having cut down with the strong axe of non-attachment —
BG_C15_V03::block-0:
But this tree of saṃsāra that has been thus described —

Its form is not perceived here as it has been described, since it is alike a dream, a mirage, a city of the gandharvas, or a magician's illusion: for its very being is, the moment it is seen, already lost. For that very reason it has no end (anta), that is, no termination or final coming to a conclusion. So too there is no beginning — "this has come into being commencing from this point" — [such a determination] is not arrived at by anyone. Nor is there "saṃpratiṣṭhā" — a stable middle point of stay; that too is not perceived by anyone. This aśvattha as described, "with roots so firmly grown" (suvirūḍha-mūlam) — that whose roots have grown forth abundantly and become very firm, that very [tree] with such firm-rooted roots; with the axe of non-attachment (asaṅga-śastreṇa) — non-attachment is rising up away from the cravings for sons, wealth and worlds; with that axe of non-attachment, made firm (dṛḍhena) by the steadfast resolve of facing toward the supreme Self, and whetted upon the whetstone of the repeated practice of discrimination — having cut down the tree of saṃsāra together with its seed, and uprooted it.
BG_C15_V04: Thereafter, that abode is to be sought, attaining which they return no more; and saying, "To that primordial Puruṣa Himself I take refuge, from whom this ancient course [of saṃsāra] has streamed forth."
BG_C15_V04::block-0: Thereafter, after [that cutting], that vaiṣṇava abode is to be sought out (parimārgitavyam) — parimārgaṇa is searching, that is, it is to be known. The pada (abode) — entering which they return not (na nivartanti) — they do not turn back again to saṃsāra. How is it to be sought? He says: that very [Puruṣa], who has been spoken of by the word pada, the primordial (ādya), being in the beginning, the primordial Puruṣa — "in Him I take refuge" (prapadye) — thus is it to be sought out, namely by way of taking refuge in Him; this is the meaning. Who is that Puruṣa? It is said: from whom (yataḥ) — from which Puruṣa — the engagement (pravṛttiḥ) of the māyā-tree of saṃsāra has streamed forth (prasṛtā), gone forth — like the māyā of a magician — "ancient" (purāṇī), longstanding.
BG_C15_V05: Free from pride and delusion, having vanquished the fault of attachment, ever dwelling on the supreme Self, with desires wholly turned away, freed from the dualities known as pleasure and pain — the undeluded reach that imperishable abode.
BG_C15_V05::block-0:
How disposed do they go to that abode? It is said —

"Free from pride and delusion" (nirmāna-mohāḥ): māna is pride, moha is delusion; "māna-moha" is the pair, those by whom pride and delusion have departed are nirmāna-mohāḥ — devoid of pride and delusion. "Having vanquished the fault of attachment" (jita-saṅga-doṣāḥ): attachment itself is a fault — saṅga-doṣa; those by whom that fault of attachment has been vanquished are jita-saṅga-doṣāḥ. "Adhyātma-nityāḥ" — those constantly engaged in contemplation upon the nature of the supreme Self, intent upon that. "With desires wholly turned away" (vinivṛtta-kāmāḥ): those whose desires have, in a special way, with full detachment, turned away — these are vinivṛtta-kāmāḥ, the yatis, the saṃnyāsins, freed from the dualities of the dear and the unbidden, called pleasure and pain, abandoned by these — they go, the undeluded, devoid of delusion, to that imperishable abode as already described.
BG_C15_V06: Neither does the sun illumine that, nor the moon, nor fire; that, having reached which they return not, is My supreme abode.
BG_C15_V06::block-0:
That very abode is again specified —

"Tat" — that — connects through interposition with "dhāma." That dhāma, the lustrous pada, the sun does not illumine, even though it has the power of illumining all. So too the moon, the cool-rayed, illumines it not, nor does pāvaka, fire. That dhāma, the vaiṣṇava abode, having gone to which (gatvā) — having attained which — they return not; and which the sun and the rest do not illumine — that dhāma is the supreme pada of Viṣṇu, My pada.
BG_C15_V07: A portion of My very Self, become the jīva in the world of the living, eternal, draws to itself the senses with the mind as the sixth, [though they are] resting in their own nature.
BG_C15_V07::block-0:
It has been said "on attaining which they return not." But surely, every going has return as its end — "unions terminate in disunion" is well established. How then is it said, "For those who have gone to that abode there is no return"? Hear the reason for this —

"Of My very [Self]" — of Me, the supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa; aṃśa is part, member, a [partial] locus — these mean nothing different. "In the world of the living" — in the world of jīvas, that is, in saṃsāra, having become the jīva — well known as the doer and the experiencer — eternal (sanātana), longstanding; just as the reflection of the sun in water is a portion of the sun, [yet] when the cause, the water, departs, it goes to the sun itself and does not return, but rather goes [as it were] by that very [sun's own] Self; even so [is it here]; just as the ākāśa enclosed by the limiting adjunct of a pot etc., though [seeming to be] a portion of ākāśa, on the disappearance of the pot etc. as its cause, attains the [great] ākāśa and returns not. Therefore what has been said, "having gone to which they return not" (Bh.G. 15.6), stands established. — "But how can the partless supreme Self have a partial locus, an aṃśa? And were He to have parts, the contingency of destruction by the partition of parts would arise." — There is no such fault, since the partial locus, the aṃśa, is only as it were superimposed (kalpitaḥ), being delimited by the limiting adjunct fashioned by avidyā. And this matter has been shown at length in the chapter on the kṣetra. — How does that jīva, who is [thus] superimposed as My aṃśa, transmigrate and depart? It is said: the senses, sound and the rest, with the mind as the sixth, dwelling in their own seats — in the cavities of the ear and the rest, that is, abiding in [their respective] prakṛti — these he draws — pulls them along.
BG_C15_V08: When the Lord [of the body] takes on a body, and likewise when He departs from one, He goes carrying these [senses] with Him — even as the wind carries fragrances from their resting-place.
BG_C15_V08::block-0:
At what time? —

"Yac cāpi" — and likewise when the Īśvara, the lord of the aggregate of the body and the rest, namely the jīva, departs (utkrāmati), then "karṣati" — the second pāda of the verse is, by the force of the meaning, connected first. And when from a previous body He attains another body, then having taken (gṛhītvā) these — the senses with the mind as the sixth — He goes well (saṃyāti), goes thoroughly. Like what? He says: as the wind, the breeze, [carries] fragrances from their resting-place — from a flower and the like.
BG_C15_V09: Presiding over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, the nose, and likewise the mind, this one (the embodied Self) enjoys the objects of the senses.
BG_C15_V09::block-1: Ear, eye, the sense of touch — namely the skin-organ — taste, and likewise smell, and the mind as the sixth, each conjoined with its respective sense-organ: presiding over these (adhiṣṭhāya), this one, abiding in the body, enjoys (upasevate) the objects — sound and the rest.
BG_C15_V10: Whether departing (from the body), or remaining within it, or experiencing — joined with the guṇas — the deluded do not perceive him; those whose eye is wisdom (jñāna-cakṣus) do perceive.
BG_C15_V10::block-0: Thus the one in the body — and (severing) from the body —
BG_C15_V10::block-1: Departing (utkrāmantam) — abandoning the previously acquired body; or else remaining (sthitam) in the body; or experiencing (bhuñjānam) — that is, apprehending sound and the rest; conjoined with the guṇas (guṇānvitam) — joined with, accompanied by, fully linked to the guṇas such as pleasure, pain, delusion, and the like — that is the meaning. Although he is set forth thus, well within the very range of vision, the deluded (vimūḍhāḥ) — those whose minds are dragged hither and thither by the lure of seen and unseen sense-enjoyments, deluded in many ways — do not behold him. The Blessed One laments compassionately: "Alas, what a piteous state prevails!" Those, however, who possess the eye of knowledge born of the (six) means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) — they see him; jñāna-cakṣuṣaḥ means they whose vision is discriminative (viviktadṛṣṭi) — that is the meaning.
BG_C15_V11: And those yogins who strive behold him established in the Self; but those of unrefined being, even though striving, being undiscerning, do not behold him.
BG_C15_V11::block-1: Those striving (yatantaḥ), making effort, and the yogins (yoginaḥ) — those of well-collected mind (samāhita-citta) — behold this one, the Self under discussion: "This very one am I" — thus they apprehend him as established in the Self (ātmani), that is, in their own intellect (svasyāṃ buddhau). But the undiscerning (acetasaḥ) — those without discrimination — even though striving by means of scripture and other valid means, being of unrefined being (akṛtātmānaḥ) — that is, those whose self has not been purified by austerity and the conquest of the senses — not turned away from evil conduct, of unstilled pride, even though making effort, do not thus behold him.
BG_C15_V12: That brilliance, dwelling in the sun, which illumines the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in fire — know that brilliance to be Mine.
BG_C15_V12::block-0: That Pada (supreme abode) which the lights such as fire, sun and the rest — though themselves illuminators of all — do not illumine; on attaining which the seekers of liberation do not turn back, facing transmigration once more; and of which Pada the individual jīvas, modulating themselves according to the diversity of upādhis (limiting adjuncts), are mere portions — as pot-space and the like are portions of space (ākāśa); intending to declare the all-Self-nature (sarvātmatva) of that Pada and its being the substratum of every empirical transaction, the Blessed One states a brief epitome of His vibhūti (manifest glories) in four verses —
BG_C15_V12::block-1: That which dwells in the sun (ādityagatam) — that is, has the sun as its locus. What is it? Tejas — splendour, light — which illumines (bhāsayate) the world, the entire universe, in its totality (akhilam); and that which abides as illuminator in the moon, the bearer of the hare-mark; and that which is in fire, the carrier of oblations — know (viddhi) that brilliance to be Mine (māmakam), belonging to Me, that light of Mine, Viṣṇu's. Or alternatively: the brilliance dwelling in the sun is the light whose nature is consciousness (caitanyātmaka jyotis); that which is in the moon and that which is in fire — know that brilliance to be Mine, belonging to Me, that light of Mine, Viṣṇu's.
BG_C15_V12::block-2: Objection: But that consciousness-natured light is alike in things stationary and in things moving. How then can this specification — "That which dwells in the sun" and the rest — hold? The answer: This is no defect, for it is logical that, owing to the predominance of sattva, the manifestation be more abundant. In the sun and the rest, sattva is exceedingly luminous and exceedingly resplendent; hence the light is manifest there in a heightened degree, and so it is singled out — not, however, that the light is greater there in itself. Just as a face, though uniformly present (capable of reflection), does not become manifest on a piece of wood or a wall, but in a clear mirror — and still more in one yet clearer — manifests in graded measure: even so here.
BG_C15_V13: Entering the earth, I sustain the beings by My vigour; and becoming the moon — whose essence is sap (rasa) — I nourish all the herbs.
BG_C15_V13::block-1: Entering (āviśya) the earth (gām), pervading it, I sustain (dhārayāmi) the beings, the world, by My vigour (ojasā), by strength — that strength, devoid of desire and attachment, the Lord-form, by which, having entered into the earth for upholding the world, the earth, though heavy, neither falls down nor splits asunder. Thus too proclaims the mantra-utterance: "By whom the heavens are fierce and the earth firm" (Tai. Saṃ. 4.1.8), and "He upheld the earth" (Tai. Saṃ. 4.1.8), and so on. Therefore it is rightly said, "Entering the earth, I bear up the moving and unmoving beings." Furthermore, the herbs born on earth — all of them, rice, barley, and the rest — I nourish (puṣṇāmi); I render them full of nutriment and savoured with sap, becoming the moon (somo bhūtvā) whose essence is sap (rasātmaka) — that is, becoming Soma whose intrinsic nature is sap.
