The moon (Soma) is the storehouse of all sappy savours; he, being himself the embodiment of every rasa, infusing his own sap into all the herbs, nourishes them.
BG_C15_V14: Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire, lodged in the body of beings, conjoined with prāṇa and apāna, I digest the four kinds of food.
BG_C15_V14::block-1: I Myself, becoming the Vaiśvānara — the fire seated in the belly — as the śruti says, "This fire that is Vaiśvānara is that which is within man, by which this food that is eaten is digested" (Bṛ. Up. 5.9.1) and the like; being Vaiśvānara, taking refuge in (i.e., entering) the body (deham āśritaḥ) of beings — those endowed with prāṇa — and conjoined (samāyukta) with prāṇa and apāna, I digest (pacāmi) — that is, I effect digestion of — the food (annam), of food in the four kinds (caturvidham), the four-fold edible: that which is chewed (bhakṣya), that which is sucked (cūṣya), that which is licked (lehya), and that which is drunk/eaten (bhojya). For one who beholds, "The eater is Vaiśvānara fire; the eaten is food, Soma; both these together — agni-ṣomau — constitute the entire universe," no defilement of food can ever cling.
BG_C15_V15: And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me are memory, knowledge, and their loss; by all the Vedas am I alone the One to be known; the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda, that too am I.
BG_C15_V15::block-1: Being the Self of every being-class, I am seated within the heart (hṛdi), in the intellect (buddhi). Hence from Me, the Self of all beings, arise memory (smṛti), knowledge (jñāna), and their removal (apohanam) — their departure. As the memory and knowledge of those of meritorious deeds arise corresponding to their meritorious karma, so for those of demerit-filled deeds the dimming, the loss, the receding (apāyana, apagamana) of memory and knowledge proceeds in conformity with their evil karma. By all the Vedas (vedaiḥ ca sarvaiḥ) I alone, the supreme Self, am to be known (vedyaḥ) — that is, am the One to be cognised. I am the author of Vedānta (vedānta-kṛt) — namely, the originator of the tradition of the Vedānta-meaning — that is the sense; and I alone am the knower of the Veda (vedavit), the one who knows the meaning of the Veda.
BG_C15_V16: Two are these puruṣas in the world, the perishable and the imperishable: all beings are the perishable; the kūṭastha is called the imperishable.
BG_C15_V16::block-0: The compendium of the Lord's vibhūti — of the Blessed Lord, the Īśvara called Nārāyaṇa — has been declared, made through the medium of specific limiting adjuncts (viśiṣṭa-upādhi-kṛta), beginning with "That brilliance dwelling in the sun" (Bh.Gī. 15.12) and the rest. Now, henceforth, the following verses are commenced, with the desire to determine the very nature, in itself, of that same (Lord) — the unconditioned, the absolute (nirupādhika kevala), distinct from the differentiation effected by the upādhis of the perishable and the imperishable. There, gathering up into three masses the entire content of the topic-meaning of the past and the coming chapters, He says —
BG_C15_V16::block-1: These two puruṣas, set forth as separate masses, are spoken of in the world (loka) — that is, in saṃsāra — as two: the perishable (kṣara), so called because it perishes (kṣarati), the destructible — that is one mass; and the other puruṣa, the imperishable (akṣara), its opposite — namely the māyā-power of the Blessed Lord, the seed of the rise of the puruṣa called "perishable," the substratum of the impressions (saṃskāras) of the desires, karmas, and the rest of innumerable transmigrating creatures — this is called the imperishable puruṣa. Who are those two puruṣas? The Blessed Lord himself states: the perishable consists of all beings (sarvāṇi bhūtāni) — that is, the entire mass of modifications (vikāra-jāta) — that is the meaning. Kūṭastha — kūṭa means a heap, and standing as a heap; or alternatively, the synonyms of kūṭa are māyā, deception (vañcanā), crookedness (jihmatā), tortuousness (kuṭilatā) — standing in many modes of māyā, deception, and the rest, is kūṭastha. Because of the endlessness of the seed of saṃsāra, it does not perish (na kṣarati) — therefore it is called akṣara.
BG_C15_V17: But the Supreme Puruṣa is another, declared as the Paramātman — He who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them, the imperishable Lord. (17)
BG_C15_V17::block-0: Different from these two — the perishable (kṣara) and the imperishable (akṣara) — distinct from them, untouched by the twofold defect of these two upādhis (the kṣara-upādhi and the akṣara-upādhi), of the very nature eternally pure, awake, and free —
BG_C15_V17::block-1: The Uttama Puruṣa — uttama in the sense of 'most exalted' — is, however, another, utterly distinct from these two. Paramātman: He is parama, supreme, in relation to the selves fashioned by avidyā, namely the body and the rest; and He is ātman, the inner conscious principle of all beings; therefore He is celebrated in the Vedānta texts under the name 'Paramātman.' This very one is now further specified: He who, having entered (āviśya — having pervaded) the three worlds known as bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, and svaḥ, by His own innate power of consciousness, sustains them — bibharti — sustains and upholds them merely by the fact of His own being (svarūpa-sad-bhāva-mātreṇa). Avyaya: He in whom no decay (vyaya) is found is avyaya. Who is this? The Īśvara — the omniscient one called Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is to rule (īśana-śīla).
BG_C15_V18: Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, therefore am I celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama. (18)
BG_C15_V18::block-0: For the Īśvara as thus expounded, the name 'Puruṣottama' is well known. By showing — through the well-established etymology of the name — that the name is meaningful, the Lord reveals Himself as 'I am the unsurpassed Īśvara' —
BG_C15_V18::block-1: Because I have transcended (atītaḥ) the perishable — that is, I have crossed over the saṃsāra-māyā tree known as the aśvattha — and because I am uttama, most exalted, or highest (ūrdhvatama), in comparison even with the imperishable — that imperishable which is the seed-source of the saṃsāra-māyā tree — therefore, on account of My pre-eminence over both the kṣara and the akṣara, I am celebrated, well known, in the world and in the Veda. Thus do devotees know Me as 'Puruṣottama.' Poets too inscribe this name in their kāvyas and elsewhere. They invoke and extol Me by this very appellation, 'Puruṣottama.'
BG_C15_V19: He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as Puruṣottama — he, knowing all, worships Me with his whole being, O Bhārata. (19)
BG_C15_V19::block-0: Now then, the fruit attained by him who knows the Self as just expounded is set forth —
BG_C15_V19::block-1: He who knows Me — the Īśvara possessed of the qualities just stated — in the manner just explained, free from delusion (asaṃmūḍhaḥ), being devoid of confusion, knowing 'this very Puruṣottama, that I am' — he is the sarvavit, the all-knower: in his very Self he knows all, hence omniscient. He worships Me, who abide in all beings, with sarvabhāva — with his whole being, as his very Self in every aspect, O Bhārata.
BG_C15_V20: Thus has this most secret teaching been declared by Me, O sinless one. Knowing this, one becomes wise and accomplished in all that is to be done, O Bhārata. (20)
BG_C15_V20::block-0: In this chapter, having declared the knowledge of the truth of the Lord, whose fruit is liberation (mokṣa), now indeed He extols it —
BG_C15_V20::block-1:
'Iti' — that is, 'thus.' Guhyatamam — most secret to be guarded, that is, the highest hiddenness. What is so? The śāstra. Although the entire work known as the Gītā is called 'śāstra,' yet here this very chapter is called 'śāstra' for the sake of praise, by force of context (prakaraṇa). For the entire purport of the Gītā-śāstra has been stated in this chapter in a condensed form. Nay, not merely the purport of the Gītā-śāstra, but the whole purport of the Veda is here brought to completion. So has it been said: 'He who knows that, he is the knower of the Veda' (Bh. Gī. 15.1), and 'By all the Vedas am I alone to be known' (Bh. Gī. 15.15).

This has been declared, expounded, by Me, O Anagha — O sinless one. Having understood this śāstra, with its meaning as shown forth, one becomes wise (buddhimān) — not otherwise — and kṛta-kṛtya, O Bhārata: he by whom that which is to be done has been done is kṛta-kṛtya. The sense is: by him who has been born into the highly distinguished birth of a Brāhmaṇa, all that is to be done becomes done once the truth of the Lord has been known; and the intent is that for none whatever is the duty fulfilled in any other way. So too has it been said: 'All action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge' (Bh. Gī. 4.33). And there is the Mānava utterance: 'For this is the consummation of birth, especially of a Brāhmaṇa; having attained this, the twice-born indeed becomes accomplished, and not otherwise' (Manu 12.93). Since you have heard this supreme reality from Me, therefore you, O Bhārata, are kṛtārtha — your purpose is fulfilled.
BG_C16_V01::block-0: The natures of beings — divine (daivī), demonic (āsurī), and rākṣasic — were indicated in the ninth chapter. To set them forth in detail, the chapter beginning 'fearlessness, purity of inner being' is now commenced. Therein the daivī prakṛti is shown for the sake of release from saṃsāra, while the āsurī and rākṣasī are shown for the sake of bondage; and so the daivī is set forth that it may be embraced, the other two that they may be shunned.
BG_C16_V01::block-1:
Abhayam — fearlessness. Sattva-saṃśuddhiḥ — purity of sattva, the inner instrument (antaḥkaraṇa); namely, in dealings with others, the avoidance of cheating, deceit, falsehood and the like — conduct conducted with a pure-sattva disposition. Jñāna-yoga-vyavasthitiḥ: jñāna is the apprehension, from scripture and from the teacher, of the realities such as the Self; and yoga is the bringing of those things, once apprehended, to the state of being directly cognized in one's own Self by single-pointedness, through the withdrawal of the senses and the rest. The vyavasthiti — being firmly established — in those two, jñāna and yoga: this is steadfastness in them. This is the foremost daivī sāttvikī wealth (sampat). Whatever prakṛti arises in the qualified ones in their respective sphere is called sāttvikī.

Dānam — sharing food and the like according to one's capacity. Damaḥ — restraint of the outer organs; the restraint of the inner instrument, called śānti, He will speak of further on. Yajña — both the śrauta sacrifice such as Agnihotra and the smārta such as Devayajña and the rest. Svādhyāya — study of the Ṛgveda and the rest with an end unseen (adṛṣṭārtham). Tapas — the bodily and other tapas to be expounded later. Ārjavam — uprightness, at all times.
BG_C16_V02: Non-injury, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquillity, freedom from slander, compassion to creatures, non-covetousness, gentleness, modesty, freedom from fickleness — (2)
BG_C16_V02::block-1: Ahiṃsā — non-injuring; the avoidance of pain to living beings. Satyam — speaking of things as they truly are, free of what is unpleasant or untrue. Akrodha — the quelling of anger that has arisen towards one who has reviled or struck one. Tyāga — renunciation (saṃnyāsa), since dāna has already been spoken of earlier. Śānti — the quieting of the inner instrument. Apaiśuna — the absence of slandering: paiśuna is the disclosing of another's faults to a third party; its absence is apaiśuna. Dayā — compassion for beings in suffering. Alolutva — the non-perturbation of the senses in the proximity of objects. Mārdava — softness, absence of cruelty. Hrī — modesty, the sense of shame. Acāpalam — refraining from the unnecessary employment of speech, hands, feet and so on, when there is no occasion.
BG_C16_V03: Vigour, forbearance, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, absence of pride — these come to be in him who is born to the divine wealth, O Bhārata. (3)
BG_C16_V03::block-1:
Tejas — vigour, forcefulness; not the lustre of the skin. Kṣamā — the non-arising of inner perturbation in one who has been reviled or struck; whereas akrodha, as we have already said, is the quelling of perturbation once it has arisen. Such is the difference between kṣamā and akrodha. Dhṛti — that special function of the inner instrument which checks despondency when body and senses sink into it, by which the senses and the body, sustained, do not collapse. Śaucam is twofold: the outer, brought about by earth and water, and the inner, namely the cleanness of mind and intellect — the absence of contamination such as deceit, attachment, and the like. Such is the twofold purity. Adroha — the absence of any wish to harm others, non-injury. Nātimānitā — atimāna is excessive self-esteem; one in whom this exists is atimānin; that state is atimānitā; the absence of it is nātimānitā — the sense being, the absence of any conceit of one's surpassing worthiness of honour.

These — beginning with abhaya and ending here — come to be in one who is born to (i.e. born for) the wealth (sampat) — what kind of wealth? Daivī, the wealth that belongs to the gods; with reference to that he is born; that is, one fit for godly splendour, of auspicious destiny, O Bhārata.
BG_C16_V04: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and indeed ignorance — these belong, O Pārtha, to one born to the demonic wealth. (4)
BG_C16_V04::block-0: Now then, the demonic wealth (āsurī sampat) is set forth —
BG_C16_V04::block-1: Dambha — the parading of dharma as a mere flag (dharma-dhvajitva), hypocrisy. Darpa — exhilaration occasioned by learning, wealth, kinsmen and the like. Atimāna — already explained. And krodha. And, indeed, pāruṣya — harsh speech: as when calling a one-eyed man 'the seeing one,' a deformed man 'the well-formed,' one of low birth 'of high birth,' and so forth. Ajñāna — the cognition opposed to discrimination, the false notion concerning what is to be done and what is not to be done, and the like. To one born — born to what? He says: to the sampat, the wealth — the wealth of the asuras, that is, the āsurī sampat — born for that, O Pārtha. Such is the meaning.
BG_C16_V05: The divine endowment is held to lead to liberation, the demoniac to bondage. Grieve not, O Pāṇḍava: thou art born to the divine endowment.
BG_C16_V05::block-0: The fruit of these two endowments is now stated —
BG_C16_V05::block-1:
The divine endowment that has been described — that leads to liberation, that is, to release from the bondage of saṃsāra. The demoniac endowment is regarded as leading to bondage — to that bondage which is fixed and binding (ni-bandha), being its cause; and likewise the rākṣasic endowment too.

When this had been said, the Lord, observing in Arjuna an inward reflection of this kind — "Am I one endowed with the demoniac endowment? Or am I one endowed with the divine endowment?" — addressed him: Mā śucaḥ — do not grieve, do not entertain sorrow. Thou art born unto the divine endowment, that is, thou art born marked out for it; the meaning is, thou art destined for future blessedness, O Pāṇḍava.
BG_C16_V06: Two are the orders of created beings in this world — the divine and the demoniac. The divine has been described at length; hear from Me, O Pārtha, the demoniac in detail.
BG_C16_V06::block-0:
Dvau — two in number; bhūta-sargau — the creations of beings, that is, of human beings. The compound is resolved: that which is created is sarga; the very beings being created, conjoined with one or the other of the two endowments — divine and demoniac — are spoken of as the "two creations of beings." So the Śruti declares: "Two indeed are the offspring of Prajāpati, gods and asuras" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.3.1). Loke asmin — in this world, that is, in saṃsāra, since the twofold division applies to all.

Which are these two creations of beings? It is said: in primal nature itself there are precisely the divine and the demoniac. As to the purpose of restating what has already been told, He says: the divine creation has been recounted at length, in many modes, beginning with "Fearlessness, purity of mind" (Gītā 16.1) and so on; but the demoniac has not been told at length. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding it, hear from Me, O Pārtha — that is, by My word — the demoniac, being now recounted at length; mark it well.
BG_C16_V07: Demoniac people know not engagement nor withdrawal; neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth is found in them.
BG_C16_V07::block-0: From here up to the close of the chapter, the demoniac endowment is set forth as the qualifying mark of a particular kind of beings; for, by direct presentation, it becomes possible to shun it —
BG_C16_V07::block-1:
Pravṛttim — engagement: that engagement which is to be undertaken in respect of any means to a human goal — that engagement; nivṛttim ca — and withdrawal, the contrary of that, withdrawal from that which is the cause of harm and from which one ought to turn back — that is nivṛtti, and that too — these the demoniac people do not know, do not recognise.

Not only do they not know engagement and withdrawal, but neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth is found in them; for the demoniac are indeed unclean, lacking in right conduct, deceitful, and speakers of untruth.
BG_C16_V08: They say the world is unreal, without foundation, without an Īśvara, brought into being by the mutual union (of male and female), produced by desire alone — what else?
BG_C16_V08::block-1:
Asatyam — "Just as we ourselves are mostly given to falsehood, even so this whole world is unreal"; aprathiṣṭham ca — and without foundation: dharma and adharma are not its foundation, hence it is without foundation; thus those demoniac people declare the world. Anīśvaram — without an Īśvara: there exists no ruling Īśvara who governs it with regard to dharma and adharma; therefore they declare the world to be without an Īśvara.

Further: aparaspara-sambhūtam — the whole world has come into being from the mutual union of male and female impelled by desire. Kim anyat kāma-haitukam — "caused by desire alone" is kāma-haitukam. What other cause has the world? There is no other cause — no unseen cause such as dharma and adharma — for the world; "desire alone is the cause of beings." This is the view of the Lokāyatikas (the materialists).
BG_C16_V09: Holding fast to this view, lost in their very nature, of small intelligence, men of fierce deeds rise up as enemies of the world, for its destruction.
BG_C16_V09::block-0: Holding fast to — taking refuge in — this view, naṣṭa-ātmānaḥ: those whose true nature has perished, who have fallen away from the means to the next world; alpa-buddhayaḥ: those whose intelligence is small, having only the sense-objects for its sphere — these are alpa-buddhayaḥ; they rise up — come forth — as ugra-karmāṇaḥ — those of cruel deeds, of violent disposition. The construction is: "they come forth for the destruction of the world." Of the world they are enemies; the meaning is, foes.
BG_C16_V10: Resorting to insatiable desire, filled with hypocrisy, conceit and pride, having from delusion taken up evil resolves, they engage in action with impure vows.
BG_C16_V10::block-1: Kāmam — a particular kind of longing — āśritya: holding fast to it; duṣpūram — incapable of being filled; dambha-māna-mada-anvitāḥ — dambha (hypocrisy), māna (conceit), and mada (pride) — by these conjoined; mohāt — through want of discrimination; gṛhītvā — having taken up; asad-grāhān — inauspicious resolves; pravartante — they engage themselves in the world; aśuci-vratāḥ — those whose vows are impure are aśuci-vratāḥ.
BG_C16_V11: Given over to immeasurable cares, ending only with death, holding the enjoyment of desires as the highest, convinced that this is all —
BG_C16_V11::block-1:
Cintām aparimeyām ca — and care that is immeasurable: that care of which the limit cannot be measured is aparimeyā, that care; pralaya-antām — ending in destruction, that is, ending in death; upāśritāḥ — having taken refuge in; the meaning is, ever absorbed in care.

Kāmopabhoga-paramāḥ — that which is desired is kāma — sound and the other sense-objects; for whom the enjoyment of these is the highest goal; whose minds are settled in the conviction "This very enjoyment of desires is the supreme human end"; etāvat iti niścitāḥ — convinced that "this much, and no more" is all.
BG_C16_V12: Bound by hundreds of cords of expectation, given over to lust and wrath, they strive after hoards of wealth by unjust means, for the enjoyment of desires.
BG_C16_V12::block-0: Āśā-pāśa-śataiḥ — by hundreds of the cords that are very expectations themselves; baddhāḥ — bound, controlled, being drawn in every direction; kāma-krodha-parāyaṇāḥ — those whose supreme resort and refuge are lust and wrath are kāma-krodha-parāyaṇāḥ; īhante — they strive; kāma-bhoga-artham — for the sake of the enjoyment of desires, not for the sake of dharma; anyāyena — by injustice, namely by the seizure of others' goods and the like, that is the meaning. What do they strive for? Artha-sañcayān — heaps of wealth.
BG_C16_V13: “This has been gained by me today; this further longing of the heart I shall yet attain. This wealth is mine; this other wealth too shall be mine in time to come.”
BG_C16_V13::block-0: And of this very kind is their inner resolve —
BG_C16_V13::block-1: “This object — this wealth — has been gained by me today, at this very moment. And this other thing I shall yet obtain — a longing of the heart, that which gladdens the mind. This much already is mine; and this further wealth too shall be mine next year, and through it I shall be renowned as a wealthy man.” Such, says the Lord, is the brooding of the demoniac.
BG_C16_V14: “This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay these others as well. I am the lord; I am the enjoyer; I am accomplished, mighty, and happy.”
BG_C16_V14::block-0: “This man named Devadatta, an enemy hard to vanquish, has been slain by me. And I shall slay these others as well — these miserable wretches. What can these mere ascetics do? In every way there is none equal to me. How? — I am the lord, I am the enjoyer. I am in every respect accomplished, well provided with sons and grandsons; I am no mere mortal, but mighty and happy too — I alone. The rest are but burdens that have descended to weigh down the earth.”
BG_C16_V15: “I am wealthy and of high birth — who else is there equal to me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice” — thus are they bewildered by ignorance.
BG_C16_V15::block-0: Wealthy in money, and abhijanavān — endowed for seven generations with vedic learning and the like — even by such excellence none is equal to me. Who else is there sadṛśa, equal, to me? Moreover, yakṣye — I shall by sacrifice too overpower others; dāsyāmi — I shall give to actors and the like; modiṣye — I shall obtain abundant joy: thus, ajñāna-vimohitāḥ — bewildered by ignorance, fallen into manifold non-discrimination.
BG_C16_V16: Distracted by many thoughts, enveloped by the net of delusion, addicted to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
BG_C16_V16::block-0: Aneka-citta-vibhrāntāḥ — variously distracted by the many kinds of thinking just described; moha-jāla-samāvṛtāḥ — moha is non-discrimination, ignorance; that very ignorance, being of the nature of a covering, is like a net (jāla); enveloped by it. Prasaktāḥ kāma-bhogeṣu — clinging only to the enjoyment of desires, with their sins thereby accumulated, they fall patanti narake aśucau — into a foul hell, such as Vaitaraṇī and the rest.
BG_C16_V17: Self-conceited, stiff-necked, filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth, they perform sacrifices that are sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy and not in accordance with scriptural injunction.
BG_C16_V17::block-0: Ātma-sambhāvitāḥ — esteemed by their own selves alone as endowed with every excellence, not by the good. Stabdhāḥ — those whose minds never bow. Dhana-māna-madānvitāḥ — māna and mada caused by wealth; possessed of these. They sacrifice yajante nāma-yajñaiḥ — by sacrifices that are sacrifices in name only, with dambha — by parading the flag of dharma — and avidhi-pūrvakam — devoid of those auxiliaries and procedures that scripture prescribes.
BG_C16_V18: Resorting to egotism, force, arrogance, lust and wrath, these envious ones hate Me dwelling in their own and others' bodies.
BG_C16_V18::block-0: Ahaṅkāra — ahaṅ-karaṇam — is the act of saying ‘I’: by qualities both real and unreal superimposed upon the Self, one thinks ‘I am the Self qualified thus.’ That is ahaṅkāra, known as avidyā — the most grievous of all, the root of every fault and of all activity productive of evil; that he resorts to. So too balam — strength, the cause of overpowering others, joined with passion and lust. Darpa — dharpa is that special fault, lodged in the inner organ, on whose arising one transgresses dharma. Kāmam — desire for women and the rest. Krodham — wrath directed toward what is unwelcome. These and other great faults they have resorted to. Further, they hate Me, the Lord — Me who, in their own and others' bodies, am the witness of their thoughts and deeds; their hatred consists in transgressing My ordinance; they engage in such transgression as abhyasūyakāḥ — those who cannot bear the qualities of those established on the path of the good.
BG_C16_V19: These haters, cruel, the lowest of men, inauspicious in this round of births, I cast unceasingly into demoniac wombs alone.
BG_C16_V19::block-0: Tān — those, the opponents of the path of the good, haters of the saintly and of Me; cruel; in the rounds of saṃsāra — that is, in the courses of transmigration through many hells; nara-adhamān — the lowest of men, because they are full of the fault of unrighteousness — I cast (kṣipāmi), I hurl, ceaselessly, the inauspicious — those who do inauspicious deeds — into demoniac wombs only, namely the wombs of tigers, lions and the like, where cruel actions predominate. The construction is to be carried with ‘kṣipāmi.’
BG_C16_V20: Having entered demoniac wombs, deluded, birth after birth, without ever attaining Me, O son of Kuntī, they go thence to a yet lower goal.
BG_C16_V20::block-0: Having entered, attained to, demoniac wombs, the deluded — those without discrimination — birth after birth, in every successive birth being born only in wombs where tamas predominates, going downward, the deluded, without attaining Me, the Lord — without reaching Me — O son of Kuntī, thence — even from that demoniac womb — go to a still lower goal, the most degraded of states. As to ‘without attaining Me at all’ — there is not the slightest possibility of their attaining Me; therefore the meaning is: without attaining the path of the good which I have prescribed.
BG_C16_V21: Threefold is this gateway of hell, destructive of the Self — desire, anger, and likewise greed. Therefore one should abandon this triad. (21)
BG_C16_V21::block-0: A summary of the entire demoniac endowment is now stated, in which threefold root every variety of demoniac endowment, though endless, is comprehended. By avoiding this, the whole is avoided; for it is the root of every calamity. That very root is now declared —
BG_C16_V21::block-1: "Threefold," of three kinds, is "this gateway of hell," the gateway leading to the attainment of hell, "destructive of the Self" — that gateway upon entering which the Self perishes; that is, becomes unfit for any human end. Hence it is called "a gateway destructive of the Self." What is it? Desire, anger, and likewise greed. "Therefore one should abandon this triad." Since this is a gateway destructive of the Self, therefore one should renounce this triad of desire and the rest. (21)
BG_C16_V22: The man, O son of Kuntī, who is freed from these three gateways of darkness, practises what is good for the Self; thereafter he attains the supreme goal. (22)
BG_C16_V22::block-1: "Freed from these," O son of Kuntī, "gateways of darkness" — the gateways of darkness, that is, of hell whose nature is sorrow and delusion, namely desire and the rest — "freed from these three," the man "practises," performs. What? "That which is good for the Self." That which formerly, being obstructed, he did not practise — upon the removal of that obstruction he now practises. "Thereafter," through that practice, he "attains the supreme goal," liberation as well. (22)
BG_C16_V23: He who, casting aside the injunction of scripture, conducts himself by the impulse of desire, gains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. (23)
BG_C16_V23::block-0: For all this — both the abandonment of the demoniac endowment and the practice of what is conducive to the highest good — scripture is the cause. Both can be accomplished only on the authority of scripture, and not otherwise. Hence —
BG_C16_V23::block-1: "He who, casting aside the injunction of scripture" — "scripture" is the Veda; its "injunction," the cause of the knowledge of what ought and ought not to be done, called the rule of command and prohibition — "casting it aside," abandoning it, "conducts himself by the impulse of desire," being impelled by desire, "he gains not perfection," the fitness for the human end; nor does he gain happiness even in this world, nor the "supreme," the most exalted, "goal" — that is, neither heaven nor liberation. (23)
BG_C16_V24: Therefore let scripture be your authority in determining what should and should not be done. Knowing what is declared in the injunction of scripture, you ought to perform action here. (24)
BG_C16_V24::block-0: "Therefore scripture is the authority," the means of knowledge, "for you," "in determining what should and should not be done," in establishing what ought and ought not to be performed. Therefore, having known, having ascertained, what is declared in the "injunction of scripture" — "injunction" is rule; the rule itself is scripture; hence "the injunction of scripture" is the rule which is scripture, characterised by "do this, do not do that" — that action, namely your own duty, declared by it, you ought to perform "here." The word "here" is used to indicate the field of qualification for action. (24)
BG_C17_V01::block-0: Having obtained the seed of his question from the Lord's statement, "Therefore let scripture be your authority" (Bg. 16.24), Arjuna said —
BG_C17_V01::block-1: Those who, without any qualification, casting aside, abandoning, the injunction of scripture — that is, the prescription of Śruti and Smṛti — worship, that is, render homage to, the gods and others, "endowed with faith," united with faith, with the conviction of orthodoxy: those who, not perceiving any injunction of scripture characterised by Śruti or Smṛti, simply by the sight of the practice of elders worship the gods and others out of trustfulness — these are the ones taken up here by the words "who, casting aside the injunction of scripture, sacrifice endowed with faith." But those who, while indeed perceiving some injunction of scripture, cast it aside and worship the gods and others contrary to the rule — these are not included here in "those who sacrifice casting aside the injunction of scripture." Why? Because of the qualifying epithet "endowed with faith." For it cannot be supposed that those who do see some scripture which lays down the rule of worshipping the gods, having cast that very scripture aside out of want of faith, would yet engage in the worship of those very gods enjoined by it endowed with faith. Therefore the former are precisely the ones taken up in the words "those who, casting aside the injunction of scripture, sacrifice endowed with faith." Of such men, what indeed is the standing — "sattva" — O Kṛṣṇa: is it sattva, or rajas, or tamas? Is sattva their standing, their stationing? Or rajas? Or tamas? This is what is conveyed: that worship of theirs directed to the gods and the rest — is it sāttvika, or rājasa, or tāmasa? (1)
BG_C17_V02::block-0: Since this question pertains to a general subject and does not admit of an undivided reply, the Blessed Lord said —
BG_C17_V02::block-1: "Threefold," of three kinds, is the faith of embodied beings — those possessing bodies — concerning which standing you are asking; that faith "is born of their own nature." The impressions of dharma and the like accumulated in previous births, becoming manifest at the time of death, are called nature; what is born from that is "born of nature." The sāttvikī, produced by sattva, is directed to the worship of the gods and the like; the rājasī, produced by rajas, is directed to the worship of yakṣas, rākṣasas and the like; the tāmasī, produced by tamas, is directed to the worship of pretas, piśācas and the like. Such threefold faith, as it is being declared, hear — that is, fix in your understanding. (2)
BG_C17_V03: The faith of every being conforms to his inner constitution, O Bhārata. Man is made up of faith; whatever his faith, that verily is he. (3)
BG_C17_V03::block-0: That very faith is threefold thus —
BG_C17_V03::block-1: "Conforming to the inner constitution" — conforming to the inner organ as endowed with its specific impressions — is the faith "of every," that is, of every class of living being, O Bhārata. If this be so, then what follows? It is said — "made up of faith" — predominantly of faith — is this man, the saṃsārin, the jīva. How? "Whatever his faith" — whatever faith belongs to whichever jīva — that jīva is precisely "he of that faith," that is, conforming to that faith. (3)
BG_C17_V04: The sāttvika worship the gods; the rājasa, the yakṣas and rākṣasas; while others — the tāmasa folk — worship pretas and hosts of bhūtas. (4)
BG_C17_V04::block-0: Therefore, by the effect — that is, by the indicative mark which is the worship of gods and the rest — the standing in sattva and the others can be inferred. So He says —
BG_C17_V04::block-1: "They worship," that is, render homage to: the sāttvikas, those established in sattva, worship the gods; the rājasas worship yakṣas and rākṣasas; while others, the tāmasa folk, worship pretas and hosts of bhūtas — the Sapta-Mātṛkās and the like. (4)
BG_C17_V05: Those people who undertake terrible austerity not enjoined by scripture, joined with hypocrisy and egotism, possessed of the force born of desire and attachment — (5)
BG_C17_V05::block-0: Thus, by their effects, those grounded in sattva and the rest have been determined within the general scope of the scriptural injunction. Therein, only some rare one among thousands, devoted to the worship of the gods and the like, becomes grounded in sattva; but in the main, beings are grounded in rajas and grounded in tamas. How so? — to show this, He says:
BG_C17_V05::block-1: "Not enjoined by scripture" (aśāstra-vihitam) — that is, not laid down by scripture; "terrible" (ghoram), causing pain to other beings and to one's own self — such austerity (tapaḥ) those people "undertake" (tapyante), bring to performance. And they are "joined with hypocrisy and egotism" (dambha-ahaṅkāra-saṃyuktāḥ): the compound is dambhaś ca ahaṅkāraś ca dambha-ahaṅkārau, joined with these two, hence dambha-ahaṅkāra-saṃyuktāḥ. "Possessed of the force of desire and attachment" (kāma-rāga-balānvitāḥ): kāmaś ca rāgaś ca kāma-rāgau; the force produced by these is kāma-rāga-balam; possessed of (anvitāḥ) that, they are kāma-rāga-balānvitāḥ. (5)
BG_C17_V06: Emaciating the group of elements situated in the body, and Me too, who am situated within the body — know them to be of demonic resolve. (6)
BG_C17_V06::block-0: "Emaciating" (karśayantaḥ), making lean, the "group of elements" (bhūta-grāmam) — the aggregate of organs (karaṇa-samudāyam) — "situated in the body" (śarīra-stham); being "unintelligent" (acetasaḥ), devoid of discernment; and "Me too" (māṃ caiva), who, as Nārāyaṇa situated within the body (antaḥ-śarīra-stham), am the witness of their actions and intentions — emaciating Me as well: the very non-performance of My ordinance is itself the emaciating of Me. "Know them" (tān viddhi) to be "of demonic resolve" (āsura-niścayān): those whose resolve is demonic are āsura-niścayāḥ; this teaching is given so that they may be shunned. (6)
BG_C17_V07: Food too, that is dear to everyone, becomes of three kinds; so also sacrifice, austerity, and gift. Hear this distinction of theirs. (7)
BG_C17_V07::block-0: Now is undertaken the demonstration that foods, divided into the three groups of the savoury, the unctuous, and so on, are respectively dear to the sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa person. The purpose is that, having recognised — by the indicatory mark of one's excessive liking for some particular food, savoury or unctuous and the rest — one's own sāttvika, rājasa, or tāmasa nature, one may shun those foods that bear the marks of rajas and tamas, and take up those that bear the marks of sattva. Likewise, the threefold division of sacrifice and the rest according to the difference of guṇas of sattva and so on is also set forth here, with this purpose: "having recognised the rājasa and tāmasa kinds, how indeed shall one give them up and undertake only the sāttvika ones?" Accordingly He says —
BG_C17_V07::block-1: "Food too" (āhāras tu api), of "everyone" (sarvasya), of every enjoying creature, "becomes of three kinds" (trividho bhavati) as "dear" (priyaḥ), desired; "so likewise" (tathā) sacrifice, so likewise austerity, so likewise gift. Hear this distinction — to be stated — of these foods and the rest. (7)
BG_C17_V08: Foods that augment lifespan, vigour, strength, health, comfort, and gladness, that are savoury, unctuous, lasting, and pleasing to the heart — these are dear to the sāttvika. (8)
BG_C17_V08::block-0: Lifespan and vigour and strength and health and comfort and gladness — these are āyuḥ-sattva-bala-ārogya-sukha-prītayaḥ; their augmenters are āyuḥ-sattva-bala-ārogya-sukha-prīti-vivardhanāḥ. And they are "savoury" (rasyāḥ), endowed with sap; "unctuous" (snigdhāḥ), having oil; "lasting" (sthirāḥ), abiding for a long time in the body; "pleasing to the heart" (hṛdyāḥ), dear to the heart — such foods are "dear to the sāttvika" (sāttvika-priyāḥ), desired by the sāttvika person. (8)
BG_C17_V09: Foods that are excessively bitter, sour, salty, hot, pungent, dry, and burning are desired by the rājasa; they bring sorrow, grief, and sickness. (9)
BG_C17_V09::block-0: In "kaṭu-amla-lavaṇa-aty-uṣṇa-tīkṣṇa-rūkṣa-vidāhinaḥ," the word "ati" (excessively) is to be construed with each of the items beginning with kaṭu — thus "excessively bitter," "excessively pungent," and so forth. Bitter and sour and salty and excessively hot and pungent and dry and burning — these foods are "desired by the rājasa" (rājasasya iṣṭāḥ); they are "bringers of sorrow, grief, and sickness" (duḥkha-śoka-āmaya-pradāḥ): sorrow and grief and sickness — they bestow these, hence duḥkha-śoka-āmaya-pradāḥ. (9)
BG_C17_V10: What is half-cooked, devoid of taste, foul-smelling, and stale, the leavings as well, and what is unfit for sacrifice — such food is dear to the tāmasa. (10)
BG_C17_V10::block-0: "Yāta-yāmaṃ" — half-cooked; for that which is wholly devoid of essence is denoted by the word "gata-rasam" (devoid of taste). "Gata-rasam" — bereft of sap; "pūti" — foul-smelling; "paryuṣitam" — and what, after being cooked, has been kept overnight; "ucchiṣṭam api" — also the leavings of what others have eaten; "amedhyam" — unfit for sacrifice; such food is "dear to the tāmasa" (tāmasa-priyam). (10)
BG_C17_V11: The sacrifice that is offered as enjoined in scripture by those not desiring fruit, having settled the mind on the sole resolve "this is to be sacrificed," — that is sāttvika. (11)
BG_C17_V11::block-0: Now next, sacrifice is declared to be of three kinds —
BG_C17_V11::block-1: By those who are "not desiring fruit" (a-phala-ākāṅkṣibhiḥ), not seeking any reward, the sacrifice that is "enjoined as seen in the scriptural injunction" (vidhi-dṛṣṭaḥ, sanctioned by the directive of scripture) is performed (ijyate, brought to completion); having "settled the mind" with the resolve "yaṣṭavyam eva" — "the very accomplishment of the form of sacrifice itself is the duty," determining thus, "no purpose of mine is to be served by it" — that is called sāttvika sacrifice. (11)
BG_C17_V12: But that which is offered with an aim at fruit, and even for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas — know that sacrifice to be rājasa. (12)
BG_C17_V12::block-0: But "having aimed at," having intended, the fruit, and "even for the sake of ostentation" (dambha-artham api caiva), that which is performed (ijyate), O best of the Bharatas — know that sacrifice to be rājasa. (12)
BG_C17_V13: A sacrifice that is bereft of injunction, in which no food is distributed, that is devoid of mantras, that has no dakṣiṇā, and that is wholly without faith — that they declare to be tāmasa.
BG_C17_V13::block-0: *Vidhi-hīnam* — opposed to what has been ordained by the scripture; *asṛṣṭa-annam* — that sacrifice in which the food is *na sṛṣṭam, na dattam* (not let forth, not given) to the brāhmaṇas, that is called *asṛṣṭa-anna*, and so [the Lord declares] *asṛṣṭa-annam*; *mantra-hīnam* — wanting in respect of mantra, of svara, or of varṇa (intonation or syllabic articulation); *adakṣiṇam* — destitute of the dakṣiṇā prescribed [for that rite]; and *śraddhā-virahitam* — wholly devoid of faith — such a sacrifice they declare to be *tāmasa*, brought into being by tamas.
BG_C17_V14: Worship offered to the gods, to the twice-born, to the teacher and to the wise; cleanliness, straightforwardness, brahmacarya and non-injury — this is called the austerity of the body.
BG_C17_V14::block-0: Now is told the threefold austerity —
BG_C17_V14::block-1: *Devāḥ ca dvijāḥ ca guravaḥ ca prājñāḥ ca* — gods, twice-born, teachers, and the wise; the worship of these is *deva-dvija-guru-prājña-pūjanam*; *śaucam* (cleanliness); *ārjavam* — straightness, *ṛjutvam*; *brahmacaryam* and *ahiṃsā* — these, accomplished by the body, *śarīra-nirvartyam*, that is *śārīram*: that austerity which is brought to fulfilment by all the agents and instruments — the body and the rest — with the body as the principal one, [though] requiring agent and the others, is called *śārīram tapas*. For He will declare further on, *pañcaite tasya hetavaḥ* (Bh. Gī. 18.15) — these five are its causes.
BG_C17_V15: Speech that causes no agitation, that is true, agreeable and salutary, together with the regular recitation of the Veda — this is called the austerity of speech.
BG_C17_V15::block-0: *Anudvegakaram* — what does not cause distress to living beings; *vākyam* — speech; *satyam priya-hitam ca yat* — true, agreeable and salutary, the agreeable and salutary having reference to seen and unseen ends. The speech is qualified by the attributes of non-distress and the rest. The word *ca* serves to gather these qualifying attributes together. If a speech, used with the intent of conveying meaning to another, were lacking in any one, two, or three of [these four] — truthfulness, agreeableness, salutariness and non-distress — it would not be the austerity of speech. So too with truthful speech: should it be wanting in any one, two, or three of the others, it does not become the austerity of speech. Likewise with agreeable speech: if it is wanting in any one, two, or three of the others, it does not become the austerity of speech. Likewise with salutary speech: if it is wanting in any one, two, or three of the others, it does not become the austerity of speech. Then what is that austerity? That speech which is at once true, non-agitating, agreeable and salutary — that is the austerity of speech; as in the saying, “Be tranquil, child; perform your study and yoga; thereby will be your good.” And the regular practice of one's own scriptural recitation, *yathā-vidhi*, is also called the austerity of speech.
BG_C17_V16: Tranquillity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of heart — this is called the austerity of the mind.
BG_C17_V16::block-0: *Manaḥprasādaḥ* — the calming of the mind, the bringing of clarity, that is *prasāda*. *Saumyatvam* is what they call *saumanasya* — that mode of the inner organ which is to be inferred from such effects as serenity of countenance and the rest. *Mauna* — even the restraint of speech proceeds, having mental restraint as its antecedent; hence by [naming] the effect, the cause is named: mental restraint itself is *mauna*. *Ātmavinigrahaḥ* — restraint of the mind in its general aspect, of every form, is *ātmavinigraha*; the restraint of the mind specifically with reference to its objects of speech is *mauna* — such is the distinction. *Bhāva-saṃśuddhiḥ* — guilelessness in dealings with others at the time of transaction is *bhāva-saṃśuddhi*. This — *iti etat* — is called the austerity of the mind.
BG_C17_V17: That threefold austerity, performed by men of concentrated mind with supreme faith and without longing for fruit, they call sāttvika.
BG_C17_V17::block-0: How does the bodily, vocal and mental austerity already described, undertaken by men, become threefold by the differentiation of the guṇas, sattva and the rest — this is now told —
BG_C17_V17::block-1: *Śraddhayā* — by faith, the conviction grounded in āstika-belief; *parayā* — by the most exalted [faith]; *taptam* — practised; that *tapas* — the threefold one already under discussion, of three kinds, having three seats; *naraiḥ* — by men, by the practitioners; *aphalākāṅkṣibhiḥ* — by those bereft of the longing for fruit; *yuktaiḥ* — by those who are concentrated [in mind] — when the austerity is of such a kind, it is *sāttvika*, brought into being by sattva; thus do the cultured proclaim it.
BG_C17_V18: That austerity which is performed for the sake of welcome, honour and worship, and out of ostentation — that, here, is declared to be rājasa, unsteady and impermanent.
BG_C17_V18::block-0: *Satkāra* — *sādhukāra*, the saying, “This ascetic brāhmaṇa is good” — for the sake of such [acclaim]; *māna* — the showing of honour, by rising up, by saluting, and the like — for the sake of that; *pūjā* — the washing of the feet, the worshipful offerings, the providing of a resting place, and the rest — and for the sake of that; the austerity that is *satkāra-māna-pūjā-artham*; *and* that which is performed *dambhena ca eva* — through ostentation also — that austerity is *iha proktam* — said here — to be *rājasa*, *calam* (unsteady), since its fruit is occasional, and therefore *adhruvam* (impermanent).
BG_C17_V19: That austerity which is performed with deluded notion, by causing pain to oneself, or for the destruction of another — that is declared to be tāmasa.
BG_C17_V19::block-0: *Mūḍha-grāheṇa* — by an undiscriminating resolve; *ātmanaḥ pīḍayā* — by the inflicting of pain upon oneself — what austerity is performed; or *parasya utsādana-artham* — for the sake of another's ruin, for [his] destruction — that austerity is declared to be *tāmasa*.
BG_C17_V20: That gift which is given with the thought, “It ought to be given,” to one from whom no return is expected, in [a holy] place, at [an auspicious] time, and to a worthy recipient — that gift is held to be sāttvika.
BG_C17_V20::block-0: Now is told the threefold division of dāna —
BG_C17_V20::block-1: *Dātavyam iti* — having so resolved in the mind, the gift that *dīyate* — is given — *anupakāriṇe* — to one incapable of making a return; even to one capable [of returning], it is given without [any such] expectation; *deśe* — in a holy place, such as Kurukṣetra and the like; *kāle* — at [a sacred] time, such as the saṅkrānti and the rest; *pātre ca* — and to a worthy recipient, such as one who has crossed the Veda together with the six aṅgas, and the like — that gift is remembered as *sāttvika*.
BG_C17_V21: But that gift which is given for the sake of a return-favour, or again with an eye on its fruit, and which is given with vexation — that gift is declared to be rājasa.
BG_C17_V21::block-0: But that gift which is given for the sake of a return-favour — that is, with the motive 'in due time he will reciprocate towards me' — or again, given with this aim, 'some unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit of this gift will accrue to me,' and which is moreover given with vexation, that is, accompanied by distress — that gift is declared (smṛta) to be rājasa.
BG_C17_V22: That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients, without honour and with contempt — that is declared to be tāmasa.
BG_C17_V22::block-0: At an improper place — that is, in a place not sanctified, contaminated by mlecchas, impurity and the like; at an improper time — that is, at a time not renowned as a cause of merit, devoid of the special occasions such as the saṅkrānti and the rest; and to unworthy recipients — that is, to fools, thieves and such persons; or, even when the conditions of place and so forth are met, that gift which is asat-kṛta — devoid of kindly speech, washing of the feet, worship and the rest — and avajñāta — accompanied by disrespect of the recipient — that gift is declared (udāhṛta) to be tāmasa.
BG_C17_V23: 'Oṁ Tat Sat' — this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman. By it, in olden times, were the brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices ordained.
BG_C17_V23::block-0: In order to bring about the perfection (sād-guṇya-karaṇa) of sacrifice, gift, austerity and the rest, this teaching is now spoken —
BG_C17_V23::block-1: 'Oṁ Tat Sat' — such is the designation (nirdeśa); that by which something is pointed out is a nirdeśa. The threefold name-designation of Brahman has been thus pondered (smṛta, cintita) in the Vedānta-texts by the knowers of Brahman. By that threefold designation were the brāhmaṇas and likewise the Vedas and the sacrifices ordained (vihita), that is, fashioned, in olden times, formerly. This is stated by way of praising the designation.
BG_C17_V24: Therefore, after pronouncing 'Oṁ', the acts of sacrifice, gift and austerity, as enjoined by scripture, ever proceed among those who speak of Brahman.
BG_C17_V24::block-0: Therefore, having pronounced — that is, uttered — 'Oṁ', the acts in the form of sacrifice and the rest, namely the actions of sacrifice, gift and austerity, proceed (pravartante), being enjoined by the ordinance, prompted by śāstra, ever (satatam, sarvadā) among the brahma-vādins, those of the habit of speaking of Brahman.
BG_C17_V25: Saying 'Tat', without aiming at the fruit, the manifold acts of sacrifice, austerity and gift are performed by those who long for liberation.
BG_C17_V25::block-0: Having uttered 'Tat' — that is, having pronounced 'Tat', the appellation of Brahman — and not aiming at the fruit of acts such as sacrifice, the acts of sacrifice and austerity, viz. the sacrificial actions and the austerity-actions taken together as yajña-tapaḥ-kriyāḥ, and the gift-actions of various kinds, characterised as the giving of fields, of gold and the like, are performed (kriyante, nirvartyante) by those who long for liberation (mokṣa-kāṅkṣibhiḥ) — that is, by mumukṣus, seekers of mokṣa.
BG_C17_V26: In the sense of reality (sad-bhāva) and in the sense of goodness (sādhu-bhāva), the word 'Sat' is employed; and so too, O Pārtha, the word 'Sat' is applied to a praiseworthy act.
BG_C17_V26::block-0: The application of the words 'Oṁ' and 'Tat' has been told. Now, presently, the application of the word 'Sat' is being narrated —
BG_C17_V26::block-1: Sad-bhāva — that is, the coming-into-being of what was non-existent, as in the birth of a son who hitherto did not exist; and likewise sādhu-bhāva — that is, the becoming-virtuous of one of bad conduct, who is not a sādhu, his attaining the state of good conduct, which is sādhu-bhāva — in that sādhu-bhāva also, the word 'Sat', the appellation of Brahman, is employed (prayujyate, abhidhīyate). And so too, O Pārtha, in a praiseworthy act such as marriage and the like, the word 'Sat' is applied (yujyate, prayujyate).
BG_C17_V27: Steadfastness in sacrifice, in austerity, and in gift is also called 'Sat'; and so too the act done for the sake of That is spoken of as 'Sat'.
BG_C17_V27::block-0: That steadfastness which exists in sacrifice — in the sacrificial act — and that which exists in austerity, and that which exists in gift, that is called 'Sat' by the wise. And the act done for the sake of That — that is, for the sake of sacrifice, gift and austerity; or alternatively, the act done for the sake of That to which the threefold appellation is being applied — namely for the sake of sacrifice, gift and austerity, that is to say, for the sake of the Lord (Īśvara) — is itself spoken of as 'Sat'. Thus, this act of sacrifice, gift, austerity and the rest, even when non-sāttvika and defective, when undertaken with faith and through the application of the threefold appellation of Brahman, becomes endowed with quality (sa-guṇa) and rendered sāttvika.
BG_C17_V28: What is offered in oblation, what is given, the austerity practised, and whatever is done without faith — it is called 'Asat', O Pārtha; and that is of no avail hereafter, nor here.
BG_C17_V28::block-0: Therein, since in every case everything is accomplished only with faith as the foremost element, therefore —
BG_C17_V28::block-1: What is offered in oblation without faith — the homa performed without faith; what is given without faith to brāhmaṇas; the austerity practised, undertaken, without faith; and likewise whatever is done without faith — such as praise, salutation and the rest — all that is called 'Asat', because it is outside the path of the means to the attainment of Me, O Pārtha. And that, even if performed with much exertion, is of no avail for the fruit hereafter (pretya), nor (no api) is it for the sake of this world here, since it is censured by the good (sādhus).
BG_C18_V01::block-0: This concluding chapter is begun with the purpose that the meaning of the entire Gītā-śāstra, and indeed the meaning of all the Vedas, should be summed up here. The substance taught throughout the previous chapters is to be grasped in this chapter. Arjuna, however, being especially desirous of knowing the meaning of the two terms saṃnyāsa (renunciation) and tyāga (relinquishment) in particular, said —
BG_C18_V01::block-1: "Of saṃnyāsa"—that is, of the meaning of the word saṃnyāsa—"O mighty-armed one, I wish to know the truth"—the truth, its real nature, that is, the actual import; "and of tyāga"—of the meaning of the word tyāga—"O Hṛṣīkeśa, separately," each distinguished from the other. "O Keśiniṣūdana"—Keśin was a certain Asura disguised as a horse whom the Lord Vāsudeva slew; by that name Arjuna addresses Him.
BG_C18_V02::block-0: The words saṃnyāsa and tyāga have been used here and there, but their full import has not been settled in the previous chapters. Hence, when Arjuna asked, the Lord, in order to settle the matter, said —
BG_C18_V02::block-1: Some sages, that is, certain learned ones, know the renouncing (nyāsa) of desire-prompted works such as the Aśvamedha—works which one has begun to perform because they have been enjoined—as the meaning of the word saṃnyāsa. The discerning, the wise, declare the relinquishment of all the fruits of all works being performed—of the obligatory (nitya) and the occasional (naimittika)—the giving up of the fruit which would otherwise accrue to oneself, that is, the relinquishment of the fruits of all karma, as tyāga, the meaning of the word tyāga. If either the abandoning of desire-prompted works or the relinquishing of fruit alone were to be stated as the meaning, then in every case mere abandonment would be the single meaning of both saṃnyāsa and tyāga, and they would not denote distinct categories like the words "pot" and "cloth."
BG_C18_V02::block-2: Objection (pūrvapakṣa): It is held that the obligatory and occasional rites have no fruit at all. How then is the relinquishment of their fruit spoken of, like the abandonment of a barren woman's son? Reply (siddhānta): That is no fault, for the Lord here regards even the nitya rites as having fruit. Indeed the Lord will say, "undesired, desired, and mixed" (BG 18.12), and "but not for renouncers" (BG 18.12). Showing that for renouncers alone there is no connection with the fruit of works, He shows by "after death there is, for non-renouncers" (BG 18.12) that for non-renouncers the fruit of even the nitya karma does accrue.
BG_C18_V03: Some thinkers say that karma should be relinquished as being defective; others say that the rites of sacrifice, gift, and austerity should not be relinquished.
BG_C18_V03::block-0: "Should be relinquished" (tyājyam)—should be given up—"as defective" (doṣavat); doṣavat means "that which has a defect." What is it that has the defect? Karma—all of it, since it is the cause of bondage. Or, just as a defect like attachment is given up, so likewise karma should be given up: thus some thinkers, the wise, leaning on the Sāṅkhya and like views, declare—including with reference to those qualified karmīs (workers). Concerning that very same karma others say: "the rites of sacrifice, gift, and austerity are not to be given up."
BG_C18_V03::block-1: It is the karmīs alone, the qualified ones, with reference to whom these alternative views arise; not with reference to those established in jñāna-niṣṭhā, the renouncers who have risen out of activity. Those who have been removed from the sphere of karma by the verse, "For the Sāṅkhyas through jñāna-yoga the niṣṭhā was previously declared by Me" (BG 3.3)—about them there is here no consideration.
BG_C18_V03::block-2: Objection: But just as those qualified by "and through karma-yoga for the yogins" (BG 3.3), even though already assigned to a distinct niṣṭhā, are here considered in this section that sums up the meaning of all the śāstras, so let the Sāṅkhyas, the jñāna-niṣṭhas, also be considered. No, because for them no relinquishment caused by delusion or by suffering is possible. The Sāṅkhyas do not see any suffering caused by bodily exertion as inhering in the Self, since desire and the rest have been shown to be properties of the kṣetra (field). Hence they do not give up karma out of fear of the suffering from bodily exertion. Nor do they see actions in the Self, on account of which they would, out of delusion, give up enjoined karma. They renounce the actions of the guṇas with the conviction "I do not act at all" (BG 5.8). Through verses such as "having renounced all actions mentally" (BG 5.13), the mode of renunciation belonging to the knowers of truth has been declared. Therefore, those others who are qualified for karma, who are not knowers of the Self, in whom giving up due to delusion or due to fear of bodily exertion is possible—they alone are censured here as tāmasa renouncers and rājasa renouncers, in order to praise the relinquishment of the fruit of action by the karmīs who are not Self-knowers; and because the supreme renouncer (paramārtha-saṃnyāsin) is distinguished by the marks given to the one beyond the guṇas: "abandoning every undertaking" (BG 12.16), "silent, content with anything, homeless, of stable mind" (BG 12.19); and He will say "the supreme niṣṭhā of jñāna" (BG 18.58). Hence the jñāna-niṣṭha renouncers are not intended here. The relinquishment of the fruit of action alone, being sāttvika by guṇa, is, with reference to the tāmasa and so forth, called saṃnyāsa—not the principal renunciation of all action.
BG_C18_V03::block-3: Objection: From the impossibility of complete renunciation of all action and from the causal statement "For not by an embodied being [is it possible to relinquish actions entirely]" (BG 18.11), only the principal sense (mukhya) is meant. No; for that causal statement is by way of praise. Just as "From relinquishment, peace immediately" (BG 12.12) is itself merely praise of the relinquishment of fruit, since it is enjoined for Arjuna, who is unlearned (ajña) and incapable of practising the many alternatives that have been described—so this too, "For it is not possible for an embodied one" (BG 18.11), is for the praise of the relinquishment of the fruit of action; it cannot be shown by anyone to be a refutation of the position "having mentally renounced all actions, neither acting nor causing to act, he abides" (BG 5.13). Therefore, this alternative regarding saṃnyāsa and tyāga concerns only those qualified for action. But those who behold the supreme reality, the Sāṅkhyas, are qualified solely for the jñāna-niṣṭhā characterised by complete renunciation of all action, and for nothing else; hence they are not subject to this alternative. And we have established this in the passage "Know that to be indestructible…" (BG 2.21) and at the beginning of the third chapter and elsewhere.
BG_C18_V04: Hear from Me, O best of the Bharatas, the conclusion regarding that relinquishment; for relinquishment, O tiger among men, has been clearly declared to be of three kinds.
BG_C18_V04::block-1: "Hear the conclusion"—grasp it firmly—"from My word." "There," in that matter—in the alternative concerning tyāga and saṃnyāsa as set forth—"O best of the Bharatas," most excellent among the Bharatas. "For relinquishment"—because the meaning denoted by the words tyāga and saṃnyāsa is one and the same; with this intention He says "For relinquishment." "O tiger among men, three-fold"—of three kinds, by the modes of tāmasa and the rest—"has been thoroughly proclaimed" in the śāstras. Since the meaning denoted by the words tyāga and saṃnyāsa, in the case of the qualified karmī who is not a knower of the Self, becomes three-fold by the distinction of tāmasa and so on, but not so for the seer of the supreme reality, this matter is hard to know; therefore none other is competent to declare the truth here. Hence "hear from Me"—from My word—the conclusion, the divine determination, regarding the meaning of the supreme purport of the śāstra.
BG_C18_V05: The acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity should not be relinquished; they are to be performed. Sacrifice, gift, and austerity are indeed purifiers of the discerning.
BG_C18_V05::block-0: What then is that conclusion? He says —
BG_C18_V05::block-1: Sacrifice, gift, and austerity—this three-fold karma is not to be relinquished, not to be given up; it is to be done, to be performed. Why? Because sacrifice, gift and austerity are purifiers, the means of inner purification, for the discerning, for those who do not seek their fruit—this is the meaning.
BG_C18_V06: Yet even these works should be performed, abandoning attachment and the fruits, O Pārtha. This is My settled and supreme view.
BG_C18_V06::block-0: Yet even these works—the works of sacrifice, gift and austerity already declared to be purifying—must, having abandoned saṅga (attachment) to them and likewise relinquishing their fruits, be undertaken; this is My settled, supreme view.
BG_C18_V06::block-1: Having vowed "hear the conclusion from Me on that" (BG 18.4) and having stated purifying-power as the reason, the words "these works also are to be done" with "this is My settled supreme view" merely sum up the previously declared theme; they are not the statement of any new matter, since "these also" naturally refers to what has been the topic close at hand. The meaning of the word "also" (api) is: even these works, which are causes of bondage for one full of attachment seeking the fruit, are nevertheless to be performed by the one seeking liberation. "These also" is not said with reference to other (i.e., kāmya) works.
BG_C18_V06::block-2: Others, however, explain it thus: since the nitya works have no fruit, the phrase "having abandoned attachment and the fruits" is unfitting (with respect to nitya karma); hence the meaning of "these also" is that the kāmya works which are other than the nitya are also to be done—how much more so the nitya rites of sacrifice, gift and austerity. That is wrong, for the fruit-bearing nature of even the nitya works has here been established by the verse "sacrifice, gift, and austerity are indeed purifiers" (BG 18.5) and so on. For the seeker of liberation, who, fearing that even the nitya works may cause bondage, wishes to give them up—how could there arise an inclination toward kāmya works? Since "karma is far inferior" (BG 2.49) is censure, since the bondage-causing nature of kāmya works is fixed by "except for action done for sacrifice" (BG 3.9), and from the verses "the Vedas have the three guṇas as their subject" (BG 2.45), "the knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of soma, [worshipping] Me" (BG 9.20), "with merit exhausted they enter the world of mortals" (BG 9.21), and because of the great distance (in the text), the designation "these also" cannot refer to kāmya works.
BG_C18_V07: But the renunciation of an enjoined work is not proper; the relinquishment of it through delusion is declared to be tāmasa.
BG_C18_V07::block-0: Therefore, for the unenlightened, qualified seeker of liberation —
BG_C18_V07::block-1: But the renunciation, the giving up, of niyata (obligatory, daily) karma is not proper; for in the case of the unenlightened its purifying-power is desired. The relinquishment of that niyata karma through delusion, through ignorance—since the niyata is what must necessarily be done and yet it is being given up, this is self-contradictory; hence the relinquishment caused by delusion is declared to be tāmasa, for delusion is tamas itself.
BG_C18_V08: Whoever should relinquish a work merely thinking "It is painful," through fear of bodily exertion—he, having performed a rājasa relinquishment, gains by no means the fruit of relinquishment.
BG_C18_V08::block-1: Whatever karma he should relinquish merely with the thought "it is painful," out of kāya-kleśa-bhaya—out of fear of bodily suffering—he, having performed a rājasa relinquishment, one wrought by rajas, gains by no means the fruit of relinquishment, namely the fruit of the renunciation of all action preceded by knowledge—what is called mokṣa; he never attains it.
BG_C18_V09: When that obligatory work is performed simply because it ought to be done, O Arjuna, abandoning attachment and the fruit as well — that renunciation is held to be sāttvika.
BG_C18_V09::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: But what then is the sāttvika renunciation? In reply, the Lord says —
BG_C18_V09::block-1:
Bhāṣya: That work which, simply on the ground that ‘it must be done’ as a duty, is performed — that is, accomplished — as nityam (constantly enjoined), O Arjuna, having abandoned attachment and the fruit as well. As for the question whether the obligatory rites bear fruit, we have already stated that the Lord’s own word is the authority. Or alternatively, even though no fruit is heard of for the nityakarma, the ignorant man none the less imagines that the obligatory rite, when done, produces some fruit — either the refining of the self (ātmasaṃskāra) or the warding off of demerit (pratyavāya-parihāra). To check that imagination too, the Lord says ‘abandoning the fruit’. Hence it is well said: ‘abandoning attachment and the fruit as well’. That renunciation — the abandonment of attachment and fruit in the obligatory rites — is held to be sāttvika, born of the sattva-guṇa, and so intended.

Objection: But the renunciation of work and saṃnyāsa was begun as threefold; among them, the tāmasa and rājasa renunciations have been described. How then is the abandonment of attachment and fruit being spoken of as the third? Reply: It is like saying ‘three brāhmaṇas have come’ when two are versed in the six aṅgas and the third is a kṣatriya — the third is included by way of generic resemblance. So here, this is no flaw; it is by way of praise that all are gathered under the common notion of ‘renunciation’. For the renunciation of action and the renunciation of clinging to its fruit do share the common feature of being a kind of renunciation. There, by censuring the renunciation of action as rājasa and tāmasa, the renunciation of attachment to the fruit of action is praised as sāttvika in the words ‘that renunciation is held to be sāttvika’.
BG_C18_V10: He neither hates disagreeable work nor clings to agreeable work — the renouncer pervaded by sattva, intelligent, his doubts cut asunder.
BG_C18_V10::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: But the qualified man who, abandoning attachment and the longing for fruit, performs the obligatory rite — his inner organ, no longer being soiled by craving for fruit and the rest, and being at the same time refined by the obligatory works, becomes pure. That, when purified, becomes serene and capable of looking into the Self. For such a man, his inner organ purified by the performance of obligatory karma and now turned toward Self-knowledge, the steps by which his abiding in That comes about are now to be set forth. Hence the Lord says —
BG_C18_V10::block-1:
Bhāṣya: He does not hate akuśala — the unwholesome, that is, kāmya work, which through the begetting of a body is the cause of saṃsāra — thinking ‘what use is this?’. Nor does he, regarding the kuśala — the wholesome, namely the obligatory rite, which is the cause of inner purity, of the rise of knowledge, and of one’s settling in That — get attached, thinking ‘this is the means to mokṣa’; that is to say, he forms no fond clinging to it. And who is this person? The renouncer (tyāgī), endowed with the renunciation of attachment and fruit just described — he who, having abandoned attachment to the work and its fruit, performs the obligatory rites is the tyāgī. And when does he neither hate the unwholesome work nor cling to the wholesome? It is then explained — when he is sattva-samāviṣṭa, that is, pervaded, fully suffused, conjoined with sattva, which is the cause of the discriminative knowledge of Self and not-Self. And precisely on that account he is medhāvī, endowed with medhā — the wisdom (prajñā) characterised as Self-knowledge — and so he is medhāvī, ‘the wise’. Just because he is wise, his doubts are cut asunder (chinna-saṃśaya): the doubts wrought by avidyā are cut for him, by the firm conviction that ‘abiding in the Self’s own nature alone is the supreme means to the highest good, and nothing else’.

That qualified man, refined by stages through the practice of karma-yoga in the manner already described, having recognised the Self — which is free from the modifications of birth and the rest, and therefore actionless (niṣkriya) — as his own Self, mentally renouncing all karmas, neither doing anything nor causing anything to be done, sits at ease and attains to the steadfastness in jñāna characterised as naiṣkarmya — that is the meaning. The fruit of the karma-yoga spoken of earlier is thus stated by this very verse.
BG_C18_V11: It is not possible for an embodied being to give up actions wholly; but he who renounces the fruit of action — he is called the renouncer.
BG_C18_V11::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: But that man who, though qualified, on account of his identifying himself with the body is a ‘deha-bhṛt’, an ignorant person, whose conviction ‘I am the doer’ has not been falsified by the knowledge of the Self’s non-doership — for him, since the entire renunciation of works is impossible, his eligibility lies only in the performance of the enjoined rites coupled with the renunciation of their fruit, not in their abandonment. To bring out this point, the Lord says —
BG_C18_V11::block-1: Bhāṣya: ‘For (hi) — that is, since — by an embodied being’ (deha-bhṛt: he who bears a body is deha-bhṛt; and the term ‘deha-bhṛt’ is used of one who identifies himself with the body, not of the discriminating man — for the latter has been turned away from the office of agency by the words ‘he who knows This as indestructible’ (BG 2.21) and the like). Hence, by such an ignorant deha-bhṛt, it is not possible to renounce — to lay down — works wholly, in their entirety. Therefore that ignorant qualified man who, while performing the obligatory rites, is a tyāgī of the fruit of action — that is, a renouncer of the mere clinging to its fruit — he is called a tyāgī, by way of praise, even though he is yet a doer of works. Hence it is only the seer of the highest reality, the ‘un-embodied’ one (a-deha-bhṛt) — he who is free from the notion ‘I am the body’ — who can effect the entire renunciation of works.
BG_C18_V12: Threefold is the fruit of action — undesired, desired, and mixed — accruing after death to the non-renouncers; but to the saṃnyāsins, never anywhere.
BG_C18_V12::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: But what then is that purpose which would be served by the renunciation of all works? It is now stated —
BG_C18_V12::block-1: Bhāṣya: Aniṣṭa — characterised by hell, animal birth, and the like; iṣṭa — characterised by becoming a god and the like; and miśra — mixed, conjoined with the desired and the undesired, and characterised by human birth. There, threefold, of three kinds, is the fruit of work — work characterised as dharma and adharma — produced by the operation of many external instruments, wrought by avidyā, comparable to the magic of an Indra-jāla and a great deluder, as if creeping up to the inner Self — for ‘phala’ is etymologised thus: that which goes to dissolution, to disappearance, by reason of its triviality (phalgutā). Such, then, is the fruit which accrues to the atyāgins, the ignorant doers of works who are not renouncers in the highest sense, ‘pretya’ — after the falling of the body. But not so, never, for the saṃnyāsins, the renouncers in the highest sense, the paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas, who abide solely in knowledge — anywhere whatever. For the abiding in pure right vision never fails to uproot the seed of saṃsāra, namely avidyā and the rest — that is the meaning.
BG_C18_V13: Learn from Me, O mighty-armed one, these five causes laid down in the Sāṅkhya — that is, the Vedānta, the consummation of works — for the accomplishment of all actions.
BG_C18_V13::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: Hence the entire renunciation of works is possible only for the seer of the highest truth, since for him action, agent, and fruit are seen to have been superimposed on the Self by avidyā; whereas for the ignorant man who looks upon substratum and the rest — the agent and the instruments of action — as themselves the Self, the entire renunciation of works is not possible. This very point He sets forth in the verses that follow —
BG_C18_V13::block-1: Bhāṣya: ‘These five’, about to be enumerated, O mighty-armed one, are the causes (kāraṇa), the producers. ‘Learn from Me’ — this is said in order to gather his attention to what follows, and also to bring out the great difference of the matter to be taught. He praises those causes as worth knowing — sāṅkhya: that scripture in which the things to be known are reckoned (saṅkhyā) is sāṅkhya, namely the Vedānta. ‘Kṛtānta’ is its qualifier. ‘Kṛta’ means ‘action’; that wherein its end (anta), that is, its consummation (parisamāpti), takes place, is the kṛtānta — ‘the end of action’. By the words ‘so much use is there in a tank…’ (BG 2.46) and ‘all action without remainder, O Pārtha, is consummated in knowledge’ (BG 4.33), it is shown that on the rise of Self-knowledge all actions cease. Hence, in that sāṅkhya, that kṛtānta — that Vedānta — which is for the sake of Self-knowledge, these five have been declared (prokta) for the accomplishment, the bringing-to-completion, of all actions.
BG_C18_V14: The substratum, likewise the agent, the manifold instruments, the various separate functions, and divine providence as the fifth among these.
BG_C18_V14::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: What are they? It is said —
BG_C18_V14::block-1: Bhāṣya: Adhiṣṭhāna — the body, which is the seat (āśraya) of the manifestation of desire, hate, pleasure, pain, knowledge and the rest, is the adhiṣṭhāna. Likewise the kartā — the experiencer (bhoktā) marked off by the upādhi. The karaṇa, the instrument — the ear and the rest, for the apprehension of sound and so forth — is manifold, of various kinds, and twelve in number. The various, separate cheṣṭās are the airy functions, prāṇa, apāna and the rest. And ‘daiva’ alone — daivam eva — among these four is the fifth, the completer of the five — the sun and the like, which favour the eye and the other organs.
BG_C18_V15: Whatever action a man undertakes by body, speech, or mind — whether right or contrary — these five are its causes.
BG_C18_V15::block-0:
Bhāṣya: Whatever action a man begins — that is, accomplishes — by these three, body, speech, and mind, whether nyāyya, ‘right’, namely conformable to dharma and to scripture, or viparīta, ‘contrary’, namely opposed to scripture and unrighteous; and even those activities such as the winking of the eye and the like, which are the means of mere life, being themselves the effects of dharma and adharma already wrought — these too are taken in by the very mention of the right and the contrary. These five, as just enumerated, are the causes, the kāraṇas, of every action whatsoever.

Objection: But these — the substratum and the rest — are the producers of all actions; how then is it said, ‘whatever action one begins by body, speech, and mind’? Reply: This is no flaw. All action characterised as the enjoined and the prohibited has body, speech, and mind as its primary instruments; and the activities such as seeing, hearing, and so on, which fall under the head of life and form their accessories, are gathered under those three heads alone, and are accordingly said to be ‘begun by the body and the rest’. At the time of the fruit too, it is by means whose principal members are these very same that the fruit is enjoyed. Hence the fivefold causality is not contradicted.
BG_C18_V16: This being so, the dull-witted man who, owing to an unrefined understanding, looks upon the unmingled Self alone as the agent — he, perverse-minded, does not see.
BG_C18_V16::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘There’ (tatra) connects with what has been the topic. ‘Such being the case’ — when, that is, work has to be effected through the five causes mentioned. The phrase ‘this being so there’ is then construed as the ground for being a dur-mati, a perverse-minded one. Among these — that is, of the action wrought by these things imagined, by avidyā, as non-different from the Self — he who looks upon the kevala, the unmingled, pure Self alone as the agent, with the thought ‘I myself am the doer’, he is the unwise. Why? Because his buddhi is unrefined (akṛta-buddhitvāt) — that is, unrefined by the methods of Vedānta, the teaching of the ācārya, and reasoning. And even he who, holding the Self to be other than body and the rest, looks upon the Self alone, the unmingled, as the agent — he too is akṛta-buddhi. Hence, owing to his unrefined understanding, he does not see — does not see the truth of the Self or of action, that is the meaning. Therefore he is dur-mati: his mati is despicable, perverse, vitiated, the cause of incessant attainment of birth and death — and so he is dur-mati. He, though seeing, does not see — like a man with timira-affected eyes who sees many moons, or like one who, when the clouds are racing, sees the moon racing, or like a man seated in a moving vehicle who, when other things are moving, sees himself moving.
BG_C18_V17: He whose state of mind is not tainted by egoity, whose understanding is not stained — even having slain these worlds he does not slay, nor is he bound. (17)
BG_C18_V17::block-0: Who, then, is that wise one who sees rightly? In answer it is said —
BG_C18_V17::block-1:
He whose self has been refined by the teaching of the scripture, the teacher, and reasoning — in him there does not arise the egoised conviction "I am the doer" (ahaṅkṛto bhāvaḥ = bhāvanā, pratyaya). On the contrary, he sees thus: "These very five — the seat (adhiṣṭhāna) and the rest — superimposed upon the Self by avidyā, are the doers of all actions; not I; I, indeed, am the witness of their operations, 'breathless, mindless, pure, higher than the imperishable Higher' (Muṇḍ.
