Up. 2.1.2), alone (kevala) and changeless." Whose buddhi — the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is but an upādhi of the Self — is not stained, that is, does not become attached by the after-thought "I did this; therefore I shall go to hell" — he is the wise one (sumati), he it is who sees. Even having slain (hatvā api) these worlds — that is, all these living beings — he does not slay, he does not perform the act of slaying; nor is he bound (na nibadhyate), nor is he linked with its consequence in the form of the fruit of unrighteousness.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): To say "having slain, he slays not" is a self-contradiction, granted that it is praise. — Reply (siddhānta): There is no fault here, for it is reconciled by reference to the worldly (laukika) and the absolute (pāramārthika) standpoints. Resorting to the worldly outlook in which, through the conception of the Self as the body etc., one thinks "I am the slayer," he says "having slain"; resorting to the absolute outlook already shown, he says "he does not slay, he is not bound." Both, accordingly, are entirely consistent.

Objection: But the Self does indeed act, in conjunction with the seat and the rest — for the very word "alone" is used in "the Self alone as the doer" (Gītā 18.16). — Reply: There is no fault. Since the Self is by nature changeless, conjunction with the seat etc. is itself impossible. For only that which undergoes change can be conjoined with others, and only by being so conjoined could it become a doer. But for the changeless Self there is no conjunction with anything whatever; therefore agency by way of conjunction is not possible. Hence the aloneness (kevalatva) of the Self is its very nature, and the word "alone" is merely a restatement (anuvāda) of this. The changelessness of the Self, moreover, is established by śruti, smṛti, and reasoning. "It is said to be unmodifiable" (Gītā 2.25), "actions are wrought wholly by the guṇas" (Gītā 3.27), "though seated in the body, He does not act" (Gītā 13.31), and so forth — established repeatedly in the Gītā itself. And in the śrutis: "as it were He thinks, as it were He moves" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7), and the like. By reasoning too: the principle of the Self is partless (niravayava), independent (aparatantra), and changeless — this is the royal road. Even granting modifiability to the Self, only its own modification could belong to it; the actions of the seat etc. could not have the Self as their agent. For the action of one cannot, unwrought, come over to another. Whatever is conveyed onto something by avidyā does not really belong to it. Just as silverness does not belong to the mother-of-pearl; or as the dark surface attributed by children through avidyā does not belong to the sky, so too the modifications of the seat etc. belong only to those very things, not to the Self. Therefore it has been rightly said: "Because there is neither egoity nor stain on the buddhi, the wise man neither slays nor is bound." Having declared as a thesis "This neither slays nor is slain" (Gītā 2.19), having established the changelessness of the Self by reasoning beginning with "It is not born" (Gītā 2.20), and having concisely stated at the outset of the śāstra, in "He who knows it as imperishable" (Gītā 2.21), the cessation of competence for action in the case of the knower, and having expanded that theme contextually here and there in the middle, He now sums it up here for the consolidation of the meaning of the śāstra in the words "the wise man neither slays nor is bound." This being so, since the conceit of being a body-bearer cannot stand and the renunciation of the entire mass of action wrought by avidyā becomes possible, it is established that for renunciants the threefold fruit of action — undesired and the rest — does not arise; and, by the contrary reasoning, that it inevitably arises for others. Thus is summed up the import of the Gītā-śāstra. This very import, the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas, is to be ascertained and accepted by acute-minded learned ones after due deliberation; this we have shown here and there by the division of topics, in accordance with the reasoning of the śāstra.
BG_C18_V18: Knowledge, the knowable, and the knower — this is the threefold impulse to action; the instrument, the object of the act, and the agent — this is the threefold collocation of action. (18)
BG_C18_V18::block-0: Now, then, the impeller of actions is being declared —
BG_C18_V18::block-1: Knowledge (jñāna) — "that by which one knows" — is here spoken of generally, embracing every object. So too the knowable (jñeya), "that which is to be known," is spoken of generally, embracing all. Likewise the knower (parijñātā), the enjoyer characterised by upādhi and fashioned by avidyā. These three, indistinguishably taken, constitute the threefold (trividhā), three-formed impulse to action of all actions. For only when these three — knowledge and the rest — meet together, does the entire undertaking of action, having for its purpose abandonment, acquisition, and so on, become possible. Then the action that has been set in motion by the five — the seat and the rest — falling into three heaps according to the divisions of speech, mind, and body, is contained within three: instrument, object, and agent. This is what is being stated. The instrument (karaṇa) — "that by which it is done" — comprises the outer (śrotra etc.) and the inner (buddhi etc.); the object (karma) is what is most desired by the agent and is pervaded by the action; the agent (kartā) is the one who sets the instruments in operation, characterised by upādhi. Thus is the threefold (trividhaḥ), three-formed collocation of action (karma-saṅgraha) — "that wherein it is gathered together" is the saṅgraha; the gathering of action is the karma-saṅgraha; for the action inheres in these three; therefore this is the threefold collocation of action.
BG_C18_V19: Knowledge, action, and agent are declared to be threefold according to the differences of guṇa in the enumeration of guṇas; hear of these too as they really are. (19)
BG_C18_V19::block-0: Now, since action, instrumentalities, and fruit are all of the nature of the guṇas, the threefold division according to the difference of the guṇas — sattva, rajas, and tamas — must be set forth; hence this is begun —
BG_C18_V19::block-1: Knowledge and action — "action" (karma) here means the activity (kriyā), not the technical "object of action" which is what is most desired — and the agent (kartā), the accomplisher of activities, are threefold (tridhā eva); the restrictive "only" (eva) is to show the absence of any other class besides the guṇas — "according to the difference of the guṇas" means by the difference of sattva and the rest. "Are declared" — that is, spoken of — "in the enumeration of guṇas," i.e. in the Kāpila śāstra. That śāstra of the enumeration of guṇas (Sāṅkhya) is, indeed, an authority in matters concerning the guṇas and the enjoyer. Although on the topic of the absolute oneness of Brahman it stands contradicted, still, since those Kāpilas are skilled in describing the operation of the guṇas as guṇas, that śāstra too is here adduced by way of laudatory reinforcement of the meaning to be set forth — so there is no contradiction. "As they really are" — that is, according to right reasoning, according to the śāstra — "hear those too," i.e., those forms of knowledge etc. born of the guṇa-difference — meaning, fix the mind in concentration upon the meaning to be declared.
BG_C18_V20: That knowledge by which one beholds in all beings one imperishable Being, undivided amid the divided — know that knowledge to be sāttvika. (20)
BG_C18_V20::block-0: First, then, the threefold nature of knowledge is being declared —
BG_C18_V20::block-1: In all beings — from the unmanifest down to the immobile — "by which knowledge one beholds" one Being (bhāva), one Reality — for the word bhāva denotes a thing — that is, the one Self-substance; "imperishable" (avyaya), which does not perish either in its own being or in its own attribute, that is, kūṭastha (immutable, fixed as an anvil-stand); "by which knowledge one sees" (īkṣate), and that Being undivided (avibhakta) — not divided despite the divisions of bodies, body by body — that Self-substance, like space (vyoma), uninterrupted — that knowledge, the very immediate right vision pertaining to the non-dual Self, know to be sāttvika.
BG_C18_V21: But that knowledge which, by way of separateness, knows in all beings manifold beings of distinct kinds — know that knowledge to be rājasa. (21)
BG_C18_V21::block-0: Those views which posit duality are imperfect (asamyak); being rājasa or tāmasa, they do not directly serve to uproot saṃsāra —
BG_C18_V21::block-1: But that knowledge which, by way of separateness — by difference, body by body, otherness by otherness — knows manifold beings (nānā-bhāvān), the manifold selves of separate kinds (pṛthag-vidhān), of differing characteristics — that is the meaning — "knows" (vetti, vijānāti) which knowledge, in all beings; since knowledge cannot itself be the agent, the meaning is "that knowledge by which one knows" — know that knowledge to be rājasa, born of the rajas-guṇa.
BG_C18_V22: But that which is attached to a single effect as if it were everything, devoid of reasoning, not attaining the real, and limited — that is declared to be tāmasa. (22)
BG_C18_V22::block-0: That knowledge which is attached "as if all-comprehending" — as if covering every object — to a single effect (eka kārya), namely the body, or to something external, an idol and the like, with the conviction "this much alone is the Self or the Lord; nothing exists beyond this" — just as the naked Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas) hold the soul to be the size of the body and contained within the body, or as those who hold the Lord to be merely a stone or a piece of wood; thus attached to a single effect; devoid of reasoning (ahaitukam), bereft of any cause, lacking argument; not attaining the real (atattvārthavat) — that is, not attaining things as they are: the real (tattvārtha) is the thing as it is in fact; if it possesses such a real as its object known, it is tattvārthavat; what is not so is atattvārthavat; and on account of being itself reasonless, it is also limited (alpa) — because of having a small object, or because of yielding small fruit. That is declared to be tāmasa. For such knowledge is seen in tāmasa beings, the unreflective.
BG_C18_V23: An action that is enjoined, free of attachment, performed without rāga or dveṣa by one not seeking its fruit — that is called sāttvika. (23)
BG_C18_V23::block-0: Now, then, the threefold nature of action is being declared —
BG_C18_V23::block-1: Enjoined (niyatam) — meaning, fixed and obligatory (nitya); free of attachment (saṅgarahitam) — devoid of clinging; performed without rāga or dveṣa (arāgadveṣataḥ kṛtam) — that is, the opposite of one performed under the impulse of rāga or under the impulse of dveṣa; performed by one not seeking the fruit (aphalaprepsunā) — "one who seeks the fruit" is phalaprepsu, one thirsting for fruit; the opposite, one not seeking the fruit, is the agent — that action which is performed by such a one, that is called sāttvika.
BG_C18_V24: But that action which is performed by one seeking desire, or again with egoism, with much exertion — that is declared to be rājasa. (24)
BG_C18_V24::block-0: But that which is performed by "one seeking desire" — meaning, one seeking the fruit of action — and "with egoism" (sāhaṅkāreṇa); the latter is not in reference to the absence of egoity born of true knowledge of the Self. Then with reference to what? With reference to the worldly absence of egoism such as is conceded to the Vedic learned (laukika-śrotriya). For one who is truly without ego in the highest sense — namely the knower of the Self — such qualifications as "seeker of desire" and "performer of much-laboured action" do not at all apply. Even of sāttvika action the agent, if he be not a knower of the Self, performs it with egoity — what then to say of the rājasa and tāmasa? In common usage, even one who is not a knower of the Self, if he is a Vedic-learned man (śrotriya), is spoken of as without egoism: "this Brahmin is without egoism." It is therefore in this sense alone that "with egoism" is said. The word "again" (punaḥ) is for filling out the metre. "Performed with much exertion" — accomplished by the agent with great labour — that action is declared to be rājasa.
BG_C18_V25: That action is called tāmasa which is undertaken from delusion, without considering its consequence, the loss it entails, the injury it causes, and one's own capacity. (25)
BG_C18_V25::block-0: Anubandha — that thing which comes about afterwards is called the after-consequence; that anubandha; kṣaya — that loss of strength or loss of substance which would arise in the doing of the action, that loss; hiṃsā — and the injury, the harming of living beings; anapekṣya ca pauruṣam — and without taking into account one's own manliness, that is, one's personal capacity in the form of the conviction 'I am able to bring this action to completion' — without taking into account these things beginning with anubandha and ending with pauruṣa, the action that is undertaken from moha, that is, from non-discrimination, that action is called tāmasa, that which has issued forth from tamas.
BG_C18_V26: Free from attachment, not given to self-assertion, endowed with steadfastness and zeal, unaffected in success and failure — such a doer is called sāttvika. (26)
BG_C18_V26::block-0:
Now the distinction among doers is set forth —

Muktasaṅgaḥ — he by whom attachment has been let go, abandoned, is muktasaṅga; anahaṃvādī — not of the nature of speaking with the assertion of 'I'; dhṛtyutsāhasamanvitaḥ — dhṛti is firmness in upholding, utsāha is exertion; one who is endowed with, conjoined with these two is dhṛtyutsāhasamanvita; siddhyasiddhyoḥ — in the success and the non-success — that is, in the gaining or non-gaining of the fruit of the action being performed — nirvikāraḥ, free from modification; he who is impelled solely by the authority of scripture and not by craving for the fruit and the like, he is called nirvikāra. The doer who is of such a nature is called sāttvika.
BG_C18_V27: Passionate, eager to grasp the fruit of action, greedy, of an injurious nature, impure, swayed by joy and grief — such a doer is proclaimed rājasa. (27)
BG_C18_V27::block-0: Rāgī — he in whom rāga exists is rāgī; karmaphalaprepsuḥ — one who seeks the fruit of action, this is the meaning; lubdhaḥ — one in whom thirst has arisen for the wealth of others, or one who refuses to part with his own wealth at sacred fords and the like; hiṃsātmakaḥ — of a nature that causes pain to others; aśuciḥ — devoid of outer and inner cleanliness; harṣaśokānvitaḥ — joy at the gaining of what is desired, and grief at the gaining of the undesired and at the loss of what is desired — conjoined, joined together, with these two, joy and grief; and indeed it is from the success and failure of that very action that joy and grief would arise; the doer who is joined with these two is proclaimed rājasa.
BG_C18_V28: Unconcentrated, vulgar, stiff-necked, deceitful, malicious, indolent, despondent, and procrastinating — such a doer is called tāmasa. (28)
BG_C18_V28::block-0: Ayuktaḥ — not yoked, that is, not collected within; prākṛtaḥ — of utterly uncultivated intellect, like a child; stabdhaḥ — like a staff, who does not bend before anyone; śaṭhaḥ — given to māyā, one who hides his own capacity; naikṛtikaḥ — bent on causing breach among others; alasaḥ — of a disposition not to engage even in what ought to be done; viṣādī — possessed of dejection, of a perpetually downcast nature; dīrghasūtrī ca — and one who endlessly draws out his obligations, of a perpetually slow disposition; what ought to be done today or tomorrow he does not accomplish even in a month; he who is of such a kind, that doer is called tāmasa.
BG_C18_V29: Hear now, O Dhanañjaya, the threefold division of intellect and likewise of steadfastness, distinguished according to the guṇas, being declared exhaustively and in their separate forms. (29)
BG_C18_V29::block-0: 'Hear the threefold division of buddhi, and likewise the division of dhṛti, according to the guṇas, that is, according to the sattva-and-other guṇas' — this is the announcement-aphorism of the topic. Procyamānam — being expounded; aśeṣeṇa — without remainder, just as it is; pṛthaktvena — through discrimination, separately; Dhanañjaya — in the conquest of the quarters he won abundant wealth, both human and divine; therefore he, Arjuna, is Dhanañjaya.
BG_C18_V30: That intellect, O Pārtha, is sāttvika which knows pravṛtti and nivṛtti, what ought to be done and what ought not, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation. (30)
BG_C18_V30::block-0:
Pravṛttiṃ ca — pravṛtti is engagement, the path of action which is the cause of bondage and which has scripturally enjoined matters as its province; nivṛttiṃ ca — nirvṛtti is the path of saṃnyāsa which is the cause of mokṣa — since pravṛtti and nivṛtti stand in a single sentence with bondage and liberation, they are to be understood as the path of action and the path of renunciation of action; kāryākārye — what is enjoined and what is prohibited, that which is to be done and that which is not to be done by an intellect grounded in scripture, whether worldly or vedic, that is, doing and not-doing; with respect to whom? With respect to actions whose ends are seen and unseen, conditioned by place, time and the like.

Bhayābhaye — bhaya is that from which one fears, such as thieves, tigers and the like; not bhaya is abhaya; bhaya and abhaya, that is, bhayābhaye — the meaning is, the causes of fear and fearlessness with seen and unseen objects. Bandhaṃ — bondage along with its cause, and mokṣaṃ — liberation along with its cause — that intellect which knows, comprehends these — that intellect, O Pārtha, is sāttvikī.

Now, knowledge is a modification of buddhi; buddhi, however, is that which possesses the modification. Dhṛti too is just a particular modification of buddhi.
BG_C18_V31: That intellect, O Pārtha, is rājasī by which one cognises imperfectly dharma and adharma, and likewise what ought and what ought not to be done. (31)
BG_C18_V31::block-0: That buddhi by which one knows dharma — that which is enjoined by scripture — and adharma — that which is prohibited thereby — and likewise kārya and akārya — these very same enjoined and prohibited acts spoken of before — ayathāvat, not as they are, not by way of a settled determination from every side — that intellect, O Pārtha, is rājasī.
BG_C18_V32: That intellect, O Pārtha, is tāmasī which, enveloped by tamas, takes adharma to be dharma and views all things in a perverted manner. (32)
BG_C18_V32::block-0: Adharmaṃ — that which is prohibited — dharmam iti — as if it were what is enjoined — yā manyate — that intellect which thinks, knows, while being enveloped by tamas; sarvārthān — all knowable objects whatsoever — viparītāṃśca — knows just in the perverted way; that intellect, O Pārtha, is tāmasī.
BG_C18_V33: That unwavering steadiness, O Pārtha, by which one upholds, through yoga, the activities of mind, prāṇa and the senses — that steadiness is sāttvika.
BG_C18_V33::block-0:
By which steadiness — the qualifier 'unwavering (avyabhicāriṇyā)' is to be construed across the intervening words — one upholds; what does one uphold? The activities of mind, prāṇa and the senses: 'mind, prāṇas and senses' is the dvandva 'manaḥ-prāṇa-indriyāṇi'; their activities (kriyāḥ), that is, their movements (ceṣṭāḥ); these one upholds, restraining them from veering into paths contrary to scripture (uc-chāstra-mārga-pravṛtteḥ) — for activities upheld by such steadiness do not become engaged in objects outside the path of scripture. Through yoga, that is, through samādhi; unwavering — meaning, attended by unbroken samādhi.

This is what is meant: by the unwavering steadiness, the activities of mind, prāṇa and the senses, while being upheld, are upheld through yoga. Whatever steadiness has this character, that, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
BG_C18_V34: But that steadiness, O Arjuna, by which one holds onto dharma, kāma and artha, desiring their fruits as the occasion of each arises — that steadiness, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
BG_C18_V34::block-0: But that steadiness by which one holds onto dharma, kāma and artha — 'dharma, kāma and artha' (dharma-kāma-arthāḥ) being the dvandva — these one fixes in the mind perpetually as things to be done; O Arjuna, by occasion (prasaṅgena), that is, on every occasion of upholding this or that — dharma and the rest — by that very occasion the man becomes a craver of fruits as well; whatever steadiness such a man possesses, that, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
BG_C18_V35: That steadiness by which the dull-witted man does not let go of sleep, fear, sorrow, dejection and intoxication — that steadiness is held to be tāmasa.
BG_C18_V35::block-0: By which the dull-witted man (durmedhāḥ — of contemptible understanding) does not let go of sleep (svapnaṁ — nidrām), fear (bhayaṁ — trāsam), sorrow (śokaṁ), dejection (viṣādaṁ — viṣaṇṇatām), and intoxication (madam) — namely, the indulgence in objects, in which one, esteeming oneself highly, becomes as it were drunk — but rather holds onto them, perpetually entertaining them in the mind as things to be done; whatever steadiness such a one possesses, that is held to be tāmasa.
BG_C18_V36: Now hear from Me, O bull of the Bharatas, of the threefold happiness — that in which one, by repeated practice, comes to delight, and through which one attains the cessation of sorrow.
BG_C18_V36::block-0: By the difference of the guṇas the threefold distinction of actions and of the factors of action has been stated. Now, at this point, the threefold distinction of the fruit, namely happiness, is being declared —
BG_C18_V36::block-1: Now hear of the threefold happiness, that is, fix your attention upon it (samādhānaṁ kuru), from Me, O bull of the Bharatas. Through practice (abhyāsāt — paricayāt, āvṛtteḥ — through familiarity, through repetition) one comes to delight (rati), that is, takes pleasure in it, in which experience of happiness; and one definitely (niścayena) attains (nigacchati) the end of sorrow (duḥkha-antam — duḥkha-avasānam, duḥkha-upaśamam, the cessation, the quieting of sorrow).
BG_C18_V37: That happiness which at the start is like poison but in its outcome is like nectar — that happiness is declared sāttvika, born of the serenity of the intellect concerning the Self.
BG_C18_V37::block-0: That happiness which at the beginning, that is, at first, at the very onset (prathama-sannipāte) — at the inception of jñāna, vairāgya, dhyāna and samādhi — is, owing to its requiring the most strenuous exertion, like poison, of the nature of suffering; but in the outcome (pariṇāme), happiness born of the maturing of jñāna, vairāgya and the rest, is like nectar — that happiness is declared by the wise to be sāttvika. The buddhi of the Self is ātma-buddhi; the prasāda of that ātma-buddhi is its purity (nairmalyam), like the limpidity of water; born from that, it is ātma-buddhi-prasāda-jam. Or else, the buddhi having the Self as its object, or the buddhi resting on the Self, is ātma-buddhi; born from the abundance of its serenity (tat-prasāda-prakarṣāt) — this is what is meant. For that reason it is sāttvika.
BG_C18_V38: That happiness which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, which at the start is like nectar but in its outcome is like poison — that happiness is recorded as rājasa.
BG_C18_V38::block-0: That happiness which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects — at the beginning, at the first moment, is like nectar, equal to nectar; but in its outcome (pariṇāme), at the end of the run of its enjoyment, is like poison — because it is the cause of the loss of bodily strength, virility, beauty, wisdom, intelligence, wealth and zeal, and because it is the cause of unrighteousness (adharma) and of hell and the like that arise from that — that happiness is recorded as rājasa.
BG_C18_V39: That happiness which both at the beginning and in its consequence is delusive to the Self, arising from sleep, indolence and heedlessness — that is described as tāmasa.
BG_C18_V39::block-0: That happiness which both at the beginning and in its sequel (anubandhe — that is, in the time after its end, avasāna-uttara-kāle) is delusive (mohanam — productive of delusion) to the Self, arising from sleep, indolence and heedlessness — meaning, sleep, indolence and heedlessness, from which it springs up (samuttiṣṭhati), hence 'sleep-indolence-heedlessness-arisen' (nidrā-ālasya-pramāda-uttham) — that is described as tāmasa.
BG_C18_V40: There is no being whatever, on the earth or again among the gods in the heavens, that could be free from these three guṇas born of primal nature.
BG_C18_V40::block-0: Now, at this stage, a verse summing up the topic is begun —
BG_C18_V40::block-1: It does not exist, that is, there is not, on the earth, that is, among men and the rest, any being (sattvam — the host of living creatures, or anything else non-living); nor again, in the heavens, among the gods, is there any being, that would be free, that is, separated, from these three guṇas — beginning with sattva — born of primal nature, that is, arising from prakṛti. 'There is not such a thing' — this is the connection with the preceding.
BG_C18_V41: O scorcher of foes, the duties of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, and likewise of śūdras, have been distributed in accordance with the guṇas that arise from their own innate nature.
BG_C18_V41::block-0: The whole transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) — characterised by action, agent and fruit, constituted of the three guṇas sattva, rajas and tamas, fabricated by avidyā together with its very root — has been declared to be wholly an evil; and by the figure of the tree, beginning with 'with its roots above' (BG 15.1), this very saṃsāra has been described, and it has been said: 'having cleft it with the firm sword of non-attachment' and 'thereafter that abode is to be sought out' (BG 15.3, 15.4). Now, since everything is of the nature of the three guṇas, the cessation of the cause of saṃsāra would seem impossible; therefore the manner in which such cessation may come about must be stated, and the entire teaching of the Gītā-śāstra must be drawn to its conclusion. This and only this much constitutes the import of the whole Veda and Smṛti, and is to be put into practice by those who desire the supreme human goal — for this purpose the passage beginning 'of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas' is now commenced.
BG_C18_V41::block-1:
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas — these together are 'brāhmaṇa-kṣatriya-viśaḥ'; of these brāhmaṇa-kṣatriya-viśaḥ and of the śūdras (the śūdras are not compounded with the others because, although they belong to the human species, they have no eligibility for the Veda), O scorcher of foes, the duties have been 'distributed' — assigned in mutual distinction from one another. By what? By the guṇas that arise from svabhāva. Svabhāva is the prakṛti of the Lord, namely māyā composed of the three guṇas; that is the source (prabhava) of these guṇas, and they are therefore svabhāva-prabhava — by these the duties such as śama (control of mind) and the rest have been distributed among brāhmaṇas and the others.

Or alternatively: of the brāhmaṇa-svabhāva, the sattva-guṇa is the source (cause); of the kṣatriya-svabhāva, rajas with sattva subordinate is the source; of the vaiśya-svabhāva, rajas with tamas subordinate is the source; of the śūdra-svabhāva, tamas with rajas subordinate is the source — for in the four classes one observes the natures of inner peace, lordliness, exertion, and bewilderment respectively.

Or again: the saṃskāra accumulated in past births, manifesting itself in the present birth as the inclination toward its specific effect, is the svabhāva of living beings; and the guṇas of which that is the source are svabhāva-prabhava guṇas — for the manifestation of the guṇas cannot occur without a cause. The phrase 'svabhāva is the cause' is the specification of a particular cause. Thus, by the guṇas of sattva, rajas and tamas which arise from svabhāva, that is, which arise from prakṛti, the duties of śama and the rest have been distributed in accordance with the effect appropriate to each.
BG_C18_V41::block-2:
Objection: But the duties such as śama and the rest pertaining to brāhmaṇas and the others are distributed by the śāstra, that is, enjoined by the śāstra; how then is it said that they are distributed by the guṇas such as sattva and the rest?

Reply: This is no defect; for even by the śāstra the duties such as śama and the rest are distributed among brāhmaṇas and the others only with regard to their respective predominance of sattva and the other guṇas, and not without regard to the guṇas. Hence, although distributed by the śāstra, the duties are correctly said to be distributed by the guṇas.
BG_C18_V42: Inner control, outer control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness; knowledge, realisation, and faith in what transcends — this is the duty of a brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature.
BG_C18_V42::block-0: What then are those duties? It is now stated:
BG_C18_V42::block-1: Śama (control of the inner organ) and dama (control of the external senses) are with the meanings already explained; tapas is bodily and other austerity as previously stated; śauca (purity) has been explained; kṣānti is forbearance; ārjava is straightforwardness alone; jñāna is knowledge from scripture and teacher; vijñāna is its direct realisation; āstikya is the disposition of an āstika, namely faith in the meanings of the āgama (revealed scripture). 'Brahma-karma' is the duty of one belonging to the brāhmaṇa class, and it is svabhāvaja, 'born of one's own nature' — that which was previously said to be 'distributed by the guṇas arising from svabhāva' is the very same thing now spoken of as 'born of svabhāva'.
BG_C18_V43: Heroism, vigour, fortitude, dexterity, not fleeing in battle, generosity, and lordly bearing — this is the duty of a kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
BG_C18_V43::block-0: Śaurya is the disposition of a hero; tejas is dignified prowess (prāgalbhya); dhṛti is steady upholding — that fortitude by which one upheld is not cast down in any condition whatever; dākṣya is the disposition of one who is dexterous, namely the unimpeded engagement, without bewilderment, in tasks suddenly arising; 'and not fleeing in battle' is not turning the back to enemies; dāna is open-handedness with respect to gifts that are to be bestowed; īśvara-bhāva is the disposition of a ruler — the manifestation of the lord's power toward those who are to be governed. Kṣātraṃ karma — the duty enjoined for the kṣatriya class — kṣātraṃ karma is svabhāvajam, born of one's own nature.
BG_C18_V44: Agriculture, the keeping of cattle, and trade are the duty of the vaiśya, born of his nature; the duty of the śūdra also, consisting in service, is born of his nature.
BG_C18_V44::block-0: Kṛṣi-gauarakṣya-vāṇijyam — agriculture, cattle-keeping, and trade — that is, kṛṣi is the ploughing (lit. furrowing) of the land; gauarakṣya: he who protects cows is a go-rakṣa, and his function is gauarakṣya — the meaning is animal husbandry; vāṇijya is the merchant's work characterised by buying, selling, and the like. Vaiśya-karma is the duty of the vaiśya class; vaiśya-karma is svabhāvajam, born of his own nature. The duty of the śūdra also, consisting in service (paricaryā) — having servitude as its very nature — is svabhāvajam, born of his own nature.
BG_C18_V45: A man devoted to his own duty attains complete accomplishment. How one engaged in his own duty finds that accomplishment, hear that.
BG_C18_V45::block-0: Of these duties enjoined for each class, when properly performed, the natural fruit is the attainment of heaven, as is shown by such smṛtis as: 'The varṇas and the āśramas, devoted to their own duties, after death enjoy the fruit of their actions; thereafter, by the residue [of merit], they obtain birth with distinguished region, caste, family, dharma, longevity, learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence' (Gautama Dharma-sūtra 2.2.29; Maitri Gautama Dharma-sūtra 11.31), and the like; and from the Purāṇas there is recollection of the specific differences of worldly fruits for those of the varṇas and āśramas. But from a different cause comes the fruit now to be declared:
BG_C18_V45::block-1: 'In his own respective duty', that is, in the duty distinguished by characteristics already stated, 'devoted', that is, intent on it; saṃsiddhi — the man who is qualified attains, namely obtains, the saṃsiddhi consisting in the body's and senses' fitness for jñāna-niṣṭhā, which arises when impurity has been worn away by the performance of one's own duty. Is this complete accomplishment a direct result of the performance of one's own duty alone? No. How then? Hear that — by what method one engaged in his own duty finds that accomplishment.
BG_C18_V46: From whom is the activity of beings, by whom all this is pervaded — worshipping Him by his own duty, a man finds accomplishment.
BG_C18_V46::block-0: Yataḥ — from whom — that is, from which inner ruler, the Lord, the activity, namely the origination or movement, of beings, of living creatures, takes place; by whom, by which Lord, all this universe is pervaded, that is, filled — Him, the Lord, having worshipped with one's own duty (mentioned above for each varṇa), that is, having venerated and propitiated Him, the man, the human being, finds, obtains, the sole siddhi consisting in the fitness for jñāna-niṣṭhā.
BG_C18_V47: One's own duty, even though deficient in quality, is more praiseworthy than another's duty well performed. Performing the action determined by one's own nature, one incurs no sin.
BG_C18_V47::block-1: Śreyān — more praiseworthy — is svadharma, one's own dharma; even though deficient in quality (the word 'api' is to be supplied), in comparison with another's dharma. 'Determined by svabhāva' means 'fixed by one's own nature'; what was previously called 'born of svabhāva' is the very same thing here called 'determined by svabhāva'. Just as the poison of a worm born of poison does not cause harm to it, even so, performing the action determined by one's own nature, one does not incur sin (kilbiṣa).
BG_C18_V48: One should not abandon, O son of Kuntī, the action that is born together with one, even though it be flawed; for all undertakings are enveloped by flaw, as fire by smoke.
BG_C18_V48::block-0: It has been said that one performing the action determined by one's own nature, like the worm born of poison, does not incur sin; and that another's dharma is fraught with fear; and that, for one ignorant of the Self, 'no one indeed remains for even a moment without performing action' (BG 3.5). Hence —
BG_C18_V48::block-1: Sahajam — born together with birth itself, that is, arisen along with one's very birth. What is that? 'Action', O son of Kuntī, even though flawed because it is constituted of the three guṇas, one should not abandon. Sarvārambhāḥ — those things which are undertaken are 'undertakings', meaning all actions. By the context, whatever undertakings there be — whether one's own dharma or another's dharma — all of them, since they are constituted of the three guṇas (this being the cause assigned here), are enveloped by flaw, as fire by its co-arisen smoke. Hence, by abandoning the action born with oneself, namely one's own dharma, and undertaking another's dharma instead, one does not become free from flaw; and another's dharma is fraught with fear. Moreover, the ignorant cannot wholly abandon action; therefore he should not abandon it. This is the meaning.
BG_C18_V48::block-2:
Objection: Is it that one should not abandon action because it is impossible to abandon it wholly? Or because there is a flaw in abandoning the action that has arisen with oneself? Of what consequence is this distinction? If, indeed, the connatural action is not to be abandoned merely because it is impossible to abandon it wholly, then it follows that there would actually be merit in abandoning it wholly, were that possible.

Reply: Quite so. But — Objection: Total abandonment is itself not possible. — Why? Is the puruṣa of the nature of constant flux, like the guṇas of the Sāṃkhyas? Or is action itself the agent, as the skandhas of the Buddhists are momentary, perishing the next instant? On either alternative, total abandonment of action is not possible. There is yet a third position: when one acts, the substance is endowed with action; when one does not act, that very substance is actionless. On this view, action could indeed be wholly abandoned. The peculiarity of this third position, however, is this: the substance is not in constant flux, nor is action itself the agent. Then what? In an established substance, an action that did not exist before arises, and having existed, perishes again; the substance itself remains pure and endowed with potency. So say the followers of Kaṇāda. And that very substance, they hold, is the agent. What flaw, then, is there in this view? — This very flaw: this doctrine is contrary to the doctrine of the Lord. How is this known? Because the Lord declares: 'Of the unreal there is no being' (BG 2.16) and so on. For the Vaiśeṣikas hold that there is being of the non-existent and non-being of the existent — this doctrine is therefore not the Lord's. — Objection: Even if it is not the Lord's, what is the flaw in it, if it is logical? — Reply: It is itself flawed, for it is at variance with all means of valid knowledge. How? If the dyad and other substances were absolutely non-existent before their origination, and after originating and existing for some time again come to absolute non-existence, then it follows that the non-existent itself comes into being and the existent itself comes to non-existence; non-being becomes being, and being becomes non-being. Now, if non-being, being born, were comparable to a hare's horn before its origination, would it be born depending upon causes called the inherent, the non-inherent, and the efficient? But it cannot be said that non-being arises in this manner, depending upon a cause, since non-existents like hare's horns are nowhere observed. If, however, pots and the like, being of the nature of being, arise depending upon causes only as far as their manifestation goes, that may be intelligible. Moreover, if the non-existent has being and the existent has non-being, no one would have any confidence in any of the dealings between pramāṇa and prameya, since the determination 'the existent is just existent, the non-existent is just non-existent' would be impossible.
BG_C18_V48::block-3: Further, when they say 'it arises', they mean that the dyad and other substances enter into a relation of being with their own causes. Before origination it is non-existent; subsequently, in dependence on the operation of causes, it is connected with its own causes — the atoms — by the relation called samavāya, which is sat (existence). Once thus connected, it becomes existent and inherent in its causes. Here it must be answered: how can the non-existent have its own cause, or have a relation with anything? For of a barren woman's son one cannot, by any pramāṇa, postulate either his own cause or a relation with anything.
BG_C18_V48::block-4: Objection: But the Vaiśeṣikas do not postulate the relation of a non-being. The relation, characterised as inherence in their own causes, is asserted only of dyads and other substances that are existent. — Reply: No; for they do not admit existence prior to the relation. The Vaiśeṣikas do not hold that pots and the like exist prior to the activity of the potter, the staff, the wheel, and so forth. Nor do they admit that clay itself attains the form of the pot. As the only remaining alternative, the relation must be admitted to be of the non-existent.
BG_C18_V48::block-5: Objection: But the relation of inherence is not contradictory even in the case of the non-existent. — Reply: No, for barren women's sons and the like are nowhere observed [to enter such relations]. Why does the prior non-existence of a pot have a relation with its own cause, while the prior non-existence of a barren woman's son does not — when both are equally non-existent? Some peculiarity of the non-being would have to be stated. As to definitions, no peculiarity at all can be shown between the non-being of one, the non-being of two, the non-being of all, prior non-being, posterior non-being (destruction), mutual non-being, and absolute non-being. And in the absence of any peculiarity, that the prior non-existence of a pot becomes the existent pot through the potter and the rest, and is connected with that being called potsherds, and being so connected becomes fit for all dealings — while the posterior non-existence of that very pot, though equally non-being, does not — and that thus posterior non-being and the rest are unfit for any dealings, while the prior non-being alone, called by the names of dyad and other substances, is fit for the dealings of origination and so on — this is incoherent. For non-being is uniform, just as in the case of absolute non-being and posterior non-being.
BG_C18_V48::block-6: Objection: But we do not say that prior non-being attains the state of being. — Reply: Then it must be that being itself attains the state of being, just as a pot attains the state of pot, or a cloth that of cloth. This too is just as contrary to pramāṇa as the doctrine that non-being attains being. Even the Sāṃkhya's view of pariṇāma (transformation), since it accepts the origination and destruction of unprecedented properties, is not different from the Vaiśeṣika's. And even if abhivyakti (manifestation) and tirobhāva (occultation) be admitted, when one investigates whether manifestation and occultation are themselves existent or non-existent, the same contradiction with pramāṇa as before arises. By this, the view that origination and the rest are merely the configuration of the cause is also refuted.
BG_C18_V48::block-7: Hence, by the residue [of options], the one and only existent reality is, by avidyā, imagined in many ways, like an actor, with properties of origination, destruction, and the rest. This is the doctrine of the Lord, declared in the verse 'Of the unreal there is no being' (BG 2.16) — for the cognition 'is' never strays, while the others stray.
BG_C18_V48::block-8:
Objection: Then, since the Self is changeless, how is it that wholesale abandonment of action is not possible?

Reply: Whether the guṇas are real entities, or whether they are imagined by avidyā, action being their property, in the case of one who is ignorant it stands superimposed upon the Self by avidyā; hence it has been said: 'No one is able even for a moment to abandon it wholly' (BG 3.5). But the wise man, when avidyā has ceased through vidyā, is indeed able to abandon action wholly, since there is no residue left of what was superimposed by avidyā. For of the second moon and the rest superimposed upon a man's vision by timira (eye-disease), no residue remains when the timira is gone. Such being the case, the following statements are perfectly intelligible: 'Renouncing all actions in mind' (BG 5.13) and so on; 'A man devoted to his own duty attains complete accomplishment' (BG 18.45); and 'Worshipping Him by his own duty, a man finds accomplishment' (BG 18.46).
BG_C18_V49: He whose understanding is unattached everywhere, who has conquered the self, from whom longing has departed — through renunciation he attains the supreme perfection of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
BG_C18_V49::block-0: The karma-born perfection has been declared, characterised by fitness for jñāna-niṣṭhā; now its fruit, the perfection of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya-siddhi), characterised by jñāna-niṣṭhā itself, must be stated. With this aim the verse is begun —
BG_C18_V49::block-1: Asakta-buddhiḥ — he whose buddhi, the inner organ, is asakta, free of attachment, sarvatra, everywhere, in all the occasions for attachment such as son, wife and the rest. Jitātmā — he whose ātman, the inner organ (here taken in its psychological sense), is jita, conquered, brought under control. Vigata-spṛhaḥ — he from whom spṛhā, thirst, has gone with respect to the body, life and enjoyments. Such a knower of the Self attains naiṣkarmya-siddhi. The samāsa is unfolded thus: he is niṣkarmā from whom karmas have departed by reason of the realisation of his identity with the actionless Brahman; the abstract noun of this is naiṣkarman = naiṣkarmya, and naiṣkarmya being itself the siddhi yields naiṣkarmya-siddhi. Or else, it is the siddhi, the consummation, of niṣkarmatva in the form of abiding as the actionless Self. That naiṣkarmya-siddhi which is paramā — supreme, distinct from karma-born perfection, of the nature of immediate liberation (sadyo-mukti) — he attains by saṁnyāsa, that is, by samyag-darśana, true vision, or by the renunciation of all karmas which is preceded by such vision. To this very effect it has been said: "Mentally renouncing all actions, he sits neither acting nor causing action" (BG 5.13).
BG_C18_V50: How one who has thus attained perfection reaches Brahman — that supreme niṣṭhā of jñāna — learn from Me in brief, O son of Kuntī.
BG_C18_V50::block-0: When, by the previously stated performance of one's own duty in the form of worship of the Lord, the perfection of the previously described kind (i.e. fitness of body and senses for jñāna-niṣṭhā) is engendered, and discriminative knowledge of the Self has arisen — by what sequence does the perfection characterised by naiṣkarmya, consisting in steadfastness in pure Self-knowledge alone, then come about? That is to be told. With this purpose he says —
BG_C18_V50::block-1: Siddhiṁ prāptaḥ — having, by his own karma, worshipped the Lord and obtained from His grace the perfection of the body and senses, characterised by fitness for jñāna-niṣṭhā. The clause "having attained perfection" is here a recapitulation (anuvāda) for the sake of what follows. And what is that subsequent matter, for the sake of which there is the recapitulation? It is being stated: yathā — by what manner, namely the manner consisting in jñāna-niṣṭhā, one attains brahma, the supreme Self — that manner, that sequence by which jñāna-niṣṭhā is reached, niboḏha me — learn from My word, that is, ascertain decisively from what I say. Why at length? "No," he says: samāsenaiva — in brief alone, O Kaunteya, learn the way by which one reaches Brahman. By this much the attainment of Brahman has been promised; in order to display it as "this is it," he says, "the supreme niṣṭhā of jñāna." Niṣṭhā means the culmination, the consummation. Of what? Of brahma-jñāna. The supreme one. Of what kind is it? Of the kind that the knowledge of the Self is. And of what kind is that? Of the kind that the Self itself is. And of what kind is He? Of the kind which the Lord has declared, and which the Upaniṣadic texts and reasoning establish.
BG_C18_V50::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa: Knowledge takes the form of its object. But the Self is neither an object of knowledge, nor is It accepted anywhere as having form. — Objection: "Of the colour of the sun" (Śvet. Up. 3.8), "luminous in nature" (Chānd. Up. 3.14.2), "self-luminous" (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.9) — thus form is heard of the Self. Reply: No; for those passages serve only to negate the inference that the Self is of the nature of darkness. When the form of substance, quality and the rest is denied of the Self, the suspicion arises that the Self may be of the form of darkness; to repel that, texts such as "of the colour of the sun" (Śvet. Up. 3.8) are uttered. "Formless" (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15) specifically negates form. And from non-objectivity also: "Its form does not stand within sight; none beholds Him with the eye" (Śvet. Up. 4.20), "soundless, intangible" (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15), and so on. Therefore, the view that knowledge has the form of the Self is untenable.
BG_C18_V50::block-3: How then is there knowledge of the Self at all? For all knowledge whatsoever takes the form of its object, while the Self has been said to be without form. If both knowledge and the Self are formless, how can there be steadfastness consisting in the contemplation (bhāvanā) of the Self? — Not so; for the Self admits of supreme purity, supreme transparency and supreme subtlety. The buddhi too, like the Self, admits of purity and the rest, and hence admits of taking on the semblance of the consciousness-form of the Self. The mind has the semblance of the buddhi; the senses have the semblance of the mind; and the body has the semblance of the senses. Hence the worldly people superimpose the seeing of the Self on the body alone.
BG_C18_V50::block-4: The Lokāyatas, who hold that consciousness belongs to the body, declare: "The body characterised by consciousness is the puruṣa." Similarly others hold that consciousness belongs to the senses; others to the mind; and yet others to the buddhi. Beyond all these, certain others have taken as the Self the inner unmanifest — that which is termed avyākṛta and is in the state of avidyā. Throughout, from buddhi up to the body, this very semblance of the Self's consciousness is the cause of the delusion regarding the Self. Therefore, the knowledge whose object is the Self need not be enjoined as something to be produced. What then is to be done? Only the cessation of the superimposition (adhyāropa) of the non-Self — name, form and the rest — upon the Self is to be effected; the cognition of the Self's consciousness is not something to be brought about, since it appears uniformly through the forms of all things superimposed by avidyā. It is on this very account that the Buddhist Vijñāna-vādins have arrived at the view that no real entity exists distinct from cognition, and that cognition is independent of any other means of valid knowledge, on the ground of its self-luminosity. Therefore, with regard to Brahman, only the elimination of avidyā-superimposition is to be done; no effort is to be made for the cognition of Brahman, since It is supremely self-evident. To those whose buddhi is carried away by the particular forms of name and form imagined by avidyā, that very Self — though supremely well-known, easily known, the very nearest, indeed one's own being — appears as little known, hard to know, very far away, as it were something other. But to those whose buddhi has turned away from external forms, who have obtained the grace of the Self through the teacher, there is no bliss greater than this, well-known, easily known and very near them. So too it has been said: "Directly perceptible, in accord with dharma" (BG 9.2) and so forth.
BG_C18_V50::block-5: Some who fancy themselves learned object: "Because the Self-entity is formless, the buddhi cannot reach It; therefore steadfastness in true knowledge is hard to accomplish." True — for those who lack the tradition of teachers, who have not heard the Vedānta, whose buddhi is intensely attached to external objects, who have made no exertion in the right means of valid knowledge. But for the opposite kind — those whose right cognition (sad-buddhi) is fixed on the dual reality of grasper and grasped of common experience — that very dual reality is exceedingly hard to establish, since apart from the consciousness of the Self no other entity is grasped at all; and we have already said that "this is just so, not otherwise." The Lord too has said: "That which is night to all beings is the time of waking for the self-controlled sage" (BG 2.69). Therefore, the cessation of the buddhi's apprehension of external forms and distinctions is itself the means of taking refuge in the Self's own being. The Self is never, for anyone, anywhere, unknown, to-be-attained, to-be-rejected or to-be-accepted. For if the Self were unknown, all activities undertaken for one's own sake would become purposeless. It cannot be supposed that they exist for the sake of the body or other insentient objects; nor that pleasure exists for the sake of pleasure, or pain for the sake of pain. Indeed, every transaction terminates in the awareness of the Self. Therefore, just as no other means of valid knowledge is needed to determine one's own body, so much the more — since the Self is more inward than even that — no other means of valid knowledge is needed for Its cognition. Thus jñāna-niṣṭhā regarding the Self is, for the discriminating, well-established. This is settled.
BG_C18_V50::block-6: Even for those who hold that knowledge is formless and not directly perceptible, the apprehension of the knowable comes about by the power of knowledge alone; hence knowledge must be admitted to be supremely well-known, just like pleasure and the rest. Also from the impossibility of the desire to know it: if knowledge were not well-known, it would be sought after just as the knowable is. Just as the knower wishes by knowledge to encompass the knowable — a pot and the like — so knowledge too would have to be sought to be encompassed by another knowledge. But this is not the case. Therefore knowledge is supremely well-known, and on the same ground the knower also is well-known. Hence no effort is to be made for the production of knowledge; only the removal of the false notion of self in the non-self is to be effected. Therefore jñāna-niṣṭhā is easy to accomplish.
BG_C18_V51: Endowed with a purified buddhi, restraining the self with firmness, abandoning sound and the other sense-objects, and casting off attraction and aversion —
BG_C18_V51::block-0: That very supreme niṣṭhā of jñāna is now spoken of: how is it to be brought about? —
BG_C18_V51::block-1: Buddhyā — by the buddhi, characterised by determination (adhyavasāya); viśuddhayā — purified, free of māyā; yuktaḥ — endowed, equipped therewith. Dhṛtyā — with firmness, fortitude; ātmānam — the aggregate of body and senses (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta); niyamya ca — and having restrained, having brought into one's own control. Śabda-ādīn viṣayān tyaktvā — having abandoned sound and the rest of the sense-objects. By implication, having let go of those that are mere supports of bodily subsistence in their bare necessity and abandoned anything beyond that which serves pleasure. Towards those that come naturally for the sake of bodily subsistence, vyudasya — casting off, completely setting aside — rāga-dveṣau, attraction and aversion.
BG_C18_V52: Resorting to a solitary place, eating little, with speech, body and mind controlled, ever intent on the yoga of meditation, established in dispassion —
BG_C18_V52::block-1: Vivikta-sevī — he whose habit is to resort to solitary places such as forests, river-banks, mountain-caves and the like is vivikta-sevī. Laghv-āśī — of the habit of eating little. The mention of these two — resort to solitude and light eating — is because they remove the faults of sleep and the rest, and thereby cause clarity (prasāda) of mind. Yata-vāk-kāya-mānasaḥ — that yati, that one steadfast in jñāna, whose speech, body and mind are restrained, is yata-vāk-kāya-mānasaḥ. With all his organs thus quiescent, dhyāna-yoga-paraḥ — dhyāna is the contemplation of the Self's own nature, yoga is the one-pointed concentration on the Self; he by whom these two are pursued as paramount is dhyāna-yoga-paraḥ. Nityam — "always"; this is included to indicate that there is no other duty such as the recitation of mantras and the like. Vairāgyam — the state of vi-rāga, the freedom from thirst with regard to objects seen and heard of (the visible and unseen-fruit kinds); samupāśritaḥ — perfectly resorted to, that is, perpetually established in it.
BG_C18_V53: Letting go of egoism, force, pride, desire, anger and possession, free from "mine," tranquil — he is fit to become Brahman.
BG_C18_V53::block-1: Ahaṅkāra — the act of "I-making" with regard to the body and the rest. Bala — strength conjoined with desire and attachment; not the natural strength of the body and so on, since the giving up of that is not possible. Darpa — pride, which is what arises immediately after exhilaration and is the cause of transgression of dharma — for the smṛti says, "Being elated he becomes proud; being proud he transgresses dharma" (Āp. Dh. Sū. 1.13.4). Kāma — desire; krodha — aversion; parigraha — even when the inner faults of the senses and mind have been given up, on account of the maintenance of the body or the necessity of dharma-performance external possession may yet present itself; that too — vimucya — letting go, completely abandoning. Having become a paramahaṁsa-parivrājaka, in respect of even the bare maintenance of the body's life he is nirmamaḥ — devoid of "mine"; for that very reason śāntaḥ — at peace, withdrawn; he in whom delight and exertion have been reabsorbed, the yati steadfast in jñāna, brahma-bhūyāya kalpate — becomes fit, capable, for becoming Brahman.
BG_C18_V54: Become Brahman, with serene self, he neither grieves nor longs; equal towards all beings, he obtains supreme devotion to Me.
BG_C18_V54::block-1: Brahma-bhūtaḥ — having attained Brahman; prasannātmā — of the nature of having obtained the inner clarity of the Self; na śocati — he does not grieve, that is, he is not pained over any deficiency of property or any defect with respect to himself. Na kāṅkṣati — for the longing for an unattained object is not possible in the knower of Brahman. Hence this is a description, by way of recapitulation, of the very nature of the brahma-bhūta — "he neither grieves nor longs." There is also a variant reading, "na hṛṣyati" ("he does not exult"). Samaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu — equal towards all beings, that is, by the analogy of one's own self he sees pleasure or pain in all beings as equally one's own. The seeing of all as identical with the Self is not what is meant here, since that is to be told later in "by devotion he comes to know Me" (BG 18.55). Such a one steadfast in jñāna obtains mad-bhakti — devotion (bhajana) to Me, the supreme Lord — paraṁ — supreme, the highest, of the form of jñāna, the fourth kind; for it has been said: "Of four kinds are those who worship Me" (BG 7.16).
BG_C18_V55: By that devotion he comes to know Me truly — how vast I am and who I am in essence; then, having known Me as I am in truth, he immediately enters into Me.
BG_C18_V55::block-0: By that — by devotion in the form of knowledge —
BG_C18_V55::block-1: Bhaktyā mām abhijānāti — by that devotion he truly knows Me — how vast I am, with the manifold differentiation set up by upādhis, and who I am, with all upādhi-distinctions wholly destroyed, the Highest Person, like ākāśa. Such Me — the non-dual, the single homogeneous mass of consciousness, ageless, fearless, deathless — he knows in truth (tattvataḥ). Tataḥ — having thus known Me in truth, viśate tad-anantaram — he enters Me immediately upon knowledge. Here the knowing and the entering are not intended as two distinct acts spoken of by "having known he enters thereafter"; rather, since there is no other fruit, knowledge alone is meant — for it has been said, "Know Me also as the kṣetrajña" (BG 13.2).
BG_C18_V55::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa: But this is contradictory: "that supreme niṣṭhā of jñāna by which he knows Me." How contradictory? It is replied — at the very moment in which, regarding any object, knowledge arises in the knower, in that very moment the knower knows that object. Hence no jñāna-niṣṭhā in the form of repeated repetition of the knowledge is required. Therefore he does not know by knowledge but, rather, by the repetition of knowledge, namely jñāna-niṣṭhā. Reply: This is no defect. The jñāna in question, which is endowed with the causes that bring about its origination and ripening, free from any opponent, has its consummation in the firm direct experience of the Self; that is what is signified by the word niṣṭhā. By the instruction of scripture and teacher, depending on auxiliary causes — the purity of the buddhi and the like, and qualities such as humility — the knowledge of the unity of the kṣetrajña and the supreme Self is engendered, accompanied by the renunciation of all karmas which is rooted in the dichotomous notion of agency and the rest. The abiding of that knowledge in the form of the firm direct experience of one's own Self — this is called the supreme jñāna-niṣṭhā. This very jñāna-niṣṭhā has been described, in relation to the three other devotions of the afflicted and so on, as the supreme, fourth devotion. By that supreme devotion he knows the Lord truly, immediately upon which the dichotomous notion of Lord and kṣetrajña is utterly destroyed. Hence the statement "He knows Me by devotion characterised by jñāna-niṣṭhā" is not contradictory.
BG_C18_V55::block-3: And here all the scriptural texts that enjoin nivṛtti — those of the Vedānta, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, Smṛti — and that are established by reasoning become meaningful: "Having known... they rise up and roam as mendicants on alms" (Bṛh. Up. 3.5.1); "Therefore they declare renunciation to be supremely above these austerities" (Tai. Nār. 79); "Renunciation alone surpassed [them]" (Tai. Nār. 78); "Saṁnyāsa is the laying down of karmas" ( ? ); "Abandoning the Vedas and this world and the next" (Āp. Dh. 2.9.13); "Give up dharma and adharma" (Mo. Dh. 329.40); and the rest. The texts adduced here also belong here. The purposelessness of those texts cannot be admitted; nor can they be explained as mere arthavāda, since they stand in their own context, and since liberation, whose nature is steadfastness in the unchanging inmost Self, is what is being treated. For one who wishes to go to the eastern sea, and one who wishes to go in the opposite direction, to the western sea, there cannot be a common road. Jñāna-niṣṭhā is the engagement in producing a continuous current of cognition concerning the inmost Self; it is opposed to coexistence with karma, just as travelling toward the western sea is opposed to travelling toward the eastern. The opposition here is settled, like that between a mountain and a mustard-seed, by those who know the means of valid knowledge. Therefore, jñāna-niṣṭhā is to be brought about only through the renunciation of all karmas. This is established.
BG_C18_V56: Even when performing all actions always, taking refuge in Me, by My grace he attains the everlasting, imperishable abode.
BG_C18_V56::block-0: The fruit of the bhakti-yoga of worshipping the Lord through one's own karma is the attainment of the perfection consisting in fitness for jñāna-niṣṭhā; that jñāna-niṣṭhā, occasioned by it, has liberation as its terminal fruit. That bhakti-yoga to the Lord is now eulogised in the concluding section that sums up the meaning of the śāstra, for the strengthening of the resolve regarding the import of the śāstra —
BG_C18_V56::block-1: Sarva-karmāṇi api — even all karmas, even those that are prohibited; sadā kurvāṇaḥ — always performing them; mad-vyapāśrayaḥ — he in whom the refuge is I, Vāsudeva, the Lord — that is, he by whom all dispositions are deposited in Me. Such a one too — mat-prasādāt — by My grace, the grace of the Lord — avāpnoti — attains; śāśvataṁ — eternal; the Vaiṣṇava abode (Vaiṣṇavaṁ padam); avyayaṁ — imperishable.
BG_C18_V57: Mentally renouncing all actions in Me, having Me as the supreme goal, and resorting to the yoga of (steadied) intellect, be ever absorbed in Me in mind.
BG_C18_V57::block-1: With the mind — that is, with the discriminating intellect — renouncing all actions, those aimed at seen and unseen ends, in Me, the Lord, by the principle stated in "Whatever you do, whatever you eat" (BG 9.27), and being mat-paraḥ — "He of whom Vāsudeva, that is, I, am the supreme (paraḥ) [resort]; that art thou" — having thus dedicated your entire being to Me, taking refuge in the buddhi-yoga, the state of the intellect's collected concentration (samāhita-buddhitva), having recourse to it as your sole shelter (apāśraya), with no other refuge — being mac-cittaḥ, "he whose citta (mind) is in Me alone; that art thou" — be such ever, at all times.
BG_C18_V58: With mind fixed on Me, you shall, by My grace, cross over all difficulties; but if from egotism you will not heed, you shall perish.
BG_C18_V58::block-0: Being mac-cittaḥ — having mind fixed on Me — you shall by My grace cross over, that is, transcend, all the difficulties (sarva-durgāṇi), all the host of well-nigh impassable causes of saṃsāra. But if (atha cet) you, out of egotism — "I am a learned man" — will not hearken to, that is, will not accept, what I have spoken, then you shall perish (vinaṅkṣyasi), come to ruin.
BG_C18_V59: If, taking refuge in egotism, you think "I shall not fight," vain is this resolve of yours; (your own) nature will compel you.
BG_C18_V59::block-0: And this should not be entertained by you — "I am independent (svatantraḥ); why should I do what another bids?" —
BG_C18_V59::block-1: If, taking refuge in egotism, you think — that is, ponder, resolve — "I will not fight, I shall not engage in battle," vain (mithyā) is this resolve, this determination, of yours; for prakṛti — your kṣatriya nature — will compel you (niyokṣyati).
BG_C18_V60: O son of Kuntī, bound by your own action born of (your) nature, what you out of delusion do not wish to do, that you shall do, even helplessly.
BG_C18_V60::block-1: Bound — fastened with certainty — O Kaunteya, by that which is born of (your) nature, namely the heroism etc. described above, by your own (svena), that is, intrinsic, action: that action which, out of delusion (mohāt), out of want of discrimination, you do not wish to do — that very action you shall do, helpless (avaśaḥ), entirely under another's sway.
BG_C18_V61: The Lord, O Arjuna, abides in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve, as though mounted on a machine, by His māyā.
BG_C18_V61::block-1:
Īśvara — He whose nature is to rule, Nārāyaṇa — abides, that is, takes up His seat, in the heart-region (hṛd-deśe), in the seat of the heart, of all beings, of all living creatures. "Arjuna" — "of pure innermost nature, of cleansed inner organ" — as is shown by the śruti, "the day too — the dark day and the bright (arjuna) day" (Ṛg-Veda Maṇḍala 6.1.9.1).

How does He abide in them? He answers: causing them to revolve (bhrāmayan) — making them whirl about — all beings as it were mounted on a machine (yantrārūḍhāni) — that is, as if stationed upon machines: the word iva, "as it were," is to be understood here — just as wooden figures of men and the like are mounted upon machines. By māyā, by deception (chadman), causing them to revolve, He abides — such is the construction.
BG_C18_V62: Take refuge in Him alone, with all your being, O Bhārata; by His grace you shall attain supreme peace, the eternal abode.
BG_C18_V62::block-0: Him alone — that Īśvara — go for refuge, take as your shelter (āśraya), for the removal of the affliction of saṃsāra; with all your being (sarva-bhāvena), that is, with your entire self (sarvātmanā), O Bhārata. Thence, by His grace (tat-prasādāt) — by the favour of the Lord — you shall attain supreme peace (parām śāntim), the highest cessation, and the abode (sthānam) — namely My, that is, Viṣṇu's, supreme state — eternal (śāśvatam), everlasting.
BG_C18_V63: Thus has the knowledge, more secret than secrecy itself, been declared to you by Me; reflecting upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.
BG_C18_V63::block-0: Thus — this — the knowledge has been declared, that is, told, to you, more secret than the secret (guhyāt guhyataram) — exceedingly secret, profoundly hidden (rahasyam) — that is the meaning, by Me, the omniscient Īśvara. Having reflected (vimṛśya) — that is, having pondered, having examined — upon this, the scripture as set forth, in its entirety (aśeṣeṇa), the whole body of meaning thus declared — act as you wish (yathecchasi tathā kuru).
BG_C18_V64: Hear again My supreme word, the most secret of all secrets; since you are firmly dear to Me, therefore I shall declare what is salutary for you.
BG_C18_V64::block-0: Hear once more what is being uttered by Me —
BG_C18_V64::block-1:
Sarva-guhyatamam — most secret among all secrets, surpassingly secret (atyanta-guhyatamam), utterly hidden (atyanta-rahasyam) — though already spoken not once but many times, hear yet again (bhūyaḥ punaḥ) My supreme (paramam), highest (prakṛṣṭam) word (vacaḥ), utterance.

Not from fear, nor from any motive of self-interest do I declare it; what then? — "You are dear (iṣṭaḥ), beloved (priyaḥ), to Me firmly (dṛḍham), without lapse (avyabhicāreṇa)" — for that reason (tataḥ), on that account, I shall speak, I shall tell you (te tava) what is salutary (hitam) — the supreme means to the attainment of knowledge (jñāna-prāpti-sādhanam); for that is, of all that is salutary, the most salutary (hitatamam).
BG_C18_V65: Have your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, prostrate before Me. You shall come to Me alone — this I promise you truly, for you are dear to Me. (65)
BG_C18_V65::block-1: Have your mind on Me (man-manāḥ bhava) — let your thought be set on Me. Be My devotee (mad-bhaktaḥ bhava) — be one whose worshipful service is to Me. Be My sacrificer (mad-yājī) — be one whose nature is to sacrifice to Me. Prostrate to Me (māṁ namaskuru) — even your act of prostration, let it be to Me alone. Thus abiding, with goal, means and purpose all surrendered into Vāsudeva alone, you shall come to Me alone (mām eva eṣyasi) — you shall reach Me. "Truly to you I promise (satyaṁ te pratijāne)" — I make a true vow regarding this matter; this is the meaning. The reason: because you are dear to Me. Having thus understood the Lord's truthfulness of vow, and having ascertained that the fruit of liberation is unfailing for one devoted to the Lord, one should become wholly given over to taking refuge in the Lord — this is the purport of the sentence.
BG_C18_V66: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone, the One. I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (66)
BG_C18_V66::block-0: Having concluded the supreme secret of the karma-yoga discipline, namely taking refuge in the Lord, He now declares the fruit of the karma-yoga discipline — the right vision (samyag-darśana) which is the essence of the entire Vedānta —
BG_C18_V66::block-1:
All dharmas (sarva-dharmān) — "all" qualifies "dharmas," hence sarva-dharmāḥ; them. Here, by the word dharma, adharma also is included, since what is intended is naiṣkarmya (state of actionlessness), and on the strength of śruti and smṛti — "Not he who has not desisted from evil conduct" (Kaṭha 1.2.24), "Abandon both dharma and adharma" (Mahābhārata, Mokṣa-dharma 329.40), and the like. "Abandoning all dharmas" means renouncing all actions. "Me alone (mām ekam)" — the Self of all, the same, abiding in all beings, the Lord, the Imperishable, free from being conceived in the womb, birth, old age and death — "I alone am That": thus take refuge; assert that there is nothing other than Me. This is the meaning. "I shall liberate you (ahaṁ tvā)" — you, of such firm understanding, from all sins (sarva-pāpebhyaḥ) — from the bondages in the form of all dharma and adharma — I shall liberate by manifesting your own Self-nature. As also said: "Abiding in their Self, I destroy [the darkness born of ignorance] with the luminous lamp of knowledge" (Gītā 10.11). Therefore, do not grieve (mā śucaḥ) — do not lament. This is the meaning.

In this scripture of the Gītā, what has been ascertained as the means to the supreme good — knowledge, action, or both? Whence the doubt? Sentences such as "By knowing which one attains immortality" (Gītā 13.12) and "Then, having known Me in truth, he enters [Me] immediately thereafter" (Gītā 18.55) demonstrate the attainment of supreme good from knowledge alone. Sentences such as "Your right is to action only" (Gītā 2.47) and "Do action only" (Gītā 4.15) demonstrate the unfailing duty of performing actions. Thus, since both knowledge and action are taught as duties, the combination of the two might also be a cause of supreme good — so might arise the doubt of someone. But what then is the fruit of this enquiry (mīmāṁsā-phala)? Indeed it is just this: ascertaining which one of these is the means to supreme good. Hence this is to be enquired into more extensively.

The knowledge of the Self alone is the cause of supreme good, since by removing the cognition of difference it terminates in the fruit of absolute aloneness (kaivalya). The cognition of difference among action, agent, and fruit is constantly active in the Self through avidyā — "This is my action; I am the doer; for such-and-such fruit I shall do this action" — this avidyā is operative from beginningless time. The remover of this avidyā is knowledge regarding the Self of the form: "This very 'I' am, alone, non-doer, action-less, fruit-less; there is none other than I" — when this arises, since it removes the cognition of difference which is the cause of engagement in action. The word "tu" ("alone") serves to exclude alternatives — it negates the two views that supreme good is attained from actions alone, and from a combination of knowledge and actions. Further, since supreme good is not something to be produced, action cannot be its means. For an eternal entity is not produced by action or by knowledge. "Then is knowledge alone fruitless?" No, for being the remover of avidyā it is observed to terminate in the fruit of kaivalya. The terminating in kaivalya as fruit is observed of the knowledge that removes the darkness of avidyā, just as the result of the lamp's light, which removes the darkness of ignorance about a serpent etc. mistaken in a rope, is the rope's aloneness with the snake-imagination dispelled. So too with knowledge. Just as in observable matters, in actions like cutting, fire-churning and the like, the engaged agent and other factors do not engage in another fruit or another action apart from their observed result of producing two pieces, fire-vision, etc., so in the action of abiding in knowledge with its observable purpose, the engaged knower and other factors cannot engage in any other action apart from the fruit of the Self's aloneness. Hence abiding in knowledge accompanied by action is impossible. "It can be like the actions of eating, agnihotra etc." — no, for in knowledge whose fruit is kaivalya, desire for the fruit of action is impossible. Indeed when knowledge whose fruit is kaivalya is attained, just as for one whose fruit is water flooded all around, there is no desire for the fruit of digging wells, ponds and the like, so desire is impossible for any other fruit or for action as the means to it. For one engaged in an action whose fruit is the obtaining of a kingdom, engagement in an action whose fruit is the obtaining of a mere field is impossible, nor is desire for that. Therefore action does not have the character of being the means to supreme good. Nor does the combination of knowledge and action. Nor does knowledge whose fruit is kaivalya require the assistance of action, since being the remover of avidyā it is contrary to it. Darkness does not remove darkness. Therefore knowledge alone is the means to supreme good — [if this be said:] No, because of the incurring of sin (pratyavāya) by non-performance of obligatory rites, and because kaivalya is eternal. The contention that supreme good is attained from knowledge alone — that is wrong; for from non-performance of the obligatory rites enjoined in the śruti, sin in the form of attaining hell etc. would result. "Then on this view there is no liberation from karmas, hence no release at all." This is no fault; for liberation is eternal. From performance of obligatory rites, sin is not incurred; from not doing the prohibited, an unwanted body does not arise; from abstention from optional desire-prompted rites, a desired body does not arise; and on the exhaustion through enjoyment of the karma that initiated the present body, when this body has fallen, due to the absence of cause for the production of another body — through the non-performance of [the operations] of the Self [associated] with attachment etc. — abiding in one's own nature alone is kaivalya. Thus kaivalya is established without effort.

As for those who say: obligatory rites, being of the nature of suffering, are themselves the fruit of previously performed evil deeds; they have no fruit other than their own form, since none is heard of, and since they are enjoined upon occasions like "as long as one lives." — No: since karmas not yet sprouted cannot bear fruit; and a particular fruit of suffering would be unaccountable. The contention that the suffering of the toil of performing obligatory rites is enjoyed as the fruit of the evil karmas done in past births is wrong. For it is not consistent that the fruit of a karma which has not sprouted at the time of death for fruit-giving is enjoyed in a birth initiated by another karma. Otherwise, in a birth initiated by agnihotra etc. for the enjoyment of heaven's fruit, the non-experience of hell-fruit would not occur. Also, since that evil karma cannot have a particular suffering as its fruit — for among many evils, with their varied means to varied fruits of suffering, when only the suffering of toil in obligatory rites is imagined as fruit, the affliction of pairs-of-opposites, disease and the like cannot be made to be without cause: it cannot be imagined that only the suffering of the toil of obligatory rites is the fruit of previously acquired evil and not the suffering of carrying stones on one's head and the like. Further, this is unrelated to the topic — the contention that the suffering of toil in obligatory rites is the fruit of previously done evil karma. How? For the topic was that the destruction of previously done evil whose fruit has not sprouted is not consistent. There you say it is the fruit of karma whose fruit has sprouted — namely the suffering of toil in obligatory rites — not of one whose fruit has not sprouted. If you hold that all previously done evil is one whose fruit has sprouted, then your specification "only the suffering of toil in obligatory rites is its fruit" is inappropriate; and the obligatory injunction would become purposeless, since the destruction of evil karma whose fruit has sprouted is consistent through enjoyment alone. Moreover, if suffering be the fruit of the obligatory rite as heard, it is seen to come from the very toil of performance, like exercise; the supposition that it is the fruit of something else is unwarranted. From the injunction relative to occasions like "as long as one lives," the obligatory rites cannot be the fruit of previously done evil, in the manner of a prāyaścitta (expiation). For the prāyaścitta enjoined upon a particular sinful act is not the fruit of that sin. If the suffering of the prāyaścitta is held to be the fruit of that very sin which is its occasion, then in the case of obligatory rites also, since they too are conditioned by an occasion (like jīvana, life), the suffering of their performance would have to be the fruit of that very life-condition — for there is no difference in being naimittika between the obligatory and the prāyaścitta. Further: since the suffering of performance is equal in the obligatory and the optional agnihotra etc., why should only the suffering of obligatory performance be the fruit of past evil and not that of optional performance — there being no distinguishing mark? Hence even that of the optional would be the fruit of past evil.
