And so being, since no fruit of obligatory rites is heard, and since otherwise their injunction would be unaccountable, the postulation by arthāpatti that the suffering of obligatory performance is the fruit of past evil is unwarranted; rather, by the same impossibility of the injunction otherwise and by inference, a fruit other than the suffering of performance is established for the obligatory. There is also contradiction; for what is being said is contradictory: if it be admitted that, on performing the obligatory rite, the fruit of some other karma is enjoyed, then that very enjoyment is the fruit of the obligatory rite, while it has been said that the obligatory has no fruit. Further, when optional agnihotra etc. is being performed, the obligatory agnihotra also [is performed simultaneously, etc.].

"That all action is preceded by avidyā is unestablished" — no; like brahminicide and the like. Even though the obligatory action is known from the scripture, yet it occurs in one possessed of avidyā. Just as the action of brahminicide and the like — even though known through prohibitive scripture — is a cause of harm and arises in one possessed of the defects of avidyā, desire and the like, otherwise such engagement being inexplicable; so too the obligatory, occasional and optional. "In the absence of knowledge of the Self distinct from the body, engagement in obligatory and other actions is unaccountable" — no; for it is observed that the action which is mere movement, not really done by the Self, is engaged in with the cognition "I do." "The cognition of 'I' in the body-aggregate is figurative, not false" — no; for the figurative interpretation also applies to its effects. The cognition of "I" with respect to one's own body-aggregate is figurative, just as in one's own son: "You verily are the self by name 'son'" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, Ekāgnikāṇḍa 2.11), and in the world: "This bull is verily my breath." Such cognition is not false. False cognition is rather of post and man when their distinguishing features are not grasped. The figurative cognition does not have the function of producing the result proper to the principal, since it serves only the praise of its substratum, with the implied comparison being elliptical. Just as in "Devadatta is a lion" or "the boy is fire": from possession of a generic property like cruelty or tawniness similar to a lion or fire, it is only for the praise of Devadatta or the boy as substratum; nothing is accomplished as the lion's effect or fire's effect, the cause of the figurative word and cognition; whereas the effect of false cognition is experienced as harm. The locus of figurative cognition is known: "Devadatta is not a lion," likewise "this boy is not fire." Likewise, the action done by the Self in the figurative sense — namely the body-aggregate — is not done by the Self in the principal sense — the object of the cognition "I." For the action done by the figurative lion or fire is not done by the principal lion or fire. Nor does cruelty or tawniness produce any effect of the principal lion or fire, since it is exhausted in the purpose of praise. And the praised ones know: "I am not a lion," "I am not fire"; not "the lion's action is mine," "the fire's action is mine." So too: "the action of the aggregate is not mine, the principal Self's" — this cognition would be more proper; not "I am the doer, the action is mine." As to the contention that the Self performs action through its own memories, desires and efforts which are causes of action — no; for these are preceded by false cognition. Memories, desires, efforts etc. are preceded by impressions generated by experienced fruits of action conditioned by false cognition with respect to the desirable and undesirable. Just as in this birth, dharma and adharma are produced by attachment, aversion and the like that arise from identification with the body-aggregate, and there is enjoyment of their fruit, so in past and yet earlier births: thus saṁsāra, brought about by beginningless avidyā, is to be inferred for past and future. Therefore, by knowledge-abiding accompanied by renunciation of all karmas, absolute cessation of saṁsāra is established. Since identification with the body is of the nature of avidyā, with its cessation no body arises, and so saṁsāra ceases. Identification with the Self in the body-aggregate is of the nature of avidyā. None in the world, knowing "I am other than the cow etc., and the cow etc. are other than me," thinks of them as "I." But not knowing, like the cognition of a man in a post, one who lacks discrimination forms the cognition "I" with respect to the body-aggregate; not the discriminating one who knows. As for the case of "You verily are the self by name 'son'" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, Ekāgnikāṇḍa 2)…

"From the authoritativeness of injunction regarding what is unseen, what is to be done by the Self is in fact done by the figurative selves — body, sense-organs and the like" — if so said, no; because their selfhood itself is brought about by avidyā. Body, senses etc. are not figurative selves. Then what? Being non-Self, they are made to acquire selfhood by false cognition alone, since [the cognition of selfhood] exists when [false cognition] exists, and is absent when [false cognition] is absent. In the time of ignorance, in the non-discriminating, in children, the cognition "I am tall," "I am fair" with respect to the body-aggregate is observed; but not in the discriminating who know "I am other than the body-aggregate" — at that time the cognition of "I" in the body-aggregate does not occur. Therefore, since it is absent in the absence of false cognition, it is brought about by it alone, not figurative. For figurative cognition or word-usage applies to a lion and Devadatta or fire and a boy when their specific and generic features are separately apprehended; not when these are not apprehended. As to what was said "on the strength of śruti's authoritativeness" — no; that authoritativeness is regarding matters unseen. Śruti's authoritativeness pertains to a matter unobtained by perception etc., such as the relation of means and end in agnihotra etc., not to a matter of perception, since the authoritativeness aims at showing the unseen. Therefore the figurative status of the cognition of "I" in the body-aggregate, conditioned by an evidently false notion, cannot be assumed. Even hundreds of śruti-passages declaring "fire is cold or non-luminous" cannot become authoritative. If they were to declare "fire is cold or non-luminous," still some other meaning of the śruti is to be assumed as intended, on the principle that otherwise its authoritativeness would not stand; not what contradicts another pramāṇa or is self-contradictory. "Since action has an agent involving false cognition, in the absence of an agent the śruti would lose authority" — no, for in brahma-vidyā [the śruti] retains purposefulness.

"Then like the karma-injunction-śruti, the brahma-vidyā-injunction-śruti also would be without authority" — no; because no contradicting cognition arises [against it]. Just as the cognition of "I" in the body-aggregate is sublated when the Self is realized through the brahma-vidyā-injunction-śruti, so the realization of the Self in the Self itself can never, by anyone, in any way, be sublated, since cognition is not separate from its fruit, just as fire is hot and luminous. Nor in this way is the karma-injunction-śruti without authority, since it serves to produce engagement towards the inner Self by suspending each previously active engagement and producing a new engagement at every step. Even though the means be illusory, due to the truth of the end, it would be true, like arthavādas which supplement injunctions; in the world too, in giving milk etc. to children and the deranged, the words "this lengthens your hair-tuft." The authoritativeness of those at other levels is established directly, just as the authoritativeness of perception etc. dependent on body-identification before Self-knowledge. As to what you think — that the Self, even without itself acting, by mere proximity does the action; that very is the principal agency of the Self; just as a king is said to fight when his soldiers fight, although he himself does not fight, having merely been present he is known as victor or vanquished; or as the commander does it merely by speech; and the connection of king and commander with the fruit of action is observed; and as the priest's action is the sacrificer's; so too the action of body etc. would be done by the Self, since the fruit accrues to the Self; or as the magnet, although not engaged, yet, since it causes iron to revolve, has principal agency, so too the Self — that is wrong; for it would lead to the absurdity that a non-doer is yet a kāraka (factor of action). "There are many kinds of factors" — no; for in the case of king and others, principal agency itself is observed. The king for his part fights through his own activity; and in causing the soldiers to fight and giving wealth, his agency is principal, as also in enjoying the fruit of victory or defeat. In the case of the sacrificer too, in giving up the principal substance and giving the dakṣiṇā, his agency is principal. Hence the figurative use of agency for one not engaged is understood as figurative. If principal agency of the form of one's own activity were not observed in king, sacrificer etc., then agency by mere proximity might be assumed to be principal; as in the case of the magnet through the iron's revolution — but not so in the case of king, sacrificer etc., whose own activity is observed. Therefore agency by mere proximity is figurative alone. And so being, the connection with its fruit too would be figurative alone. The principal effect is not accomplished by the figurative. Therefore what is sung — "By the activity of body and the like, the Self, though not engaged, is the doer and enjoyer" — is wholly false. But everything is consistent on the basis of error, as in dream; and so in māyā. And in suṣupti, samādhi etc., where the chain of erroneous cognition of "I" with respect to the body etc. is broken, the harm of doership, enjoyership and the like is not observed. Therefore this saṁsāra-confusion is conditioned by erroneous cognition alone, and not real; hence by right vision, absolute cessation [of saṁsāra] is established.
BG_C18_V67: This is not to be told to one without austerity, nor ever to one without devotion, nor to one not desirous of hearing, nor to one who carps at Me. (67)
BG_C18_V67::block-0: Having gathered up the entire purport of the Gītā-śāstra in this chapter, and especially at its end, having for the firmness of the scripture's purport made a brief recapitulation, He now states the rule for the transmission of the scripture —
BG_C18_V67::block-1: This scripture (idam) — taught by Me for your good, for the cessation of saṁsāra — is not to be spoken to one without austerity (atapaskāya); the connection "is not to be spoken" stands at a distance. Even to one with austerity, if devoid of devotion (abhaktāya) — without devotion to teacher and to God — at any time (kadācana), in any state, it is not to be spoken. Even one who is devoted and an ascetic, if not desirous of hearing (aśuśrūṣave) — to him also it is not to be spoken. And one who carps at Me (mām abhyasūyati) — Vāsudeva — taking [Me] to be a mere ordinary man, by superimposing defects such as self-praise, not knowing My Lordhood, not bearing [it] — he too is unfit; to him also it is not to be spoken. To one free from carping at the Lord, an ascetic, a devotee, desirous of hearing — to such the scripture is to be spoken: this is gathered by implication. There, from the alternative shown in "to one of intelligence or to one of austerity" (Yāska, Nirukta 2.1.6), the scripture is to be taught to an ascetic equipped with desire-to-hear and devotion, or to one of intelligence equipped with the same. To one devoid of desire-to-hear and devotion — neither to an ascetic nor to one of intelligence is it to be spoken. To one who carps at the Lord, even though endowed with all virtues, it is not to be spoken. And to one possessing devotion and desire to serve the teacher, it is to be spoken: this is the rule for the transmission of the scripture.
BG_C18_V68: He who shall declare this supreme secret to those devoted to Me, having shown supreme devotion to Me, shall come to Me alone — there is no doubt. (68)
BG_C18_V68::block-0: Now He states the fruit for the one who effects the transmission —
BG_C18_V68::block-1: He who (yaḥ) shall expound this — said as above, supreme — directed to the supreme good, the text in the form of the dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna — secret, most to be guarded — among My devotees (mad-bhakteṣu) — among those who possess devotion to Me — shall declare, shall expound, that is, shall establish through both text and meaning; just as it has been done by Me to you. From the repeated mention of devotion (bhaktiḥ), it is gathered that by mere devotion alone one becomes a fit recipient for the transmission of the scripture. How shall he expound it? It is said: having shown supreme devotion to Me (bhaktiṁ mayi parāṁ kṛtvā) — having taken it that "the service of the Lord, the supreme guru, the Imperishable, is being rendered by me." His fruit is this — He shall come to Me alone (mām eva eṣyati) — that is, he is liberated indeed. "Without doubt (asaṁśayaḥ)" — herein no doubt should be entertained.
BG_C18_V69: And no one among men shall be a more loved doer of dear deeds for Me than he, nor shall there be on earth another more dear to Me than he. (69)
BG_C18_V69::block-1: And no one among men (na ca tasmāt manuṣyeṣu) — that is, among men, none other than that one who effects the transmission of the scripture — is a more dear-deed-doer (priya-kṛttamaḥ) — one who does dear deeds excellently — for Me; meaning, there is none other such who does deeds dearer to Me; this is the meaning, regarding those existing now. And there shall not be (na ca bhavitā) — even in time to come — another (anyaḥ), a second more dear (priyataraḥ) — a doer of dearer deeds — than he, on this earth (bhuvi).
BG_C18_V70: And he who shall study this dharma-laden dialogue of ours — by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge: such is My conviction. (70)
BG_C18_V70::block-1: He who (yaḥ) shall study (adhyeṣyate) — recite — this dharma-laden — not deviating from dharma — dialogue-form text of ours (āvayoḥ) — by him this would be done. By the sacrifice of knowledge (jñāna-yajñena) — among the sacrifices of injunction (vidhi), recitation (japa), undertone (upāṁśu) and mental (mānasa), the jñāna-yajña, being mental, is the most distinguished; hence, by that sacrifice of knowledge the recitation of the Gītā-śāstra is praised; or it is itself an injunction of fruit, since this fruit is equal to the fruit of the jñāna-yajña concerning deities and the like. By that recitation I shall have been worshipped (iṣṭaḥ) — honoured: such is My (me) conviction (matiḥ), determination.
BG_C18_V71: And the man who, full of faith and free of cavil, even but listens to it — even he, liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of the meritorious. (71)
BG_C18_V71::block-0: Now the fruit for the listener —
BG_C18_V71::block-1: He who, full of faith (śraddhāvān), endowed with faith, and free of cavil (anasūyaḥ), shall but hear (śṛṇuyāt api) this text — that man (naraḥ) — by the word "even" (api), how much more is implied for one who knows its meaning — even he, freed from sin, shall attain the auspicious — praiseworthy — worlds (lokān) of the meritorious — of those possessing actions like agnihotra and the like.
BG_C18_V72: Has this been heard by you, Pārtha, with one-pointed mind? Has the bewilderment born of ignorance been destroyed for you, Dhanañjaya? (72)
BG_C18_V72::block-0: Out of the desire to know whether the disciple has grasped the purport of the scripture or not, He asks. The questioner's intent is: should I know that he has not grasped, I shall make him grasp again by some other means as well. And by undertaking another effort, the disciple's accomplishment is to be effected — thus the teacher's duty is shown —
BG_C18_V72::block-1: Has (kaccit) this — what has been spoken by Me — been heard, that is, ascertained through hearing, O Pārtha, by you, with one-pointed mind, with attentive thought? Or, free from heedlessness? Has the bewilderment born of ignorance (ajñāna-saṁmohaḥ) — the bewilderment caused by ignorance, the state of indistinction, the natural lack of discrimination — been destroyed (praṇaṣṭaḥ)? For the sake of which this effort of yours in hearing the scripture, and My effort in teaching, has been undertaken — has it [been destroyed] for you, O Dhanañjaya?
BG_C18_V73::block-0:
Destroyed is the delusion (moha) born of ignorance — that delusion which is the cause of the entire mass of saṃsāric calamity, and which, like the ocean, is most difficult to cross. And memory (smṛti) — memory whose object is the truth of the Self (ātma-tattva) — has been gained, by the gaining of which there comes about the complete loosening of all the knots of the heart. "Through Thy grace" means: by Thy grace, by me, who has taken refuge in Thy grace, O Acyuta.

By this question and answer concerning the destruction of delusion, it is established and shown that the fruit of the knowledge of the entire scriptural meaning is just this much, and nothing more — namely, that from knowledge there results the destruction of delusion together with the obtaining of the memory of the Self. So too in the śruti, having begun with "I, the non-knower of the Self, grieve" (Chānd. Up. 7.1.3), the loosening of all the knots is declared to be by means of the knowledge of the Self. And there are the mantras: "The knot of the heart is cut asunder" (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.2.9); and "There, what delusion, what sorrow, for one who beholds the oneness?" (Īśā Up. 7).

"Now, at this very moment, I am established in Thy command (śāsana), my doubt gone, my hesitation released. I shall do Thy word." The intention is: "By Thy grace I have accomplished my purpose; there remains nothing yet to be done by me."
BG_C18_V74::block-0: The meaning of the śāstra has been brought to its consummation. Now, in order to show the connection of the narrative, Sañjaya says —
BG_C18_V74::block-1: "Thus" — in this manner, this conversation between Vāsudeva and Pārtha, the great-souled one, just as it has been related, did I hear, did I attend to. "Wonderful" — exceedingly astonishing; "hair-thrilling" — causing the hairs of the body to stand on end.
BG_C18_V75: Through the grace of Vyāsa I have heard this supreme, most secret yoga, from the Lord of yoga, Kṛṣṇa Himself, who declared it in person.
BG_C18_V75::block-1: "Through Vyāsa's grace" — through the divine vision (divya-cakṣus) gained from him — I have heard this conversation, the supreme, most secret yoga. Since the textual treatise has yoga for its content, the granthah itself is also "yoga"; or else it refers to this very conversation as "yoga" itself. [I heard it] from the Lord of yoga, Kṛṣṇa, while He Himself was declaring it directly (sākṣāt) — not by tradition through intermediaries (paramparā).
BG_C18_V76: O King, recalling again and again this wondrous and holy conversation between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again.
BG_C18_V76::block-0: "O King" — O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, recalling again and again, that is, every moment, this wondrous conversation between Keśava and Arjuna, this conversation which is "holy" (puṇyam) — by the mere hearing of which sin is removed — having heard it, I rejoice again and again, that is, at every instant.
BG_C18_V77: And recalling again and again that supremely wondrous form of Hari, great is my astonishment, O King; and I rejoice again and again.
BG_C18_V77::block-0: And recalling, recalling again that supremely wondrous form of Hari — the universal form (viśva-rūpa) — great is my astonishment, O King; and I rejoice again and again.
BG_C18_V78: Where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, is, where Pārtha the bowman is — there is fortune, victory, prosperity, and steadfast polity. Such is my conviction.
BG_C18_V78::block-1: "Where" — on whichever side — is the Lord of yoga (yogeśvara), the Lord of all the yogas, since He is the source of every yoga, being the seed of all yoga, namely Kṛṣṇa; and "where" — on whichever side — is Pārtha the bowman, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva — "there" — on that side, the side of the Pāṇḍavas — is fortune (śrī), is victory (vijaya), and on that very side is bhūti — bhūti meaning the special expansion, the wide outflow of fortune; and steadfast (dhruvā), unswerving, is polity (nīti), that is, statecraft (naya). Such is my conviction (matiḥ) — this is my settled judgement.
